papers.title: A Sampling Complexity-aware Framework for Discrete-time Fractional-Order Dynamical System Identification
papers.abstract: A variety of complex biological, natural and man-made systems exhibit non-Markovian dynamics that can be modeled through fractional order differential equations, yet, we lack sample comlexity aware system identification strategies. Towards this end, we propose an affine discrete-time fractional order dynamical system (FoDS) identification algorithm and provide a detailed sample complexity analysis. The algorithm effectively addresses the challenges of FoDS identification in the presence of noisy data. The proposed algorithm consists of two key steps. Firstly, it avoids solving higher-order polynomial equations, which would otherwise result in multiple potential solutions for the fractional orders. Secondly, the identification problem is reformulated as a least squares estimation, allowing us to infer the system parameters. We derive the expectation and probabilistic bounds for the FoDS parameter estimation error, assuming prior knowledge of the functions \( f \) and \( g \) in the FoDS model. The error decays at a rate of \( N = O\left( \frac{d}{\epsilon} \right) \), where \( N \) is the number of samples, \( d \) is the dimension of the state variable, and \( \epsilon \) represents the desired estimation accuracy. Simulation results demonstrate that our theoretical bounds are tight, validating the accuracy and robustness of this algorithm.
papers.summary: Many biological, natural, and engineered systems show non-Markovian behavior that fractional-order differential equations can model, yet no identification method for such systems comes with sample complexity guarantees. The authors propose an affine discrete-time fractional-order dynamical system (FoDS) identification algorithm that avoids solving higher-order polynomial equations for the fractional orders, which would yield multiple candidate solutions, and recasts parameter inference as least squares estimation to handle noisy data. Assuming the model functions f and g are known, they derive expectation and probabilistic bounds on the parameter estimation error showing the sample requirement scales as **N = O(d/ε)** in state dimension d and target accuracy ε, and simulations indicate the bounds are tight.

papers.title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly add intermediate reasoning for robot manipulation, but they mostly reason about the observed scene, and explicitly rolling out future frames at every inference step is computationally expensive. `IG-VLA` learns to anticipate task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space rather than generating pixels, and a Scene Gist Memory distills those reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token so the deployed policy can skip explicit future prediction. On `LIBERO`, `LIBERO-Plus`, and `VLABench`, both the reasoning and gist policies beat the strongest baseline by nearly 6% success rate on the `LIBERO-Plus` language suite, and **the gist policy cuts latency from 1081 ms to 169.5 ms per action chunk, a 6.38x speedup**, on a single A6000 GPU.

papers.title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot
papers.abstract: METR's 50\% time horizon measures the human completion time of software tasks that an AI solves with 50\% probability, allowing AI capabilities to be expressed in interpretable units. On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, we recompute the time horizons using splines and item-response theory to relax the assumption that the AI difficulty of a task depends linearly on the log of human time. Our fitted spline can be interpreted as a function that \emph{converts} human time to AI difficulty; it is nearly flat in a region from 2--30 min but close to linear elsewhere. Hence, a time-horizon jump from 3 min to 30 min is much easier than one from 30 min to 5 hours despite the same multiplier of $10 \times$. Overall, we contribute time-horizon point estimates that perform better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, as well as diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity. We suggest that time horizons be interpreted together with the diagnostic plots, especially as new time-horizon-based benchmarks are proposed or existing ones grow to include longer tasks.
papers.summary: METR's 50% time horizon expresses an AI system's capability as the human completion time of software tasks it solves half the time, but the standard estimate assumes a task's difficulty for AI is linear in the log of human time. Using 228 tasks and 26 models, the authors refit the horizons with splines and item-response theory, producing a learned function that converts human time into AI difficulty. **That function is nearly flat between 2 and 30 minutes and roughly linear elsewhere**, so a horizon jump from 3 to 30 minutes is far easier than one from 30 minutes to 5 hours despite both being a 10x multiplier. The spline estimates score better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, and the paper adds diagnostic plots for assessing construct validity as time-horizon benchmarks expand to longer tasks.

papers.title: Neuromorphic Satellite Intelligence: A Formal Framework for Event-Driven Architectures, Spike-Based Algorithms, and Quantitative Energy-Accuracy Trade-offs
papers.abstract: Satellite onboard computing faces an irreducible tension: mission intelligence requirements grow monotonically while power, mass, and radiation budgets remain fixed. This paper advances the state of the art on three fronts. First, we develop a formal mathematical model of spiking neural computation for satellite workloads, deriving closed-form expressions for energy consumption as a function of network sparsity, firing rate, and synaptic fan-out. Second, we propose three original algorithms -- a Spiking Kalman-Complementary Filter (SKCF) for attitude estimation, a Temporal Contrast Anomaly Detector (TCAD) for spacecraft health monitoring, and a Spike-Based Adaptive Modulation and Coding (SAMC) scheme for cognitive satellite links -- each with pseudocode and analytical complexity bounds. Third, we introduce a quantitative Energy-Accuracy-Latency (EAL) trade-off surface and populate it with numerical estimates derived from published silicon measurements of Loihi and SpiNNaker, enabling direct comparison with FPGA and GPU baselines. A taxonomy of four radiation-aware neuromorphic architecture classes is refined with fault-rate models. Continual on-orbit learning is formalized through a constrained Spike-Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) rule that provably bounds weight drift. Case studies for a 12U CubeSat Earth observation mission, a GEO communications payload, and an autonomous deep-space probe provide concrete, quantified design points. Our analysis shows that neuromorphic implementations can achieve 8 to 47 times energy reduction over GPU baselines while maintaining inference accuracy within 2.1\% for representative satellite workloads.
papers.summary: Satellite onboard computing must deliver growing mission intelligence under fixed power, mass, and radiation budgets. The authors formalize spiking neural computation for satellite workloads with closed-form energy expressions in terms of sparsity, firing rate, and synaptic fan-out, propose three spike-based algorithms for attitude estimation (`SKCF`), spacecraft health anomaly detection (`TCAD`), and adaptive modulation and coding (`SAMC`), and define an Energy-Accuracy-Latency trade-off surface populated with estimates derived from published Loihi and SpiNNaker silicon measurements. A constrained spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) rule bounds weight drift for on-orbit learning, and case studies for a 12U CubeSat, a GEO communications payload, and a deep-space probe lead the authors to estimate **8 to 47 times energy reduction over GPU baselines with accuracy within 2.1%**.

papers.title: TTS-Q: Perception-Guided Post-Training Quantization of Text-to-Speech Diffusion Transformers
papers.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) can clone a voice from seconds of audio. Yet the quality comes from billion-parameter diffusion transformers whose size and multi-step sampling put them out of reach of the on-device, assistive, and real-time applications that need them most. Post-training quantization (PTQ) shrinks such models without retraining, but it has been built for language and vision, not speech. At 4 bits, a strong quantizer leaves intelligibility close to full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre, so error rates stay low while the voice drifts from the target speaker. We ask why quantization hurts speech, where the damage lives, and whether it can be repaired without retraining. To find out, we run the first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B. The timbre cost comes from both the weight and the activation quantization, but only the activation part has the timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. We therefore introduce TTS-Q, which selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that assigns higher precision to late-step feed-forward activations. TTS-Q recovers timbre best at both scales, at no cost to intelligibility. Separately, the deployed calibrated-W4A4 reference reduces peak memory on GPU, providing a practical reference for resource-constrained TTS deployment.
papers.summary: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) built on billion-parameter diffusion transformers is too large and slow for the on-device, assistive, and real-time uses that need it most, and post-training quantization (PTQ) methods were designed for language and vision rather than speech. The first 4-bit weight-and-activation (W4A4) PTQ study of a TTS diffusion transformer at 1B and 3.5B parameters finds that **quantization leaves intelligibility near full precision but consistently erodes speaker timbre**, with damage from both weights and activations though only the activation error has a timestep structure a precision schedule can exploit. `TTS-Q` selects hard-to-quantize items from task-matched calibration candidates and applies a budget-balanced mixed-precision schedule that gives late-step feed-forward activations more bits, recovering timbre best at both scales with no intelligibility cost, while the calibrated W4A4 reference also cuts peak GPU memory.

papers.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
papers.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) tools have often been presented as methods to increase trust in machine learning models by making aspects of their algorithms more human-understandable. However, evidence accumulated over the last decade points to an overall failure of this objective, instead promoting overreliance on incorrect predictions, which can subsequently lead to algorithmic aversion. Rather, XAI appears to function primarily as a debugging tool, useful for obtaining anecdotal insights into, for example, features learned by the model. One of the main issues underlying this limitation is that XAI methods often oversimplify the inner workings of the model, resulting in misalignment between the explanation and the model itself - a behavior referred to as unfaithfulness or infidelity. Faithfulness can be interpreted as the degree of approximation between an explanation and the model. Computing faithfulness in a rigorous manner would thus make it possible to quantify one of the various elements of trustworthiness of an explanation. However, existing metrics present significant limitations, making this quantification either infeasible or computationally expensive. In this position paper, we outline five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics and propose four possible avenues for research to bolster their reliability.
papers.summary: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) was meant to build trust in machine learning models, but a decade of evidence suggests it mostly promotes overreliance on wrong predictions and works better as a debugging aid for anecdotal insight into learned features. A central cause is unfaithfulness, where an explanation oversimplifies and fails to approximate the model it describes, and existing faithfulness metrics for feature-importance explanations are either infeasible or too expensive to compute rigorously. The position paper lays out **five major shortcomings of current faithfulness metrics** and proposes four research avenues to make them more reliable.

papers.title: Algebraic Integer Quantization for Machine Learning Applications
papers.abstract: In this article, we propose algebraic integer number formats (AINF) as a framework for highly configurable and accurate compressed computation. A key property of AINF is its straightforward reduction to purely integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. We develop a matrix multiplication engine that exploits this property, obtaining performance within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical counterparts on modern hardware accelerators. Another key advantage of AIQ is the freedom to select algebraic integers tailored to the numerical characteristics of a given use case, offering optimization opportunities that are fundamentally unavailable in floating-point or fixed-point formats. Motivated by these properties, we introduce algebraic integer quantization (AIQ), a lossy compression format for large language model (LLM) inference, and provide results demonstrating that AIQ achieves competitive accuracy compared to the industry-standard MX format across a diverse set of models and benchmarks at equivalent bit-per-parameter budgets. The experiments presented in this article employ algebraic integers of degree two (quadratic integers); generalizations to higher-order and, in particular, multidimensional algebraic integers promise even greater computational advantages and remain a promising direction for future work.
papers.summary: Algebraic integer number formats (AINF) are proposed as a configurable framework for compressed computation whose key property is a straightforward reduction to pure integer arithmetic, enabling error-free multiply-accumulate operations. The authors build a matrix multiplication engine around this property that runs within a predictable factor of the most efficient numerical kernels on modern accelerators, and note that the algebraic integers can be chosen to match a workload's numerical characteristics in ways floating-point and fixed-point formats cannot. From this they derive algebraic integer quantization (`AIQ`), a lossy format for large language model (LLM) inference, and report that **`AIQ` matches the accuracy of the industry-standard `MX` format at equal bits per parameter** across a range of models and benchmarks, using degree-two (quadratic) algebraic integers with higher-degree and multidimensional generalizations left for future work.

papers.title: Kairos: Toward a Byte-Level Foundation Model for Every Modality
papers.abstract: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error. Kairos combines bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (LiZAttention2), block-wise Attention-Residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer and a multi-scale byte-level codec, trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space shared by text, image, audio, video, lidar and control streams; this report asks whether the combination optimizes at all before asking whether it is useful. We give code-derived algorithms for each component, including a cross-session recurrent-state memory gate, then run convergence sanity checks: overfittinga single 440-byte sentence at 1--15M parameters, text only, with three seeds for codec and attention choices and single-run sweeps for seven further factors. The two attention variants tested at 3\,000 steps (LiZAttention2 and window attention alone) reach a minimum loss near $10^{-3}$. After 600 steps, the mean minimum loss ranges from 0.018 (patch codec) to 0.354 (depthwise convolutional codec) with an identical ranking on three seeds. An apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections closes with more steps or more diverse data and reverses when the projections are frozen: it is a convergence-speed effect, not a capacity effect. These checks suggest that the implementation optimizes; they say nothing about generalization, multimodal training or comparison with existing models, which a planned pretraining run is meant to address. The Discussion sizes a 200M-total/25M-active target analytically; none of its throughput figures is measured. Code is available at https://github.com/fabienfrfr/Kairos . Python package at https://pypi.org/project/kairos-fm/ .
papers.summary: Small language models trained on a single local machine leave little room for architectural trial and error, so `Kairos` bundles several ideas at once: bidirectional gated-DeltaNet linear attention and sliding-window attention over shared projections (`LiZAttention2`), block-wise attention-residual aggregation, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) feed-forward layer, and a multi-scale byte-level codec trained with a uniform-noise denoising objective over one byte space intended to cover text, image, audio, video, lidar, and control streams. The report asks only whether this combination optimizes, overfitting a single 440-byte sentence at 1 to 15M parameters, text only, with multi-seed comparisons of codec and attention choices. Both attention variants reach a loss near 0.001 at 3000 steps, codec choice ranks identically across seeds, and **an apparent advantage of shared over separate attention projections turns out to be a convergence-speed effect rather than a capacity effect**. The authors state the checks say nothing about generalization, multimodal training, or comparisons with existing models, and the sizing of a 200M-total/25M-active target is analytical with no measured throughput.

papers.title: An Input-Dependent Readout Phase for Resonant Sequence Models
papers.abstract: Sequence models with a fixed-size state avoid the quadratic cost of attention, but face a design choice. An input-dependent state transition gives content-dependent memory at the cost of FFT-based training, while a fixed transition keeps the O(T log T) convolutional path but reads memory the same way for every input. ResonatorLM, a recent model of the second kind, reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head. We make that readout phase a function of the current token, which adds input dependence to the read only, keeps the convolution exact, and costs 0.2 percent more parameters. An analysis of the untrained bank shows that phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below the background within 2-8 steps and no choice of damping extends linear reconstruction beyond about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on WikiText-2, the input-dependent phase matches the original at the training length and removes its failure beyond it: trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024, perplexity falls from 12.81 to 3.76. We trace the failure to long-memory heads that accumulate more history than training exposed them to. The learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.
papers.summary: Fixed-size-state sequence models avoid attention's quadratic cost but must choose between input-dependent state transitions, which give content-dependent memory at the price of FFT-based training, and fixed transitions, which keep an O(T log T) convolutional path but read memory identically for every input. `ResonatorLM`, a fixed-transition model that reads a bank of damped complex oscillators through a fixed learned phase per head, is modified so the readout phase depends on the current token, adding input dependence only to the read while keeping the convolution exact and adding 0.2% more parameters. Analysis of the untrained bank shows phase does encode elapsed time, but an ordinary token falls below background within 2 to 8 steps and no damping extends linear reconstruction past about 16 tokens. In 6M-parameter character-level models on `WikiText-2`, the change matches the original at training length and **removes its length-generalization failure, cutting perplexity from 12.81 to 3.76 when trained on 256 tokens and tested on 1024**, which the authors trace to long-memory heads accumulating more history than training exposed them to, though the learned phase tracks the current character rather than distance and does not improve retrieval.

papers.title: Acoustic Biomarkers for Alzheimer's Disease Detection from Spontaneous Speech
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major public health challenge, and early identification is crucial for timely intervention and care planning. Recent work has shown that speech-based digital biomarkers can capture subtle changes in vocal production, prosody, and timing that often precede or accompany cognitive decline. In this study, we investigate whether acoustic features extracted from spontaneous speech can reliably distinguish individuals with AD from healthy controls. Using a structured speech dataset derived from the Cookie Theft picture-description task, we extract clinically informative low-level descriptors spanning prosodic, spectral, and temporal domains, and evaluate a range of machine learning classifiers. Our results indicate that acoustic biomarkers carry strong discriminative value, with the best-performing models achieving clinically meaningful separation between diagnostic groups. These findings support the use of non-invasive, low-cost audio-based screening tools and motivate further work on multimodal and longitudinal assessment frameworks for dementia risk detection.
papers.summary: Early identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD) matters for intervention and care planning, and speech-based digital biomarkers can capture subtle changes in vocal production, prosody, and timing that accompany cognitive decline. Using spontaneous speech from the Cookie Theft picture-description task, the study extracts low-level prosodic, spectral, and temporal descriptors and evaluates a range of machine learning classifiers for separating people with AD from healthy controls. The authors report that **acoustic features alone carry strong discriminative value**, with the best models achieving what they describe as clinically meaningful separation, and argue this supports low-cost, non-invasive audio screening with multimodal and longitudinal follow-up.

papers.title: EarLog: Opportunistic Ear Physiology Sensing toward Personalized Hearing Risk Awareness
papers.abstract: Many headphone users risk irreversible hearing damage during high-load listening, yet current protection still relies on sound-pressure limits. Clinical tests detect damage after it becomes measurable, leaving the risk-accumulating process unobserved. The acoustic reflex (AR), an involuntary response to high acoustic load, marks when the ear enters a protective state. AR traces are weak, and existing measurements require dedicated probes and controlled conditions that are difficult to maintain during everyday audio. We present EarLog, which turns playback, the dominant interference, into an opportunistic probe. EarLog introduces content-conditioned residual sensing to suppress variations caused by nonstationary content, individual ear acoustics, and device response. It identifies weak AR through loudness-dependent changes and localized spectral irregularities in the residual. A resonance-constrained sparse finite impulse response (FIR) model captures the short-window response. Dual-microphone observations, mild-distortion recovery, and cross-session reference updates keep detection usable under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), fit changes, and environmental drift. EarLog runs in real time on an embedded controller using a low-cost dual-microphone add-on. We evaluate it with 81 participants, 16 headphone models, and more than 400 hours of recordings. EarLog achieves 99.0% sensitivity and 98.7% specificity on a clinically referenced benchmark. EarLog records listener-specific AR events during everyday listening, providing data for future longitudinal studies of hearing risk.
papers.summary: Headphone users accumulate hearing damage during high-load listening that sound-pressure limits do not capture, and the acoustic reflex (AR), an involuntary protective response of the ear, is normally measurable only with dedicated probes under controlled conditions. `EarLog` turns the audio playback itself into an opportunistic probe, using content-conditioned residual sensing to suppress variation from nonstationary content, individual ear acoustics, and device response, then detects weak AR events through loudness-dependent changes and localized spectral irregularities captured by a resonance-constrained sparse finite impulse response (FIR) model. Dual-microphone observations, mild-distortion recovery, and cross-session reference updates keep detection usable under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), fit changes, and environmental drift, and the system runs in real time on an embedded controller with a low-cost add-on. Across 81 participants, 16 headphone models, and over 400 hours of recordings, it reaches **99.0% sensitivity and 98.7% specificity** on a clinically referenced benchmark.

papers.title: Energy-Efficient Spiking Neural Networks for Sensing-Aided Beam Prediction
papers.abstract: Sensing-aided beam prediction can reduce the beam-training overhead of millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems by leveraging environmental information from complementary modalities such as vision and position. However, the resulting sensing and inference pipeline can be energy-intensive, motivating the use of energy-efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) as an alternative to conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs). In this work, we develop SNN architectures for beam prediction and systematically compare them with ANNs using position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs. Our results show that compact ANNs consistently outperform SNNs for position-only sensing. In contrast, for vision and multimodal sensing, SNNs achieve higher accuracy than ANNs at similar energy costs and require up to an order of magnitude less energy at a comparable accuracy. For example, the multimodal SNN achieves 58.08% top-1 accuracy, outperforming the closest-energy ANN by 18.11 percentage points. We further show that SNN accuracy is limited by the binary communication between layers rather than by model size. These results demonstrate the potential of SNNs for energy-efficient sensing-aided beam prediction while highlighting their accuracy limitation.
papers.summary: Sensing-aided beam prediction uses vision and position information to cut beam-training overhead in millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems, but the sensing and inference pipeline is energy-intensive, motivating spiking neural networks (SNNs) as an alternative to conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs). The authors develop SNN architectures for beam prediction and systematically compare them with ANNs on position-only, vision-only, and multimodal inputs. Compact ANNs win on position-only sensing, but for vision and multimodal inputs SNNs are more accurate at similar energy and need up to an order of magnitude less energy at comparable accuracy, with **the multimodal SNN reaching 58.08% top-1 accuracy, 18.11 points above the closest-energy ANN**. Further analysis attributes the SNN accuracy ceiling to binary communication between layers rather than model size.

papers.title: CORAL-KV: Compact Cross-Layer Prediction and Residual Coding for Autoregressive Video KV Caches
papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models maintain a growing attention key-value (KV) cache, making memory a key bottleneck for long video generation. Recently, clustering-based quantization has emerged as an effective method to compress video KV caches by grouping similar key and value vectors then quantizing residual errors. However, when later frames attend to the compressed history, small reconstruction errors can compound as the video grows. Beyond the within-layer similarity exploited by clustering, we find strong dependencies across cache layers in video models. This motivates Coral-KV - Calibrated Offline, Residual-coded, and Adapted Locally - a KV-cache compression framework that uses cache states in each layer to predict keys and values in subsequent layers, then quantizes the remaining prediction residuals. We construct compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank (block-DPLR) predictors: block-diagonal components model channel relationships within each attention head, while a global low-rank term models dependencies between heads. Coral-KV exposes a flexible fidelity-memory trade-off: it can reuse its predictors across videos or refit lightweight block-diagonal predictors to the current video for higher fidelity. Across extensive evaluations on both HY-WorldPlay and MAGI-1, our reusable configuration improves PSNR over QVG-4 by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB, respectively, while using 48% and 37% less cache memory. Against QVG-Pro, our video-adapted configuration improves MAGI-1 PSNR by 3.77 dB while using 33.7% less cache memory. Coral-KV also maintains higher reconstruction fidelity over extended generation and reduces temporal discontinuities while retaining comparable generation latency.
papers.summary: Autoregressive video diffusion models keep a growing attention key-value (KV) cache that becomes the memory bottleneck for long generation, and existing clustering-based quantization lets small reconstruction errors compound as later frames attend to the compressed history. Observing strong dependencies across cache layers, `Coral-KV` uses each layer's cache state to predict the keys and values of subsequent layers with compact block-diagonal-plus-low-rank predictors, where block-diagonal parts model within-head channel relationships and a global low-rank term models cross-head dependencies, then quantizes only the prediction residuals. Predictors can be reused across videos or lightweight block-diagonal ones refit to the current video for higher fidelity. On `HY-WorldPlay` and `MAGI-1`, the reusable configuration **improves PSNR over `QVG-4` by 0.32 dB and 4.95 dB while using 48% and 37% less cache memory**, the video-adapted configuration beats `QVG-Pro` on `MAGI-1` by 3.77 dB with 33.7% less memory, and fidelity holds up better over extended generation with fewer temporal discontinuities at comparable latency.

papers.title: Looking Under the Streetlight: Evaluation in Generative Molecular Dynamics
papers.abstract: This position paper argues that the generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) community is not properly evaluating its progress: current evaluations let a model match what is reported while being arbitrarily wrong on what was claimed, which risks over-claiming advantage over classical baselines. This reflects a structural misalignment between common evaluation practices and the scientific tasks the field sets for itself. The reason is that the ground truth---exhaustive molecular dynamics on the systems of interest---is computationally costly, and this cost is what motivates the field. With ground truth inaccessible, evaluation drifts toward convenient proxies, and the resulting norms entrench easily. We identify misaligned evaluation patterns that persist as a community-level equilibrium, and propose concrete observables, reporting standards, and benchmark designs, both computational and experimental, that better reflect what GenMD aspires to deliver. Our aim is to give the field shared language and tools for evaluation that match its scientific ambitions before today's conventions calcify into norms.
papers.summary: Generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) aims to replace costly molecular dynamics simulation with learned models, but this position paper argues the field's evaluations let a model match what is reported while being arbitrarily wrong about what was actually claimed, risking over-stated advantages over classical baselines. The root cause is that the ground truth, exhaustive simulation on the systems of interest, is exactly the expensive computation the field wants to avoid, so evaluation drifts toward convenient proxies that harden into norms. The authors identify **misaligned evaluation patterns that persist as a community-level equilibrium** and propose concrete observables, reporting standards, and both computational and experimental benchmark designs that better reflect what the field aims to deliver.

papers.title: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
papers.abstract: The goal of circuit discovery is to decompose a monolithic neural network into tiny modular subnetworks which are interpretable in the sense that each does an identifiable subtask. We develop a practical method for composing arbitrarily many circuits into a single model. We propose a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm that overcomes limitations of previous attempts to compose circuits by naive union, then generalize it to $N$ circuits via CircuitTree, a new data structure built on a $\Theta(N\log N)$ tree-compose schedule. We compose circuits pruned from HuBERT for classifying individual phonemes into a syllable classifier, a capability none of the 39 phoneme circuits has individually. Chaining CircuitTrees into a hierarchy-of-circuits pipeline, we transcribe open syllables at 64.8\% accuracy, within 1.2 points of a 66.0\% ceiling that shares no circuitry at all, with 99.5\% of circuit components shared.
papers.summary: Circuit discovery decomposes a neural network into small subnetworks that each perform an identifiable subtask, but reassembling many such circuits into one working model has been limited by naive union approaches. The authors propose a greedy, density-scaled composition algorithm and generalize it to N circuits via `CircuitTree`, a data structure built on a Θ(N log N) tree-compose schedule. Combining 39 phoneme-classification circuits pruned from `HuBERT` yields a syllable classifier, a capability none of the individual circuits has, and chaining CircuitTrees into a hierarchy-of-circuits pipeline **transcribes open syllables at 64.8% accuracy, within 1.2 points of a 66.0% ceiling that shares no circuitry, while sharing 99.5% of circuit components**.

papers.title: MolP2SBench: Do LLMs Really Reason from Molecular Properties to Structure?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in molecular discovery and structure elucidation, where decisions depend on physical observations. Existing evaluations primarily focus on end-to-end molecular reconstruction, where correct predictions do not necessarily indicate reliance on the supplied properties. We introduce MolP2SBench, a benchmark for molecular property-to-structure (P2S) reasoning in LLMs. Each task presents a masked molecular scaffold with given properties and asks the model to select the missing structure from plausible candidates. We shuffle or replace properties to test reliance on correct property-structure pairing and responsiveness to counterfactual property changes. A channel-wise leaderboard uses Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), giving equal weight to source and counterfactual recovery. Evaluating seven models, we find that LLMs can use physical properties for structure prediction, but performance varies substantially across property types. Higher accuracy with a property does not necessarily imply greater responsiveness to it: a model may benefit more from $^1$H NMR than from $^{13}$C NMR, yet be less likely to change its prediction when the $^1$H data is replaced. LLM performance also need not reflect the relative difficulty of these properties for human chemists. Although UV-Vis spectra provide less direct structural information than NMR spectra, Astra achieves higher accuracy with UV-Vis data than with NMR peaks. MolP2SBench supports studying how LLMs extract and use physical-property information, revealing patterns that may differ from conventional chemical intuition and providing a foundation for more reliably property-grounded models for molecular and quantum-chemical inference. Code and dataset: https://github.com/DUAL-Xiao/MolP2SBench.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used in molecular discovery and structure elucidation, but end-to-end reconstruction evaluations cannot tell whether a correct prediction actually relied on the supplied physical properties. `MolP2SBench` presents a masked molecular scaffold with given properties and asks the model to pick the missing structure from plausible candidates, then shuffles or replaces the properties to test both reliance on correct property-structure pairing and responsiveness to counterfactual changes, scored by Property-Grounded Recovery (PGR), which weights source and counterfactual recovery equally. Across seven models, LLMs do use properties but unevenly across property types, and **higher accuracy with a property does not imply greater responsiveness to it**: a model may gain more from 1H NMR than 13C NMR yet be less likely to change its answer when the 1H data is swapped. Performance also departs from human chemical intuition, with `Astra` scoring higher using UV-Vis spectra than NMR peaks despite UV-Vis carrying less direct structural information.

papers.title: Behind-the-Meter Photovoltaic Visibility from Net Smart Meters: Deployment Regimes and Operational Insights
papers.abstract: Distribution operators need visibility of behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, yet most residential customers are observed only through net smart meters. Deep-learning-based PV disaggregation can restore this visibility, but its operational value depends on whether the model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. We quantify this dependence using four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, applied to Ausgrid smart-meter data with cross-dataset adaptation to the Pecan Street data. Using a fixed training protocol, we benchmark representative deep sequence architectures for PV disaggregation under regime-matched evaluation. At a fixed 48-hour context length, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104~kW on seen households in the future test period to 0.185~kW on unseen households over the same period, and under a fixed training contract the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice. Under target-domain normalization, fine-tuning on five target-region households reduces source-model transfer error by 28\%--36\%. Long input windows help known-customer extrapolation, while their new-customer benefits vary by model. These findings suggest regime-matched error budgets, limited target supervision for model adaptation in new regions, and use-case-dependent context selection for energy data analytics.
papers.summary: Distribution operators need visibility into behind-the-meter photovoltaic (PV) generation, but most households are observed only through net smart meters, and the operational value of deep-learning PV disaggregation depends on whether a model serves known customers, new customers, future periods, or new regions. The study defines four deployment regimes that separate household transfer from temporal extrapolation, benchmarks representative deep sequence architectures under a fixed training protocol on `Ausgrid` smart-meter data, and tests cross-dataset adaptation to `Pecan Street`. At a 48-hour context, daylight mean absolute error (MAE) of the best model rises from 0.104 kW on seen households to 0.185 kW on unseen households in the same period, and **the deployment regime explains far more of the error variation than model choice**. Fine-tuning on five target-region households cuts source-model transfer error by 28% to 36%, and long input windows help known-customer extrapolation while their benefit for new customers varies by model.

papers.title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
papers.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that mixes who the person is, what happened that day and how the sensor measured it, so measurement differences travel with the representation into new cohorts. We ask whether pretraining can place the measurement component that harms transfer in known coordinates, so that deployment drops them with a fixed projection and no target data. GlucoPRISM supervises a GlucoFM backbone with response contracts, rules for how each part of the representation should change when only the day or only the sensor changes: a 64-dimensional Trait band should change with neither, a 48-dimensional State band only across days, and a 16-dimensional Sensor band should track the device. Synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings, different-day pairs and glucose-summary targets supply this supervision without clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, dropping the Sensor band from the same frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57, against 69.3 for GlucoFM. The gain has two parts. Into CGMacros, the one target cohort recorded with two sensor types, filtering adds 11 to 19 points, and this holds when the generator is recalibrated on half of the participants and scored on the other half. On the other eight directions filtering is neutral and the encoder itself exceeds GlucoFM by 3.5 points. The device remains linearly decodable after filtering, so the filter removes a device-related component that harms transfer rather than all measurement information. The retained bands improve window AUROC on thirteen of fourteen public task--cohort cells (Holm-adjusted p=0.031) and correlation on fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.
papers.summary: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models encode each day as one vector that entangles the person, the day's events, and the sensor's measurement characteristics, so device differences travel into new cohorts and hurt transfer. `GlucoPRISM` supervises a `GlucoFM` backbone with response contracts that split the representation into a Trait band that should change with neither day nor sensor, a State band that changes only across days, and a Sensor band that tracks the device, using synthetic sensor views calibrated on paired Dexcom and Libre recordings rather than clinical labels. Across twelve cross-cohort directions, **dropping the Sensor band from the frozen encoder raises mean transfer AUROC from 68.75 to 73.57**, against 69.3 for `GlucoFM`, with gains of 11 to 19 points into the one cohort recorded with two sensor types and a 3.5-point encoder advantage on the remaining directions. The device stays linearly decodable after filtering, indicating the filter removes a transfer-harming component rather than all measurement information, and the retained bands improve thirteen of fourteen public task-cohort cells and fourteen of fifteen clinical endpoints in an external cohort of 9,303 participants.

papers.title: CacheScope: Exact-Compute Allocation for Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
papers.abstract: Training-free feature reuse accelerates diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising computation at selected steps with cached approximations. Existing methods mainly improve the reconstruction of skipped features, but we find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is used, increasing reconstruction complexity brings limited gains, whereas the placement of exact-computation steps has a much larger effect on fidelity. More importantly, absolute shallow-probe variation is jointly affected by input-trajectory displacement and network response strength, and therefore does not directly reflect cache risk. We address this confounding by normalizing probe-output variation with the corresponding input displacement, yielding a directional gain per unit trajectory movement. Based on this signal, we propose CacheScope, which identifies high-risk reuse steps online and selectively falls back to full denoising computation while leaving the underlying cache reconstructor unchanged. CacheScope requires no additional training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedule optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev, Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, and Open-Sora 1.2, CacheScope achieves up to 3.57x acceleration and reduces median LPIPS by up to 70.1% over the strongest probe-based baseline.
papers.summary: Training-free feature reuse speeds up diffusion transformer inference by replacing full denoising at selected steps with cached approximations, and the authors find that once a stable first-order reconstructor is in place, where exact-computation steps are placed matters far more than how elaborate the reconstruction is. They also show that raw shallow-probe variation conflates input-trajectory displacement with network response strength, so they normalize probe-output change by input displacement to obtain a directional gain per unit of trajectory movement. `CacheScope` uses this signal to flag high-risk reuse steps online and fall back to full computation at those steps, leaving the cache reconstructor unchanged and requiring no training, gradients, auxiliary networks, or prompt-specific offline schedules. Across `FLUX.1-dev`, `Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B`, and `Open-Sora 1.2`, it reaches **up to 3.57x acceleration and cuts median LPIPS by up to 70.1%** relative to the strongest probe-based baseline.

papers.title: Structural and Representational Agency in LLM-Driven Timbre Generation and Interpolation
papers.abstract: Generative creative interfaces routinely report the user's position within a space of possibilities. Such displays imply that the quantities shown were measured from the artefact; in a growing class of systems they are instead predicted by a language model describing its own output, and the two are indistinguishable on screen. Most creative domains lack an agreed measurement against which such a self-report can be checked; audio admits one. In a measurement study of a working LLM-driven timbre interface, what a user can cause proves separable from what the interface reports. The first is exactly characterisable: the reachable set is a zonotope whose dimension increases by one per sound placed, so the space the model may act within is demonstrably the user's own. The second is inaccurate. The displayed position differs from measurement by approximately three times the width of that region, and the error has two independent sources: model-predicted coordinates, whose accuracy varies twofold between the two models evaluated, and the interpolation step, which arises from combining synthesiser parameters and is unaffected by model quality. End to end, 26 of 36 refinement instructions produced no perceptible change, and under the weaker model the facility performed no action while reporting convergence. Effective agency (what a user can cause) and epistemic agency (whether they can know it) are therefore separable and independently engineered: structurally enforced constraints survive model failure, whereas guarantees resting on the model's own report do not. The failure mode that remains is silence presented as success. We close with a short protocol for building and auditing such displays.
papers.summary: Generative creative interfaces display the user's position within a space of possibilities as if it were measured from the artefact, but in a growing class of systems that position is predicted by a language model describing its own output, and audio is one of the few creative domains where such self-reports can be checked against an agreed measurement. In a measurement study of a working LLM-driven timbre interface, what the user can cause is exactly characterizable as a zonotope whose dimension grows by one per sound placed, while the displayed position is off by roughly three times the width of that region, with errors from both model-predicted coordinates, whose accuracy varies twofold between the two models tested, and a model-independent interpolation step. **End to end, 26 of 36 refinement instructions produced no perceptible change**, and under the weaker model the system performed no action while reporting convergence. The authors separate effective agency (what a user can cause) from epistemic agency (whether they can know it), argue that structurally enforced constraints survive model failure while guarantees resting on the model's own report do not, and close with a short protocol for building and auditing such displays.

papers.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
papers.abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-guided program search for executable control policies often lacks a structured way to reuse earlier high-scoring programs. `EliteTable` keeps a fixed-capacity table of top solutions and uses it to steer three kinds of proposals: new programs, edits of a single stored solution, and remixes of several. Across six `Gymnasium` control tasks with ten generations of fifty candidates each and ten independent searches per task, **candidate-score medians rose from the first to the final generation in all six tasks**, held-out gains appeared in four, and the `CartPole-v1` winner hit the search-score ceiling in the first generation of every search. Results on `Acrobot-v1` were mixed, with six of ten searches declining on held-out episodes, and the authors note that comparisons and ablations are still needed to establish relative performance and the contribution of each component.

papers.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
papers.abstract: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book ($+0.38$ pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from $+0.68$ to between $+0.92$ and $+0.96$, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.
papers.summary: Estimating the price impact of a large trade is a counterfactual question, but classical models such as `Almgren-Chriss` and propagator models regress price on order flow and are biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. The authors build a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow-price relation, with confounding strength as an exact per-episode knob. On that prior the naive estimator overestimates impact by up to 68% while **the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding**, and a twin model with the intervention inputs removed collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at ground-truth scale to metaorders in an `ABIDES` limit-order-book simulator, and its intervention response replicates on thousands of detected flow bursts in crypto perpetuals and Nasdaq equities, which the authors describe as consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer.

papers.title: Efficient Learning of Survival Analysis Models Under Outcome-Dependent Truncation and Censoring
papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models are typically trained on data assumed to be representative of the predictive tasks the model will face in the future, but practical datasets violate this assumption. We focus on outcome-dependent truncation in which an observation appears in the training data depending on its label. Our work connects two largely distinct literatures: efficient learning under truncation and survival analysis. Existing methods for truncated survival analysis do not characterize the optimization landscape and instead rely on iterative procedures such as expectation maximization. We address this gap and prove that Cox regression can be efficiently learned under truncated and right-censored data using first-order optimization when the baseline hazard is known (despite nonconvexity). In contrast, when the baseline hazard is learned jointly, we construct identifiable and correctly specified models whose negative log-likelihood contains strict suboptimal local minima. On experiments with four survival datasets, we show that accounting for truncation reduces the prediction bias induced by naive Cox regression and extends to neural networks. We also show orders of magnitude speedups compared to standard expectation maximization.
papers.summary: Training data for survival models often suffers from outcome-dependent truncation, where whether an observation appears at all depends on its label, yet existing truncated survival methods rely on iterative expectation-maximization procedures without characterizing the optimization landscape. Connecting the literatures on efficient learning under truncation and survival analysis, the authors prove that `Cox regression` can be learned under truncated and right-censored data with first-order optimization when the baseline hazard is known, despite nonconvexity. **When the baseline hazard is learned jointly, they construct identifiable and correctly specified models whose negative log-likelihood contains strict suboptimal local minima.** On four survival datasets, accounting for truncation reduces the prediction bias of naive Cox regression, extends to neural networks, and runs orders of magnitude faster than standard expectation maximization.

papers.title: Enriched Holomorphic Neural Networks for 2D and 3D Laplace Problems
papers.abstract: Boundary-value problems for the Laplace equation develop singular behaviour near corners, edges and junctions that smooth approximators resolve poorly. We combine holomorphic neural networks with singular functions derived from the local geometry and boundary conditions. The representation is harmonic by construction, so no interior residual is needed: the network fits the smooth remainder from boundary data alone, and the enrichment terms capture the singular behaviour. Singular exponents are trainable, so the construction also applies when the local expansion is not known in advance. We extend the approach to three dimensions using independent networks evaluated along complex null directions. The enriched model is the most accurate tested method on every problem. Its margin is several orders of magnitude where the enrichment captures the singularity exactly, and a factor of about 1.7-2.1 over the next-best method on a CdZnTe radiation detector with many singular sites, in both two and three dimensions.
papers.summary: Solutions to boundary-value problems for the Laplace equation develop singularities near corners, edges, and junctions that smooth neural approximators capture poorly. The approach combines holomorphic neural networks, which are harmonic by construction and therefore need no interior residual loss, with singular enrichment functions derived from the local geometry and boundary conditions, so the network fits only the smooth remainder from boundary data; singular exponents are trainable for cases where the local expansion is unknown, and a three-dimensional extension evaluates independent networks along complex null directions. The enriched model is the most accurate method tested on every problem, with margins of **several orders of magnitude when the enrichment captures the singularity exactly** and a factor of about 1.7 to 2.1 over the next-best method on a CdZnTe radiation detector geometry with many singular sites, in both two and three dimensions.

papers.title: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
papers.abstract: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is often proposed for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows, yet most studies never run the comparison that could refute it - giving a much simpler method the same search effort. We run that comparison under a controlled protocol. All arms receive an identical budget - the same number of candidate schedules built and evaluated: an MCTS scheduling method, preregistered as the main arm; a randomized-restart list scheduler with no search tree as the control; and a textbook-UCT MCTS arm as a registered follow-up on the same domain. The analysis plan was locked before data collection; an independent checker confirmed all 768 confirmation-stage schedules valid with correct finish times. At the main budget of 2048 evaluated schedules, MCTS is 2.88% worse than the restarts (95% CI [-3.62%,-2.15%]; the 72 of 96 held-out instances with positive baseline-relative headroom). The deficit is not budget starvation: on the separate exploration pool restarts self-improve by 1.85% where MCTS gains 0.24%, and 700 of 720 of MCTS's first results are merely the warm start it was handed. The studied selection rule locks deterministically onto the first-expanded child, keeping its trials correlated while restarts draw gains from the tails; the causal link to makespan remains an inference. A structural map locates where the tree stops paying: restarts win on sparse irregular workflows, no difference is detectable on regular layered ones, and dense ones leave no room to improve. Swapping the rule for textbook UCT removes most of the deficit (-0.26%, 95% CI [-0.71%,+0.23%]) without reversing its sign. Results are confined to a controlled synthetic domain (N in {8,16,32} tasks, 2-8 processors, budgets up to 2048); we make no claim about larger budgets.
papers.summary: Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) is frequently proposed for scheduling directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) workflows, but studies rarely give a simpler method the same search effort. Under a preregistered protocol with a locked analysis plan and an independent validity checker, the authors compare an MCTS scheduler against a randomized-restart list scheduler with no search tree, plus a textbook-UCT MCTS arm, all with an identical budget of built and evaluated schedules. **At the main budget of 2048 schedules, MCTS produced makespans 2.88% worse than the restarts**, a deficit attributed to a selection rule that locks onto the first-expanded child while restarts draw gains from the tails, though the authors note the causal link to makespan remains an inference; swapping in textbook UCT removes most of the gap without reversing its sign. Restarts win on sparse irregular workflows, no difference is detectable on regular layered ones, and the claims are confined to a synthetic domain of 8 to 32 tasks, 2 to 8 processors, and budgets up to 2048.

papers.title: Transformer-Based Masked Diffusion Models Provably Learn Distributions with Latent Structure
papers.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate discrete data by iteratively unmasking multiple tokens in parallel using a learned mask predictor. Their output carries two errors: parallelization error due to parallel sampling, and estimation error from the mask predictor learned with finite samples. Existing theory treats these errors separately, and the available statistical bounds typically scale with the number $V^L$ of length-$L$ sequences over a vocabulary of size $V$, suffering from the curse of dimensionality. In this work, we establish end-to-end statistical guarantees showing that transformer-based MDMs learn structured distributions with a sample complexity governed by their latent structure. Specifically, we model this structure through mixtures of hidden Markov trees, which capture latent dependencies within components and heterogeneity across components. When the data distribution is well approximated by such a mixture, a transformer-based MDM with parallel unmasking schedules achieves $\varepsilon$-accurate sampling in KL divergence with $\widetilde{O}(LK_{\mathrm{par}}/\varepsilon)$ training samples, where $K_{\mathrm{par}}$ is polynomial in $L$, $V$, the number of hidden states, and the number of mixture components. The transformer network and sampling procedure require no knowledge of the tree topologies or component parameters, thereby adapting to the unknown latent structure automatically. Overall, our results provide theoretical justification for the empirical effectiveness of MDMs on real-world data.
papers.summary: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate discrete sequences by unmasking many tokens in parallel, and their output carries both a parallelization error and an estimation error from the finite-sample mask predictor, which prior theory treats separately with bounds that scale with the number of possible sequences. The authors model data as mixtures of hidden Markov trees, which capture latent dependencies within components and heterogeneity across them, and derive end-to-end statistical guarantees for transformer-based MDMs with parallel unmasking schedules. When the data distribution is well approximated by such a mixture, **epsilon-accurate sampling in KL divergence needs a number of training samples that is polynomial in sequence length, vocabulary size, hidden states, and mixture components, and inverse in epsilon**, rather than exponential in sequence length. Neither the network nor the sampler needs the tree topologies or component parameters, so the method adapts to the unknown latent structure automatically.

papers.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
papers.abstract: Autoregressive decoding is less suited to non-causally ordered data, e.g., cross-references or future dependencies, since their outputs cannot be revised post hoc, unlike iterative human reasoning. Diffusion LLMs partially mitigate this limitation but still cannot flexibly insert or remove arbitrary numbers of tokens from a pre-generated context. We design AutoIndexer as a generative model with a novel training and decoding mechanism that simulates a Chain of Edits, allowing the model to flexibly modify its prior outputs in hindsight via token insertions, substitutions, and deletions. The model learns to predict marker tokens for opening and closing edits, simultaneously moving a cursor to positions in the existing token sequence, analogous to a text editor. Training sequences are obtained by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to edit by undoing those inverses. The perturbation training allows AutoIndexer to be robust to erroneous context and adaptable to editing tasks such as code correction. We demonstrate that our method exhibits post-generation context-editing capabilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/AutodeskAILab/autoindexer.
papers.summary: Autoregressive decoding cannot revise earlier output, which suits it poorly to data with cross-references or future dependencies, and diffusion language models still cannot insert or delete arbitrary numbers of tokens in already-generated context. `AutoIndexer` trains a causal model on a Chain of Edits: it predicts marker tokens that open and close edits while moving a cursor through the existing token sequence, like a text editor, so it can insert, substitute, and delete tokens in hindsight. Training sequences are built by perturbing ground-truth labels with inverse chained edit operations, and the model learns to undo them, which also makes it robust to erroneous context and applicable to tasks such as code correction. **The model shows post-generation context-editing abilities that most autoregressive and diffusion models lack without compromising performance on standard LLM benchmarks**, and the code is released.

papers.title: Fly-by-Code: Embodied Coding Agents for Aerial Manipulation with Active Visual and Physical Feedback
papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
papers.summary: Embodied coding agents build robot policies by generating programs and refining them from execution feedback, but aerial manipulation breaks this loop: payload limits leave task-critical outcomes outside the onboard camera's view, and fragile dynamics leave failure causes unresolved, so re-examining the same feedback cannot help. The proposed `Active Feedback` (AF) framework has the agent synthesize a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation either to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints or to test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions. Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, **AF raises final task success from 31.7% to 75%** and cuts false completion declarations from 25 to 5 compared with terminal feedback under the same agent configuration and execution limit. Programs refined in simulation run unchanged on a physical aerial manipulator through shared robot APIs and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world.

papers.title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a memory-efficient alternative to backpropagation for fine-tuning large language models. However, existing ZO methods typically sample training examples uniformly, overlooking their evolving importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. To address this limitation, we propose Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (SAZO), which learns sample importance online and adaptively allocates queries to accelerate convergence. SAZO extracts gradient-norm information from existing directional differences to estimate sample importance without access to true gradients. Furthermore, to track evolving importance from sparse minibatch feedback, SAZO maintains per-example exponential moving averages that aggregate observations across updates. The method requires no additional model evaluations and only $O(N)$ additional scalar state compared with MeZO. We prove that SAZO asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of the minimum-variance sampling oracle, and achieves a strictly faster convergence rate than standard methods. Extensive experiments across four model families demonstrate improved average downstream performance and up to $6\times$ faster convergence to the same training loss in terms of query count.
papers.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization fine-tunes large language models without the memory cost of backpropagation, but existing methods such as `MeZO` sample training examples uniformly, ignoring their changing importance and leaving avoidable estimation variance. Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Optimization (`SAZO`) extracts gradient-norm information from the directional differences the method already computes, tracks it with per-example exponential moving averages, and allocates queries adaptively, adding no extra model evaluations and only linear scalar state in the number of examples. The authors prove `SAZO` asymptotically matches the leading convergence term of a minimum-variance sampling oracle and converges strictly faster than standard methods. Across four model families it improves average downstream performance and reaches the same training loss with **up to 6 times fewer queries**.

papers.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.
papers.summary: Static coding benchmarks leak into training data and saturate as agents improve, so the authors propose a self-scaling arena whose tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time by the participating agents themselves. In `SWE-Duel`, a Red agent implements a new feature in a real repository, embeds a subtle bug with sealed triggering tests, and the pull request is admitted only if it passes the feature and existing tests, fails exactly the bug tests, and a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind; a Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists, wins only if its revision passes all three suites, and the roles swap. In a tournament of 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages over 1,500 turns, `GPT-5.5` with `Codex CLI` ranked first as the strongest solver, **repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviewed**, while `Claude Opus 4.8` with `mini-swe-agent` ranked second as the strongest task author with a 27.3% Red win rate. Within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% versus 4.0%), preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with authoring capability.
papers.highlight_summary:
Static coding benchmarks leak into training data and saturate as agents improve, so `SWE-Duel` makes two coding agents author tasks for each other at evaluation time, leaving nothing to leak in advance and letting difficulty rise with the participants themselves.

- In each Red turn an agent works in three context-isolated sessions on a real repository, implementing a feature with feature tests, then embedding a subtle bug with sealed bug-triggering tests, and the task is admitted only if all visible tests still pass and a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks.
- The Blue agent reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists and wins only if its revision passes the existing, feature, and sealed bug test suites, so reverting the feature or shipping the bug both count as losses before the roles swap.
- A round-robin tournament of 11 model-harness pairs on 15 repositories in five languages ran 1,500 turns, where `GPT-5.5` with `Codex CLI` ranked first as the strongest solver, repairing **98.3%** of reviewed defects, while `Claude Opus 4.8` with `mini-swe-agent` ranked second as the strongest task author with a **27.3%** Red win rate, and the same model under `Claude Code` fell to eighth.
- Holding the solver fixed as `DeepSeek-V4-Pro` and varying only the author, tasks from `GLM-5.3` defeated it **42.9%** of the time versus 8.3% for `GLM-5.1` and 0.0% for `GLM-5.2`, giving preliminary evidence that difficulty tracks authoring capability, and a late entrant could be placed with only five matches without reordering the incumbents.
- The blind self-repair gate caps difficulty at the author's own bug-finding ability, Blue already succeeds on 87.9% of all turns so headroom at the top is thin, a manual audit found a 6.0% false-negative rate from overly specific bug tests, and the GLM ladder rests on only 12 to 14 tasks per version with wide confidence intervals.

papers.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose multiple tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by the target model. Recent diffusion-based drafters make this paradigm particularly attractive: deep attention-based neural backbones provide strong predictions, while drafting multiple future positions in parallel avoids the sequential cost of autoregressive generation. This parallelism, however, comes at a cost.
