Tokens within a draft block are predicted without access to the realized identities of preceding draft tokens, removing intra-block dependencies that would naturally be available under autoregressive generation. We introduce DCOCO (DFlash Contextual Corrector), a lightweight mechanism that restores these dependencies while preserving parallel drafting. Rather than committing to each position's top prediction, DCOCO retains multiple candidate tokens and evaluates their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, enabling contextually informed token selection at low additional cost. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks, DCOCO achieves the highest average throughput in every evaluated configuration, spanning greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding. Its advantage persists under concurrent serving: DCOCO outperforms the strongest competing method by 6-23% across 4-32 concurrent requests, while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected DFlash at these loads. These results demonstrate that recovering intra-block dependencies through parallel contextual scoring delivers consistent acceleration across decoding regimes and serving loads.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up large language model inference by having a lightweight drafter propose several tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, and diffusion-based drafters such as `DFlash` draft many positions at once, but tokens within a block are predicted without seeing the realized identities of preceding draft tokens. `DCOCO` (DFlash Contextual Corrector) keeps multiple candidate tokens per position and scores their contextual compatibility across adjacent draft positions in parallel, restoring intra-block dependencies without giving up parallel drafting. Across four verifier backbones and ten benchmarks it achieves the highest average throughput in every configuration, covering greedy and stochastic decoding with and without extended reasoning, with **speedups of up to 6.6x over vanilla decoding**. Under concurrent serving with 4 to 32 requests it beats the strongest competing method by 6 to 23% while other sequential correctors fall below uncorrected `DFlash`.

papers.title: An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning
papers.abstract: Most systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning are in the same class as multi-layer perceptrons: while they may be universal function approximators, they struggle to learn associative tasks which are easy for transformers. Equilibrium propagation relies on a bidirectional flow of information through the physical system between input and output. The reverse flow is broken by more complex nonlinear systems, such as those performing multiplication which is needed to express dot-product attention. Here we explicitly restore this bidirectional flow by introducing extra circuit elements for this purpose into a double or dyadic circuit. We then use these ideas to construct an attention mechanism exploiting the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. We show that in simulations this circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task, despite using realistic reverse components which transmit only an approximate gradient. For this training to succeed we need cross-entropy loss (not mean squared error). We generate nudges appropriate for this loss using a novel floating circuit element, based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. We train the resistors in this circuit using the Lion optimiser, which can be implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates.
papers.summary: Physical learning systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning have so far behaved like multi-layer perceptrons and struggle with the associative tasks transformers handle easily, because the bidirectional information flow those methods need breaks down in circuits that multiply, as dot-product attention requires. The authors restore that reverse flow with extra circuit elements in a dyadic circuit and build an attention mechanism from the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices, with softmax and loss nudging realized by the same sub-circuit. **In simulation the circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task** even though the realistic reverse components transmit only an approximate gradient. Training required cross-entropy rather than mean squared error loss and used the `Lion` optimizer, which can be implemented with one capacitor per parameter to store past gradient estimates.

papers.title: DiffusionART: Efficient, Stable and Scalable Reinforcement of Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tunes diffusion models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as Flow-GRPO are limited in efficiency by poor credit assignment, while forward-process methods such as DiffusionNFT are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. We show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward--reverse consistency force that joint positive--negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. We introduce DiffusionART (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting), which aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning. It requires no differentiable reward model, remains effective with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models (DiffusionART-Pairwise). Across image and video generation, DiffusionART trains efficiently and stably without per-task tuning. In particular, on HunyuanVideo-13B with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards, DiffusionART reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of DiffusionNFT and Flow-GRPO-Fast with 12.02 and 11.72 times fewer GPU hours, respectively, while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.
papers.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) can fine-tune diffusion models from black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as `Flow-GRPO` suffer from poor credit assignment while forward-process methods such as `DiffusionNFT` are efficient yet unstable without carefully tuned exponential-moving-average (EMA) off-policy training. The authors show that NFT-style objectives contain a hidden forward-reverse consistency force that joint positive-negative training cancels only partially, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration rather than off-policy rollouts. `DiffusionART` (Diffusion Reinforcement with Aggregation-First Reward Tilting) aggregates each prompt's rewards into a shared reward-improving direction for reverse-process states, removing the consistency force by construction, and adds a trust-region-masked second update for drift-adaptive restoration without EMA tuning; it needs no differentiable reward model, works with fewer samples per prompt, and supports pairwise reward models. On `HunyuanVideo-13B` with equally weighted visual and motion quality rewards it **reaches the late-stage mean reward levels of both baselines with about 12 times fewer GPU hours** while achieving 28.8% and 53.0% higher mean training rewards.
papers.highlight_summary:
Online reinforcement learning fine-tunes diffusion and flow models with black-box rewards, but reverse-process methods such as `Flow-GRPO` learn slowly because a trajectory-level advantage is smeared across every denoising transition, while forward-process methods such as `DiffusionNFT` are efficient yet collapse without an exponential moving average, or EMA, rollout policy whose lag must be tuned per task. The proposed fix aggregates each prompt's rewards into one shared reward-improving direction, regresses every visited reverse-rollout state toward it, and replaces EMA with a second trust-region-masked update that supplies restoration proportional to each state's drift.

- The diagnosis is that `DiffusionNFT`'s forward-noised targets carry a hidden forward-reverse consistency force that joint positive and negative training cancels only across samples rather than at each state, and that EMA stabilizes training through restoration toward the lagged reference rather than through off-policy data, since keeping EMA rollouts but dropping the old-policy anchor still collapses.
- For each prompt the method computes the covariance between rewards and clean endpoints over the K rollout samples, RMS-normalizes it into a guidance vector, and regresses each visited state's velocity toward the cached rollout prediction plus that vector, applying two updates on disjoint halves of the batch so the second update's gradient becomes guidance minus current drift, with a KL-proxy trust-region mask at one fixed threshold blocking excessive outward drift and a pairwise variant accepting winner/loser labels in place of scalar rewards.
- On `SD3.5-M` it matches `DiffusionNFT` with EMA in training efficiency without any EMA tuning and reaches `Flow-GRPO`'s step-500 reward with **10.0×, 5.2× and 9.6× fewer steps** on `GenEval`, OCR and `PickScore`, and on `FLUX.1-dev` it scores 0.9684 on `GenEval` versus 0.9183 for `Flow-DPPO` and 0.8490 for `DiffusionNFT`.
- On `HunyuanVideo-13B` with equal visual-quality and motion-quality weights it reaches the late-stage mean reward of `DiffusionNFT` and `Flow-GRPO-Fast` with **12.02× and 11.72× fewer GPU hours** while finishing **28.8% and 53.0% higher**, and for image-to-video on `Wan2.1-I2V-14B` it reaches motion quality 6 in 45.8 GPU hours versus 220.3 for `Flow-GRPO-Fast`, a 4.8× reduction.
- Every video gain is measured against the learned `VideoReward` model with no human evaluation or over-optimization check, the trust-region mask that prevents a mid-training drop on video slightly slows image training, and the `FLUX.1-dev` comparison runs `DiffusionNFT` with hyperparameters transferred untuned from `SD3.5-M`, so that baseline was never tuned at scale.

papers.title: CLUE: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Unsupervised Event Type Induction and Annotation
papers.abstract: Event ontology is the foundational framework for defining events in a dataset. Event type induction generally involves domain experts who define guidelines for creating event types and their names based on the dataset's domain and scope. However, this process is resource-intensive in terms of annotation costs and is prone to human biases. To alleviate the need for manual event ontology creation, we propose the CLUE framework for event type induction, naming, and annotation. Our main contributions in this work are: 1) designing a novel joint embedding representation for expressing both the verb-centric view and the semantic view of events; 2) event type induction using contrastive loss guided clustering; 3) event naming and refinement. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at https://github.com/PratikMaitra/CLUE.
papers.summary: Building an event ontology, the set of event types that defines what counts as an event in a dataset, normally requires domain experts to write guidelines and names, which is costly and prone to human bias. `CLUE` is a framework for unsupervised event type induction, naming, and annotation built on three pieces: a joint embedding that represents both the verb-centric view and the semantic view of events, clustering guided by a contrastive loss to induce event types, and a step that names and refines the induced types. **Experiments are reported to demonstrate the framework's effectiveness**, and the code is publicly available.

papers.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
papers.summary: Latent recurrent language models reuse a shared block of layers so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count, but at one loop they typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a tax that makes a separate model the better choice whenever latency matters. Elastic Latent Recurrence (`ELR`) removes this tax through a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget; mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit added cost, and keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds memory at the one-loop level while retaining most of the gain. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B mixture-of-experts hybrid models, one-loop `ELR` lands within about a point of its matched baseline on a ten-task average and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points respectively. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields `Koi-4B`, a single checkpoint that matches `Qwen3.5-4B` with an estimated 18 on the `Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index` at one loop and **rises to 29 at four loops**.

papers.title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective
papers.abstract: Event sequences are chains of random events, each described by heterogeneous (numerical and categorical) features. The problem of event sequence forecasting occurs in finance, healthcare, business process intelligence, and other fields. In this work, we study multi-horizon forecasting of event sequences as a conditional generative modeling problem. We evaluate forecasts not only for prediction accuracy, but also for distributional realism. To this end, we present a benchmark comprising metrics for both quality aspects, strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. Careful evaluation reveals that no method excels at both accuracy and realism, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between the two. Finally, we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an algorithm that aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, demonstrating that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/xaosina/event-sequence-forecasting.
papers.summary: Event sequences, chains of random events with mixed numerical and categorical features, arise in finance, healthcare, and business process intelligence, and forecasting them over multiple horizons is framed here as conditional generative modeling. The authors present a benchmark that scores forecasts on both prediction accuracy and distributional realism, with strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. **Careful evaluation finds that no method excels at both accuracy and realism**, pointing to a fundamental trade-off between the two. They then introduce `Wasserstein BaryBooster`, which aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, showing that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy, and release the code.

papers.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
papers.abstract: The continued improvement of large language models increasingly depends on synthetic experience, yet effective data synthesis for interactive agents requires not only executable and verifiable trajectories, but also interactions that provide learning value for the current task agent. Existing methods increasingly incorporate environment feedback, data validation, or learner failures, but still face a feedback-to-decision gap: observed weaknesses do not directly specify how future synthesis should change, or whether they can be represented by the current synthesis space. To address this gap, we propose EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework that organizes synthesis around a revisable state specifying what interaction factors can be deliberately generated and where synthesis effort should be allocated. A role-specialized multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, while a Designer allocates synthesis directions and a Planner grounds them into executable experience. This process enables within-space adaptation toward weak or under-covered regions and synthesis-space expansion that promotes newly discovered factors into explicit generation controls. Experiments on $\tau^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench show that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over the strongest synthesis baseline, while producing higher-quality and structurally broader synthetic experience and discovering controllable factors missed without learner feedback.
papers.summary: Improving interactive language model agents increasingly depends on synthetic experience, but existing data synthesis methods face a feedback-to-decision gap: observed learner weaknesses do not directly say how future synthesis should change or whether the current synthesis space can even express them. `EvoSyn` is a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework organized around a revisable state that specifies which interaction factors can be deliberately generated and where synthesis effort should go, with role-specialized agents translating learner feedback into revisions, a Designer allocating synthesis directions, and a Planner grounding them into executable experience. This supports both adaptation toward weak or under-covered regions within the current space and expansion of the space by promoting newly discovered factors into explicit generation controls. On `τ²-Bench` and `CAR-Bench`, the framework **improves average task success by 13.3 points over the strongest synthesis baseline** while producing higher-quality, structurally broader synthetic experience and discovering controllable factors that go unnoticed without learner feedback.

papers.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
papers.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.
papers.summary: Most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, so strategic reasoning over long horizons remains under-studied and hard to separate into stored knowledge, reasoning, and luck. `SpireBench` has models play the complete commercial deck-builder `Slay the Spire` at its highest difficulty, where early decisions determine long-term success, and the harness is the first to give a model the full original game. Across 20 large language models (LLMs), **frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts**, winning the first act as often as experts and then falling behind; what separates strong from weak models is per-fight play, while all of them misjudge risk over a run by preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A self-consistent renaming of every game term shows part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious.

papers.title: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable supervision for software engineering agents through executable tests, but binary rewards fail to distinguish trajectories with substantially different debugging quality. We investigate whether the current policy can judge its own trajectories and use these judgments to improve task performance without a separately trained reward model. To this end, we introduce Behavioral Self-Rewarding (BSR), a reward-refinement method that reuses the policy to compare observable debugging behavior among trajectories from the same task with the same verifier outcome. BSR aggregates pairwise preferences into task-local scores and converts them into bounded auxiliary rewards, introducing reward contrast while preserving the verifier-defined pass/fail ordering. This provides additional supervision from already-collected trajectories without requiring new environment interactions. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench-Live show consistent improvements across the evaluated Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B configurations, supporting using the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary learning signal for training software engineering agents.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) supervises software engineering agents through executable tests, but a binary pass/fail reward cannot tell apart trajectories whose debugging quality differs substantially. Behavioral Self-Rewarding (`BSR`) reuses the current policy to compare observable debugging behavior between trajectories from the same task that share a verifier outcome, aggregates the pairwise preferences into task-local scores, and converts them into bounded auxiliary rewards that add contrast while preserving the verifier-defined ordering, all without a separately trained reward model or new environment interactions. Experiments on `SWE-bench Verified` and `SWE-bench-Live` with `Qwen3-14B` and `Qwen3-32B` **show consistent improvements across all evaluated configurations**, supporting the policy's own comparative judgments as a complementary training signal for software engineering agents.

papers.title: STAPLE: Static Sparse Upcycling of Pretrained Checkpoints via Embedding Modules
papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
papers.summary: Sparse computation can grow a language model's parameter count without proportionally increasing active compute, but sparse pretraining is expensive and existing upcycling methods target Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads limit scalability. `STAPLE` builds on `STEM`, which replaces feed-forward up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, but instead keeps the up-projections and adds the static sparse embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information. On `OLMo-2 1B` it improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on `HumanEval`, 2.80 on `MBPP`, 2.27 on `GSM8K`, and 1.65 on `DROP`, the gains grow with static capacity and persist on `OLMo-2 7B`, and it beats `STEM`, an Engram-style model, and an MoE upcycling baseline on average **while decoding 2x faster than the MoE baseline with less than half its GPU memory and energy per token**. A host-offloaded implementation that caches only the roughly 5% most frequent embeddings on GPU keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline despite adding billions of parameters late in training.

papers.title: Reflective Prompt Optimization of a Deep-Research Agent: A Topic-Disjoint, Multi-Seed Protocol for Measuring Transferable Gains and Prompt-Level Overfitting
papers.abstract: Prompt optimization is an attractive alternative to reinforcement learning for adapting language-model agents, since it is cheap and produces human-readable artifacts. On factual tasks, however, it carries a failure mode that scalar-reward reinforcement learning does not. An optimizer that reads the training examples can write their answers into the prompt, so an in-distribution gain may be memorization rather than transferable behaviour. We apply reflective prompt evolution (GEPA) to the two system prompts of a multi-agent deep-research agent and evaluate it under a topic-disjoint split in which no topic is shared across train, validation, and test. Held-out citation reward rises by 0.079, from 0.702 to 0.781, with a bootstrap 95\% confidence interval of [0.051, 0.107], and the gain replicates across three seeds (mean 0.107). Nearly half of the winning prompt is a memorized answer key, yet a controlled ablation shows this content earns no reward even on the exact training questions it encodes. The large validation-minus-held-out gap is therefore small-sample selection under a noisy judge, not memorization. Varying the verifier isolates what makes the gain transfer. Decomposed per-dimension feedback is the causal ingredient, and collapsing it to a single scalar reward makes held-out transfer negative. The gain persists under an out-of-family judge and is largely reproduced by a hand-written version of the discovered recipe. Credible evaluation of prompt optimizers therefore requires held-out topics, multiple seeds, and verifier ablations. We release the candidate prompts, lineage diffs, figures, tables, and analysis.
papers.summary: Prompt optimization is a cheap, human-readable alternative to reinforcement learning for adapting language-model agents, but on factual tasks an optimizer that reads training examples can simply write the answers into the prompt, so in-distribution gains may be memorization. The authors apply reflective prompt evolution (`GEPA`) to the two system prompts of a multi-agent deep-research agent and evaluate under a topic-disjoint split, so no topic is shared across train, validation, and test. **Held-out citation reward rises from 0.702 to 0.781, replicating across three seeds**, and although nearly half of the winning prompt is a memorized answer key, an ablation shows that content earns no reward even on the exact training questions it encodes. Verifier ablations show decomposed per-dimension feedback is the causal ingredient, since collapsing it to a single scalar reward makes held-out transfer negative, and the gain survives an out-of-family judge and is largely reproduced by a hand-written version of the discovered recipe.

papers.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.
papers.summary: Continual learning aims to adapt pretrained models without losing prior capabilities, but the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend well beyond them. The authors organize task descriptions and examples into Task Banks whose entries a frozen model selects and combines to guide generation of replay data, then run continual instruction tuning on `Qwen` models of several sizes. Tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy hides, and **generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank, with combined partial banks retaining more than either bank alone**. Letting the model choose replay targets based on the new task beats random selection at the 4B scale but not at smaller sizes, and under a fixed example budget replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains.

papers.title: Knowing Is Not Telling: Identity Ossification in LLM Representations of Trans-border Communities
papers.abstract: Ethnic and cultural identities rarely align with political borders, a tension made sharper by migration and long-standing cross-border ties. Communities such as the Sami, the Rohingya, and the Kurds have long lived across more than one state. This tension is especially clear in mainland Southeast Asia, where many communities share history, language, and culture across state lines. We study nine such transborder ethnic communities along China's southwestern border with mainland Southeast Asia, looking at how large language models (LLMs) represent them. We define and study identity ossification: a pattern where LLMs turn a fluid, cross-border ethnic identity into a single, fixed nation-state identity. We introduce the Transborder Identity Ossification Diagnostic Framework (TIODF) that compares direct factual questions with open-ended narrative questions to test whether ossification comes from missing knowledge or from how models frame their answers. We test GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.2 in English and Chinese. Ossification varies substantially across models and query languages. It appears in only 10.1% of GPT-5.1's English answers, but in 62.6% of DeepSeek-V3.2's Chinese answers. Models often still tell a single-nation story even when they answer the factual question correctly. This decoupling suggests that ossification reflects narrative framing rather than simple knowledge absence, which matters for how we test cultural fairness in multilingual AI systems.
papers.summary: Many ethnic communities live across state borders, and the authors ask whether large language models flatten such fluid identities into a single nation-state framing, a pattern they call identity ossification, studying nine transborder communities along China's southwestern border with mainland Southeast Asia. They introduce the Transborder Identity Ossification Diagnostic Framework (`TIODF`), which pairs direct factual questions with open-ended narrative questions to separate missing knowledge from narrative framing, and test `GPT-5.1` and `DeepSeek-V3.2` in English and Chinese. **Ossification appears in 10.1% of GPT-5.1's English answers but 62.6% of DeepSeek-V3.2's Chinese answers**, and models often tell a single-nation story even when they answer the factual question correctly. The decoupling suggests ossification is a framing effect rather than a knowledge gap, which bears on how cultural fairness in multilingual systems should be tested.

papers.title: GeopoliticalQA: Benchmarking Retrieval and Generation over Intelligence Reports
papers.abstract: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports constitute a rich source of expert knowledge and have increasing value in the current political climate, but their heterogeneity and analytical complexity pose challenges for retrieval-augmented question answering. We introduce a benchmark for grounded question answering over 415 open-source geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports, comprising 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions. We propose a document-aware generation pipeline that profiles reports before generating questions and validate dataset quality through expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Using the benchmark, we evaluate 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs for RAG. We find that models perform similarly on document-level retrieval, while at the harder chunk level retrieval quality is not driven by embedding-model scale: bge-m3, a mid-size open encoder matches an order of magnitude larger ones and outperforms commercial embedding APIs. In contrast, answer generation remains challenging even given the gold evidence, particularly for inferential and risk-oriented questions.
papers.summary: Geopolitical and strategic intelligence reports are a rich but heterogeneous source for retrieval-augmented question answering, and no benchmark has targeted them. The authors build `GeopoliticalQA`, 5,525 document-grounded question-answer pairs over 415 open-source reports spanning factual, inferential, comparative, and risk-oriented questions, generated by a pipeline that profiles each report before writing questions and validated with expert annotation and an LLM-as-judge protocol. Evaluating 15 retrieval systems and six open-weight LLMs, they find document-level retrieval is similar across systems, while **at the chunk level the mid-size open encoder `bge-m3` matches embedding models an order of magnitude larger and beats commercial embedding APIs**. Answer generation remains hard even with gold evidence, especially for inferential and risk-oriented questions.

papers.title: Mesh-Native Tokenisation: Retrofitting Foundation Models to Unstructured Data
papers.abstract: Physics foundation models are an increasingly popular approach for building versatile emulators for spatiotemporal systems. They require tokenisation layers that lift physical field data into a latent representation suitable for dynamic processing. A typical choice for this layer is a convolutional encoder, which lifts field information in a locality-aware way and can be trained very efficiently. However, this choice cannot be applied to a large class of scientific computing problems where data are represented on unstructured meshes, for example simulations on domains with curved boundaries. Such data typically require graph neural network architectures, which are more expensive to train and, in the form currently used, encode information differently from their CNN counterparts, thus limiting the portability of physics emulators between these data regimes. In this work we introduce Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC), a locality-aware tokenisation layer that encodes unstructured mesh-based data in a way that is analogous to CNNs. This approach leads to models that can be trained once on mesh data and then deployed to arbitrary unstructured meshes, even if these are irregular, with minimal retraining. We show that this tokenisation approach can be used to retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models efficiently on unstructured meshes and provide theoretical results to confirm the consistency of this approach with classical CNN encoders. We demonstrate the favourable performance of this retrofitting approach, which in many cases reaches acceptable accuracy even in zero-shot deployment, and outperforms existing baselines after only a few epochs of fine-tuning, thus providing an efficient bridge between the two data regimes.
papers.summary: Physics foundation models typically tokenise field data with convolutional encoders, which cannot be applied to the many scientific simulations defined on unstructured meshes, such as domains with curved boundaries, where graph neural networks are the usual but costlier and less portable choice. The authors introduce Mesh-Native Convolution (`MNC`), a locality-aware tokenisation layer that encodes mesh data in a way analogous to a CNN, so a model trained once on mesh data can be deployed to arbitrary irregular meshes with minimal retraining. They provide theoretical results showing consistency with classical CNN encoders and use the layer to retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models onto unstructured meshes. **Retrofitted models often reach acceptable accuracy zero-shot and outperform existing baselines after only a few epochs of fine-tuning**, bridging the grid and mesh data regimes.

papers.title: Machine Learning and Time-Series Foundation Models for Day-Ahead Electricity Forecasting in a University Building
papers.abstract:
Day-ahead electricity forecasts can help building operators schedule heating, ventilation, and other services around anticipated demand. Choosing a forecasting model also requires balancing accuracy with its forecast-time inputs, local training, and computational requirements.
  We benchmark statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural-network, and pretrained TimesFM models for a university building. We use chronological validation and evaluate all configurations on the same 57 test days, comparing accuracy across workdays, weekends, and holidays alongside local fitting and forecasting time. Weather covariates use retrospective observations.
  TimesFM 3.0 with covariates achieves the lowest overall errors, reducing mean absolute error by approximately 43\% relative to weekly seasonal-naive forecasting. XGBoost remains competitive, although paired daily comparisons do not establish a clear mean-absolute-error advantage for TimesFM. TimesFM also performs strongly using only past electricity consumption. Adding covariates improves its holiday forecasts but slightly worsens workday and weekend forecasts, leaving overall mean absolute error almost unchanged. TimesFM requires no building-specific weight training, while XGBoost offers rapid local fitting and inference. The evaluated LSTM takes longer to fit without outperforming either approach.
  An exploratory historical evaluation reveals seasonal variation, while a separate weather-source comparison produces only small changes in the selected TimesFM configuration's accuracy. These results support pretrained TimesFM as a strong initial forecasting baseline for this building, with XGBoost as a competitive locally fitted alternative. Covariates are particularly useful when improved holiday forecasts justify the additional input preparation.
papers.summary: Day-ahead electricity forecasts help building operators schedule heating and ventilation, but choosing a model means balancing accuracy against input requirements, local training, and compute. The authors benchmark statistical, machine-learning, recurrent neural-network, and pretrained `TimesFM` models on a university building using chronological validation over the same 57 test days, comparing workdays, weekends, and holidays alongside fitting and forecasting time. **`TimesFM 3.0` with covariates cuts mean absolute error by about 43% relative to a weekly seasonal-naive forecast**, though paired daily comparisons do not establish a clear advantage over `XGBoost`, which remains competitive with rapid local fitting. Weather covariates improve TimesFM's holiday forecasts but slightly hurt workdays and weekends, leaving overall error nearly unchanged, and the evaluated `LSTM` takes longer to fit without outperforming either approach.

papers.title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
papers.abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.
papers.summary: Backdoor attacks on large language models normally follow a trigger-response pattern in which one condition activates a single terminal behavior, leaving unexplored attacks where malicious behavior builds through intermediate stages. The authors present `Cancerous Backdoor Attack`, which gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions using invisible tokens, which supply hidden stage signals absent from the visible request, and a stage controller that tracks progression during inference. Across several reasoning datasets and models the attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption and outperforms prior backdoor baselines. **Reasoning can be corrupted progressively before any visible change in answers, so answer accuracy alone is insufficient for detecting backdoors.**

papers.title: SynAct: Synergistic Active Feedback Learning for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents executing multi-step workflows fail in two fundamentally different ways: recoverable slips, which further attempts can repair, and knowledge gaps, which retrying cannot resolve. Expert feedback can address the latter, but expert attention is scarce. The key challenge is therefore not whether to ask for feedback, but where feedback can change the outcome. Existing approaches either avoid expert feedback, allowing agents to reinforce their own errors, or allocate feedback at the task level without identifying consequential decisions. We present SynAct, an active learning framework that treats expert attention as the binding constraint and allocates feedback at the level of individual decisions. SynAct ranks decisions by the mutual information between the selected action and the terminal outcome across repeated rollouts, queries an expert at the highest-value decisions, and distills the resulting corrections into transferable rules that the agent can reuse without expert access at deployment. We theoretically characterize what this signal identifies under finite repeated sampling: with k rollouts and at least m observations per action, outcome-constant decisions have zero mutual information, while outcome-separating decisions have mutual information at least H2(m/k) bits, yielding exact separation for any threshold t in (0,H2(m/k)). This also explains why success-based acquisition can be blind when all rollouts fail: success is constant even when failed runs reach different outcomes. Across four agent benchmarks and four models spanning three families, SynAct improves held-out accuracy in all 16 evaluated settings, by +11.7pp on average. The same signal transfers to inference-time routing, where SynAct outperforms budget-matched cascade, uncertainty, and expert-judge routers in 15 of 16 settings, while a single targeted correction outperforms seven additional unaimed retries.
papers.summary: LLM agents running multi-step workflows fail either through recoverable slips, which retries can fix, or knowledge gaps, which they cannot, and scarce expert feedback is only worth spending where it changes the outcome. `SynAct` is an active learning framework that ranks individual decisions by the mutual information between the chosen action and the terminal outcome across repeated rollouts, queries an expert at the highest-value decisions, and distills corrections into reusable rules the agent applies without expert access at deployment. The authors prove that with k rollouts and at least m observations per action, outcome-constant decisions have zero mutual information while outcome-separating ones have at least H2(m/k) bits, giving exact separation, and that success-based acquisition goes blind when all rollouts fail. **Across four agent benchmarks and four models from three families, held-out accuracy improves in all 16 settings by 11.7 percentage points on average**, the same signal beats budget-matched cascade, uncertainty, and expert-judge routers in 15 of 16 inference-time routing settings, and one targeted correction outperforms seven unaimed retries.

papers.title: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents can execute increasingly complex tasks, but effective assistance also requires aligning their actions with goals and constraints that users may leave unstated. We study this problem as interactive intent alignment through clarification. Yet clarification is useful only when the agent can turn the answer into better decisions. As training changes how the agent handles incomplete information and uses additional answers, the same clarification can become more or less useful. We introduce CLEAT (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training), a framework that co-trains a clarification-value controller and the task policy from shared interaction outcomes. We formulate residual query value to measure the task utility gained by asking rather than proceeding under the current policy, and estimate it through paired rollouts from the same interaction history. These paired returns train the controller to predict clarification value and the task policy to select useful questions and act on the answers. The controller guides subsequent rollout collection, while outcomes from the updated agent provide new value labels that allow clarification guidance to adapt as the agent learns. With Qwen3-4B, CLEAT achieves the highest mean score in all ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks. Gains over the strongest baseline reach 13.2 and 6.5 percentage points on UserGym Travel and IN3 underspecification judgment accuracy, respectively. Ablations show that co-training improves the task policy even when the controller is removed at inference, while adapting clarification guidance to the evolving policy yields further gains.
papers.summary: LLM agents must align their actions with goals and constraints users leave unstated, and asking a clarifying question only helps if the agent can turn the answer into better decisions, a relationship that shifts as the agent trains. `CLEAT` (CLarification through valuE-guided Agent co-Training) co-trains a clarification-value controller and the task policy from shared interaction outcomes, defining residual query value as the task utility gained by asking rather than proceeding, estimated through paired rollouts from the same history. The controller guides subsequent rollout collection while outcomes from the updated agent supply fresh value labels, so clarification guidance adapts as the policy learns. **With `Qwen3-4B`, CLEAT achieves the highest mean score in all ten evaluation settings across four benchmarks**, with gains over the strongest baseline reaching 13.2 points on `UserGym Travel` and 6.5 points on `IN3` underspecification judgment, and ablations show co-training helps the policy even when the controller is removed at inference.

papers.title: Kronecker Product Attention: Memory-Efficient KV Compression via Structured Factorization
papers.abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and depth, and existing remedies such as Multi-Query Attention (`MQA`), Grouped-Query Attention (`GQA`), Multi-Head Latent Attention (`MLA`), and Tensor Product Attention (`TPA`) trade away expressivity, add positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. Kronecker Product Attention (`KPA`) represents keys and values as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors, strictly generalizing TPA since its rank-one outer products arise as a degenerate Kronecker split while non-degenerate factors capture richer block-structured patterns. A structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker form preserves the relative-position property of `RoPE` while rotating only the compact factors, removing the decoupled RoPE branch MLA needs. **KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine benchmarks under identical training while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression**, with the Kronecker head split acting as a tuneable knob on the compression-accuracy trade-off.

papers.title: Data-driven Optimal Sensor Placement for Aerosol Monitoring in the UK
papers.abstract: We develop a data-driven sensor-placement framework and apply it to aerosol monitoring in the United Kingdom (UK). A trained convolutional Gaussian neural process is embedded within the DeepSensor optimisation framework. Genetic optimisation with lazy evaluation and caching reduces mean computational time by 60\% (10$\pm$3 versus 25$\pm$7 minutes) while producing sequential placement performance comparable to the greedy solver. Using the CAMS reference field to construct a retrospective oracle benchmark, Joint NLL improves by about 22\% for Joint-MI-driven genetic placement after five locations for aerosol stations are identified. Seasonal and wind-regime analyses show that agreement between model-based criteria and oracle benchmarks varies with meteorological transport conditions. These results show a computationally efficient approach for data-informed expansion of environmental observing systems.
authors: Talha Ansar (University of Engineering and Technology
Waqar Muhammad Ashraf (The Alan Turing Institute
J. Scott Hosking (The Alan Turing Institute
papers.summary: Deciding where to place new aerosol monitoring stations across the United Kingdom is framed as a data-driven sensor-placement problem. A trained convolutional Gaussian neural process is embedded in the `DeepSensor` optimisation framework, and a genetic optimiser with lazy evaluation and caching is compared against a greedy solver, using the `CAMS` reference field to construct a retrospective oracle benchmark. **The genetic approach cuts mean compute time by 60%, from about 25 to 10 minutes, while matching the greedy solver's sequential placement performance**, and joint-mutual-information-driven placement improves joint negative log-likelihood by about 22% after five stations are chosen. Seasonal and wind-regime analyses show that agreement between model-based criteria and the oracle varies with meteorological transport conditions.

papers.title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
papers.abstract: Data-centric scaling of RLVR has focused on collecting or generating verifiable training problems. However, corpus size alone does not determine whether the dataset provides a useful learning signal for a target policy. To guide the synthesis of effective RLVR data, we experimentally characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of its problems, the target policy, and the training rollout budget. Under this characterization, we show that a large open-source math corpus pooled from widely used RLVR datasets falls almost entirely into a zero-advantage trap: for a fixed target policy and rollout budget, roughly 88% of its problems are solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout. Filtering concentrates what remains, but it can only select, discarding the hard problems. Effective synthetic problems should therefore require the reasoning operations and compositions required to solve those hard problems. Yet their difficulty must be calibrated, so that some rollouts succeed, some fail, and at least one correct solution fits within the training budget. Prompting a teacher to vary hard problems directly does not achieve this. Guided by these empirical principles, we introduce MagicBeanStalk, a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive data-synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of substantively new, policy- and budget-calibrated training problems while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints. Across 8 math benchmarks, continual RLVR on MagicBeanStalk problems improves gpt-oss-120b from 61.2 to 69.8 (+8.6) and DeepSeek v4Flash from 72.4 to 77.9 (+5.4) on a 16K-token budget. Training on the full 78K source corpus improves by only +1.1 and its best filtered real data subset by +5.8. In finance, we synthesize over 14K verifiable problems from only 340 solutions and improve over base by 6.9 and 2.4 points on SecQue and FinanceBench, respectively.
papers.summary: Scaling reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has focused on collecting more verifiable problems, but corpus size alone does not guarantee a learning signal for a given policy. The authors characterize dataset effectiveness as a function of the problems, the target policy, and the rollout budget, and show that **roughly 88% of a large pooled open-source math corpus falls into a zero-advantage trap, solved in every rollout or failed in every rollout**, so filtering can only select and must discard the hard problems. `MagicBeanStalk` is a top-down decomposition and bottom-up recursive synthesis algorithm that grows seed problems into families of new problems calibrated to the policy and budget while preserving the seeds' reasoning blueprints, something direct teacher prompting fails to do. Continual RLVR on the synthesized problems lifts `gpt-oss-120b` from 61.2 to 69.8 and `DeepSeek v4Flash` from 72.4 to 77.9 across eight math benchmarks at a 16K-token budget, versus +1.1 from the full 78K source corpus and +5.8 from its best filtered subset, and in finance over 14K problems synthesized from 340 solutions improve `SecQue` and `FinanceBench` by 6.9 and 2.4 points.

papers.title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
papers.abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.
papers.summary: Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assumes a static knowledge base, but many decision-support settings start with an empty one that fills up through human decisions. `iRAG` combines RAG with hybrid decision-making, storing prior decisions as retrievable precedents and moving through three phases: silent observation, evidence-grounded contestation of human choices, and finally autonomous handling with abstention. **Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations.** Retrieval decay helps on changed knowledge but raises error on stable knowledge, a stability-plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage, and the human-oversight workflow has not yet been evaluated with real users.

papers.title: perturber: A Stateless Service for Semantics-Preserving Text Perturbations
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) evaluations on clean benchmarks overstate model robustness: real inputs arrive perturbed, and these meaning-preserving variants routinely move model answers. Studying this systematically requires applying perturbations one at a time, reproducibly, and identically wherever they run, yet existing tools couple them to a benchmarking stack rather than packaging them as a reusable transform layer. We present perturber, a stateless service and Python library that applies exactly one semantics-preserving perturbation per call, drawn from a first-party catalog of 68 perturbations across 11 families. It turns on a single primitive, with composition left to the caller chaining calls, so the service and the library produce identical output by construction. We evaluate the tool itself, its correctness, reproducibility, and cost, rather than any model's robustness, measuring meaning-preservation per perturbation rather than assuming it. The demonstration adds a live playground, an introspectable catalog for benchmark selection, and a one-command reproducible evaluation.
papers.summary: Evaluations on clean benchmarks overstate robustness because real inputs arrive perturbed, and meaning-preserving variants routinely change model answers, yet existing perturbation tools are coupled to particular benchmarking stacks. `perturber` is a stateless service and Python library that applies exactly one semantics-preserving perturbation per call, drawn from a first-party catalog of **68 perturbations across 11 families**, with composition left to the caller so the service and library produce identical output by construction. The evaluation targets the tool itself, its correctness, reproducibility, and cost, measuring meaning preservation per perturbation rather than assuming it, and the demonstration includes a live playground, an introspectable catalog, and a one-command reproducible evaluation.

papers.title: Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Language model agents increasingly operate over long interaction streams, requiring online adaptation to distribution shifts through continual learning. However, existing agent harnesses typically either evolve their states only through forward information flow or rely on additional replay or validation data for harness optimization. To address this, we propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that complements forward read and write with backward revision under a strictly online streaming protocol. We ask what information could have been captured differently in the harness state to better inform the current instance in the stream. Specifically, after each instance, we leverage the resulting trajectory as feedback to revise the reflections retrieved for that instance, thereby propagating feedback backward through the textual harness state. Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms strong raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces source-grounded and meaningful revisions, corrects overgeneralized or outdated experience under distribution shifts, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.
papers.summary: Language-model agents operating over long interaction streams need to adapt online to distribution shift, but existing harnesses either update their state only through forward information flow or require extra replay or validation data. `ReHarness` is a recurrent harness that adds backward revision to forward read and write under a strictly online streaming protocol: after each instance, the resulting trajectory serves as feedback to revise the reflections that were retrieved for that instance, propagating the signal backward through the textual harness state. **Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language-model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches.** Analysis shows the revisions are source-grounded, correct overgeneralized or outdated experience under shift, and improve both stability and plasticity.
papers.highlight_summary:
Language-model agents that learn from a stream of tasks typically store memories or reflections and only ever read them forward, so an overgeneralized or outdated reflection persists and keeps misleading later decisions after a distribution shift. `ReHarness` adds a backward revision step: after every instance, a revision agent rewrites the reflections that were retrieved for it, using the new trajectory as feedback while keeping any new content grounded in each reflection's original source trajectory, all under a strictly online protocol with no replay, validation set, or gradient updates.

- Each step runs forward read (retrieve the top-5 reflections with `Qwen3-Embedding-8B`), backward revision (independently rewrite each retrieved reflection given its source trajectory and the current outcome), and forward write (a memory agent produces a new reflection using the revised ones as demonstrations).
- Across `CL-Bench`, `MemoryBench`, and `MemoryArena` with `Claude Opus 4.8`, `GPT-5.5`, and `Gemini 3.7 Flash`, `ReHarness` reaches a mean normalized gain of **0.240** versus **0.168** for `Top-K Raw` and **0.164** for `Full Raw`, ranks first or tied in **8 of 9** benchmark-backbone combinations, and beats every baseline including `Mem0`, `RBank`, `DoT`, `ACE`, and `GEPA-Online` under Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon tests (p_adj 0.039 vs `Top-K Raw`, 0.043 vs `Full Raw`).
- A claim-level audit finds over 95% of revised-reflection claims stay grounded in the source trajectory with only 0.8–2.1% leakage from the downstream instance, and on `CL-Bench` the method posts the highest average stability (0.015) and plasticity (0.241) while all other structured memory and reflection baselines show negative stability on average.
- Dropping revision entirely cuts the `CL-Bench`/Claude gain from 0.217 to 0.144, and a diagnostic counterfactual replay that reapplies the revised state to the same instance (which violates the streaming protocol) lifts it to 0.335, confirming the revisions carry real information.
- On `CL-Bench` with Claude, `ReHarness` consumes ~41.6M total tokens versus 52.7M for `Top-K Raw` and 142.1M for `Full Raw`, but its heavier output-token use puts its cost at about $254, cheaper than `Full Raw` ($314) yet far above `Top-K Raw` ($85), and gains are marginal on exploitable poker where noisy hand-level rewards give the revision agent little diagnostic signal.

papers.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
papers.summary: Large language models increasingly drive GeoAI systems, yet evaluations rarely test whether they can elicit the geospatial data requirements a retrieval-oriented analytic task needs before any data is fetched. `GeoFitBench-LLM` assesses whether models can infer the datasets, supporting resources, and constraints implied by natural-language geo-analytic requests, organized around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, with ground truth encoded in a fixed provider-independent schema. Across seven models under minimal prompting, identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with **`GPT-5.4 Thinking` recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of requests**, while accurate fitness-for-use specification grows harder as inferential demands increase.

papers.title: Amortised Inference through One-Step Implicit Sampling
papers.abstract: Efficient sampling from Bayesian posterior distributions in high dimensions remains a hard problem, despite advances in theory and algorithms. Multiple steps are usually required to draw unbiased samples, for example, iterations of an MCMC algorithm or integration steps in a diffusion-based amortised sampler. However, scalable one-step amortised inference remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we build upon recent progress in data-driven generative modelling to offer a possible solution for one-step amortised sampling. Our one-step implicit sampler (OSIS) uses short-time MCMC dynamics to define a local target for the evolution of an implicitly modelled distribution. In the asymptotic limit, the modelled distribution is a fixed point of the MCMC kernel and thus samples from the target. We analyse the convergence properties of OSIS and show connections with other generative modelling and sampling algorithms. We study various design choices and show that OSIS performs well compared to multi-step amortised samplers and non-amortised MCMC baselines while being far more efficient at sampling time.
papers.summary: Drawing unbiased samples from high-dimensional Bayesian posteriors usually takes many steps, whether MCMC iterations or integration steps in a diffusion-based amortised sampler, and scalable one-step amortised inference has remained open. The one-step implicit sampler (`OSIS`) uses short-time MCMC dynamics to define a local target for the evolution of an implicitly modelled distribution, so that in the asymptotic limit the modelled distribution is a fixed point of the MCMC kernel and therefore samples from the target. The authors analyse convergence, draw connections to other generative modelling and sampling algorithms, and study design choices. **OSIS performs well against multi-step amortised samplers and non-amortised MCMC baselines while being far more efficient at sampling time.**

papers.title: Expert-level detection of low-voltage intervals in EEG as a robust biomarker of neonatal encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Background: Discontinuity in neonatal EEG is a critical marker of brain dysfunction but can be difficult to quantify visually. Inter-burst intervals (IBIs) are a key characteristic of discontinuity, yet their definition does not easily translate to AI detection. Objectives: To introduce low-voltage intervals (LVIs), defined exclusively by amplitude and duration, as a context-independent alternative to IBIs, develop an AI detection method for LVIs, and assess their clinical utility as a marker of brain injury. Methods: We developed a ConvNeXt model to detect LVIs and compared its performance with existing methods. We then tested the clinical relevance of detected LVIs across four applications: 1) grading background EEG abnormalities on an open benchmark dataset, 2) classifying clinical hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) grades and comparing with a normal EEG dataset, 3) seizure prediction, and 4) association with seizure burden. Results: For training and validation, 654 hours of per-channel EEG from 123 neonates were reviewed and 51,162 LVIs were annotated. On held-out validation, ConvNeXt had an AUC of 0.996 and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.926. Model-reader agreement exceeded inter-reader agreement ($\Delta \kappa = 0.025$, 95% CI: 0.007 to 0.045, $p<0.001$), attaining expert-level equivalence. On a combined dataset of 444 neonates, percentage LVI showed a strong association with EEG grades (Spearman's $\rho=0.801$), a moderate association with HIE grades ($\rho=0.384$), a weaker association with seizure burden ($\rho=0.244$), and a strong seizure prediction capacity (AUC $=0.872$). Conclusion: AI detection of LVIs achieves expert-level equivalence, whereas quantitative features do not. Automated LVI quantification provides a robust clinical biomarker of neonatal encephalopathy associated with background EEG activity, HIE severity, and seizure risk.
papers.summary: Discontinuity in neonatal EEG marks brain dysfunction, but inter-burst intervals (IBIs), its key characteristic, are defined in ways that translate poorly to automated detection. The authors define low-voltage intervals (LVIs) purely by amplitude and duration as a context-independent alternative, annotate 51,162 of them across 654 hours of EEG from 123 neonates, and train a `ConvNeXt` detector. **On held-out validation the detector reaches an AUC of 0.996, and its agreement with expert readers exceeds inter-reader agreement, establishing expert-level equivalence.** On 444 neonates, percentage LVI correlates strongly with EEG grades and seizure prediction, moderately with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE) grades, and weakly with seizure burden, supporting automated LVI quantification as a clinical biomarker of neonatal encephalopathy.

papers.title: Critical Mass: Structure-Disjoint Splits Drift With the Libraries They Are Built On
papers.abstract: Molecular machine learning evaluates out-of-distribution performance with structure disjoint splits, a construction rule fixed once at the scale its library happened to have: threshold a pairwise distance, then assign whole connected components to folds. For predicting structures from mass spectra, the field has converged on single-linkage clustering under the myopic Maximum Common Edge Subgraph (MCES) distance at a threshold of 10. This convention was set on 29,000 molecules but public libraries now hold 227,690 molecules. MCES is NP-hard per pair over a quadratically growing set, and so the criterion has never been evaluated at that scale. We propose an optimized version of this criterion, allowing for computationally feasible application on the public libraries: Admissible bounds and a union-find skip reduce $2.6 \times 10^{10}$ molecular pairs to only $1.15 \times 10^{7}$ integer programs, a $2{,}259\times$ saving, while provably producing the lossless partition. We find that at this scale the graph percolates. A single component holds $95.5\%$ of the library, capping any test set at $4.5\%$. What remains is not merely smaller, but systematically different: a held-out compound outweighs a training compound 88.1\% of the time, because a fixed absolute budget is a tighter relative tolerance on a larger molecule. Large library benchmarks using this splitting rule naively therefore conflate structural novelty with extrapolation to larger, more complex chemistry.
papers.summary: Molecular machine learning measures out-of-distribution performance with structure-disjoint splits, and for predicting structures from mass spectra the field settled on single-linkage clustering under the Maximum Common Edge Subgraph (`MCES`) distance at a threshold of 10, a rule fixed when libraries held 29,000 molecules that has never been checked at today's 227,690. Because MCES is NP-hard per pair, the authors introduce admissible bounds and a union-find skip that reduce about 26 billion molecular pairs to 11.5 million integer programs, a 2,259-fold saving, while provably producing the same lossless partition. **At this scale the similarity graph percolates: a single component holds 95.5% of the library, capping any test set at 4.5%.** What remains is systematically different, since a held-out compound outweighs a training compound 88.1% of the time, so large-library benchmarks using this rule conflate structural novelty with extrapolation to larger, more complex chemistry.

papers.title: Toward Maximizing Algebraic Connectivity via Density-Dependent Backbone Construction and Reinforcement Learning Completion
papers.abstract: This paper studies an open network design problem of constructing graph topologies with maximum algebraic connectivity under fixed numbers of vertices and edges. A density-dependent approach is proposed that decomposes the design task into two stages: a high-quality, low-cost structural backbone construction and a reinforcement learning completion stage. The method selects the backbone based on density, using complete multipartite graphs in dense regimes and Cayley graphs in low-to-intermediate regimes, and then refines the remaining edges through a learning-based procedure. Numerical results show that the proposed method achieves high algebraic connectivity with favorable runtime scalability, outperforming existing methods. These results support a structural-family-first strategy for scalable network design.
