papers.summary: Constructing graph topologies that maximize algebraic connectivity for a fixed number of vertices and edges is an open network design problem. The proposed method splits the task into two stages: a low-cost structural backbone chosen by edge density, using complete multipartite graphs in dense regimes and Cayley graphs in low-to-intermediate regimes, followed by a reinforcement learning completion stage that places the remaining edges. **Numerical results show the approach achieves high algebraic connectivity with favorable runtime scalability and outperforms existing methods**, supporting a structural-family-first strategy for scalable network design.

papers.title: Primal-Dual Flow Matching for Sample-Wise Constrained Generation
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of learning to generate data while satisfying a prescribed \emph{sample-wise} constraint with a user-specified probability of constraint satisfaction. Starting with a population-level constrained negative log-likelihood minimization and using a flow-matching (FM) parameterization, under regularity assumptions and sufficient expressivity of the velocity field family, we derive guarantees on the probability of constraint satisfaction for the corresponding primal-dual optimization algorithm. We provide a practical implementation of this approach, called Primal-Dual Flow Matching (PDFM), which has direct control over constraint satisfaction rate and requires only binary membership oracle feedback for constraint satisfaction, avoiding the need for differentiable distances, projections, or special structure of the constraint set, such as convexity. We show that PDFM improves constraint satisfaction over vanilla FM and achieves competitive performance against constraint-aware baselines while maintaining distributional fidelity. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhengyanHuan/PDFM.
papers.summary: Generative models often need to satisfy hard constraints on individual samples, such as keeping outputs inside a feasible region, while still matching the target distribution. Starting from a population-level constrained negative log-likelihood objective with a flow-matching (FM) parameterization, the authors derive guarantees on the probability of constraint satisfaction for a primal-dual optimization scheme and implement it as `PDFM`. The method gives direct control over the constraint satisfaction rate and **requires only a binary membership oracle for the constraint**, with no need for differentiable distances, projections, or convexity of the constraint set. Experiments show improved satisfaction over vanilla FM and competitive results against constraint-aware baselines without sacrificing distributional fidelity.

papers.title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
papers.abstract: Perspectivist NLP has established that annotator positionality shapes labels for subjective tasks, but the field still lacks methods for operationalising it. Positionality is typically operationalised as a demographic form completed at recruitment: a static attribute recorded once and treated as a covariate, on the assumption that the knowledge it indexes is active when the annotator reads an item. This paper treats that assumption as a design problem and asks whether lived experience can instead be primed by the task itself. We introduce AXLE, a pre-annotation stage in which a scenario vignette anchors a short, axis-guided conversation that is synthesised into a first-person micro-narrative and returned to the annotator before labelling begins. In a 2x2 between-subjects study (104 annotators, 30 items, 1,040 annotations) on ambiguous hate speech spanning immigration, religion and gender, elicitation was associated with higher identity resonance and higher sensitivity to harm. It also increased label entropy and lowered inter-annotator agreement: the stage appears to surface plurality rather than manufacture consensus, which distinguishes it from annotator training, whose success criterion is convergence.
papers.summary: Perspectivist NLP holds that annotator positionality shapes labels on subjective tasks, yet positionality is usually recorded once as a demographic form and treated as a static covariate. `AXLE` is a pre-annotation stage in which a scenario vignette anchors a short axis-guided conversation, which is synthesized into a first-person micro-narrative and returned to the annotator before labelling begins. In a 2x2 between-subjects study on ambiguous hate speech about immigration, religion, and gender, with **104 annotators producing 1,040 annotations**, the elicitation stage was associated with higher identity resonance and higher sensitivity to harm. It also raised label entropy and lowered inter-annotator agreement, suggesting it surfaces plurality rather than manufacturing consensus, unlike annotator training whose goal is convergence.

papers.title: Product Monte Carlo: Expectation Under a Product of Densities
papers.abstract: Aggregating independently computed sub-sample inferences is a well-known challenge in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, and opinion pooling. The core problem is to approximate a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. We propose Product Monte Carlo (PMC), an algorithm for computing arbitrary expectations under a product of densities using only Monte Carlo draws from individual densities. We turn the intractable product expectation into a regression problem by expressing it through a family of computable conditional expectations. Besides the point estimate, our fully Bayesian regression formulation provides coherent uncertainty quantification and principled diagnostics. We establish theoretical guarantees on consistency and characterize convergence rates for the PMC estimator. Across simulated and real-data experiments varying the number, dimensionality, and heterogeneity of the component distributions, PMC achieves higher estimation accuracy, better-calibrated uncertainty coverage, and improved scalability at a lower computational cost than existing methods. In addition, PMC requires no density evaluation, making it applicable to simulation-based inference, as we demonstrate in an application with protein images.
papers.summary: Combining independently computed sub-sample posteriors in large-scale Bayesian computation, federated learning, or opinion pooling requires approximating a distribution whose density is proportional to a product of individual densities. `Product Monte Carlo` computes arbitrary expectations under such a product using only Monte Carlo draws from each component, recasting the intractable product expectation as a regression problem over a family of computable conditional expectations, with a fully Bayesian regression formulation that yields uncertainty quantification and diagnostics. The authors prove consistency and characterize convergence rates, and across simulated and real-data experiments varying the number, dimensionality, and heterogeneity of components, report higher accuracy, better-calibrated coverage, and lower computational cost than existing methods. Because it **needs no density evaluations**, it also applies to simulation-based inference, demonstrated on protein images.

papers.title: Bridging Human and Model Attention: Explainability Analysis of CNN, Mamba, and ViT Architectures with Gaze-Based Validation
papers.abstract: High-risk applications of deep learning require precise characterization of model decision-making. We conduct a systematic explainability evaluation across Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba (ViM). Unlike predominantly qualitative studies, we quantify the alignment between model attention and human visual perception using eye-tracking ground truth. We formalize this comparison via a standardized normalization pipeline mapping post-hoc attribution maps and gaze heatmaps onto spatial probability distributions. Alignment is evaluated across fine-grained classification, medical imaging, and emotion recognition using architecture-specific XAI methods. We measure fidelity using Jensen-Shannon similarity, Chi-square similarity, and Pearson correlation, three complementary estimators capturing support overlap, mass discrepancy, and structural co-variation. Our results reveal distinct attention dynamics: CNNs tend to exhibit a more global focus, with spatially more diffuse saliency maps that correlate well with human perception in general contexts, while ViTs demonstrate fine-grained, patch-level attention, often focused on discriminative microfeatures. The Mamba architecture shows biased behavior: it achieves strong explainability in medical tasks but exhibits divergent intensity distributions in natural images; our analytical characterization of the metrics makes this dissociation explicit, since near-unit support overlap is attained simultaneously with a vanishing linear correlation. We further analyze the effect of backbone freezing and ensemble strategies on model interpretability. The results highlight how architectural and training choices influence the alignment between model saliency and human visual attention.
papers.summary: High-risk uses of deep learning require knowing whether a model attends to the same image regions a human would, but most explainability studies are qualitative. The authors map post-hoc attribution maps from Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and Vision Mamba (ViM) onto spatial probability distributions and compare them to eye-tracking heatmaps using Jensen-Shannon similarity, Chi-square similarity, and Pearson correlation across fine-grained classification, medical imaging, and emotion recognition. CNNs produce diffuse, globally focused saliency that correlates well with human gaze in general settings, while ViTs concentrate on fine-grained discriminative patches. **The Mamba architecture aligns strongly on medical tasks but diverges on natural images**, reaching near-unit support overlap with vanishing linear correlation, and the paper further examines how backbone freezing and ensembling affect alignment.

papers.title: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
papers.abstract: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). Against an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites, PVBRF-ID with secure clipping reached 0.641, whereas FedAvg fell to 0.046; plaintext multi-Krum remained higher by 0.052. An update-inference attacker recovered each site's class mix from plaintext updates (Spearman correlation 0.81) but not from one server's view. Backdoors passed the filter, and noise-based mitigation gave only heuristic protection. The implementation uses Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3, 30 rounds and 10 seeds.
papers.summary: Federated intrusion detection across distributed oilfield sites faces a tension: Byzantine-robust aggregation rules need to inspect each client update in the clear, while secure aggregation hides those updates from the poisoning checks. `PVBRF-ID` is a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and cosine similarity against a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing only one accept bit per site, with commitments, Merkle roots, and a homomorphic audit making inclusion publicly verifiable. On a 15-class `Edge-IIoTset` task with ten non-identically distributed sites, it matched `FedAvg` on clean data and **held macro-F1 at 0.696 under sign-flip attacks where FedAvg collapsed to 0.091**, while an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites reduced it to 0.641 versus 0.046 for FedAvg, still 0.052 below plaintext multi-Krum. An update-inference attacker could recover each site's class mix from plaintext updates but not from a single server's view, though backdoors passed the filter and noise-based mitigation offered only heuristic protection.

papers.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
papers.abstract:
Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark.
  Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.

papers.title: Byzantine-Resilient Federated Large Language Model via Hypergraph Message Passing
papers.abstract: Federated Large Language Models (FedLLMs) are promising to deliver privacy-preserving, collaborative intelligence. The decentralized training process is vulnerable to Byzantine attacks that corrupt semantic consistency and factual resilience through malicious model updates. This paper presents a new resilience strategy that prevents semantically corrupted knowledge from propagating during federated aggregation. A defense problem is formulated to jointly maximize global accuracy and suppress manipulated model updates, enabling trustworthy knowledge aggregation without accessing private local data. To strengthen the resilience of FedLLMs, we develop a novel Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder (HMP-GAE) framework, where low-rank model updates are represented as nodes in a hypergraph and high-order semantic relationships among multiple agents are exploited through iterative message passing. By leveraging historical checkpoints and cross-agent relational reasoning, HMP-GAE identifies and suppresses semantically inconsistent updates while preserving knowledge alignment among agents throughout federated training. HMP-GAE is implemented using Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.2 as pretrained FedLLM backbones and evaluated on AG News and Yahoo! Answers datasets. Compared to existing defenses, HMP-GAE improves global accuracy by $1.21$\%, reduces final-model classification semantic entropy by $44.08$\%, and lowers perplexity by $13.34$\%. HMP-GAE outperforms the GAE-based defense by improving the accuracy $1.39$\%, reducing the semantic entropy by $54.5$\%, and lowering perplexity by $35.5$\%.
papers.summary: Federated Large Language Models (FedLLMs) train collaboratively without sharing private data, but malicious clients can inject model updates that corrupt semantic consistency and factual reliability during aggregation. The `HMP-GAE` framework represents low-rank model updates as nodes in a hypergraph and uses a Hypergraph Message Passing Graph Autoencoder to exploit high-order relationships among agents, drawing on historical checkpoints and cross-agent reasoning to identify and suppress semantically inconsistent updates without accessing local data. Evaluated with `Qwen-2.5` and `Llama-3.2` backbones on `AG News` and `Yahoo! Answers`, it improves global accuracy by 1.21% over existing defenses and **reduces final-model semantic entropy by 44.08%** while lowering perplexity by 13.34%, with larger margins over a plain GAE-based defense.

papers.title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.
papers.summary: Large language models are stochastic, so repeated runs under identical conditions can yield different outputs, which complicates risk management for deployed systems. The proposed framework builds an empirical response distribution via Monte Carlo simulation over repeated executions, then applies semantic interventions to the prompt or context and measures how the distribution shifts. Illustrated on borrower classification and music album recommendation, the approach quantifies robustness, control effectiveness, and residual behavior in terms that map onto model risk management and governance across the lifecycle from task design to continuous monitoring. **Because it relies only on observed responses, it works on black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.**

papers.title: Spatial Context or Memory? Sizing the Inputs of Neural Surrogates for Partially Observed Fields
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates that forecast a physical field from sparse, noisy sensors read a window of nearby sensors and a history of past snapshots. Practitioners choose both by comparing fitted models with each other. Such comparisons cannot tell a model's shortfall from missing information. We measure the trade-off between window and history against the Bayes-optimal error of the same readings. An exact Gaussian analysis shows that noisy or sparse observation of a field with local dynamics makes the optimal forecast read distant sensors only through spatial correlation. On a forced linear field with a known optimum, trained models that read only the window come within 1% of it. We then train such models on viscous Burgers flow and the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, with every deciding comparison fixed before any test evaluation. In every field except KS, eight snapshots remove a smaller fraction of the one-snapshot error as the lead time, the number of steps to the forecast target, grows. In KS, for windows up to one correlation length, they remove a larger fraction. This lead-time inversion persists across sensor densities, three architectures and a two-dimensional domain. It shrinks as damping lowers the Lyapunov exponent. Damping also removes the linear instability of KS. We therefore tie the inversion to instability and leave chaos and linear amplification unseparated. For surrogate design the results give two rules. Size the window in correlation lengths of the field. Split a fixed input budget between window and history for the lead time the model will serve, because the best split moves toward wider windows as the lead time grows. In Burgers flow the split chosen at lead time one ends with 13.5 times the best error at lead time eight.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates that forecast a physical field from sparse, noisy sensors must choose how wide a spatial window of neighboring sensors and how long a history of past snapshots to read, and practitioners usually pick these by comparing fitted models, which cannot separate model shortfall from missing information. The authors instead benchmark the window-versus-history trade-off against the Bayes-optimal error for the same readings, showing through an exact Gaussian analysis that under sparse or noisy observation of locally driven dynamics the optimal forecast uses distant sensors only via spatial correlation, and that window-only models on a forced linear field come within 1% of the optimum. On viscous Burgers flow and the chaotic `Kuramoto-Sivashinsky` equation with all comparisons preregistered, extra history helps less as lead time grows in every field except KS, where it helps more, an inversion that persists across sensor densities, three architectures, and 2D domains and shrinks as damping lowers the Lyapunov exponent. The practical rules are to size the window in correlation lengths and split the input budget for the lead time the model will serve, since **a split chosen at lead time one ends with 13.5 times the best error at lead time eight** in Burgers flow.

papers.title: Zebra3D: Efficient Hybrid Foundation Models For Scalable 3D Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits their scalability to large view sets. We present Zebra3D, a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework that improves the efficiency of pretrained 3D foundation models without training from scratch. Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and $\pi^3$, we observe a broadly consistent depth-wise pattern: early stages are relatively tolerant to linear replacement, while sensitive middle-to-late stages tend to exhibit more concentrated attention. Zebra3D exploits this structure by assigning linear-centered attention to tolerant stages and tile-sparse attention to sensitive stages, using landmark summaries to preserve unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting enables training-free conversion, while optional post-conversion training combines task supervision with output and relational feature distillation. Across all three backbones, Zebra3D achieves strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity, with training-free variants remaining close to their dense counterparts. End-to-end speedups increase with input view count, reaching up to $7.1\times$ at 1,024 views. After post-conversion training, Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5\% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94\% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data and schedule.
papers.summary: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits how many views they can process. `Zebra3D` converts pretrained models such as `VGGT`, `HunyuanWorld-Mirror`, and `π³` into layerwise sparse-linear hybrids, exploiting a consistent depth-wise pattern in which early stages tolerate linear attention while sensitive middle-to-late stages have concentrated attention and receive tile-sparse attention with landmark summaries for unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting allows training-free conversion, with optional post-conversion training combining task supervision and feature distillation. Training-free variants stay close to their dense counterparts, end-to-end speedups reach **up to 7.1x at 1,024 views**, and after post-conversion training `Zebra3D-VGGT` reaches 80.5% `RealEstate10K` AUC@30 at 94% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data.

papers.title: A Categorical Atlas of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Cones, Orbits, and Gauges
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has hundreds of methods, usually compared by parameter count and benchmark score. We compare them as maps. A pretrained checkpoint is a base point in weight space, and a weight-space method is a smooth map from a small parameter space that starts at that point. These maps form a slice category in which the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning terminal. Three invariants of the map do most of the work. Its image near the base point governs expressivity, through the first-order image, the dimension, a min-cut bound on rank and whether that point is smooth or an apex. Its fibres, with the optimizer's metric, govern training dynamics. Base change moves the base point and covers splitting initialisations, quantisation, restarts and merging. We prove, for example, that zero-initialised LoRA, and Householder reflection adaptation at its default start under stated rank and parity conditions, begin at the apex of a cone; that no exact initialisation lets LoRA reach an update of rank above twice its own; that exactly orthogonal methods never change a weight's singular values in exact arithmetic, however often they are merged; that under Adam with no epsilon, weight decay or clipping and one shared schedule, LoRA+ from the standard zero initialisation follows exactly the trajectory of plain LoRA with its scale multiplied by the learning-rate ratio; that Adam with shared hyperparameters respects only the signed permutations inside LoRA's continuous symmetry group of full-rank factors; and that the activation function decides when a scaling adapter folds into preceding weights. We classify 382 methods from 138 papers by seven coordinates read off their formulas, with 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions. Every numbered result is proved in full, and results due to others are credited where we re-derive them.
papers.summary: Hundreds of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods exist but are typically compared only by parameter count and benchmark score. The authors instead treat each method as a smooth map from a small parameter space into weight space anchored at the pretrained checkpoint, forming a slice category in which the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning terminal, and show that three invariants of the map, its first-order image, its fibres under the optimizer's metric, and base change, govern expressivity, training dynamics, and operations like quantisation and merging. Proved results include that zero-initialised `LoRA` starts at the apex of a cone, that no exact initialisation lets LoRA reach an update of rank above twice its own, that exactly orthogonal methods never alter a weight's singular values no matter how often they are merged, and that under idealised Adam `LoRA+` from zero initialisation follows plain LoRA's trajectory with a rescaled scale. The atlas **classifies 382 methods from 138 papers by seven coordinates**, with 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions between them.

papers.title: StereoEngine: Scaling Stereo Bimanual Robot Data without Stereo Cameras
papers.abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation, with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation, where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, lifting monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views, producing consistent left-right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io
papers.summary: Stereo vision is increasingly built into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for manipulation, but large-scale real-world stereo robot datasets are scarce and existing monocular-to-stereo generators target VR content or driving rather than manipulation. `StereoEngine` offers two complementary synthesis routes: warping a monocular left-view video into the right view using estimated depth and inpainting disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model, which lifts existing monocular demonstrations to stereo without training on real stereo data, and rendering a stereo pair in simulation then jointly generating both photorealistic views without any real video input. The generated stereo pairs outperform existing baselines in quality, and **using the synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation**.

papers.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability
papers.abstract: Gradient-based attribution provides input-specific information about model parameters, but computing it via backpropagation for many samples is expensive, while static importance scores discard input dependence. We derive KPSA (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel. It measures normalized parameter-group sensitivity, embeds those sources in an explicit query space, and uses a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs. We derive bounds that separate finite-source from irreducible representation error and give margin-based top-$k$ recovery. This paper studies two interpretability applications. Firstly, KPSA identifies parameter groups with high susceptibility to perturbations across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups. Across a fivefold range of parameter budgets ($0.02$-$0.1\%$), its selected groups attain $39$-$85\%$ of the perturbation susceptibility of a first-order backpropagation oracle. In vision and forecasting, these parameter groups form sparse sensitivity circuits that extend across depth and vary systematically with the input. Secondly, we use KPSA on an activation-attribution problem for MLP features in transformers. It retains $81\%$ of the gap between a backpropagation oracle and a constant-sensitivity baseline on vision while increasing batched query-time throughput from 551 to 2,041 images/s and reducing peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44GB. On the protein-modeling task, it recovers $68\%$ of this gap. An ablation of KPSA's kernel aggregation shows that nearest-neighbor retrieval in KPSA space can remain competitive. The empirics show that compact kernel atlases can store useful input-dependent parameter sensitivity while amortizing repeated gradient attribution, a step toward scalable conditional interpretability. Code can be found at https://github.com/Axym-Labs/kpsa .
papers.summary: Gradient-based attribution tells you which parameters matter for a specific input, but backpropagating for many samples is costly, while static importance scores throw away input dependence. `KPSA` (Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlas) derives from a block decomposition of the empirical neural tangent kernel, measuring normalized parameter-group sensitivity on a set of source inputs, embedding them in an explicit query space, and using a lightweight kernel to estimate sensitivities for unseen inputs, with bounds separating finite-source error from irreducible representation error and margin-based top-k recovery guarantees. Across vision, forecasting, and protein-modeling setups at parameter budgets of 0.02 to 0.1%, the selected groups reach 39 to 85% of a first-order backpropagation oracle's perturbation susceptibility and form sparse, input-dependent sensitivity circuits spanning depth. For activation attribution of MLP features in transformers it retains 81% of the oracle's gain on vision while **raising batched query throughput from 551 to 2,041 images per second and cutting peak GPU memory from 4.55 to 0.44 GB**.

papers.title: KITE: A Knowledge-Injected Temporal Encoder for Time-Series Event Forecasting
papers.abstract: Forecasting rare, high-cost events in multivariate time-series systems is hard because their precursors are seldom observed, so a purely data-driven model has little to learn from. The engineers who run these systems, however, hold knowledge that precedes such events, information absent from the scarce labels. We call this a semantic prior and inject it into a self-supervised event forecaster through two switchable mechanisms, a covariate mechanism and an attention-bias mechanism, each the identity at its null, so one architecture serves every prior type with no per-dataset architecture search. A prior helps when it supplies information the observed window does not already contain: in a short context an informative prior beats no prior in-domain (pooled h-AUROC over the no-prior baseline: a periodicity clock +14%, p<0.001; a conservation residual +47% at a 0.25 label fraction), and a working prior transfers out-of-domain (+53%), substituting for feature transfer, while priors the window already recovers stay inert and the attention-bias mechanism shows no measurable gain. KITE is a switchable, attributable route to contextual conditioning, and a substrate for scaling toward cross-domain, pretrained time-series foundation world models that carry their governing structure explicitly.
papers.summary: Rare, high-cost events in multivariate time series are hard to forecast because their precursors are seldom observed, leaving purely data-driven models little signal, even though the engineers who operate such systems hold knowledge about what precedes them. `KITE` injects this semantic prior into a self-supervised event forecaster through two switchable mechanisms, a covariate path and an attention-bias path, each reducing to the identity at its null so a single architecture handles every prior type without per-dataset search. A prior helps only when it supplies information the observation window lacks: in short contexts a periodicity clock raises pooled h-AUROC by 14% and **a conservation residual by 47% at a 0.25 label fraction**, a working prior transfers out-of-domain with a 53% gain in place of feature transfer, while priors the window already recovers stay inert and the attention-bias path shows no measurable gain.

papers.title: Minimax Rates for Estimating Powered Sliced Wasserstein Functionals
papers.abstract: We study the two-sample estimation of the powered Sliced Wasserstein functional under projected $r$-th moment assumptions. Let $N=n\wedge m$, where $n$ and $m$ are two sample sizes. We establish the minimax rates in the noncritical regimes. When $p<r<2p$, the minimax risk is of order $N^{-(r-p)/r}$, while for $r>2p$ it is of order $N^{-1/2}$. In both cases, the natural plug-in estimator is minimax rate-optimal. At the endpoint $r=p$, the minimax risk is bounded away from zero, so uniformly consistent estimation is impossible. At the critical order $r=2p$, we obtain the exact worst-case rate of the plug-in estimator and a lower bound for the minimax risk, leaving a logarithmic gap between the lower and upper bounds. The exact minimax rate in this critical case remains open.
papers.summary: Estimating the powered Sliced Wasserstein distance between two distributions from samples raises the question of how fast error shrinks under projected r-th moment assumptions, where N is the smaller of the two sample sizes. The authors establish minimax rates in the noncritical regimes: for p < r < 2p the risk scales as N to the power -(r-p)/r, while for r > 2p it scales as N to the -1/2, and **in both regimes the natural plug-in estimator is minimax rate-optimal**. At the endpoint r = p the minimax risk is bounded away from zero, so uniformly consistent estimation is impossible, and at the critical order r = 2p they obtain the exact worst-case plug-in rate and a lower bound with a logarithmic gap, leaving the exact rate there open.

papers.title: Neural expectation-maximization and meta-models
papers.abstract: We interpret Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation--Maximization (EM). In this view, a Transformer performs inference in partially observed Markov Random Fields (MRFs) whose structure and parameters are not given a priori but are inferred from data. We show that self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities. We further establish an EM correspondence at the level of depth: each layer updates latent representations in an E-step-like forward pass, while the transition $\theta^{(l)} \to \theta^{(l+1)}$ across layers acts as an implicit M-step. Building on this interpretation, we introduce \emph{meta-models}, a design paradigm in which inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying mechanisms such as self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units within a single framework. Empirical results support the proposed perspective.
papers.summary: The authors propose reading Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation-Maximization (EM) in partially observed Markov Random Fields (MRFs) whose structure and parameters are inferred from data rather than given. They argue that **self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF**, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities, and that depth corresponds to EM, with each layer's forward pass acting as an E-step and the transition between layer parameters acting as an implicit M-step. From this view they introduce meta-models, a design paradigm where inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units under one framework, and report empirical results consistent with the interpretation.

papers.title: U4RASD at KnowledgeGraphEval-2026: Ontology-Constrained Encoder and LLM Systems for Arabic Relation Extraction
papers.abstract: This paper details our submission to KnowledgeGraphEval 2026 Subtask 2 on directed Arabic relation extraction. We explored encoder-based and large language model approaches for predicting one of 40 relations or no_relation from an Arabic sentence and a subject-object pair. Our encoder systems use typed entity markers and separate relation-existence and relation-classification heads, while our LLM systems fine-tune Yehia and Qwen3.5 with QLoRA and ontology-constrained prediction. Our best system, an ensemble of Yehia-RE, Qwen-RE, and TypedPair, achieved a micro-F1 score of 94.06 and ranked 1st in Subtask 2. Yehia-RE (full-vocabulary) achieved 92.98, while the best encoder and Qwen-RE achieved 92.69 and 91.94 respectively. Our results highlight the importance of constrained prediction and complementary modeling approaches for Arabic relation extraction.
papers.summary: The submission targets `KnowledgeGraphEval 2026` Subtask 2, directed Arabic relation extraction, where a system must assign one of 40 relations or no relation to a subject-object pair in an Arabic sentence. Encoder-based systems use typed entity markers with separate relation-existence and relation-classification heads, while LLM systems fine-tune `Yehia` and `Qwen3.5` with `QLoRA` and constrain predictions to the ontology. An ensemble of `Yehia-RE`, `Qwen-RE`, and `TypedPair` reached **a micro-F1 of 94.06 and ranked first in the subtask**, with the individual full-vocabulary Yehia-RE, best encoder, and Qwen-RE systems scoring 92.98, 92.69, and 91.94, pointing to the value of constrained prediction and complementary model families.

papers.title: Static Gradient Attribution Underperforms a Density-Matched Random Mask on Loss-Based Forgetting Within LoRA B-Matrix
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning updates a restricted subset of adapter parameters to incorporate sequential tasks while limiting catastrophic forgetting. Gradient attribution is a common rule for selecting that subset, but it requires an additional backward pass over calibration data. We identify a parameter-pool confound in comparisons between initialization-time gradient masks and unrestricted random masks under standard zero-initialized LoRA ($B=0$): the gradient with respect to $A$ is identically zero ($\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A=0$), so gradient masks select strictly from the $B$ matrix whereas unrestricted random masks draw from both $A$ and $B$. Such a comparison changes both the selection rule and the candidate parameter pool. Isolating the selection criterion by restricting both approaches to the same parameter pool, we find a negative result: a uniform random mask consistently achieves lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B. The effect is concentrated on the medical task, which contributes 80\% of the aggregate; code and math move in the same direction, and legal shows no reliable difference. This advantage is consistent with a stability--plasticity trade-off under the tested task sequence, in which random masking slightly reduces single-task fitting. On the two discrete-option tasks (Medical and Legal), the mean accuracy-BWT difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.
papers.summary: Parameter-efficient continual learning updates a restricted subset of adapter parameters per task to limit catastrophic forgetting, and gradient attribution is a common way to choose that subset despite needing an extra backward pass over calibration data. The authors identify a confound in prior comparisons: under standard zero-initialized `LoRA` with B = 0, the gradient with respect to A is identically zero, so gradient masks select only from the B matrix while unrestricted random masks draw from both A and B, changing the candidate pool along with the selection rule. Restricting both methods to the same B-matrix pool on `Qwen2.5-3B` across seven seeds, **a uniform random mask consistently achieves lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution**, with the effect concentrated on the medical task, code and math moving in the same direction, and legal showing no reliable difference. The result is consistent with a stability-plasticity trade-off in which random masking slightly reduces single-task fitting, and on the discrete-option tasks the accuracy-based difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

papers.title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
papers.summary: Predicting an autonomous vehicle's own future trajectory through urban roadway work zones is underexplored, since temporary lane changes and interactions with workers make motion hard to anticipate and dedicated data is scarce. The authors collect `WZDrive-Data`, a multimodal dataset of 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers in a human-in-the-loop simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers, recording driver control and gaze signals alongside simulator trajectories and scene information. Their multimodal predictor `WZDrive` reaches a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m, **reducing minADE by 7.18% and minFDE by 13.18%** against the best state-of-the-art baseline on each metric.

papers.title: NV-Tesseract-AD: Curriculum-Enhanced Conditional Diffusion for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: We propose NV-Tesseract-AD, a curriculum learning-enhanced conditional diffusion framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection. Our central hypothesis is that reconstruction difficulty can be explicitly structured along two complementary axes, masking severity and diffusion noise level, and that training from easier to harder tasks along both axes simultaneously stabilizes optimization and improves residual discriminability. We integrate a Transformer-based diffusion backbone with a three-stage dual curriculum over masking ratios and diffusion timesteps, retaining anomalous samples throughout training and relying on structured corruption to drive self-supervised representation learning. We evaluate NV-Tesseract-AD under two regimes: in-distribution training on the TSB-UAD-M corpus and strict zero-shot transfer to ten EasyTSAD benchmark families without per-dataset tuning. The dual-axis curriculum produces masking-invariant reconstruction, confirmed by a near-zero loss gap between complementary masking strategies within the first training stage, and yields an approximately 3.7-fold improvement in F1 and a 56 percent reduction in MSE relative to a non-curriculum baseline. Zero-shot performance reaches F1 = 0.984 on NAB and F1 = 0.948 on NormA. Weaker results on heterogeneous families are traced to unsupervised threshold calibration rather than reconstruction quality, identifying calibration as the dominant remaining detection bottleneck. Accelerated inference via DPM-Solver++ reduces sampling cost by a factor of 3.5 to 5.7 at the dataset level but couples to thresholding behavior, establishing that the sampler and threshold must be validated jointly. Together, these findings demonstrate that aligning diffusion denoising difficulty with curriculum learning principles provides a principled and practical approach for robust anomaly detection in complex multivariate time series.
papers.summary: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors for multivariate time series can be unstable to train and produce residuals that poorly separate normal from anomalous windows. `NV-Tesseract-AD` pairs a Transformer-based conditional diffusion backbone with a three-stage dual curriculum that ramps difficulty along two axes at once, masking ratio and diffusion noise level, keeping anomalous samples in training and relying on structured corruption for self-supervised representation learning. Trained in-distribution on `TSB-UAD-M`, the curriculum yields masking-invariant reconstruction and **roughly a 3.7-fold F1 improvement and 56% lower MSE over a non-curriculum baseline**, and zero-shot transfer to ten `EasyTSAD` families without per-dataset tuning reaches F1 of 0.984 on `NAB` and 0.948 on `NormA`. Weaker results on heterogeneous families trace to unsupervised threshold calibration rather than reconstruction quality, and accelerated sampling with `DPM-Solver++` cuts cost 3.5 to 5.7x but interacts with thresholding, so sampler and threshold must be validated together.

papers.title: MADS: Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation for Robust Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: Task-oriented conversational agents remain fragile under realistic conditions, especially when users exhibit non-cooperative behavior. Existing function-calling benchmarks underrepresent adversarial conversation trajectories, thereby limiting the training resources available for developing robust agents. We present MADS (Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation), a synthetic data generation pipeline that produces structured, diverse dialogue trajectories. We inject adversarial conversation, producing validated conversation trajectories that capture realistic, unhappy paths. Using MADS, we construct MADS-Bench: a benchmark spanning six domains, 55 personas, and 1095 conversations, with approximately 66% of conversations containing failure-prone conversation scenarios. We evaluate the robustness of the trained models using a two-stage training approach that combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).
papers.summary: Task-oriented conversational agents break down when users are uncooperative, and existing function-calling benchmarks contain few adversarial trajectories to train on. `MADS` (Multi-Agent Dialog Simulation) is a synthetic data pipeline that generates structured, diverse dialogues and injects adversarial conversation to produce validated unhappy-path trajectories. From it the authors build `MADS-Bench`, which spans six domains, 55 personas, and 1095 conversations, **about 66% of which contain failure-prone scenarios**, and they assess robustness by training models with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

papers.title: DistressBench: Evaluating Multi-Dimensional Crisis Support in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Language models have been adopted faster than evaluation practices that reliably assess their risks, and a growing share of use is affective rather than informational. Within that traffic users disclose suicide and self-harm (SSH) crises. Existing safety benchmarks score models primarily on refusal, but refusal is not the desired behavior here; the conversation requires a substantive supportive response. We introduce DistressBench, 718 English conversations with clinician-authored user turns spanning 23 SSH subcategories, each paired with a task-specific rubric of weighted atomic criteria across seven dimensions of crisis support and a clinician reference response. A model's score is the weighted average over the criteria its reply satisfies, reading directly as the fraction of required care delivered. The best of 25 frontier models satisfies 88.4% of weighted criteria and the median model 71.4%, against 98.7% for clinician references scored on the same criteria. Pooled across all 25 models, in 35.3% of conversations where a model satisfied every criterion for recognizing the crisis, it failed to route the user toward human help. The shortfall concentrates in the dimensions requiring the model to act rather than withhold. Contrasting each dimension's median model against its best separates capability limits from choices: de-escalation reaches 74.6% in the strongest model against a median of 46.0%, and safety disclaimers 84.6% against 8.3%. Multi-turn conversations score below single-turn ones (68.5% against 74.2%). We release the corpus, rubrics, judge calibration labels, and a companion annex of 20 long-horizon red-team transcripts. These results argue for evaluating crisis safety on the care a model delivers rather than on what it declines to say, and for treating de-escalation and resource routing as deployment requirements.
papers.summary: A growing share of language model use is affective rather than informational, and some users disclose suicide and self-harm (SSH) crises, where refusal is the wrong behavior and a substantive supportive response is required. `DistressBench` contains 718 English conversations with clinician-authored user turns across 23 SSH subcategories, each paired with a weighted rubric spanning seven dimensions of crisis support and a clinician reference response, so a model's score reads directly as the fraction of required care delivered. The best of 25 frontier models satisfies 88.4% of weighted criteria and the median 71.4%, against 98.7% for clinician references, and **in 35.3% of conversations where a model fully recognized the crisis it still failed to route the user toward human help**, with shortfalls concentrated in dimensions that require acting rather than withholding. The authors argue that crisis safety should be evaluated on the care a model delivers rather than on what it declines to say, with de-escalation and resource routing treated as deployment requirements.

papers.title: Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs
papers.abstract:
Hardware datasheets contain engineering specifications essential for component selection, system integration, and hardware compatibility verification. However, manual inspection is tedious and error-prone because datasheets are lengthy and heterogeneous, with dense information fragmented across tables, figures, and text. Although large language models (LLMs) can automate this process, na\"ive one-shot processing omits relevant specifications even when the document fits within the model's context window.
  We present an automated LLM-driven pipeline that transforms hardware datasheets into general-purpose hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs through chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement. The framework uses LLMs for information extraction and semantic reasoning while preserving source provenance and applying graph updates through validated instructions and deterministic local execution. This staged design reduces per-query context and maintains traceable intermediate representations. The resulting knowledge graphs provide semantically organized, source-grounded hardware properties for downstream retrieval and reasoning.
  We evaluate the framework on 20 hardware datasheets spanning diverse component types and document lengths. We assess property faithfulness and introduce inter-graph completeness to measure relative semantic coverage without exhaustive ground truth. Our framework achieves 98.8% property faithfulness compared with 76.1% for the one-shot baseline, while fully covering 83.6% of faithful baseline properties; in the reverse direction, the baseline fully covers only 10.5% of ours. These improvements provide more reliable and comprehensive engineering information for downstream hardware design and verification, reducing the risk of overlooked constraints and incorrect decisions.
papers.summary: Hardware datasheets scatter dense specifications across tables, figures, and text, and even when an entire datasheet fits in a large language model's context window, one-shot extraction omits relevant properties. The proposed pipeline turns datasheets into hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs through chunk-based property extraction, hierarchical routing, and iterative refinement, with the LLM handling extraction and semantic reasoning while graph updates are applied through validated instructions and deterministic local execution that preserves source provenance. On 20 datasheets of varied component types and lengths, the pipeline reaches **98.8% property faithfulness versus 76.1% for a one-shot baseline**, fully covers 83.6% of the baseline's faithful properties, and is covered only 10.5% in the reverse direction under a new inter-graph completeness measure that avoids exhaustive ground truth.

papers.title: Provenance-grouped protocol for evaluating machine learning in perovskite photovoltaics
papers.abstract: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are typically evaluated using random data splits, which we show systematically leak information through massive internal duplication. Because nearly two-thirds of curated devices share their exact recipe with another, random splits primarily reward the mere recall of historical data rather than testing true physical generalisation. To solve this, we mapped the institutional provenance of the Perovskite Database and established a rigorous hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively isolate duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models establishes new state-of-the-art performance across all splits and reveals a critical regime shift: while tree ensembles dominate random splits by recognising familiar recipes, their ranking collapses on genuinely unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures excel. Furthermore, feature importance demonstrates that the device architecture and fabrication methodology dictate final efficiency just as strongly as the absorber chemistry. This standardised protocol empowers the community to separate memorisation from true physical discovery.
papers.summary: Machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells are usually evaluated with random train-test splits, but nearly two-thirds of curated devices share an exact recipe with another device, so random splits leak information and mostly reward recall of historical data. The authors map the institutional provenance of the `Perovskite Database` and define a hierarchy of grouped splits that progressively hold out duplicate devices, publications, and institutions. Benchmarking thirteen models shows that **tree ensembles that lead on random splits collapse in the rankings on unseen institutions and future discoveries, where composition-aware neural architectures do best**, and feature importance indicates that device architecture and fabrication method shape efficiency as strongly as absorber chemistry.

papers.title: Semantic Views: Certified Reuse of LLM Labels Across Semantic Queries
papers.abstract: Semantic query engines evaluate natural-language filters with a large language model, and every evaluation is a costly oracle call. Optimizers that reduce these calls face a dilemma: cascades that trust a cheap proxy miss their precision and recall targets on many queries, methods with finite-sample guarantees save little, and all of them discard the oracle's labels when the query ends. We present SemViews, a certified semantic filter that orders tuples by signals that cost no oracle calls (the labels that earlier queries left behind as semantic views, a local embedding, and a helper model's score), refines that order with labels it must pay for anyway, and certifies its answer with fresh stratified oracle samples. The answer meets user precision and recall targets with probability at least $1-\delta$ for every workload and every catalog, so a stale or misleading view can cost oracle calls but never accuracy. On four workloads replayed against 725,000 recorded oracle labels, SemViews meets both targets on 99.63% of queries and saves 28%-45% of the oracle calls, whereas the only prior method in our study with the same guarantee needs 1.32x-1.71x as many calls. When a question returns in different words, views cut its calls by a further 27%-36%, with both targets met on at least 99.8% of such queries; similarity caches and entailment-based reuse meet them on only 17%-47%.
papers.summary: Semantic query engines evaluate natural-language filters by calling a large language model oracle on each tuple, and existing optimizers either miss precision and recall targets, save few calls when they offer guarantees, or discard the oracle's labels once a query ends. `SemViews` keeps those labels as reusable semantic views, orders tuples by signals that cost no oracle calls, namely earlier view labels, a local embedding, and a helper model's score, refines that order with labels it must buy anyway, and certifies the answer with fresh stratified oracle samples so that precision and recall targets hold with probability at least 1 minus delta for any workload or catalog. Replayed against 725,000 recorded oracle labels on four workloads, it meets both targets on 99.63% of queries while **saving 28% to 45% of oracle calls**, where the only prior method with the same guarantee needs 1.32 to 1.71 times as many calls, and rephrased repeat questions cut calls by a further 27% to 36%.

papers.title: REDaCT: Collapse-Free Unlearning in Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Unlearning in large reasoning models (LRMs) requires removing forget-set information from both the reasoning trace and the final answer. Existing approaches achieve this objective at the cost of reasoning collapse, where the model fails to produce a coherent chain-of-thought (CoT) and does not properly terminate its reasoning process. To address this challenge, we propose REDaCT (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning), an inference-time unlearning framework for LRMs. REDaCT consists of two key components: (1) a binary leak detector that identifies sentences in the reasoning trace that leak forget-set information, and (2) an embedding optimization module that learns a corrective embedding offline, such that when injected at the first detected leak during inference, it guides subsequent reasoning towards sentences that do not leak forget-set information. Experimental results show that REDaCT completely avoids reasoning collapse, substantially improving reasoning preservation compared to state-of-the-art unlearning methods while maintaining perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect CoT forgetting. Our code is available at: https://github.com/jmaccoby/redact.
papers.summary: Unlearning in large reasoning models (LRMs) must remove forget-set information from both the chain-of-thought (CoT) and the final answer, and existing methods achieve this at the cost of reasoning collapse, where the model stops producing coherent, properly terminated reasoning. `REDaCT` (REgenerate via Detection and Corrective Tuning) is an inference-time framework that pairs a binary leak detector, which flags reasoning sentences that leak forget-set content, with a corrective embedding learned offline and injected at the first detected leak to steer subsequent reasoning toward non-leaking sentences. In experiments it **completely avoids reasoning collapse** while maintaining perfect answer forgetting and near-perfect CoT forgetting, substantially improving reasoning preservation over state-of-the-art unlearning baselines.

papers.title: Credit Attribution in Timestamped Soccer Networks Using Multivariate Hawkes Processes
papers.abstract: The two main traditional player statistics used in soccer are goals scored and assists, with an assist credited when a player's pass immediately leads to a teammate scoring. Attributing credit solely to the player who makes the final pass before a goal fails to account for the contributions of multiple players in the buildup to the goal. Consequently, traditional statistics provide only a limited view of player involvement. In this paper, we use multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs) to model timestamped sequences of passes and shots, which form continuous-time networks. MHPs provide a branching mechanism where an event (a pass or shot) can be generated as a child of a previous event, which allows us to quantify each pass's contribution to a subsequent pass or shot. This approach distributes credit across multiple passes within an attacking sequence, making it applicable across a wide range of situations. Building on this framework, we propose expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that measures a player's involvement in creating goal scoring opportunities based on their passes. This metric identifies players who play key roles in creating goal scoring opportunities even if they do not make the final pass, offering a more comprehensive measure of attacking involvement and player performance.
papers.summary: Goals and assists credit only the scorer and the final passer, ignoring the other players who contribute to the buildup before a goal. The authors model timestamped sequences of passes and shots as continuous-time networks using multivariate Hawkes processes (MHPs), whose branching structure treats each event as a possible child of an earlier one and thereby quantifies how much each pass contributed to a later pass or shot. On this basis they define expected goal involvements (xGI), a metric that **distributes credit across every pass in an attacking sequence** and identifies players central to chance creation even when they do not make the final pass.

papers.title: Coordinate-Free Automatic Differentiation
papers.abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) is a cornerstone of modern machine learning. Since all AD frameworks implicitly fix a basis of Euclidean space to define gradients and Jacobians, they natively process mathematical objects that are arrays of a fixed set of coordinates. This makes it awkward to express objects such as rotations, volume forms, and curvatures that arise, for example, in applications of AI to science. Bespoke workarounds lack reusability. We show that (i) a single, basis-independent derivative operator can represent many geometric differential operations, and (ii) this operator can be expressed entirely in terms of existing AD primitives. This reusable transformation can be composed with JAX batching, compilation, and hardware acceleration. Geometry enters as algebraic data. We experimentally demonstrate its reuse across different manifold operators, its composition through a spacetime inverse-problem pipeline, and its use in optimization over different rotor subgroups.
papers.summary: Automatic differentiation (AD) frameworks implicitly fix a basis of Euclidean space, so they natively handle arrays of fixed coordinates and make objects such as rotations, volume forms, and curvatures awkward to express, with bespoke workarounds that do not reuse well. The authors show that a single basis-independent derivative operator can represent many geometric differential operations and that **this operator can be expressed entirely in terms of existing AD primitives**, so the transformation composes with JAX batching, compilation, and hardware acceleration while geometry enters as algebraic data. They demonstrate reuse across different manifold operators, composition within a spacetime inverse-problem pipeline, and optimization over different rotor subgroups.

papers.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders typically demands millions of paired examples. In this paper, we study the regime where only $N \sim 100$--$500$ pairs are available, while unpaired data on either side is abundant. Our method expresses every representation by its similarities to the $N$ paired anchors, which places both modalities in a common coordinate system; matches the two point clouds with a single entropic optimal transport problem solved over the entire pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching; and distills the resulting plan into two lightweight encoders, so that the correspondence becomes inductive. We additionally put this marginal constraint in relation with the one-step hub corrections of the bilingual lexicon induction literature. Pairing is required only for the anchors: the unpaired collections may be drawn independently from the two marginals, so that no item outside the anchor set needs to have both of its modalities observed. We evaluate on image-text and molecule-text alignment, where our method outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget on Flickr30k, MS-COCO and ChEBI-20.
papers.summary: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders normally requires millions of paired examples, whereas this work targets the regime of only 100 to 500 pairs alongside abundant unpaired data on each side. Every representation is re-expressed by its similarities to the paired anchors, which places both modalities in a shared coordinate system. The two point clouds are then matched with a single entropic optimal transport problem over the whole pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching, and the resulting plan is distilled into two lightweight encoders so that the correspondence becomes inductive. Only the anchors need pairing, since the unpaired collections can be drawn independently from each marginal, and the method **outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget** on `Flickr30k`, `MS-COCO`, and `ChEBI-20` for image-text and molecule-text alignment.

papers.title: EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.
papers.summary: Self-evolving LLM agents usually improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills, yet even procedurally capable agents fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, wrong, or stale. `EvoBelief` is a self-evolving world model that stores environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses: unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation, later observations and controlled experiments validate a rule before it can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope, and counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes, all with the language model frozen and each rule linked to its evidence and the decisions it changed. Across four benchmarks it improves task performance and reuses rules across tasks, raising `ALFWorld` success over a matched frozen world model by 23.9% with `Claude Haiku 4.5` and 31.3% with `GPT-5.4`, recovering from unannounced dynamics changes on `MiniGrid`, and in the Reactor Lab setting of `DiscoveryWorld` **completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances versus 0% for every baseline**.

papers.title: Large Language Models, Machine-Assisted Cultural Analytics, and the Agentic Turn
papers.abstract: Technologies like large language models make it easier to convert cultural material into analyzable variables, while LLM-driven agentic systems extend machine assistance to other parts of the research workflow. Rather than a full how-to guide or an exhaustive review of recent LLM use cases, this chapter looks at some crucial aspects of this new paradigm as well as the bigger picture. I argue that these technologies expand the scale, methodological range, and scope for delegation, while the basic logic by which those measurements support cultural claims remains mostly unchanged.
papers.summary: Large language models make it easier to convert cultural material into analyzable variables, and LLM-driven agentic systems extend machine assistance into other parts of the research workflow. This book chapter, framed as a perspective rather than a how-to guide or exhaustive review, examines key aspects of that paradigm for cultural analytics and situates it within a bigger picture. The author argues that these technologies expand scale, methodological range, and the scope for delegation, **while the basic logic by which measurements support cultural claims remains mostly unchanged**.

papers.title: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-guided evolutionary optimization has successfully improved prompts, programs, and even entire AI systems. Most optimization methods select a candidate from the search frontier, then mutate it in one LLM pass based only on its failures. This focus on the frontier can stall on production AI systems, where isolated failures reveal little about complex, hidden interactions. We introduce CoCoEvolve (Cortex Code Evolve), an evolutionary optimizer built around what we call meta-reflection, wherein an agentic mutator (Cortex Code) selectively retrieves evidence from the entire evolutionary history and probes the live system before verifying and proposing mutations. We apply CoCoEvolve to optimize three classes of production AI systems: data agents, LLM-powered data pipelines, and data engineering workflows. On DABStep, CoCoEvolve tops the public leaderboard, reaching 92.8% held-out hard accuracy compared to 78.4% for Meta-Harness and 30.4% for GEPA under matched conditions. Across six LLM data pipeline workloads, it outperforms every evaluated baseline. On data-eng-bench, CoCoEvolve lifts test-set solve rate from 59.1% to 77.4%, past the best baseline of 73.6%. It also has 11 percentage points higher accuracy than GEPA on HotpotQA while remaining competitive with specialized optimizers on established mathematical and systems benchmarks. Matched ablations confirm that each component of CoCoEvolve contributes to these gains, demonstrating the value of meta-reflection for optimizing production AI systems.
papers.summary: LLM-guided evolutionary optimizers typically select a candidate from the search frontier and mutate it in one LLM pass based only on that candidate's failures, which stalls on production AI systems where isolated failures reveal little about hidden interactions. `CoCoEvolve` (Cortex Code Evolve) is built around meta-reflection, in which an agentic mutator selectively retrieves evidence from the entire evolutionary history and probes the live system before verifying and proposing mutations. Applied to data agents, LLM-powered data pipelines, and data engineering workflows, it reaches **92.8% held-out hard accuracy on `DABStep`**, topping the public leaderboard against 78.4% for `Meta-Harness` and 30.4% for `GEPA` under matched conditions, lifts the `data-eng-bench` test solve rate from 59.1% to 77.4%, beats every baseline on six pipeline workloads, and scores 11 points above `GEPA` on `HotpotQA`, with matched ablations attributing gains to each component.

papers.title: Efficient Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement via Reinforcement Learning-Based Neural Architecture Search
papers.abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments but often relies on computationally expensive models unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework to discover compact, efficient AVSE architectures. The search space preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, while a novel reward function jointly optimises speech enhancement performance, measured by SI-SNR improvement, and model compactness. Using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking, the framework evaluates only 35 candidate architectures and identifies a model with 2.9 million parameters, compared with 22 million in the baseline. The proposed architecture achieves a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline, while reducing model size by approximately nine-fold. Evaluation on commercial mobile CPUs demonstrates a 4.3-fold reduction in real-time factor, supporting practical on-device deployment. Compared with random search, RL-NAS achieves 92% higher search efficiency. Architectural analysis reveals that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks and aggressive visual pathway pruning can maintain enhancement performance while substantially reducing computational requirements. These findings demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning-guided architecture search for developing lightweight, efficient and deployable multimodal speech enhancement systems.
papers.summary: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves intelligibility in noisy environments but typically relies on models too heavy for resource-constrained edge devices. A reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework explores a search space that preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking and a reward that jointly scores scale-invariant signal-to-noise ratio (SI-SNR) improvement and model compactness. After evaluating only 35 candidates it finds a 2.9 million parameter model, down from 22 million in the baseline, that **delivers a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline**, runs with a 4.3-fold lower real-time factor on commercial mobile CPUs, and shows that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks with aggressive visual-pathway pruning retain enhancement performance.

papers.title: Polyconvex neural-network surrogates with learned paired directional features for anisotropic hyperelastic homogenization
