papers.summary: Diffusion language models generate tokens in parallel but still need many sampling steps, so this work asks whether a model can emit an entire sequence in a single forward pass. `Seq-Drifting` applies drifting to sequences of continuous token representations, learning a direct map from Gaussian noise to text through a drift field whose per-position targets adapt to the current generated context, with attraction pulling each output toward contextually plausible token representations and repulsion discouraging collapse across samples and repetition within a sequence. **The one-step generator reaches a generative perplexity of 36.01 on `LM1B`** and is competitive on unconditional and conditional generation, with further experiments on translation, summarization, and reasoning. Code is released.

papers.title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
papers.abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. We introduce GeoSpatialBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate an escalating progression of spatial cognition, ranging from spatial relation understanding and geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Grounded in real-world urban data across six geographically diverse cities, GeoSpatialBench evaluates a comprehensive taxonomy of 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations across structured GeoJSON and map image modalities, with ground-truth references and constraints verified via GIS operations. Our empirical evaluation across frontier MLLMs uncovers a stark spatial gap: structured GeoJSON consistently outperforms map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and while models show reasonable competence on qualitative topological and ordering, performance drops on quantitative metric relations. Crucially, editing performance on ordering relations declines relative to QA, and most failed edits violate at least one specified spatial constraint. These results highlight a gap between passively recognizing spatial relations and actively manipulating geometric configurations. GeoSpatialBench provides an open, rigorous diagnostic testbed to benchmark these spatial limitations, laying essential empirical groundwork for physically grounded world models and embodied spatial AI.
papers.summary: Spatial reasoning evaluations for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mostly use static question answering over small or synthetic scenes and rarely test whether a model can modify a spatial configuration while respecting explicit geometric constraints. `GeoSpatialBench` is built from real urban data across six cities and covers 28 topological, directional, metric, and ordering relations in both structured GeoJSON and map-image modalities, with ground truth and constraints verified through GIS operations, progressing from relation understanding through geometric reasoning to constrained spatial editing. Frontier MLLMs perform consistently better on GeoJSON than on map images, with multimodal combinations offering no reliable gain over GeoJSON alone, and handle qualitative topological and ordering relations better than quantitative metric ones. **Editing performance on ordering relations drops relative to question answering, and most failed edits violate at least one stated spatial constraint.**

papers.title: HART: Hybrid Attention-RWKV Time series Foundation Model
papers.abstract: Non-autoregressive multi-step forecasting (NAF) enables time series foundation models to predict an entire future horizon in a single forward pass. Despite its strong sequence modeling capabilities, RWKV-7 exhibits long-horizon degradation in our NAF experiments. In this setup, future patches are represented as missing inputs, requiring the recurrent state to evolve across the prediction horizon without new observations. Our analysis of RWKV-7's generalized delta rule suggests a mechanism we term Placeholder Idling Decay (PID): repeated state transitions can attenuate historical information when placeholder-driven writes provide insufficient compensation. Layer-wise analysis reveals reduced state-injection norms in most layers, while transition-matrix norms remain similar between historical and prediction regions, consistent with PID. Motivated by this analysis, we propose HART, a Hybrid Attention-RWKV Time-series Foundation Model that alternates attention and RWKV blocks, combining direct access to historical tokens with recurrent temporal modeling. Controlled experiments on GIFT-Eval and TIME-Benchmark show that HART improves over pure RWKV at medium and long horizons while maintaining comparable short-horizon performance, and achieves better aggregate performance than a comparably sized pure Transformer. With 36M parameters, HART achieves long-horizon MASE comparable to Toto-2.0-1B on GIFT-Eval (0.752 vs. 0.754), using approximately 1/28 of its parameters.
papers.summary: Non-autoregressive multi-step forecasting (NAF) lets time series foundation models predict a whole horizon in one forward pass, but `RWKV-7` degrades at long horizons in this setup because future patches are represented as missing inputs and the recurrent state must evolve without new observations. An analysis of the generalized delta rule identifies Placeholder Idling Decay (PID), where repeated state transitions attenuate historical information when placeholder-driven writes do not compensate, supported by layer-wise measurements of reduced state-injection norms. `HART` alternates attention and RWKV blocks so the model retains direct access to historical tokens alongside recurrent modeling, improving over pure RWKV at medium and long horizons on `GIFT-Eval` and `TIME-Benchmark` and beating a comparably sized pure Transformer in aggregate. **With 36M parameters it matches the long-horizon MASE of `Toto-2.0-1B` on `GIFT-Eval` (0.752 vs 0.754) using roughly 1/28 of the parameters.**

papers.title: CoGameReg: Cooperative-Game-Based Collaborative Semi-Supervised Regression for Seismic Reservoir Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of reservoir properties from seismic data remains challenging when well-log labels are sparse but three-dimensional seismic observations are abundant. We present CoGameReg, a cooperative-game-based semi-supervised regression framework that uses contribution-weighted predictions of heterogeneous regressors to construct shared pseudo-labels. This design makes each regressor's influence explicit in the learning targets generated for unlabeled seismic samples under sparse well control. The Tri-Game Shapley mechanism combines a rank-MSE performance game with a pairwise consistency game to estimate nonnegative regressor weights from labeled training data. These weights remain fixed during collaborative training and are reused for final prediction fusion. Candidate pseudo-labels are screened using a common local k-nearest-neighbor error-reduction criterion before retraining. We evaluate CoGameReg on 10 public regression datasets, a synthetic three-dimensional P-wave velocity prediction task, and a field water-saturation application. The benchmark advantage is most pronounced at the 2.5% labeled-data ratio and decreases as supervision increases. CoGameReg obtains the best blind-well metrics in the synthetic experiment. In the field application, predictions clipped to 0-100% yield a pooled coefficient of determination of 0.5942, a root mean square error of 5.7441 percentage points, and a Pearson correlation of 0.8265 across three blind wells. CoGameReg has the highest Pearson correlation among the four field methods. The results support the use of CoGameReg to integrate sparse well labels with dense seismic attributes, with performance varying across metrics and well locations.
papers.summary: Estimating reservoir properties from seismic data is hard when well-log labels are sparse but three-dimensional seismic observations are plentiful. `CoGameReg` is a semi-supervised regression framework in which heterogeneous regressors produce shared pseudo-labels for unlabeled seismic samples, weighted by a Tri-Game Shapley mechanism that combines a rank-MSE performance game with a pairwise consistency game to estimate nonnegative weights from labeled data; candidate pseudo-labels pass a local k-nearest-neighbor error-reduction screen before retraining. On 10 public regression datasets the benefit is largest at a 2.5% labeled-data ratio and shrinks as supervision grows, the method obtains the best blind-well metrics on a synthetic P-wave velocity task, and in a field water-saturation application it achieves **a pooled coefficient of determination of 0.5942 and a Pearson correlation of 0.8265 across three blind wells**, the highest correlation among the four field methods compared.

papers.title: Personalized Federated Direct Preference Optimization via LoRA Adapters
papers.abstract: Federated Direct Preference Optimization (FedDPO) enables privacy-preserving alignment of language models across distributed agents without centralizing sensitive preference data. However, existing FedDPO analysis assumes all clients converge to a single shared policy, which is fundamentally at odds with the heterogeneous preference distributions present in practice. We propose Personalized FedDPO (pFedDPO), in which each client maintains a small private LoRA adapter atop a shared global base model. In pFedDPO, the base model is synchronized via FedAvg each round, while LoRA adapters remain local and capture client-specific preference patterns. We prove that this decomposition replaces the gradient diversity $\kappa^2$ in the FedDPO bound with a residual heterogeneity $\kappa^2_{\mathrm{eff}}$, which is no larger than $\kappa^2$ when adapters absorb client-specific directions, at the cost of an additive adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge. Experiments on preference datasets show that pFedDPO consistently attains a lower gradient norm than vanilla FedDPO while remaining competitive in training loss and per-client reward accuracy.
papers.summary: Federated Direct Preference Optimization (FedDPO) aligns language models across distributed clients without centralizing preference data, but existing analysis assumes every client converges to one shared policy, which conflicts with heterogeneous real-world preferences. `pFedDPO` gives each client a small private LoRA adapter on top of a shared base model: the base is synchronized with FedAvg each round while the adapters stay local to capture client-specific preference patterns. The analysis shows this decomposition **replaces the gradient diversity term in the FedDPO bound with a residual heterogeneity term that is no larger when adapters absorb client-specific directions**, at the cost of an additive adapter-bias term that vanishes as adapters converge. Experiments on preference datasets show consistently lower gradient norms than vanilla FedDPO with competitive training loss and per-client reward accuracy.

papers.title: Generalized Determinantal Point Processes for Attraction and Repulsion with Distinct Interaction Kernels
papers.abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) model subset selection probability with repulsion, but many applications also exhibit attraction arising from pairwise relations or shared latent structures. Nonsymmetric DPPs (NDPPs) capture both effects, but their kernels are difficult to interpret and specify. We propose the determinant-ratio point process (DRPP), which models repulsion and attraction via a ratio of the determinants of two symmetric positive-definite kernels. This formulation preserves the feature-based interpretation of standard DPPs while allowing the two effects to be specified separately. Furthermore, we introduce an auxiliary-variable representation that enables efficient MCMC sampling and yields tractable expectation formulas for key statistics including the normalizing constant, which together facilitate maximum-likelihood learning. We theoretically characterize the interaction structures well suited to DRPPs: for clustered attraction with $C$ latent groups, DRPPs exactly realize the target pairwise interactions with an attraction rank $C$, whereas NDPPs can require a rank that grows with the number of items given the same repulsion component. Conversely, nontransitive pair-specific attraction may require compensation through the DRPP repulsion kernel. Experiments support these predictions, showing that DRPPs fit transitive attraction with substantially fewer parameters than NDPPs.
papers.summary: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) model subset selection with repulsion, and nonsymmetric DPPs (NDPPs) add attraction, but their kernels are hard to interpret and specify. The determinant-ratio point process (`DRPP`) expresses repulsion and attraction as a ratio of determinants of two symmetric positive-definite kernels, preserving the feature-based interpretation of standard DPPs while letting the two effects be set independently, and an auxiliary-variable representation enables efficient MCMC sampling and tractable expectations, including the normalizing constant, for maximum-likelihood learning. Theory shows that **for clustered attraction with C latent groups a DRPP realizes the target pairwise interactions exactly with attraction rank C, whereas an NDPP may need rank growing with the number of items**, while nontransitive pair-specific attraction may require compensation through the repulsion kernel. Experiments confirm that DRPPs fit transitive attraction with substantially fewer parameters than NDPPs.

papers.title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation
papers.abstract: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model. We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information, while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices. Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L token-level states to K << L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively. Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8-16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11. These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder.
papers.summary: In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs) the diffusion prior must encode fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space because latents map almost deterministically to tokens, which makes the joint latent distribution hard to model. Predictive-State Flows (`PSF`) splits generative roles: a sequence is partitioned into blocks, each associated with a predictive state computed only from preceding context, a rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, and a block-causal decoder then generates all blocks in parallel while remaining autoregressive within each block, reducing diffusion from L token-level states to K much smaller than L and sequential depth to L/K. On unconditional `OpenWebText` generation, **a 197M-parameter model with K=8 reaches generative perplexity 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, versus 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for `ELF-B` with 32 steps**, with MAUVE@512 of 0.93 versus 0.73. Controlled comparisons show content states that also encode their own blocks give 8-16% worse perplexity than predictive states, and replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11.

papers.title: GIST: Generator-state-Informed Supervision for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) based on prior-data fitted networks typically use sampled hard query labels, leaving avoidable sampling variability in pretraining. A key observation is that intermediate generator states can reveal label uncertainty beyond a sampled outcome. We propose Generator-state-Informed Supervision for TFMs (GIST), which uses these states to average query losses over conditional label distributions. GIST jointly designs task generation and query supervision, using entropy-calibrated encodings to obtain tractable, input-consistent targets on supported label-dependent branches. We show that this averaging preserves the population objective and yields no larger gradient covariance at fixed parameters within each generating distribution. Under matched pretraining schedules, GIST improves mean rank across three architectures on both TabArena and TALENT without changing architecture or inference. Across these benchmarks and architectures, GIST wins 62.1% of paired dataset-level comparisons against the corresponding hard-label controls.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) built on prior-data fitted networks are pretrained on sampled hard query labels, which injects avoidable sampling variability even though the synthetic generator's intermediate states reveal label uncertainty beyond any single sampled outcome. Generator-state-Informed Supervision (`GIST`) uses those states to average query losses over conditional label distributions, jointly designing task generation and query supervision with entropy-calibrated encodings that yield tractable, input-consistent targets on supported label-dependent branches. The averaging is shown to preserve the population objective and to yield no larger gradient covariance at fixed parameters within each generating distribution. Under matched pretraining schedules it improves mean rank across three architectures on `TabArena` and `TALENT` without changing architecture or inference, **winning 62.1% of paired dataset-level comparisons against hard-label controls**.

papers.title: BLEND: Balancing Personalization vs. Generalization in Federated Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Federated vision-language models (FedVLMs) represent one of the emerging frontiers of machine learning, aiming to integrate federated learning within the fine-tuning pipelines of vision-language models (VLMs). In this work, we introduce BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance the personalization and generalization capabilities of FedVLMs. BLEND proposes a selective VLM parameter fine-tuning and aggregation strategy that consists of (i) global vision and text adapters shared across clients, and (ii) a personalized vision projection adapter tailored to each client. BLEND further introduces a novel loss function that blends the outputs of the global and personalized adapters to achieve personalization, while simultaneously promoting generalization through a principled anchor design implemented via the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BLEND consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting its ability to effectively balance personalization and generalization across diverse system settings. (Code is available at: https://github.com/payamsiabd/BLEND.git)
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning of vision-language models (VLMs) must serve clients with different data while still generalizing beyond any one client. `BLEND` fine-tunes and aggregates a selected subset of VLM parameters: global vision and text adapters shared across clients plus a personalized vision projection adapter per client, together with a loss that blends the outputs of global and personalized adapters for personalization while anchoring to the projection heads of the zero-shot VLM to preserve generalization. **Experiments across diverse federated settings show consistent gains over state-of-the-art federated VLM baselines** on both personalization and generalization, and code is released.

papers.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation are usually post-trained by step-wise imitation of demonstrations, which biases policies toward demonstrated action paths and gives little guidance for recovering once execution deviates. `OGPO` (Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization) relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and builds goal-conditioned process rewards, so the policy is optimized for reaching task-progress states rather than reproducing expert actions, without any online interaction. On `LIBERO` and `MetaWorld` it consistently improves over standard supervised fine-tuning, and **on `LIBERO-Plus` and the newly proposed `LIBERO-ReAct` mid-execution perturbation benchmark it shows stronger robustness and recovery from off-demonstration states** under distribution shift.

papers.title: Controlled-Minimax: Stabilizing Adversarial Optimization via Control Theory
papers.abstract: Minimax optimization is fundamental to adversarial learning yet suffers from severe stability challenges, often manifesting as persistent limit cycles or divergence. This paper investigates these instabilities through the lens of continuous-time dynamical systems. By modeling training dynamics as a second-order Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), we rigorously identify the root cause of non-convergence: the problematic eigenstructure of the loss function's Hessian near equilibrium points. To address this, we introduce Controlled-Minimax, a novel stabilization framework that reformulates the optimization trajectory as a controllable physical system. Unlike heuristic regularization techniques, our approach derives a specific feedback controller that provides theoretical guarantees of local exponential stability, regardless of the underlying Hessian spectrum. Consequently, our method stabilizes general minimax problems where traditional gradient descent-ascent methods fail. Extensive experiments on pathological benchmarks including the Dirac-GAN, 2D Gaussian mixtures, and Swiss Roll datasets, as well as high-resolution image synthesis with StyleGAN2-ada, demonstrate that Controlled-Minimax effectively suppresses oscillatory behavior while ensuring fast and robust convergence.
papers.summary: Minimax optimization in adversarial learning frequently falls into persistent limit cycles or diverges outright. Modeling training dynamics as a second-order ordinary differential equation (ODE) attributes non-convergence to the eigenstructure of the loss Hessian near equilibria, and `Controlled-Minimax` treats the optimization trajectory as a controllable physical system, deriving a feedback controller that **guarantees local exponential stability regardless of the Hessian spectrum**, in contrast to heuristic regularization. Experiments on pathological benchmarks including `Dirac-GAN`, 2D Gaussian mixtures, and `Swiss Roll`, as well as high-resolution image synthesis with `StyleGAN2-ada`, show suppressed oscillation and fast, robust convergence where gradient descent-ascent fails.

papers.title: DeFiRank: Federated Pairwise Ranking for Governance in Decentralized Financial Networks
papers.abstract: Existing governance approaches in decentralized financial networks rely on manual review processes conducted by human committees, which introduces subjective bias, creates a scalability bottleneck under high network volume, and fails to capture complex behavioural patterns and evolving network dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose \name, a federated learning-based pairwise ranking framework in which multiple institutions collaboratively train a ranking model without sharing their private transaction data. This collaborative learning enables the model to capture network-wide behavioural patterns that signify strong network participation and directly contribute to the network effect, including diversity of counterparties, usage of multiple applications, and frequency of transactions. The proposed system ranks providers based on the authenticity of their actions, promoting genuine contributors and demoting those exhibiting suspicious behaviour. We evaluate \name\ on a real-world blockchain transaction dataset. Results demonstrate that the federated approach achieves ranking performance modestly below the centralized baseline (NDCG@15: $\approx$0.87 vs.\ $\approx$0.92) while preserving data privacy and matching its ranking stability (Kendall $\tau$: $\approx$0.70 for both regimes), producing reliable governance decisions, including provider promotion and demotion (648 and 39 unique providers, respectively), without requiring centralized access to sensitive transaction data.
papers.summary: Governance in decentralized financial networks typically depends on manual review by human committees, which is subjective, does not scale with transaction volume, and misses evolving behavioral patterns. `DeFiRank` is a federated pairwise ranking framework in which several institutions jointly train a model over their private transaction data without sharing it, scoring providers on signals of genuine network participation such as counterparty diversity, use of multiple applications, and transaction frequency, then promoting authentic contributors and demoting suspicious ones. On a real blockchain transaction dataset **the federated model reaches NDCG@15 of about 0.87 against roughly 0.92 for a centralized baseline** while matching its ranking stability at a Kendall tau of about 0.70, and it yields concrete decisions promoting 648 and demoting 39 unique providers.

papers.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
papers.abstract:
AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model.
  Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%.
  Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.
papers.summary: AI shopping assistants increasingly decide which products a consumer sees, so a retailer choosing a catalog must account for an intermediary that forms a shortlist before the customer picks under a multinomial logit model. The study considers deterministic mediation, where the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation under the Plackett-Luce (PL) model, estimating PL ranking models from a new dataset of product rankings produced by leading AI models and validating them on held-out assortments. Combined with synthetic customer preferences, **ignoring mediation costs between 2.52% and 11.37% of mean revenue relative to the PL optimum**, while a simpler deterministic plug-in based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities loses at most 0.53%. Assortment optimization under deterministic mediation is then characterized computationally and shown to admit a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for any fixed number of customer segments.

papers.title: Beyond Second-Order Information: Paid Logistic Regression with Noisy Features
papers.abstract: We consider online binary prediction with paid stochastic features, where the learner can spend resources to obtain better observations of the underlying features. This setting is motivated by applications such as medical testing, where additional cost can provide more precise measurements of patient's features for predicting a binary outcome. At each round, a latent feature is drawn i.i.d., the response is generated through a logistic model, and the learner chooses how much to pay before observing a noisy version of the feature. The goal of learner is to jointly control prediction loss and acquisition cost. In contrast to the former result on the online linear regression with paid features, covariance information alone is no longer sufficient: two noise distributions with the same covariance may induce different optimal logistic losses, and lower variance can even lead to higher loss. Under a structural ordering in which larger payments yield better observations by removing independent noise, we obtain $\widetilde O(\sqrt{T})$ regret when the noise structure is known and $\widetilde O(T^{2/3})$ regret when it is unknown, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: In online binary prediction with paid stochastic features, a learner spends resources each round to observe a less noisy version of a latent feature before predicting a logistic outcome, a setting motivated by medical testing where extra cost buys more precise measurements. Unlike the earlier paid linear regression result, covariance alone no longer determines performance: two noise distributions with identical covariance can induce different optimal logistic losses, and lower variance can even increase loss. Under a structural ordering in which larger payments remove independent noise, the analysis gives **regret of order square root of T when the noise structure is known and T to the 2/3 when it is unknown**, with matching lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Teaching neural decoders with language
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces decode neural activity, yet class-label supervision (CLS) leaves relationships among classes implicit. We propose Language as Supervision (LaS), which aligns neural features with natural-language class descriptions through learned projections and predicts classes using candidate text prototypes. We evaluate seven encoder architectures with independently trained models for visual, motor, and speech decoding from scalp and intracranial recordings. LaS improves speech-decoding accuracy by up to 17.15~pp over matched CLS baselines. Its representations support candidate-set reuse and label-supervised subject and session adaptation, while LaS enables conditional unseen-frequency decoding in steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) responses. Correct class-description correspondence supports this generalization, and dual-sided attribution visualization shows neural and textual contributions to the same class-matching score. These findings suggest that text descriptions can serve as general-purpose references for learning and interpretation in neural decoding.
papers.summary: Brain-computer interface decoders trained with class-label supervision (CLS) treat classes as unrelated symbols, leaving the relationships among them implicit. Language as Supervision (`LaS`) aligns neural features with natural-language class descriptions through learned projections and classifies by matching against candidate text prototypes, evaluated across seven encoder architectures on visual, motor, and speech decoding from scalp and intracranial recordings. **Speech-decoding accuracy improves by up to 17.15 percentage points over matched CLS baselines**, the learned representations support candidate-set reuse and subject and session adaptation, and the method enables conditional decoding of unseen frequencies in steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP) responses, with dual-sided attribution showing how neural and textual inputs contribute to the same matching score.

papers.title: Sparse Dictionary Learning for Measure-Valued Data via Linearized Optimal Transport: Efficient Algorithms and Sample Complexity
papers.abstract: We study dictionary learning for probability measure-valued data by embedding measures into Hilbert spaces using features derived from optimal transport geometry. We learn data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations, producing fast, scalable representations of probability measures as sparse finite-dimensional codes. The resulting framework combines the rich, geometric structure of optimal transport with the interpretability and efficiency of sparse representation learning. We demonstrate its utility across diverse data modalities, including hyperspectral images, geometric point clouds, and document embeddings in large language model latent spaces. We also prove generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning objectives on broad classes of $L^2$-valued measure embeddings, expressed in terms of the metric complexity of the atom class. For optimal transport and entropic transport map dictionaries, we derive new covering number bounds that yield explicit rates. Together, our computational and theoretical results support a new, scalable model for representation learning in the space of probability measures via embedding into Hilbert spaces.
papers.summary: Dictionary learning is extended to data whose samples are probability measures by embedding each measure into a Hilbert space using features derived from optimal transport geometry, then learning data-adapted dictionaries through sparse autoencoder parameterizations that yield fast, sparse finite-dimensional codes. The approach is demonstrated on hyperspectral images, geometric point clouds, and document embeddings in large language model latent spaces. On the theoretical side, **generalization bounds for sparse dictionary learning on broad classes of L2-valued measure embeddings are proved in terms of the metric complexity of the atom class**, with new covering number bounds for optimal transport and entropic transport map dictionaries that give explicit rates.

papers.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. To address this limitation, we develop \textit{collaborative learning}, encompassing the construction of heterogeneous collaborators and the learning of effective cross-model collaboration. Specifically, \textit{model slicing} replaces a large model with smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget, enabling prior reasoning to be reassessed across distinct model parameterizations. \textit{Pyramid supervision} combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to refine reasoning and interaction decisions throughout collaboration. We evaluate our approach across four task categories: multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and open-ended constrained generation. The trained heterogeneous models achieve comparable or better task performance than the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based methods, while also achieving higher inference efficiency than the multi-agent baselines and exhibiting differentiated collaboration patterns across tasks. These findings show that learned collaboration turns model heterogeneity into complementary reasoning capabilities.
papers.summary: Single-model chain-of-thought reasoning is prone to error propagation because every step builds on the model's own earlier outputs, leaving blind spots that are hard to reassess independently. The authors propose collaborative learning: `model slicing` replaces one large model with several smaller, heterogeneous models under a comparable parameter budget so that earlier reasoning can be re-examined by differently parameterized models, and `pyramid supervision` combines protocol distillation with step-level supervision to train both the reasoning and the interaction decisions. On multi-hop question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and constrained open-ended generation, **the trained slices match or beat the original large model and established multi-agent baselines, including reinforcement-learning-based ones**, while running more efficiently than those multi-agent baselines and showing task-dependent collaboration patterns.

papers.title: SEEDS: Preview-Guided Evidence Admission for Search Agents
papers.abstract: Search agents extend large reasoning models with multi-round access to external knowledge, yet most existing systems largely conflate retrieving evidence with consuming it. Retrieved documents are commonly incorporated according to fixed or rank-based policies, despite the fact that evidence utility is conditioned on the agent's current reasoning state. Consequently, a lower-ranked candidate may be critical for the current step, while a higher-ranked candidate may provide redundant, irrelevant, or misleading information. We formulate this overlooked problem as evidence admission, which asks, at each search step, which retrieved candidates should be allowed to enter the agent's evolving reasoning context. To enable such selective control, we introduce SEEDS (Selective Evidence Entry During Search), a preview-guided evidence admission framework for search agents. SEEDS first exposes lightweight previews of retrieved candidates and then lets the agent jointly determine which candidates and how many should be fully inspected, conditioned on its current reasoning state. Unlike fixed or adaptive prefix policies, SEEDS can select arbitrary subsets with flexible cardinality, and it can be instantiated directly with an existing reasoning agent or further optimized through learning. Across nine knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks under both local corpus and live web search, SEEDS consistently improves search effectiveness while substantially reducing full-evidence consumption. Experimental analyses show that SEEDS more effectively selects useful candidates beyond the corresponding retrieval prefix. These results establish evidence admission as a complementary dimension of agentic search, separating what information is retrieved from what information is ultimately allowed to shape reasoning.
papers.summary: Search agents usually feed retrieved documents into their context by fixed or rank-based rules, even though a document's usefulness depends on where the agent currently is in its reasoning. The authors frame this as an evidence admission problem and introduce `SEEDS` (Selective Evidence Entry During Search), which shows the agent lightweight previews of retrieved candidates and lets it decide which ones, and how many, to inspect in full given its current reasoning state; the method works with an existing reasoning agent as-is or can be further optimized by training. **Across nine knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks with both local corpora and live web search, `SEEDS` improves search effectiveness while substantially cutting full-evidence consumption**, and analyses show it picks useful candidates that fall outside the top-ranked retrieval prefix.

papers.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? To this end, we propose an uncertainty-guided progressive contraction framework that concentrates supervision and optimization on the reasoning trajectories most valuable for learning. Specifically, rather than treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought (CoT) as a single realized path, we construct uncertainty-profiled reasoning supervision by building Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate reasoning states to expose process-level uncertainty. This uncertainty first contracts the original corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool. A second, learner-aware contraction then performs online routing during SFT, concentrating optimization according to the student's evolving learning state. Together, the two stages progressively contract both supervision and optimization, substantially reducing the student training budget. Experiments across diverse reasoning benchmarks and LLM families show that our method uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data SFT, over 450x less training exposure, while maintaining or improving reasoning performance. Notably, our framework generalizes well across heterogeneous student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong transfer. This indicates that it is not only a way to accelerate training but can also enhance reasoning capability.
papers.summary: Scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora raises cost without proportional gains, so the authors ask how far reasoning supervision can be compressed. Instead of treating a teacher-generated chain-of-thought as a single path, they build Monte Carlo reasoning trees around intermediate states to expose process-level uncertainty, use that uncertainty to contract the corpus into a compact teacher-informed pool, and then route optimization online during supervised fine-tuning according to the student's evolving learning state. Across reasoning benchmarks and model families, the method **uses as little as 0.22% of the optimization budget of full-data supervised fine-tuning, over 450 times less training exposure, while matching or improving reasoning performance**, and it transfers across student families, black-box teachers, and weak-to-strong settings.

papers.title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding based on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured through matrix-entropy analysis, and diversity, quantified using centered kernel alignment (CKA). We investigate layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy under hidden-state concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments within decoder representations. Motivated by these findings, we propose entropy and CKA-based layer selection algorithms that favor hidden-state sets that are both highly informative and minimally redundant. As part of this framework, we introduce token-entropy filtering, which removes hidden states associated with low predictive-entropy tokens, thereby improving the quality of layer-selection statistics. In EAGLE3-style speculative decoding, our selected sets outperform fixed baseline choices, including the default $[2, N//2, N-3]$ rule, while providing a clearer explanation of why some defaults can remain competitive. Our results provide a practical recipe for multi-layer hidden-state selection for speculative decoding, insights into the geometry and information in LLM decoder states, and a foundation for extending similar analysis to related applications.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding drafters such as `EAGLE3` draw on a few target-model hidden layers chosen by fixed position heuristics, even though picking the best subset is a combinatorial problem that cannot be searched exhaustively. The authors score candidate layer sets on two criteria, informativeness measured by matrix entropy and diversity measured by centered kernel alignment (CKA), and study layer-wise entropy, entropy under concatenation, and pairwise CKA dynamics across depth, revealing distinct informational compartments in decoder representations; a token-entropy filter drops hidden states for low-predictive-entropy tokens to clean up the selection statistics. **In `EAGLE3`-style speculative decoding, the entropy- and CKA-selected layer sets outperform fixed defaults, including the standard three-layer rule**, while also explaining why some defaults remain competitive.
papers.highlight_summary:
Speculative decoding drafters such as `EAGLE3` feed on hidden states from a handful of target-model layers chosen by fixed position heuristics, even though picking the best subset is a combinatorial problem that grows infeasible for deep models. The paper replaces the heuristic with a principled selection framework that scores candidate layer sets on two complementary criteria: informativeness, measured with matrix entropy, and diversity, measured with centered kernel alignment (`CKA`).

- The analysis tracks layer-wise Shannon entropy, aggregate entropy when hidden states are concatenated, and pairwise `CKA` dynamics across depth, revealing distinct geometric and informational compartments inside the decoder representations.
- Building on these findings, the entropy and `CKA`-based selection algorithms favor layer sets that are highly informative yet minimally redundant, and a token-entropy filter discards hidden states tied to low predictive-entropy tokens so the selection statistics are computed on more discriminative positions.
- In `EAGLE3`-style speculative decoding, the **selected layer sets outperform fixed baselines, including the default `[2, N//2, N-3]` rule** (with N the number of decoder layers), while the entropy and `CKA` profiles also explain why that default remains competitive.
- The abstract reports no quantitative speedups, acceptance lengths, or model sizes, and the evaluation is confined to a single `EAGLE3`-style setup, so the practical margin over the default rule and its transfer to other speculative-decoding architectures remain to be shown.

papers.title: From Imbalance to Evidence: Deep Nonparametric Testing for Complex Data under Severe Sample Imbalance
papers.abstract: Comparing distributions under severe sample imbalance requires effectively using abundant majority observations while retaining sensitivity to differences involving the smaller sample. This challenge is particularly relevant for complex, non-Euclidean data, such as graphs, whose structural characteristics call for flexible testing procedures. Classifier two-sample tests (C2STs) provide such flexibility, but existing procedures are primarily designed for balanced or comparably sized samples. In this paper, we study C2STs in a highly imbalanced regime, and show that severe sample imbalance may substantially degrade testing performance. Different from conventional imbalanced learning approaches that treat sample imbalance merely as a nuisance for classifier training, we turn it into a source of repeated testing evidence. Building on this insight, we propose an Enhanced Imbalance-Aware Deep Classifier Two-Sample Test (EIAD-C2ST), a classifier-agnostic framework designed for sample imbalance that accommodates diverse data modalities by tailoring classifiers to data structure. For computationally expensive deep classifiers, we further develop a scalable representation-amortized implementation strategy. Theoretically, we establish rigorous guarantees on asymptotic size and characterize conditions for power consistency, allowing the imbalance ratio to diverge. We demonstrate the empirical gains using simulations and an application to blockchain forensics. The results reveal that the majority-sample surplus, when properly leveraged, can be organized into useful statistical evidence, rather than an obstacle, for distributional comparisons with complex data.
papers.summary: Classifier two-sample tests (C2STs) offer a flexible way to compare distributions of complex, non-Euclidean data such as graphs, but existing procedures assume balanced or comparably sized samples, and the authors show that severe imbalance can substantially degrade their performance. Rather than treating the surplus majority sample as a nuisance for classifier training, they organize it into repeated testing evidence through `EIAD-C2ST`, an Enhanced Imbalance-Aware Deep Classifier Two-Sample Test that is classifier-agnostic, adapts the classifier to the data modality, and includes a representation-amortized variant for costly deep classifiers. **The method comes with guarantees on asymptotic size and conditions for power consistency even as the imbalance ratio diverges**, and simulations plus a blockchain forensics application show empirical gains.

papers.title: MathVis: Can AI Reason through Drawing? A Benchmark for Mathematical Figure Generation
papers.abstract: This paper introduces MathVis, a benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' ability to visualize frontier mathematical problems and perform diagram-assisted reasoning. The benchmark consists of 512 tasks, each comprising a mathematical statement, a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a Gold Intermediate Representation (IR), atomic rubrics, and error codes. Through rigorous evaluation, GPT-6-Astra, Claude Fable 5, and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%, respectively. We found that although the tasks require visualization, LLMs produce outputs dominated by formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs, rather than explicit diagram-mediated reasoning. Furthermore, while the solutions generated by LLMs may contain all the necessary elements, they are often visually confusing to humans. Ultimately, this benchmark aims to visualize mathematical problems and promote research on enabling LLMs to simplify their reasoning via visual diagrams.
papers.summary: `MathVis` tests whether large language models can draw figures for frontier mathematical problems and reason with them, using 512 tasks that each pair a statement with a reference diagram, executable TikZ or SVG code, a gold intermediate representation, atomic rubrics, and error codes. **`GPT-6-Astra`, `Claude Fable 5`, and `Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview` reach pass@1 scores of 31.25%, 26.56%, and 22.85%**. The models tend to answer in formal languages, symbols, and graphics programs rather than reasoning explicitly through diagrams, and even solutions that contain all the required elements are often visually confusing to humans.

papers.title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
papers.summary: Embodied agents on robots and smart hardware must turn multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while respecting product constraints, revised goals, and execution feedback. `JoyInside-VLM-Agent` is a ReAct-style multimodal agent trained on trajectories from a closed-loop sandbox that covers goal revisions and failure recovery, followed by supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and reinforcement learning with `DPER` (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing), which routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student that shares the rollout policy's weights. **It scores 77.44 overall on `BFCL v4`, above the evaluated baselines**, though results on other public benchmarks are mixed; on the `JoyInside-Devices` and `JoyInside-Robotics` suites it leads on all reported metrics, and two real-world quadruped case studies show visually grounded search, replanning after failure, and explicit failure reporting.

papers.title: DataCupid: Stable Matching Repair for Training Data Acquisition with Delayed Feedback
papers.abstract: Matching repair after utility changes can reuse valid observations, but new evaluations must respect matching capacity and may return out of order. We study announced invalidations with bounded, possibly reward-dependent reporting delays and pending evaluations that do not occupy future matching capacity. Residualload repair (RLR) combines sound outcome certificates with batched matching schedules for unequal sample deficits. Its complete dyadic quota schedule admits a sharp issue-round bound with coefficient cb < 1.607 relative to the terminal residual endpoint load, together with separate delay and evidence-lifetime bounds. RLR-P monitors complete issue-order prefixes without changing the sampling plan before acceptance. With a deterministic pure oracle, a single-repair coupling from the same drained initial state guarantees no increase in certification time, issued observations, or time to a reusable checkpoint. We also derive an information-load lower bound. On fixed priority-star markets with unknown Bernoulli gaps, PrioritySearch attains the history-adjusted first-order constant for expected certification time as {\delta} {\sim} 0, under hypothesis-independent linear history scaling and sublogarithmic reporting delays. Paired simulations and measured-feedback replay quantify the trade-offs: in the replay, RLR-P has lower mean capped update-certification time than a monitored width-based baseline, at higher oracle CPU cost.
papers.summary: When the utility of candidate training data changes, a system that acquires data through capacity-limited matching would like to reuse evaluations that remain valid rather than restart, but new evaluations must respect matching capacity and may return out of order with bounded, possibly reward-dependent delays. The authors propose residual-load repair (`RLR`), which pairs sound outcome certificates with batched matching schedules for unequal sample deficits, plus a prefix-monitoring variant `RLR-P` and a `PrioritySearch` procedure for priority-star markets with unknown Bernoulli gaps. **The dyadic quota schedule admits an issue-round bound with coefficient below 1.607 relative to the terminal residual load**, a single-repair coupling with a deterministic pure oracle guarantees no increase in certification time or issued observations, and in measured-feedback replay `RLR-P` achieves lower mean capped update-certification time than a width-based baseline at higher oracle CPU cost.

papers.title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph
papers.abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. Although such evidence commonly resides in source-specific graphs, temporal snapshots, or local observations, existing graph reasoning benchmarks remain confined to a single self-contained structure, assessing only graph perception and reasoning while leaving the alignment and composition of evidence across views underexplored. MVGraph comprises 8k instances spanning 8 \textit{graph-theoretic} tasks, abstracted from two multi-graph scenarios (partial and temporal graph views). Each problem is programmatically constructed and verified to be unsolvable from a single view. Beyond end-to-end evaluation, we decompose multi-graph reasoning into four complementary capabilities---Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning---and design 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances to probe each one, along with golden intermediate representations for evaluating the intermediate process. Across 15 LVLMs, we reveal the difficulty of multi-graph reasoning and identify cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition as prominent bottlenecks through stage-oriented diagnostics. Meanwhile, temporal constraints and increasing view counts expose further capability boundaries. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AAAndy-Zhu/MVGraph.
papers.summary: Existing graph reasoning benchmarks for large vision-language models (LVLMs) present a single self-contained graph, so they never test whether a model can align and compose evidence spread across several related views such as partial observations or temporal snapshots. `MVGraph` contains 8k programmatically constructed instances over 8 graph-theoretic tasks, each verified to be unsolvable from any single view, and adds 29 diagnostic tasks with 64k instances that separately probe Perception, Alignment, Composition, and Reasoning, with golden intermediate representations for checking the intermediate process. **Across 15 LVLMs, cross-view edge alignment and relation-level composition emerge as the main bottlenecks**, and temporal constraints and higher view counts expose further capability limits.

papers.title: MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing
papers.abstract: Video editing models achieve strong performance in modifying appearance, backgrounds, styles, and motions, empowered by large-scale training data. Beyond general scenarios, professional motions are significant in performance, sports, and martial arts. This paper focuses on professional motion editing, which involves fine-grained motion technique and temporal structure. Given professional motion names but lacking detailed descriptions, existing models often fail to generate professional motions, such as incorrectly lifting the front wheel under a Stoppie instruction. To address this challenge, we introduce MotionCoach, a trained multimodal agent that uses multi-turn tools and performs self-verification, producing a grounded prompt and a reference clip as reliable and sufficient multimodal guidance to inject external professional motion knowledge into video editing models. To supply training data, we build a data pipeline to construct trajectories. We cold-start the agent on MotionCoach-SFT-10k and apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on MotionCoach-RL-2k with rewards on the motion guidance prompt, the motion outcome video, and the format. For evaluation, we introduce VPMEBench, comprising 314 professional motion editing tasks with fine-grained references and annotations. Extensive experiments show that MotionCoach improves the overall score from 55.1 to 65.6 on Seedance 2.0 and from 51.2 to 64.5 on MiniMax-H3. Learning to construct multimodal guidance enables precise professional motion editing without retraining video editing models.
papers.summary: Video editing models handle appearance, style, and generic motion well but often fail on professional motions from sports, performance, and martial arts when given only a motion name, such as lifting the wrong wheel for a Stoppie. `MotionCoach` is a multimodal agent that uses multi-turn tools and self-verification to produce a grounded prompt and a reference clip as guidance for an unchanged video editing model; it is cold-started on `MotionCoach-SFT-10k` and then trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on `MotionCoach-RL-2k` using rewards on the guidance prompt, the output video, and the format. On the new `VPMEBench` of 314 professional motion editing tasks, **the agent raises the overall score from 55.1 to 65.6 on `Seedance 2.0` and from 51.2 to 64.5 on `MiniMax-H3`** without retraining either editor.

papers.title: Minions: A Dynamic and Distributed Virtual GPU Cloud Built on Idle Apple Silicon Devices
papers.abstract: The increasing demand for GPU-accelerated machine learning inference has exposed limitations in centralized GPU infrastructures, including high cost, limited elasticity, and long wait times under resource constraints. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon-based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.
papers.summary: Centralized GPU clusters for machine learning inference are expensive, inelastic, and prone to long queues, while the GPUs in Apple Silicon Macs sit mostly idle during everyday use. `Minions` is a dynamic, distributed virtual GPU cloud that pools idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to run large-scale inference workloads, providing flexible task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization so teams can use hardware they already own instead of buying more. **The authors report that idle macOS devices can be turned into a practical distributed inference platform** in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained.

papers.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
papers.abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).
papers.summary: Task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion, which says little about how large language model (LLM) sales agents cope with buyers who push back. `SmartSalesBench` pits agents against twelve psychologically grounded resistant buyer personas in conversations of up to twenty turns, spanning five agent profiles, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments totaling 13,680 sessions, with both agent and buyer generations grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It defines nine metrics in three tiers, primary outcome metrics `CR`, `BRS`, and `RIR`, secondary quality metrics, and exploratory metrics reserved for future reporting, scored by an LLM judge; **a human assessment with n = 50 reached kappa 0.71 and a Pearson correlation of 0.81 with `BRS`**.

papers.title: Diffusion Precipitation Generation with Medium-range Weather Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate daily precipitation forecasts are important for weather-sensitive decisions. Although recent Weather Foundation Models (WFMs) have achieved significant progress, they are trained on reanalysis data, which exhibit regional and intensity-dependent biases. Since retraining WFMs on observation-based targets is costly, we study Dynamics-Precipitation Decoupling, a plug-and-play framework that uses a separately trained generator to map non-precipitation forecasts from a frozen weather model to observation-aligned daily precipitation. Its key challenges are to capture heterogeneous rainfall distributions and align daily accumulations with atmospheric signals that evolve across space and time. To address them, we train a diffusion generator conditional on atmospheric states and satellite-gauge estimates of precipitation. A multi-scale recurrent encoder summarizes atmospheric evolution, while cross-attention aligns atmospheric and precipitation features during denoising. Extensive evaluation of various backbones, including Pangu-Weather, GraphCast, and HRES, on global and regional forecasting shows improved daily precipitation accuracy and event detection, with better representation of localized accumulation patterns. Global ensemble evaluation shows lower Brier scores than ENS and training-from-scratch GenCast at all reported lead times, with lower CRPS in most comparisons. Remarkably, a heavy-rainfall case study using 2,288 stations in China further supports improved daily accumulation patterns and event detection against ground observations.
papers.summary: Weather foundation models are trained on reanalysis data whose precipitation carries regional and intensity-dependent biases, and retraining them on observation-based targets is costly. The authors instead study Dynamics-Precipitation Decoupling, a plug-and-play setup in which a separately trained diffusion generator maps the non-precipitation forecasts of a frozen weather model to observation-aligned daily precipitation, conditioning on atmospheric states and satellite-gauge precipitation estimates with a multi-scale recurrent encoder and cross-attention during denoising. Applied to `Pangu-Weather`, `GraphCast`, and `HRES`, it improves daily precipitation accuracy and event detection, and **in global ensemble evaluation it achieves lower Brier scores than `ENS` and a from-scratch `GenCast` at every reported lead time**, with a heavy-rainfall case study over 2,288 stations in China confirming better accumulation patterns.

papers.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) of social media platforms commonly retrieves items by autoregressively decoding discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) with finite-width beam search. This work examines how this output interface constrains whether held-out targets enter finite returned lists, while distinguishing catalog-wide scoreability from empirical top-K support. We introduce two continuous-query paradigms: CQG-Single generates one retrieval query in a single pass, and CQG-AR autoregressively generates continuous residual updates, retaining step-wise decoding while removing the SID item-token vocabulary, code lookup, and discrete beam expansion. These designs thereby eliminate the SID-specific reachability constraint induced by finite-beam decoding and avoid the technical challenge of aligning a discrete SID vocabulary with the pretrained backbone's vector space. Both methods make every encoded item directly scoreable through dense or approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Under a unified protocol with valid-prefix constrained decoding, CQG-Single exceeds the TIGER-style baseline in all seven runs while using 55.3% as many trainable parameters. CQG-AR remains comparable on ML-1M and is numerically stronger on Beauty and Sports datasets. A controlled depth ablation further shows that additional continuous refinement does not monotonically improve shallow accuracy. These findings motivate decoupling output representation, autoregressive modeling, and retrieval budget when evaluating generative recommendation systems.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders on social platforms retrieve items by autoregressively decoding discrete Semantic IDs (SIDs) with finite-width beam search, which limits whether a held-out target can ever appear in the returned list even when it is scoreable catalog-wide. The authors propose two continuous-query alternatives: `CQG-Single` generates one retrieval query in a single pass, and `CQG-AR` autoregressively generates continuous residual updates, keeping step-wise decoding while dropping the SID vocabulary, code lookup, and beam expansion so every encoded item can be scored by dense or approximate-nearest-neighbor retrieval. Under a unified protocol with valid-prefix constrained decoding, **`CQG-Single` beats the `TIGER`-style baseline in all seven runs with 55.3% as many trainable parameters**, `CQG-AR` is comparable on `ML-1M` and stronger on `Beauty` and `Sports`, and a depth ablation shows extra continuous refinement does not monotonically help shallow accuracy.

papers.title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Visual interventions provide a training-free way to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models. However, an intervention may have little leverage at some layers and may damage a correct answer even when it changes the output. We investigate where visual interventions retain leverage and when they improve predictions. First, we apply the same visual-residual edit at successive decoder layers, matching its RMS strength across depth. Across six checkpoints from three model families, we observe a persistent drop in intervention effect and define its operational onset for this edit as the \textbf{Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB)}. With boundaries fixed on calibration queries, held-out effects on disjoint evaluation queries before EAB are $13.78\times$--$26.10\times$ larger than those after it. Comparison with intermediate readouts shows that the edit can lose leverage before answer preferences stabilize. Second, we compare counterfactual subtraction across presence, attribute, and relation questions. Subtraction can correct a misleading preference, leave a decision unchanged, or remove a preference supporting the correct answer. Based on these observations, we develop calibrated selective routing, which preserves the original prediction unless calibration supports an intervention for the question type. It improves full-set attribute accuracy by $1.56$--$1.81$ percentage points across three checkpoints, while universal subtraction is neutral or harmful.
papers.summary: Visual interventions can reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models without training, but their leverage varies by layer and they can overturn answers that were already correct. Applying the same visual-residual edit at successive decoder layers with matched strength across six checkpoints from three model families, the authors find a persistent drop in effect and name its onset the Evidence Anchoring Boundary (EAB); **with boundaries fixed on calibration queries, held-out intervention effects before the EAB are 13.78 to 26.10 times larger than after it**, and the edit can lose leverage before answer preferences have stabilized. Counterfactual subtraction across presence, attribute, and relation questions can fix a misleading preference, change nothing, or remove support for the right answer, so they propose calibrated selective routing that keeps the original prediction unless calibration supports intervening for that question type, which improves attribute accuracy by 1.56 to 1.81 points where universal subtraction is neutral or harmful.

papers.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction
papers.abstract: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.
papers.summary: Computer-use agents still struggle with unfamiliar software and workflows that require human domain knowledge, and although human demonstrations convey that knowledge through the same GUI, reusing them means interpreting actions in context and separating general workflow rules from task-specific details. `Work2Skill` provides `WorkRecorder`, which aligns screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and accessibility-tree data, and uses it to build `WorkDemo-350`, a synchronized multimodal dataset of 350 screened human desktop demonstrations; an agentic skill-induction method then inspects this evidence on demand to write reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. With four execution models equipped with induced skills under shared settings, `Work2Skill` scores highest, **raising mean scores over a no-skill baseline by 4.67 to 10.54 points on `MyPCBench` Bounded Action and 3.11 to 7.50 points on a 286-task subset of `OSWorld-Verified`**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Computer-use agents handle increasingly complex tasks but still fail on unfamiliar software and organization-specific workflows whose procedures are not spelled out in the request. The core idea is to record human demonstrations with aligned screen video, input events, and accessibility-tree evidence, then let a tool-using agent inspect that evidence on demand and write reusable text skills that an executor can follow without ever seeing the recording.

- `WorkRecorder` groups timestamped mouse and keyboard events into actions, links each to keyframes and video intervals, and attaches accessibility-tree names, roles, and bounds for click targets, so an induction agent can read what a control means rather than infer it from pixel coordinates.
