papers.summary: E-commerce ad creatives are now optimized for click-through rate (CTR) rather than aesthetics, but reinforcement-learning methods that regenerate images from scratch penalize every attribute of an underperforming image, including the ones that help. `ECC` reframes the task as fine-grained editing, using ANOVA and random-forest regression to isolate 28 attributes correlated with CTR, then instruction-tuning a prompt model on attribute contrasts between high- and low-CTR images and refining it on real click preferences. Consistent Preference Optimization enforces agreement across semantically equivalent shuffled suggestions to curb Direct Preference Optimization (`DPO`) overfitting. The approach **improves ad-image click-through rate over state-of-the-art generators by a substantial margin**.

papers.title: Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
papers.abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
papers.summary: Extending context length does not guarantee distant information stays usable, since a fixed-size memory must hold many associations, link them across positions, and avoid being swamped by everything it sees. Studying large-chunk test-time training, the authors trace two failures: single-step writes accumulate interference and cap capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. `Double-Take` adds multi-step unpinned updates, cross-position mixing, and bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves recall at the 0.10 chance floor, **adding binding lifts it to 0.92**, and a model trained only on 32 kb genomic contexts reaches 0.927 AUROC at 131 kb and 0.856 near 1 Mb while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse.

papers.title: LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
papers.abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.
papers.summary: Agents reasoning over document collections far larger than their context window tend to tangle acquired evidence with evolving conclusions inside a growing interaction history, producing unbounded exploration and conclusions that drift from the evidence. `LongHarness` makes that interaction explicit through Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, where unresolved conclusions steer retrieval toward missing information and newly acquired evidence revises the conclusions that directed the search, paired with lifecycle management that keeps stored evidence current and traceable. On `OfficeQA Pro` it lifts `GLM-5.3-Flash` exact match **from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2** against direct reasoning with the same backbone. It also beats existing agent harnesses, by 12.0 points over `Claude Code` on V1 and 18.9 points over `Codex` on V2.

papers.title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.
papers.summary: Jailbreaks and over-refusals both hint that recognizing a harmful request and actually writing a refusal are separate computations. Measuring residual-stream updates across 18 base-and-instruct pairs from `Qwen`, `Llama`, and `Gemma`, the authors find harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, especially in early layers, while **multilayer perceptron (MLP) updates do most of the harm-selective refusal writing**, and post-training strengthens that writing in all 18 pairs without making harmfulness more decodable. Causal intervention supports the pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to clean values largely cancels the refusal shift caused by upstream attention edits. The resulting `Sentinel` method pairs an attention-derived perception score with an MLP-derived decision score, and routing on both signals yields lower aggregate error than single-signal routing across eight models.

papers.title: SWEAR: Section-Wise Efficient Audio Reasoning via Self-Rated Difficulty
papers.abstract: Recent work on large audio-language models (LALMs) explores adaptive reasoning to balance accuracy and efficiency. However, existing approaches often rely on coarse-grained difficulty estimation, overlooking the diverse factors that determine reasoning effort. We address this limitation by deriving five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments. Based on this characterization, we propose SWEAR, a difficulty-aware reasoning framework that learns difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning and uses reinforcement learning to adapt reasoning allocation across reasoning stages. Experiments on MMAU-test-mini and MMAR show that SWEAR improves accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens, shortening reasoning for easy instances without sacrificing performance on difficult ones.
papers.summary: Adaptive reasoning in large audio-language models (LALMs) has leaned on coarse difficulty estimates that ignore the varied reasons a question takes effort. `SWEAR` derives five-dimensional difficulty scores and compressed reasoning traces from complementary offline assessments, learns those difficulty signals during supervised fine-tuning, and then uses reinforcement learning to allocate reasoning effort across stages. On `MMAU-test-mini` and `MMAR` it **raises accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens**, shortening reasoning on easy instances without hurting hard ones.

papers.title: Human and LLM Facilitation in Collaborative Design Meetings: A Computational Behavioral Comparison
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as facilitators of group discussion and collaborative work, but the behavioral differences between LLM-generated and human facilitation remain insufficiently characterized. We compare human Project Manager facilitation turns from scenario-based collaborative design meetings with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct responses across 199 paired contexts from the AMI Meeting Corpus. The analysis covers five confirmatory dimensions: contextual semantic distance, a lexical elaboration proxy, empathyand-hedge lexical density, topic divergence, and phase-vocabulary alignment. An exploratory directiveness measure failed domain validation and is not interpreted. The sampled human Project Manager turns were higher on contextual semantic distance (r = 0.644) and on empathyand-hedge lexical density (r = 0.203). The second contrast is carried mainly by hedge terms, so we read it as lexical hedging rather than psychological empathy. Llama-generated facilitation was higher on topic divergence (r = 0.703), the lexical elaboration proxy (r = 0.288; lengthconfounded), and instruction-conditioned phase-vocabulary alignment (r = 0.382). A secondary no-phase check left the Llama-higher phase contrast in place. The system prompt still requested a facilitation move, so that check is not evidence of spontaneous phase awareness. These differences should not be interpreted as a ranking of facilitation quality. The resulting behavioral profile provides a reference point for later comparisons of LLM facilitators, human facilitators, prompts, models, and collaborative settings.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly proposed as facilitators of group discussion, yet how their contributions differ behaviorally from a human facilitator's is poorly characterized. Pairing 199 human project-manager turns from the `AMI Meeting Corpus` with `Llama 3.1 8B Instruct` responses to the same contexts, the study compares five confirmatory measures. Humans scored higher on contextual semantic distance and on empathy-and-hedge lexical density, a gap carried mainly by hedge words rather than empathy, while **the model scored higher on topic divergence, lexical elaboration, and phase-vocabulary alignment**. The authors stress these are not quality rankings, and that an exploratory directiveness measure failed domain validation and is left uninterpreted.

papers.title: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
papers.abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.
papers.summary: A provider facing distillation campaigns spread across thousands of ordinary-looking accounts may have nothing to work from but the queries themselves. Using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later untouched weeks as a single frozen evaluation, the study argues the detection ceiling is set by benign coordination rather than anything specific to extraction: a campaign is visible only when it looks more distinctive than the most distinctive group of normal users that week. A calibrated cross-account monitor flags coordinated activity that per-account monitors miss in most evaluation weeks, and **campaigns that evaded every detector tested produced student models retaining at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one's**. The authors are equally explicit about the gaps, including no deployable detector at low colluder shares and benign evaluation pipelines that look indistinguishable from distillation.

papers.title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. In this paper, we investigate this efficiency transfer across five agents in two representative application settings, embodied tasks in ALFWorld and mobile app use in AndroidWorld. Across 4,500 task executions, we jointly evaluate task effectiveness, decision-level and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Experimental results show that Jev integration substantially reduces decision cost and latency across all five agents, with task-level gains varying by workflow. Task success remains close to baseline levels on ALFWorld and declines more substantially in two mobile agents. Auxiliary reasoning and additional interactions absorb decision savings, while failed recovery and premature completion limit successful delivery. Mean cost per successful outcome increases in one agent even as spending per attempt falls. These findings highlight the importance of preserving progress, supporting recovery, and verifying completion when integrating efficient decision models into agent workflows. Their practical value should be assessed through successful task delivery, recovery behavior, and resources per delivered outcome.
papers.summary: Agents make many model calls per task, so a faster and cheaper decision model such as `Jev` promises large savings, but whether per-decision savings become efficient task completion is untested. Across five agents in two settings, embodied tasks in `ALFWorld` and mobile app use in `AndroidWorld`, spanning 4,500 task executions, the authors jointly measure task effectiveness, decision- and task-level resource use, and execution behavior. Decision cost and latency fall for every agent, yet **task success declines substantially in two mobile agents and mean cost per successful outcome rises in one agent even as spending per attempt falls**. Auxiliary reasoning and extra environment interactions absorb the savings, while failed recovery and premature completion eat into delivered results.

papers.title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
papers.abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.
papers.summary: Visual agents that treat scenes as executable programs improve slowly because the final render is ambiguous supervision, and existing refinement loops ignore which proposed symbolic edits survived, vanished, or interfered during execution. `VETR` keeps aligned program-and-render records with bounded runtime observations and adds an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs, validating their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state before an ordinary visual verifier judges goal relevance. **Repair construction requires no additional language-model calls**, only extra executions. On `BlenderGym` (280 tasks) and `BlenderBench` (27 tasks) with `GPT-5.6-luna` and `Qwen3.8-27B`, it beats refinement baselines including `BlenderAlchemy` and `VIGA`.

papers.title: From 2.1M Hours of Raw Broadcast Audio to Finnish Speech SSL: Confidence Filtering and Architectural Analysis at Scale
papers.abstract: Broadcast archives offer scale and diversity for self-supervised learning (SSL) but contain substantial noisy, non-speech, and multilingual content. Prior work typically relies on voice activity detection or language identification (LID) to extract speech, ensuring presence rather than quality. Whether and how to filter unlabeled speech by quality for SSL, particularly from noisy broadcasts, remains underexplored. We present a large-scale Finnish SSL study starting from 2.1M hours of unconstrained broadcast audio. We propose automatic speech recognition (ASR) confidence as a proxy for pretraining data quality and show 3-7% relative WER improvements over LID-based filtering despite a smaller training set. We further address the lack of controlled architectural comparisons in speech SSL by evaluating Transformer, Macaron-Net, Conformer, and E-Branchformer at matched parameter budgets. Our models improve upon prior Finnish SSL baselines, particularly at Base scale and out-of-domain.
papers.summary: Broadcast archives are an attractive source of data for self-supervised learning (SSL) in speech but are full of noise, non-speech, and multiple languages, and the usual voice-activity or language-identification filters confirm that speech is present without judging its quality. Starting from 2.1 million hours of unconstrained Finnish broadcast audio, the authors use automatic speech recognition confidence as a proxy for pretraining data quality and report **3-7% relative word-error-rate improvements over language-identification filtering despite a smaller training set**. A matched-parameter comparison of `Transformer`, `Macaron-Net`, `Conformer`, and `E-Branchformer` accompanies the data study, with the resulting models improving on earlier Finnish baselines especially at base scale and out of domain.

papers.title: Can Failed Trajectories Reveal Where Agents Go Wrong? Agentic Failure Attribution Without Step-Level Labels
papers.abstract: Failure attribution for LLM agents aims to identify decisive steps responsible for task failure, which is critical for debugging and improving agentic systems. Existing methods rely on costly LLM prompting, step-level error annotations, or verified successful trajectories that lack failure signals for assistance. In this paper, we study failure attribution from step-unlabeled failure trajectories, where each trajectory is known to have failed but its decisive step is unknown. We propose SOAP (Spectral scOring with Attention-guided Propagation), an effective framework requiring neither step-level training labels nor a separate success-only reference set. SOAP first constructs a spectral reference space from LLM representations and assigns each step a base error score according to its projection behavior. Importantly, later steps may exhibit stronger failure signals because they inherit an earlier mistake, causing independent scorers to favor downstream consequences over the decisive error. To address this downstream contamination, SOAP derives soft step dependencies from attention patterns and propagates downstream error evidence toward its likely upstream sources. Extensive experiments show that SOAP consistently improves attribution performance over competitive baselines.
papers.summary: Pinpointing the decisive step that doomed a failed agent trajectory normally needs expensive language-model prompting, step-level error annotations, or a reference set of verified successes. `SOAP` works from trajectories known only to have failed, building a spectral reference space from model representations and scoring each step by its projection behavior. Because later steps inherit earlier mistakes, independent scorers tend to blame downstream consequences, so `SOAP` derives soft step dependencies from attention patterns and **propagates downstream error evidence back toward its likely upstream source**, which improves attribution over competitive baselines.

papers.title: Scaling RNA Foundation Models through Iterative Refinement
papers.abstract: Biological function in RNA is encoded across scales, from local sequence motifs to long-range structural dependencies. Conventional RNA foundation models couple parameter capacity and inference depth within a fixed architecture, prescribing a fixed computation graph for each inference. Here we present Eco-RNA, an 80M-parameter RNA foundation model that makes inference depth adjustable through learned iterative refinement. Its shared, input-conditioned Transformer core refines sequence representations through repeated application. The iteration count is selected after training and controls effective depth at fixed model parameters. We train across recurrent depths with masked reconstruction, state regularization, and a one-sided loss that anchors deeper reconstruction to a shallow reference. On the 70-assay RNAGym fitness benchmark, increasing refinement from one to four iterations raises aggregate absolute Spearman correlation from 0.242 to 0.286, with the gain retained through eight iterations. At four iterations, Eco-RNA surpasses the current SOTA Evo 2 40B on all three aggregate fitness metrics despite 500x fewer parameters. Its iteration configurations advance the compute-performance Pareto frontier among the evaluated models. It also outperforms the evaluated baselines in non-coding RNA family classification, RNA secondary-structure prediction, and chemical probing profile prediction. These results establish internal inference computation as an effective scaling dimension for RNA foundation models.
papers.summary: RNA foundation models normally couple parameter capacity with inference depth, prescribing one fixed computation graph per input. `Eco-RNA` is an 80-million-parameter model whose shared, input-conditioned Transformer core is applied repeatedly, so effective depth is chosen after training by setting an iteration count, trained with masked reconstruction, state regularization, and a one-sided loss anchoring deeper reconstructions to a shallow reference. On the 70-assay `RNAGym` fitness benchmark, going from one to four refinement passes raises aggregate absolute Spearman correlation from 0.242 to 0.286, and at four passes the model **surpasses `Evo 2` 40B on all three aggregate fitness metrics with roughly 500 times fewer parameters**. It also leads the evaluated baselines on non-coding RNA family classification, secondary-structure prediction, and chemical probing profiles.

papers.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) frequently exhibit object hallucination, affirming absent sounds. The dominant mitigation, Audio-Aware Decoding (AAD), contrasts logits under real audio against an all-zero "blank" waveform, flagged by prior review as out-of-distribution. We introduce a black-box causal test that isolates the claimed evidence itself: localize a claim's evidence region via CLAP similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three LALMs. On Qwen2-Audio-7B, localized ablation's raw AUROC trails blank's (0.613 vs. 0.721); this is a duration confound, not a localization failure, since blank removes the entire clip versus the grid's 2-4 s. Holding duration fixed, localization beats random removal at every cell on both models. Raw detection value remains model-dependent, especially on Audio Flamingo 3. The same evidence corrects decoding: contrastive decoding combining blank and language-prior contrasts, gated and ensembled, raises Qwen2-Audio accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%, beating AAD alone. A unified causal-grounding profile does not transfer between models, indicating different grounding regimes. The source code and a detailed report of our findings, including identified limitations, are available at https://github.com/khalooei/causa.
papers.summary: Large audio-language models often affirm sounds that are not present, and the dominant fix, Audio-Aware Decoding (`AAD`), contrasts logits against an all-zero waveform that reviewers have flagged as out of distribution. This audit tests the claimed evidence directly instead: locate a claim's evidence region by `CLAP` similarity, remove it by spectral gating, and compare against a random-window control across a 2x2x2 grid on three models. Raw detection favors the blank baseline on `Qwen2-Audio-7B` (0.613 against 0.721 AUROC), but that reflects a duration confound, since blanking removes the whole clip against a 2-4 second window; holding duration fixed, localized removal beats random removal in every cell on two models. Applying the same evidence to decoding, a gated ensemble of blank and language-prior contrasts **lifts `Qwen2-Audio` accuracy from 57.1% to 71.9%**, and the grounding profile does not transfer between models.

papers.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation
papers.abstract: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.
papers.summary: Continual post-training must add capabilities without erasing old ones, and Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (`SDFT`) handles this by having the model rewrite its own training data, which fails on the small models that matter for low-latency on-device use because they lack the required in-context learning and instruction following. The authors show poor acquisition and forgetting both correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, pointing to in-distribution supervision as the real requirement. `SynthSelf` therefore outsources the rewrite to a **minimally larger model from the same family**, combined with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, keeping supervision quality high without pushing the small model off its own distribution. Across four acquisition datasets, 14 retention benchmarks, and three small model scales it beats six methods including off-policy and on-policy distillation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Continual post-training must teach a model new capabilities without erasing old ones, and `SDFT` (self-distillation fine-tuning) does this by having the model rewrite demonstrations in its own distribution, but it fails on small models whose in-context learning and instruction following are too weak to produce usable self-rewrites. `SynthSelf` keeps the in-distribution rewrite but outsources it to a minimally larger same-family aligner, filters the rewrites by answer match, and then runs plain supervised fine-tuning on the survivors.

- The diagnosis is that distribution shift is the culprit: across 23 math datasets fine-tuned into `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`, forgetting on five non-math benchmarks tracks the post-training KL shift at **Spearman ρ = -0.85**, and at small scale `SDFT` self-rewrites fall to roughly **60% accuracy** and drop the chain-of-thought 8.2% of the time.
- The aligner is chosen to minimize the student's negative log-likelihood on its greedy rewrites, subject to that NLL beating gold-SFT NLL and rewrite accuracy beating the base model, which in practice means `Qwen2.5-7B` or `Qwen2.5-14B` for 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B `Qwen2.5-Instruct` students, with no new hyperparameters introduced.
- Averaged over `SciKnowEval` chemistry, a four-subject science mixture, `ToolAlpaca`, and `MedMCQA` across the three student sizes, `SynthSelf` reaches **56.4 acquisition** against 52.2 for SFT and 44.1 for `SDFT`, while matching the best baseline on 14 retention tasks at 41.7 to 41.8 (still about a point below the 42.8 base), and it beats off- and on-policy distillation using the identical aligner by **+5.7 to +16.9 percentage points** in acquisition.
- Distribution match matters more than aligner strength: `Qwen3.5-27B` and `Gemma-4-31B` produce more accurate rewrites yet sit further from the student in NLL and yield equal or worse acquisition, and same-family aligners cut data-generation FLOPs by **62.9% to 76.9%**.
- The method requires a larger same-family model to exist, its advantage over same-aligner distillation disappears on `MedMCQA` where the aligner already knows the content, retention is matched rather than improved (0.5B chemistry retention drops to 27.8 from 31.8), and only the `Qwen2.5-Instruct` family is evaluated.

papers.title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess hazardous knowledge possession rather than practical application, overlook risk amplification from BDTs, and rely on unreliable, expensive, or hazardous validation methods. To address these gaps, we introduce DRYLAB-Bench (Design Risk Yielded by LLM Agent in Biodesign), the first comprehensive benchmark evaluating the high-risk biological mutation design capabilities of LLM agents. Moving beyond basic question-answering, DRYLAB-Bench tasks agents with 30 genuinely hazardous mutation-design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines. It evaluates models in a multi-round, tool-augmented environment where LLMs orchestrate BDTs to iteratively refine candidates. Crucially, it scores designs directly against 187,695 empirical wet-lab measurements from ProteinGym and ViroGym using our proposed Biosecurity Risk Score (BRS), quantifying risk-associated effects while enabling scalable and safe ground-truth verification. Evaluations of 15 frontier models reveal substantial baseline threats: without tools, 67.6% of one-shot designs exceed the average measured variant, and 21.4% reach the highest-risk decile. Equipping models with BDTs significantly amplifies this risk, raising the pooled risk by \(\Delta BRS=+0.116\) and the top-decile share to 23.5%. Code: https://github.com/drylab-bio/DRYLAB-Bench
papers.summary: Biosecurity frameworks flag dual-use risk from models with biological design ability, but existing evaluations mostly quiz models on hazardous knowledge rather than measure whether an agent can apply it, and they ignore what changes when specialized biological design tools are attached. `DRYLAB-Bench` scores agents on 30 hazardous design scenarios distilled from biosecurity guidelines in a multi-round, tool-augmented setting, grading proposals against 187,695 existing wet-lab measurements from `ProteinGym` and `ViroGym` via a Biosecurity Risk Score, which keeps ground-truth verification scalable and safe. Across 15 frontier models the authors report measurable baseline capability even without tools, and **attaching design tools raises pooled risk further, lifting the share of top-risk-decile proposals to 23.5%**.

papers.title: BenCoDiC: A Large-Scale Contextual Cyberbullying Corpus for Bengali Political News Discourse FULL VERSION
papers.abstract: Cyberbullying is a growing concern in online communities, yet existing Bengali corpora remain limited in contextual information, annotation transparency, scale, accessibility, and support for multidimensional analysis, thereby hindering robust detection and comprehensive study of harasser behaviors and networks. To address these gaps, we introduce the Bengali Contextual and Diverse Cyberbullying (\textit{BenCoDiC}) corpus, a publicly available contextual cyberbullying resource for Bengali political news discourse comprising 50,250 textual instances collected from 100 YouTube videos and their associated discussions. The corpus preserves caption--comment--reply relationships and is organized through a nine-dimensional star schema covering users, videos, textual content, context, time, engagement, political parties, target identities, and language categories. Five AI chatbots were initially evaluated for annotation but did not meet the predefined reliability criterion. Consequently, a two-tier human annotation process with expert verification was adopted, achieving Fleiss' $\kappa=0.86$ and Krippendorff's $\alpha=0.86$. Statistical analyses characterize the corpus, while transformer-based experiments show that incorporating conversational context yields modest but consistent improvements over isolated-text classification. \textit{BenCoDiC} supports context-aware cyberbullying detection and perpetrator-oriented behavioral and network analysis. The corpus is available at https://github.com/bencodic/BenCoDiC-Corpus.
papers.summary: Bengali cyberbullying datasets have lacked conversational context, transparent annotation, and scale, which limits both detection and the study of harasser behavior and networks. The authors collect 50,250 text instances from 100 YouTube videos on Bengali political news, preserving caption, comment, and reply relationships and organizing them in a nine-dimensional star schema covering users, videos, content, context, time, engagement, political parties, target identities, and language categories. Five AI chatbots were tried as annotators but failed a predefined reliability criterion, so a two-tier human process with expert verification was used instead, reaching **Fleiss' kappa of 0.86** and Krippendorff's alpha of 0.86. Transformer experiments on `BenCoDiC` show that adding conversational context gives modest but consistent gains over classifying isolated text.

papers.title: Why Heavy-Tailed Weight Spectra Predict Model Quality
papers.abstract: A solid understanding of the predictive success of deep neural networks (DNNs) remains elusive. For example, while many data-dependent metrics exist that seek to predict model quality of DNNs, these metrics may be expensive to compute for large datasets and/or may be impossible to compute when training datasets are not released. A practical and effective predictor of model quality involves analyzing DNN weight matrices, as prior work has established that heavy-tailed spectral distributions in trained weight matrices can be strongly predictive of model quality. However, such metrics lack a rigorous statistical justification. In this work, we aim to understand why these metrics perform well, from a statistical perspective. To do so, we employ a probabilistic framework to derive the marginal likelihood for a DNN, evaluated using only the final layer weights. Across large-scale convolutional DNNs and LLMs, we find that this marginal likelihood predicts model quality. To understand the role heavy-tailed spectra play in predictive performance, we derive the limiting log-marginal likelihood for spectra that follow the (heavy-tailed) High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur (HTMP) distribution. We show that this limiting quantity is convex in a heaviness parameter, and we derive an optimal heaviness that empirically predicts over-fitting for large-scale DNNs.
papers.summary: Heavy-tailed eigenvalue spectra in trained weight matrices are known to predict deep neural network (DNN) quality without access to training data, but these metrics have lacked a rigorous statistical justification. The authors use a probabilistic framework to derive a marginal likelihood for a DNN evaluated using only its final-layer weights, and show across large convolutional networks and large language models that this quantity predicts model quality. Taking the limit for spectra that follow the heavy-tailed High-Temperature Marchenko-Pastur (HTMP) distribution, they show the log-marginal likelihood is **convex in a heaviness parameter**, which yields an optimal heaviness that empirically predicts over-fitting in large-scale models.

papers.title: Locate, Judge, Read: Role-Specialized Tool Agents over a Knowledge-Point Index for Open-Domain Multimodal Document QA
papers.abstract: Question answering over large heterogeneous document collections requires first finding the right passages and then reading them, yet current retrieval-augmented agents give one model both kinds of tools and let it schedule itself. We present KnowForge, a pipeline separated by job: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index; a Locator agent that can only search; a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop; a typed, size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking; a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images and tables; and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (3B active), KnowForge reaches F1 47.5 on the full open-domain M3DocVQA (2,441 questions, 3,368 PDFs), +11.0 over the published M3DocRAG system and +7.1 over one-shot retrieve-and-answer on the same index and model, and 53.5 with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. On MultiHop-RAG it reaches 73.5 accuracy, above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results (71.2); on the single-document MMLongBench-Doc it lifts the same model from 34.8 to 47.0, level with GPT-4o reading page images (46.3). Per-job ablations on the full benchmarks attribute the gain: the Deep Reader is worth 3.8, 9.8 and 0 points on the three corpora, tracking how visual each is; merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading; a round-budget sweep shows a step at four Locator rounds and a plateau beyond; query latency scales with model calls rather than corpus size. We serve the three indexed benchmarks as read-only knowledge bases (free registration) and release all prompts and the runner code: https://github.com/metask-ai/knowforge-bench
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented agents for question answering over large heterogeneous document collections usually hand one model both search and reading tools and let it schedule itself. `KnowForge` separates the jobs instead: a hybrid-retrieval knowledge-point index, a Locator agent that can only search, a code-scheduled bridge judge that forces the missing second hop, a typed and size-bounded evidence pool that merges every search's ranking, a Deep Reader agent that can only read text, images, and tables, and a synthesizer with a format checker. With a self-hosted `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` the pipeline reaches **F1 47.5 on the full open-domain `M3DocVQA`, 11.0 points above the published `M3DocRAG` system**, 73.5 accuracy on `MultiHop-RAG` above the strongest published RAG and GraphRAG results, and 47.0 on `MMLongBench-Doc`, level with `GPT-4o` reading page images. Ablations show the Deep Reader's value tracks how visual each corpus is, and merging both agents into one with all tools and twice the rounds loses 1.9 F1 because it keeps searching instead of reading.

papers.title: Fast Gradient-Based Approximation of Continuous Dynamic Time Warping
papers.abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a common choice for measuring the discrepancy between time series. It proceeds by finding an optimal warping between timestamps through dynamic programming, which can be slow and is not differentiable. Consequently, several variants have been proposed. Among them, Soft-DTW proposes a smooth formulation of DTW, amenable to gradient computation, while Continuous-DTW (CDTW) introduces a continuous formulation through parametrizable warping functions. Yet, computational costs remain high for both methods and impractical for large datasets in modern machine learning pipelines. This paper revisits CDTW in several ways. After establishing its differentiability under mild conditions, we introduce FastCDTW, which is an efficient approximate solver with two different computational strategies: an exact closed-form scheme for piecewise-linear warping functions, and an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for smooth ones, such as implicit neural networks. Both strategies provide gradients with respect to the warping function and the input time series, and the resulting algorithm is GPU-friendly. We demonstrate its benefits through its integration into more complex learning problems, including time series averaging, classification and deep domain adaptation.
papers.summary: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) measures the discrepancy between time series by finding an optimal alignment through dynamic programming, which is slow and not differentiable. Smooth variants such as `Soft-DTW` and the continuous formulation Continuous-DTW (CDTW) with parametrizable warping functions remain too costly for large datasets in modern pipelines. After establishing that CDTW is differentiable under mild conditions, the authors introduce `FastCDTW`, an approximate solver with an exact closed-form scheme for piecewise-linear warping functions and an **unbiased Monte Carlo estimator for smooth warping functions** such as implicit neural networks. Both strategies provide gradients with respect to the warping function and the input series, run well on GPUs, and are demonstrated inside time series averaging, classification, and deep domain adaptation.

papers.title: Looking Ahead and Back: Anticipatory Generative Modeling for Road-Network Trajectories
papers.abstract: Trajectory generation underpins urban applications such as traffic management and urban planning. Within road networks, vehicle movement along road segments is largely deterministic, whereas transitions at intersections are critical--multiple outgoing paths may appear equally plausible, yet they can lead to substantially different downstream routes. Existing generative methods such as diffusion models simulate location sequences and fail short of next transition selection, even producing trajectories that drift off the road network. To fill this gap, we advocate a fundamental shift: moving beyond location simulation toward behavior modeling on the road network. In this paper, we revisit trajectory generation through the lens of generative route planning, and introduce a new graph-constrained generative paradigm, Anticipatory Generative Modeling, which resolves next transition selection by incorporating the Anticipation of how the future route may unfold toward the destination. Concretely, we propose a novel generative model named Foresight that formulates a probabilistic model for an "anticipate--select--update--re-anticipate" loop that enables longer-term foresight while continuing sequential generation along the historical trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Foresight wins state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.summary: Generating vehicle trajectories on road networks is mostly a matter of intersections, where several outgoing roads look equally plausible but lead to very different routes, and existing diffusion-style generators that simulate location sequences handle this poorly and can even drift off the network. The authors reframe the task as generative route planning and propose Anticipatory Generative Modeling, a graph-constrained paradigm that resolves each next transition by anticipating how the remaining route could unfold toward the destination. Their model `Foresight` implements a probabilistic anticipate, select, update, and re-anticipate loop that provides longer-term foresight while continuing sequential generation along the historical trajectory, and the authors report that it **outperforms state-of-the-art baselines** in extensive experiments.

papers.title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
papers.abstract:
LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation.
  In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.
papers.summary: Sending sensitive contexts to hosted large language models raises privacy concerns, and existing differential privacy (DP) inference methods are designed for short or moderate contexts and degrade badly on very long inputs. `DP-MIND` perturbs the input locally, processes it chunk by chunk, and carries a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. The memory construction policy is trained with reinforcement learning directly on perturbed inputs, rewarded for final answer correctness and memory consistency, and a local denoising module recovers perturbation-corrupted answer spans without exposing the original context to the external model. The authors give a theoretical privacy analysis and report that the framework **outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines at context lengths up to the million-token scale**.

papers.title: Neurograf v1: An End-to-End Romanian-First Language Model Family
papers.abstract:
We present Neurograf v1, an experimental end-to-end Romanian-first language-model pipeline developed to investigate the feasibility of training language models from scratch for a lower-resource European language. The pipeline comprises RoSfera, a 635 GB Romanian corpus containing 175.7 million documents; an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer; five decoder-only models ranging from 160M to 6B parameters, trained on 131 billion tokens; three instruction-tuned assistants; and two contrastively trained embedding models. Training and evaluation were conducted using computing infrastructure at ELI-NP/IFIN-HH.
  The model family exhibits consistent scaling of validation loss and increasing Romanian factual and cultural knowledge with model size. On the 1,000-question WWTBM benchmark, Neurograf-6B achieves 69.89% accuracy on Romanian-context questions, while Neurograf-3.2B reaches 67.38%. Compute-optimal analysis yields a parameter-scaling exponent of approximately 0.423.
  Neurograf v1 serves as an experimental demonstrator rather than a production system. The study identifies practical challenges involving diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency, while demonstrating the feasibility of developing Romanian-first base models, instruction-following assistants, and semantic embedding models within a unified training pipeline.
papers.summary: Training a language model family from scratch for a lower-resource European language is tested end to end for Romanian. The pipeline comprises `RoSfera`, a 635 GB corpus of 175.7 million documents, an 80k byte-level BPE tokenizer, five decoder-only models from 160M to 6B parameters trained on 131 billion tokens, three instruction-tuned assistants, and two contrastively trained embedding models. Validation loss and Romanian factual and cultural knowledge scale consistently with model size: on the 1,000-question `WWTBM` benchmark, **`Neurograf-6B` reaches 69.89% accuracy on Romanian-context questions** and `Neurograf-3.2B` reaches 67.38%, while a compute-optimal analysis gives a parameter-scaling exponent of about 0.423. The authors frame the release as an experimental demonstrator and document practical challenges in diacritic preservation, corpus quality, data composition, and tokenization efficiency.

papers.title: Competence-Aware Orchestration for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have emerged as a promising paradigm for enhancing complex reasoning through role specialization and collaboration, yet a key challenge remains: how can collaboration be adapted to a backbone's competence on the current query? This problem matters because more collaboration is not always better--richer coordination may help on difficult cases, but it also incurs additional token cost and redundant interactions. We propose a two-stage competence-aware framework for automatic MAS orchestration. It first models the LLM backbone's task-conditioned competence for the current query, and then uses this signal to adapt role activation and the communication graph. Across six benchmarks, our method achieves an average score of 93.81%. Experiments with six LLM backbones of varying competence levels further show that our method adjusts collaboration according to the inferred competence: for higher-competence backbones, it improves average accuracy from 87.22 to 89.97 while reducing token cost by 36.26%; for lower-competence backbones, it yields a further average gain of 4.58 points over existing methods. The same trend also holds on unseen backbones.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models improve complex reasoning through role specialization, but more collaboration is not always better, since richer coordination adds token cost and redundant interaction that only pays off on hard queries. The proposed two-stage framework first models the backbone model's task-conditioned competence on the current query, then uses that signal to decide which roles to activate and how to shape the communication graph. Across six benchmarks the method averages 93.81%, and with six backbones of varying strength it adapts as intended: **for higher-competence backbones it raises average accuracy from 87.22 to 89.97 while cutting token cost by 36.26%**, and for lower-competence backbones it adds 4.58 points over existing methods. The same trend holds on backbones not seen during development.

papers.title: VIGOR: Verifiable Industrial Geometry Optimization and Repair in Scene Programs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate structured layouts and executable scene programs from natural-language instructions. However, executability does not imply engineering feasibility: an industrial scene program may execute successfully while its final state still violates coupled boundary, collision, clearance, aisle, or structural constraints. We identify this mismatch as the executability-engineering-feasibility gap, where locally plausible placements can remain globally infeasible because corrections to one device may introduce violations elsewhere. To make this gap measurable in a controlled setting, we construct an execution-grounded industrial scene-program dataset with 1,749 constructible scenarios, complete executable programs, and 94 final-state geometric checks per scenario. We further propose VIGOR, which combines supervised scene-program generation with execution-grounded verification and staged geometric refinement. Supervised fine-tuning establishes complete program generation, local projection resolves independently correctable violations, and joint conflict-graph repair coordinates residual multi-object conflicts while preserving structural relations. Experiments show that VIGOR achieves 96.86% Complete Feasibility and an Overall score of 91.20, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 10.42 points in Overall. These results show that, under controlled industrial layout conditions, reliable scene-program generation requires not only executable programs, but also explicit verification and coordinated resolution of coupled engineering constraints.
papers.summary: Large language models can emit executable scene programs for industrial layouts, but a program that runs without error may still leave devices violating coupled boundary, collision, clearance, aisle, or structural constraints, a mismatch the authors call the executability-engineering-feasibility gap. To measure it they build an execution-grounded dataset of 1,749 constructible scenarios with complete programs and 94 final-state geometric checks per scenario. `VIGOR` combines supervised fine-tuning for complete program generation with execution-grounded verification, local projection that fixes independently correctable violations, and joint conflict-graph repair that coordinates residual multi-object conflicts while preserving structural relations. It reaches **96.86% Complete Feasibility** and an Overall score of 91.20, 10.42 points above the strongest evaluated baseline.

papers.title: Les Mis\'erables Dialogue: A film-based network representation of social communication
papers.abstract: In this work, we revisit the classic Les Mis\'erables benchmark network from the perspective of social communication. Using the 1998 film adaptation of the novel, we construct the publicly available Les Mis\'erables Dialogue temporal text network, which explicitly distinguishes speakers, addressees, and other recipients of each utterance, along with its content and timing. Using the ten social dimensions model, we also derive multilayer network representations of the network, in which layers correspond to distinct relational dimensions. Beyond the network dataset, this work offers a general methodology for building similarly rich communication datasets from similar narrative sources.
papers.summary: The classic Les Misérables character network is rebuilt from the standpoint of social communication rather than co-occurrence. Using the 1998 film adaptation, the authors construct a publicly available temporal text network that records, for every utterance, the speaker, the addressee, any other recipients, the content, and the timing. Applying the ten social dimensions model, they also derive **multilayer representations whose layers correspond to distinct relational dimensions**, and they describe a general methodology for building similarly rich communication datasets from other narrative sources.

papers.title: Quality, Not Just Outcome: A Structural Scoring Framework for Selecting Coding-Agent Trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Open coding agents are commonly trained through supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories whose final patches pass the benchmark test suite. However, this outcome-level filtering criterion ignores process quality: trajectories that eventually succeed may still contain inefficient interaction patterns such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification behavior, all of which become part of the imitation target. We propose TQS (Trajectory Quality Score), a structural scoring framework for coding-agent trajectories that operates directly on trajectory structure, requires no LLM judge, and runs in linear time. TQS characterizes trajectory quality through structural signals organized around structured convergence: information focus, intent--action alignment, and policy dynamics. Using 155,144 successful trajectories from a public open-license corpus, we rank trajectories by TQS and fine-tune coding agents on filtered subsets. Models trained on top-ranked trajectories consistently outperform those trained on random or bottom-ranked subsets on SWE-Bench-Verified. Our results suggest that process-level trajectory quality is an important factor in coding-agent supervision and that structural trajectory filtering provides an effective and scalable alternative to LLM-based data selection.
papers.summary: Open coding agents are usually fine-tuned on interaction trajectories selected only because the final patch passed the benchmark test suite, which lets inefficient behavior such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification become part of the imitation target. `TQS` (Trajectory Quality Score) scores trajectories from their structure alone, with no LLM judge and in linear time, using signals for information focus, intent-action alignment, and policy dynamics organized around structured convergence. Ranking 155,144 successful trajectories from a public open-license corpus and fine-tuning coding agents on filtered subsets, the authors find that **models trained on top-ranked trajectories consistently beat those trained on random or bottom-ranked subsets on `SWE-Bench-Verified`**. They conclude that process-level trajectory quality matters for coding-agent supervision and that structural filtering is a scalable alternative to LLM-based data selection.

papers.title: SOAR: Source-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Precise Credit Assignment for Search Agents
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for search agents often suffers from evidence fabrication, a failure mode where agents bypass external information ($E_{ext}$) and fabricate an incorrect answer. We argue that this fabrication arises from an over-reliance on unreliable internal knowledge ($E_{int}$) as shortcuts due to the inherent opacity of reasoning trajectories. To address this, we propose SOAR (SOurce-Aware Reinforcement learning), a paradigm that transforms monolithic reasoning into source-explicit trajectories. SOAR (i) disentangles $E_{ext}$ and $E_{int}$ into parallel, observable streams via a Source-Aware Workflow, and (ii) incorporates Source-Consistent Reward to guide the policy evolution. By making information-source attribution explicit, SOAR enables precise credit assignment between different knowledge streams. Evaluations show that SOAR outperforms baselines on 3B and 7B backbones by 7.3% and 5.4%, while reducing evidence fabrication by 74.8%. These confirm that SOAR significantly improves performance on knowledge-intensive benchmarks while effectively mitigating evidence fabrication, fostering more faithful and grounded reasoning with enhanced robustness.
papers.summary: Search agents trained with reinforcement learning (RL) often fabricate evidence, bypassing retrieved external information and answering from unreliable internal knowledge, which the authors attribute to the opacity of monolithic reasoning trajectories. `SOAR` (Source-Aware Reinforcement learning) splits external and internal evidence into parallel, observable streams through a Source-Aware Workflow and adds a Source-Consistent Reward, so that credit can be assigned precisely between the two knowledge streams. On 3B and 7B backbones the method outperforms baselines on knowledge-intensive benchmarks by 7.3% and 5.4% while **reducing evidence fabrication by 74.8%**.

papers.title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence
papers.abstract: Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real-world professional tasks. Short trajectories can demonstrate commands and tool calls, but they do not fully show how agents accumulate evidence through exploration, use it to inform judgments, continually adjust strategies based on feedback, and turn intermediate results into final deliverables. High-quality long-horizon trajectories capture these agentic behavioral patterns and their connections within a single problem-solving process, providing richer experience for sustained autonomous work. However, environment synthesis may complete or simplify the key work underlying these patterns in advance and thus remove the need for exploration, implementation, and verification that the agent was meant to perform. To address this, we introduce TerminalHorizon, a fully automated data synthesis engine for long-horizon terminal agents. Starting from real-world professional work, it uses independent execution to identify key work omitted during construction and uses the resulting evidence to guide environment reconstruction. To extend these patterns across stages, it progressively expands tasks under the same goal, introducing new requirements that build on prior results and call for further exploration and improvement. Using this engine, we construct 1.5K task environments and perform supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on the resulting dataset to obtain TerminalHorizon-27B. We achieve substantial performance gains on all 12 benchmarks spanning coding-agent tasks, agentic tasks in real-world production settings, and general reasoning. Multiple RSI case studies, each with a 12-hour research budget, further demonstrate the model's ability to continue experimenting beyond an initial solution, improve its methods based on feedback, and retain effective improvements in its final deliverables.
papers.summary: Short agent trajectories show individual commands and tool calls but not how an agent accumulates evidence through exploration, adjusts strategy from feedback, and turns intermediate results into deliverables, and synthesized environments often pre-complete the very work the agent was meant to do. `TerminalHorizon` is an automated data synthesis engine that starts from real professional work, uses independent execution to find key work omitted during environment construction, uses that evidence to rebuild the environment, and then progressively extends tasks under the same goal with new requirements that build on prior results. The authors construct 1.5K task environments and fine-tune `Qwen3.5-27B` on the resulting data to obtain `TerminalHorizon-27B`, reporting **substantial gains on all 12 benchmarks** spanning coding-agent tasks, agentic tasks in real production settings, and general reasoning. Case studies with a 12-hour research budget each show the model continuing to experiment beyond an initial solution and retaining effective improvements in its final deliverables.

papers.title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
papers.abstract: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Prior work reduces this cost by changing the sampler or the model (e.g., sequential Monte Carlo, approximate lookahead, distillation). We propose Predictive SubTree Prefetching (PreSTO), which accelerates PowerMH by prefetching future proposals and provably leaves its MH transition kernel unchanged. PreSTO views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions: in each model call, it generates the proposals of a \textit{prefetched subtree} of this tree in one batch, then follows the realized path with the original MH acceptance rule. We also observe that MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each prefetched subtree, we further design a \textit{predictive traversal rule} that chooses the subtree to maximize the predicted number of completed transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs, PreSTO achieves median speedups of $1.71\times$, $1.91\times$, and $2.33\times$ on PowerMH and its follow-ups EntropyCut and MultiTryMH, respectively; on the first two, it makes a median of $3.9\times$ fewer model calls, each only $2.1\times$ longer. On LCB V6 with Qwen3.5-9B, the predictive traversal rule is a further $1.25\times$--$1.37\times$ faster than the default breadth-first traversal.
papers.summary: Power sampling sharpens a large language model's output distribution at test time to improve reasoning, but its `PowerMH` sampler is slow because each Metropolis-Hastings (MH) accept-or-reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. Predictive SubTree Prefetching (`PreSTO`) views future MH outcomes as a tree of accept/reject decisions, generates the proposals for a prefetched subtree in one batched model call, then follows the realized path with the original acceptance rule, which provably leaves the MH transition kernel unchanged. Because MH reaches only a sparse, nearly unary part of each subtree, a predictive traversal rule chooses the subtree expected to complete the most transitions. Across seven datasets and five base LLMs the method gives **median speedups of 1.71x, 1.91x, and 2.33x on `PowerMH`, `EntropyCut`, and `MultiTryMH`**, making about 3.9x fewer model calls that are each only about 2.1x longer.

papers.title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions
papers.abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment-specific objects. To address this limitation, we introduce RoleWorld, a symbolic world modeling approach which uses reusable prototypes and environment-specific parameter values as functional role abstractions to represent how objects behave in interactions. From interaction trajectories, a teacher LLM extracts role prototypes and executable transition rules defined over role instances, together with a skill that guides the actor LLM to use role information in decision making. In a target world, without the teacher, the actor uses this skill together with its current role assignments and parameter estimates, and actively tests a role instance hypothesis through interaction when its uncertainty affects the current decision. Feedback from each action refines role assignments and estimates parameter values online, with no LLM parameter updates and the transition rules held fixed. Experiments on MARS benchmark show that RoleWorld enables robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior, suggesting that functional role abstractions can serve as an effective component for knowledge transfer in world modeling. Project Page: https://future-item.github.io/RoleWorld.
papers.summary: World models let large language model (LLM) agents anticipate the effects of actions, but recent symbolic or program-based world models organize their rules around environment-specific objects, which limits transfer to new environments with similar interaction structure and dynamics. `RoleWorld` represents how objects behave through functional role abstractions, namely reusable role prototypes combined with environment-specific parameter values. A teacher LLM extracts role prototypes, executable transition rules over role instances, and a decision-making skill from interaction trajectories, and in a target world the actor LLM alone assigns roles, estimates parameters online from action feedback, and actively tests a role hypothesis when its uncertainty affects the current decision, with no parameter updates and the rules held fixed. On the `MARS` benchmark the authors report **robust generalization across environments with significantly altered object behavior**.

papers.title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
papers.abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but its effectiveness on long-horizon multimodal tasks is underexplored. The authors introduce `FG-Sudoku`, a visual Sudoku benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps, and find that frontier multimodal models fail on puzzles with long-range dependencies such as 9x9 grids, where near-zero success rates create reward sparsity that halts standard RLVR. Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (`AdaC-GRPO`) builds training batches dynamically by tracking the model's zone of proximal development through online rollout accuracy rather than following a rigid or prior-based schedule. It lets `Qwen2.5-VL-7B` approach `Gemini-2.5-Flash` and **close 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to `Gemini-2.5-Pro`**, with the gains also holding on `InternVL-3.5` and `Qwen3-VL`.

papers.title: WaSA: Wavelet Scattering Autoencoders for Unsupervised Offline Detection of Malicious Clients in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exposing raw data, yet remains vulnerable to malicious clients injecting poisoned datasets. Existing defenses are typically reactive (operating during training) or supervised (requiring prior knowledge of attack types) - assumptions that rarely hold in open-ended IoT deployments. We propose WaSA, a fully unsupervised, offline framework for malicious client detection. Before training, each client transmits a single, privacy-preserving spectral summary of its data to the server. A denoising autoencoder, trained solely on clean auxiliary data, scores clients based on their deviation from the learned benign manifold, identifying corruptions regardless of the attack type. WaSA requires no attack labels, generalizes to unseen anomalies, and introduces a Boltzmann sampling strategy for client selection that smoothly interpolates between hard exclusion and standard aggregation. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under diverse attack scenarios (up to 90 % malicious clients) demonstrate consistent improvements over supervised baselines and robust aggregation methods, with negligible communication overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/alelicciardi99/wavelet_autoencoders_malicious.
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) trains models without exposing raw data but is vulnerable to clients that inject poisoned datasets, and existing defenses either react during training or require prior knowledge of the attack type. `WaSA` detects malicious clients offline and without supervision: before training, each client sends a single privacy-preserving spectral summary of its data, and a denoising autoencoder trained only on clean auxiliary data scores each client by its deviation from the learned benign manifold, regardless of attack type. A Boltzmann sampling strategy for client selection interpolates smoothly between hard exclusion and standard aggregation. On `MNIST`, `CIFAR-10`, and `CIFAR-100` under diverse attack scenarios with **up to 90% malicious clients**, the approach beats supervised baselines and robust aggregation methods with negligible communication overhead.

papers.title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
papers.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.
papers.summary: Landing an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on an unmanned surface vehicle (USV) in high sea states is difficult because hierarchical landing methods usually infer future deck motion only implicitly from short observation histories. The proposed framework adds a pretrained model that explicitly predicts USV attitude during high-level landing decisions, using the prediction to identify suitable landing windows and choose the touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller keeps the UAV stable and tracks motion commands.
