A real-sim setup replays USV motion data collected in real sea conditions on a `MuJoCo` USV, and the experiments show that **explicit attitude prediction improves landing-window selection** and supports timing-aware landing planning in rapidly varying marine conditions.

papers.title: JANUS: Enhancing Long-Horizon Autonomous Research with Co-Evolving World Models
papers.abstract: Long-horizon autonomous research has shown promise in accelerating scientific progress through sustained cycles of hypothesis generation, implementation, and validation. However, this Generate-Execute-Feedback paradigm relies on reactive trial-and-error, where costly and time-consuming executions introduce severe feedback delays, throttling evolutionary progress under explosively expanding search space. To address this challenge, we propose JANUS, a framework that unifies future outcomes forecasting and past experience reflection through a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model. Within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates while world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, then accordingly selects, refines, or prunes branches prior to execution. After receiving ground-truth feedback, JANUS distills experience into evolving skills: hierarchical skills for research agent, exploration-strategy skills for world model, and their coordination protocols. This mechanism enables continual co-evolution: the research agent sharpens candidate generation while the world model refines its predictive judgment over extended horizons. Extensive evaluations on MLS-Bench-Lite and real research tasks demonstrate that JANUS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving both higher evolving efficiency and ceiling.
papers.summary: Long-horizon autonomous research systems that cycle through generating, executing, and evaluating hypotheses are throttled by slow, costly executions that delay feedback in a rapidly expanding search space. `JANUS` replaces reactive trial and error with a Predict-Verify-Evolve loop driven by a co-evolving world model: within an evolving graph, the research agent proposes candidates, the world model scores them by forecasting value improvement, information gain, and exploration utility, and branches are selected, refined, or pruned before any execution. After ground-truth feedback arrives, experience is distilled into hierarchical skills for the research agent, exploration-strategy skills for the world model, and coordination protocols between them, so candidate generation and predictive judgment improve together. On `MLS-Bench-Lite` and real research tasks the authors report that the framework **outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both evolving efficiency and ceiling**.

papers.title: Does Learning Recurrent Networks Matter in Partially Observable RL?
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability usually trains a recurrent network jointly with the policy or value function to carry temporal information, which raises the question of whether learning the recurrent module is necessary at all. Motivated by Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), the authors pair a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module and evaluate it across partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Frozen recurrent networks **support recall over hundreds of steps and reach competitive control performance with less than half the trainable parameters** of fully trainable counterparts, which the authors present as a simple, parameter-efficient baseline for partially observable RL.

papers.title: S$^3$R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Fast rollout generation for long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) requires reducing KV-cache traffic without changing the response groups used for policy optimization. In our profiled RLVR workloads, attention accounts for 72--76\% of autoregressive decoding kernel time. Sparse attention reduces these reads, but sampling directly from a sparse policy changes the response groups used for learning. For group-relative optimization, we show that even exact response-wise reweighting does not generally recover the expected dense-policy update because the advantage of each response depends on the rewards of other group members. We propose Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (S$^3$R). It uses sparse attention to propose tokens, then generates responses through full-attention verification and exact speculative sampling. Drafting and verification share the same policy parameter, eliminating the need to train or update a separate drafter. The resulting response groups follow the dense-policy distribution. Under S$^3$R, we characterize speedup conditions and the costs of drafting and verification. We found that dense verification still requires the complete historical KV cache. A KV-aware scheduler therefore limits KV-cache repeated offloading and restoration while maintaining rollout parallelism. % OR thrashing In a matched ablation with an aggressive sparse drafting budget, S$^3$R maintains stable training while direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable. On long-context mathematical reasoning, S$^3$R achieves $1.39\times~1.35\times$ the end-to-end training throughput of autoregressive rollouts on Qwen3 model, with comparable task performance.
papers.summary: Long-context reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) spends most of its rollout time in attention, which the authors measure at 72 to 76% of autoregressive decoding kernel time, but sampling from a sparse-attention policy changes the response groups used for group-relative optimization, and even exact response-wise reweighting cannot generally recover the dense-policy update because each response's advantage depends on the other group members' rewards. Self-Sparse Speculative Rollouts (`S³R`) uses sparse attention to draft tokens and the same policy with full attention to verify them through exact speculative sampling, so the resulting responses follow the dense-policy distribution without training a separate drafter, and a KV-cache-aware scheduler limits repeated offloading and restoration of the history that dense verification still needs. On long-context mathematical reasoning with `Qwen3` models, **end-to-end training throughput improves by about 1.35 to 1.39 times over autoregressive rollouts** with comparable task performance, and training stays stable under an aggressive sparse drafting budget where direct sparse sampling with training-side correction becomes unstable.

papers.title: Rethinking Relative Policy Differences Transfer of On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a target policy on its own rollouts using token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, but typically relies on the teacher being substantially more capable than the target. Recent work relaxes this requirement by transferring the relative policy difference between an expert and a reference policy rather than the expert's absolute distribution. Yet it remains unclear which differences provide useful supervision and which targets can benefit from them. We develop a unified view in which the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference defines an implicit reward for KL-regularized policy optimization. This formulation induces an on-policy update for the target, recovers conventional OPD as a special case, and enables any-to-any transfer across models that differ in scale, training stage or generation. Our systematic experiments yield three findings. First, a stronger expert is not necessarily a better source of supervision: differences induced by task-specific training, including reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning, transfer consistently, whereas those arising from model scale alone transfer weakly or not at all. Second, the expert and reference serve complementary roles: the expert provides the capability to be transferred, while the reference filters out shared behavior and isolates the relevant residual. Third, even a useful difference does not transfer to every target: success requires the induced update to move the target toward the expert and generalize beyond sampled rollouts. Raw policy distance does not predict transferability, whereas an appropriate reference can rescue otherwise unsuccessful transfer. These results characterize when relative policy differences provide effective supervision for OPD.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) usually needs a teacher far stronger than the student, and recent work instead transfers the relative difference between an expert and a reference policy, but which differences carry useful signal and which targets can absorb them has been unclear. The authors frame the log-probability ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference as an implicit reward for KL-regularized policy optimization, which induces an on-policy update for the target, recovers standard OPD as a special case, and allows any-to-any transfer across models that differ in scale, training stage, or generation. Experiments show that **differences induced by task-specific training such as reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning transfer consistently, whereas differences arising from model scale alone transfer weakly or not at all**, that the reference filters out shared behavior to isolate the relevant residual, and that raw policy distance does not predict transferability while a well-chosen reference can rescue otherwise failed transfers.
papers.highlight_summary:
Conventional on-policy distillation (OPD) needs a teacher far stronger than the student, since its reward is the teacher's own log-probability on student rollouts. The paper reframes the newer alternative of transferring a teacher's *relative* policy change as an implicit reward for KL-regularized optimization, yielding an any-to-any objective (`A²-OPD`) that recovers standard OPD as a special case and lets the proxy expert/reference pair and the target be chosen independently.

- The log-ratio between a proxy expert and a proxy reference acts as a fixed token-level reward on the target's own rollouts, with a KL term anchoring the target to its own base, a centered advantage dropping the intractable normalizer, and experiments across `Qwen3` and `Qwen2.5` models trained on `DeepMath-103K` and `Eurus-RL-Code` using top-16 token distributions.
- Differences created by task-directed training transfer reliably while scale-only gaps do not: RL and SFT proxy pairs lift the fixed `Qwen3-8B` target by **9.78 to 32.23 points** on math, a 4B RL expert alone raises it from 18.43 to **45.27**, yet the `Qwen3-8B`/`Qwen3-4B` scale pair yields **−1.03**, and two updates of similar KL magnitude (0.35 vs 0.42) give gains of 25.85 vs 3.42, so direction matters more than size.
- The expert and reference play complementary roles: swapping the reference from `Qwen3-4B` base to an early-RL checkpoint collapses the target gain from 26.84 to **9.62** because the shared capability is filtered out, while a `Qwen2.5-3B` reference gives the largest gain of **29.09** despite the largest base KL distance of 1.23.
- A useful difference is not universally transferable: Qwen3 targets gain 9.78 to 29.09, but Qwen2.5 targets under a Qwen3 reference land between **−2.46 and 2.72**, raw policy distance fails to predict this, and merely switching to a same-family `Qwen2.5-3B` reference rescues them with gains of 6.74, 2.25 and 5.76.
- Limitations include testing only Qwen-family models with a fixed transfer strength of α/β = 1, much smaller gains on code than math (+2.3 vs +26.8 for the same proxy pair), lossy text-based token alignment across tokenizers, and "match the model family" being offered as an empirical fix rather than a general compatibility criterion.

papers.title: SharP: Soft and Hard Prompt-Guided Augmentation with LLM for Low Resource Fake News Detection
papers.abstract: Fake news detection under low resource conditions is challenged by the scarcity of labeled data and the difficulty of capturing subtle deceptive patterns. In this work, we focus on low resource fake news detection, where only a small labeled set is available for training, while evaluation is performed under a fixed and unchanged test protocol. This setting is motivated by costly, ambiguous fact-checking and emerging topics and domains that are poorly covered by existing benchmarks. Existing data augmentation methods, such as synonym substitution, generative adversarial networks, and large language model (LLM)-based generation, often produce fluent but overly generic content, lacking the task-specific relevance needed for accurate detection. To address this, we propose SharP, a boundary-aware text generation framework guided by soft and hard prompts, which leverages LLMs as tools adapted to produce task-specific synthetic samples. SharP employs a dual prompt mechanism: hard prompts provide structured guidance and factual constraints, while soft prompts introduce learned semantic patterns from the data. These two types of prompts are combined to guide the generation process, enabling the model to produce samples that closely align with the characteristics of news. To further enhance detection performance, we incorporate a boundary-aware strategy that steers generation toward areas where the classifier is less confident, helping to clarify subtle distinctions between real and fake content. In addition, we adopt a dual objective optimization that balances semantic alignment with the source data and classifier feedback. This encourages the generation of samples that are both domain-consistent and helpful for refining decision boundaries, ultimately improving model robustness and generalization in low resource fake news detection.
papers.summary: Fake news detection with only a small labeled set is hard because standard augmentation methods, from synonym substitution and generative adversarial networks to large language model (LLM) generation, produce fluent but generic text that lacks task-specific signal. `SharP` guides an LLM with a dual prompt mechanism in which hard prompts supply structured guidance and factual constraints while soft prompts inject learned semantic patterns from the data, combined with a boundary-aware strategy that steers generation toward regions where the classifier is least confident. A dual objective balances semantic alignment with the source data against classifier feedback, and the authors claim **the resulting synthetic samples are both domain-consistent and effective at sharpening decision boundaries**, improving robustness and generalization under a fixed test protocol.

papers.title: How Much Computation Does Every Forecast Need? Structured Block Skipping in Two Time-Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time-series foundation models use the same network depth for every input, although forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty. We test whether whole Transformer blocks can be removed at inference time in two pretrained models: Chronos-Bolt and TimesFM 2.5. Our bypasses avoid the original block computation and preserve the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. Masks are selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from ETTh1, Traffic, Weather, and Exchange. At moderate sparsity, Chronos-Bolt with 7/11 candidate blocks and TimesFM with 16/20 blocks show little change in mean relative forecasting quality across datasets while reducing median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%. More aggressive TimesFM skipping accelerates inference further but substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Across both models, different equal-budget masks win on different windows, and a retrospective oracle significantly improves over the best static mask on every dataset. However, dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently, and Chronos representations do not support reliable unseen-domain routing. These results establish cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity, but not a deployable dynamic inference method.
papers.summary: Time-series foundation models apply the same depth to every input even though forecasting windows differ in structure and difficulty, so the authors test whether whole Transformer blocks can be bypassed at inference in the pretrained `Chronos-Bolt` and `TimesFM 2.5`, using bypasses that reproduce the dense model exactly when all blocks are enabled. With masks selected only on calibration windows and evaluated on 1,088 held-out windows from `ETTh1`, `Traffic`, `Weather`, and `Exchange`, **keeping 7 of 11 candidate blocks in Chronos-Bolt and 16 of 20 in TimesFM leaves mean relative forecast quality little changed while cutting median A100 batch-1 latency by 11.2% and 13.4%**, whereas more aggressive skipping in TimesFM substantially harms Traffic and Weather. Different equal-budget masks win on different windows and a retrospective oracle beats the best static mask on every dataset, but dataset-specific masks transfer inconsistently and Chronos representations do not support reliable routing for unseen domains, so the work establishes cross-architecture structured redundancy and input-dependent opportunity rather than a deployable dynamic inference method.

papers.title: Verifiable Sampling for Delegated Generative Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract:
Generative machine learning has shown remarkable results across a wide range of interdisciplinary tasks, motivating significant efforts toward Quantum Generative Models as a path to beyond-classical performance, given their capability of generating classically intractable distributions. However, comparatively little attention has been paid to securely delegating such computations to a powerful remote quantum server. In this work, we propose a blind and verifiable protocol for sampling that can be used for the inference phase of such quantum models. Such a protocol inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and achieves verifiability by exploiting known approaches based on trapification schemes. Alongside, to delegate the training phase, we discuss an extension of the previously proposed verifiable end-to-end Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms (Inajetovic et al., Phys. Rev. Research, 2026).
  Beyond the usual Accept/Abort outcome characterizing verification protocols, the sampling protocol for inference also provides, even against a malicious server, an estimation of the amount of corrupted generated samples, i.e., a fine-grained feature describing the quality of the outcome connecting verification protocols and application-level benchmarking.
papers.summary: Quantum generative models promise distributions that are classically intractable to sample, but little work addresses securely delegating their inference or training to a powerful remote quantum server. The authors propose a blind and verifiable sampling protocol for the inference phase that inherits blindness from Universal Blind Quantum Computing and gains verifiability through trapification schemes, and they sketch an extension of earlier verifiable Delegated Variational Quantum Algorithms to cover training. Beyond the usual accept or abort verdict, **the protocol estimates the fraction of corrupted generated samples even against a malicious server**, linking verification guarantees to application-level quality benchmarking.

papers.title: Beyond Actions: Learning Future Operation Targets for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies learn mainly by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state, yet actions specify what a robot should execute rather than what those commands will achieve. Action-Future Coupled Effect Learning (`AFCE`) makes a future-grounded physical Effect the primary prediction target: an offline tokenizer builds temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions, a flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from the current images, instruction, and robot state, and a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks, with embodiment-specific interfaces letting single-arm and dual-arm tasks share one Effect model. On `DexJoCo`, AFCE reaches **50.97% overall success, 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points above** the `π0.5` and `UVT` baselines, and leads on all five bimanual tasks.

papers.title: Monarch-MoE: Structured Experts for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
papers.abstract: Learning new tasks in multimodal continual instruction tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously acquired knowledge. Although multi-expert LoRA distributes learning across experts, updates to a dense low-rank expert can still affect many output features. We introduce Monarch-MoE, which replaces the dense factors in LoRA experts with block-diagonal factors connected by a fixed permutation. This structure provides blockwise gradient isolation: individual block-pair updates affect only one output block, while connections between all input and output blocks are maintained. To make these compact experts practical on memory-limited hardware, we combine batched computation, fused forward operators, and an optimized backward pass. Across three continual-learning methods evaluated on MLLM-DCL and UCIT with LLaVA-1.5-7B, Monarch-MoE improves first-task retention while reducing adapter parameters by approximately 75% and 50%, respectively. In the main comparison, first-task forgetting is as low as 0.52 percentage points on MLLM-DCL and 0.10 on UCIT, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance. Our implementation supports fine-tuning and inference on a single 24 GB RTX 4090, with lower measured memory use and competitive runtime in the evaluated settings. Together, these algorithmic and systems improvements make structured experts a practical option for continual adaptation on memory-limited hardware.
papers.summary: Multimodal continual instruction tuning tends to forget earlier tasks, and even multi-expert LoRA does not fully isolate updates because a dense low-rank expert touches many output features. `Monarch-MoE` replaces the dense LoRA factors with block-diagonal factors joined by a fixed permutation, so each block-pair update affects only one output block while every input block still connects to every output block, and it pairs this with batched computation, fused forward operators, and an optimized backward pass. Across three continual-learning methods on `MLLM-DCL` and `UCIT` with `LLaVA-1.5-7B`, **first-task forgetting drops to as low as 0.52 and 0.10 percentage points while adapter parameters shrink by roughly 75% and 50%**, with method-dependent trade-offs in final performance, and the whole pipeline fine-tunes and runs on a single 24 GB RTX 4090.

papers.title: Golden Anchor for Video Generation
papers.abstract: Video generation supports digital content creation, with applications in virtual avatars, AI-driven filmmaking, interactive game engines, and world models. State-of-the-art systems achieve controllability primarily through image-to-video (I2V) generation, in which an injected anchor image determines the identity, composition, and style of the resulting video. In modern pipelines, this anchor is synthesized by a text-to-image (T2I) generator. This raises a largely overlooked question: Are images obtained directly from the T2I model truly suitable for current video models? Our analysis shows that anchor aesthetic and quality scores are weakly correlated with downstream video quality. The structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V video quality in both the visual and motion dimensions. Fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward accordingly yields anchors with visibly denser structural and character detail: they score higher on image metrics, yet lower the video reward on every I2V model we test and change downstream motion unpredictably. We therefore introduce Golden Anchor Learning (GAL), to our knowledge the first framework for learning golden anchors by optimizing a T2I generator with downstream video feedback. GAL evaluates candidate anchors through the videos they induce under a frozen I2V model and converts video rewards into image-level preferences for DPO fine-tuning of the T2I generator. On all four I2V models, GAL raises the VBench average by $2.97\%$--$8.46\%$ over the untuned generator. The rendered clips also score higher under VideoReward-Overall, and their extracted frames under HPSv3 and UniPercept. GAL yields consistent motion gains across all four I2V models, as measured by a $5.62\%$--$38.24\%$ increase in VBench dynamic degree. Although GAL is trained only on HunyuanVideo-1.5 renders, these gains extend to the other three I2V models.
papers.summary: Modern image-to-video (I2V) pipelines take their anchor image from a text-to-image (T2I) generator, but the authors find that anchor aesthetic and quality scores correlate only weakly with downstream video quality, that a structure-and-texture score is negatively correlated with I2V visual and motion quality, and that fine-tuning the T2I model on an image reward lowers video reward on every I2V model tested. Golden Anchor Learning (`GAL`) instead scores candidate anchors by the videos they induce under a frozen I2V model and converts those video rewards into image-level preferences for DPO fine-tuning of the T2I generator. On `VBench` across four I2V models, **GAL raises the average score by 2.97% to 8.46% over the untuned generator** and dynamic degree by 5.62% to 38.24%, with gains also under `VideoReward-Overall`, `HPSv3`, and `UniPercept`, even though training used only `HunyuanVideo-1.5` renders.

papers.title: Tensor-based Fusion of Multi-modal Data for Predicting Cancer Risk Levels
papers.abstract: Cancer diagnosis and treatment increasingly rely on multi-modal diagnostic technologies that generate high-dimensional datasets. Although these datasets are rich in pathological information, they pose considerable challenges in interpretation, dimensionality reduction, and clinical applicability. Conventional machine learning approaches often fail to extract meaningful cross-modal features, thereby limiting predictive accuracy in patient risk stratification. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an unsupervised machine learning framework that integrates feature extraction, tensor decomposition, and clustering to improve cancer risk prediction. The framework employs tensor decomposition to fuse heterogeneous genomic and clinical data, enabling the extraction of latent, biologically meaningful features that outperform unimodal feature sets. Multiple feature extraction strategies are investigated, and the resulting features are subsequently clustered using a range of clustering algorithms. Comparative evaluations based on internal and external metrics are then used to identify the most effective configurations. The framework is validated on LinkedOmics data comprising 11,158 patients across 32 cancer types. For patient risk stratification, clinically relevant attributes such as tumor purity, pathological stage, and survival outcomes serve as ground-truth indicators. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of tSVD+GMM, which consistently outperforms other configurations across clinical benchmarks.
papers.summary: Multi-modal cancer diagnostics produce high-dimensional genomic and clinical data that conventional machine learning struggles to fuse into cross-modal features useful for patient risk stratification. The proposed unsupervised framework chains feature extraction, tensor decomposition that fuses the heterogeneous modalities into latent features, and clustering, then compares multiple extraction strategies and clustering algorithms using internal and external metrics. Validated on `LinkedOmics` data from 11,158 patients across 32 cancer types, with tumor purity, pathological stage, and survival outcomes as ground-truth indicators, the `tSVD+GMM` configuration **consistently outperforms every other configuration across the clinical benchmarks**.

papers.title: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation
papers.abstract: Generative modeling for discrete data has been significantly advanced by learning continuous vector fields on the statistical manifolds to transport simple priors to target discrete distributions. However, because these continuous-time flows are not constrained to follow geodesics on the statistical manifold, thereby requiring multi-step numerical integration for simulation and leading to substantial computational costs during inference. In this work, drawing inspiration from the "straight and fast" properties of Rectified Flow in continuous Euclidean space, we propose the Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow) model, which enables one-step categorical generation on statistical manifolds by explicitly learning geodesic trajectories that adhere to the intrinsic Riemannian geometry. By rectifying the flow on the statistical manifold, we theoretically guarantee that trajectories between prior and target distributions approximate geodesics. This rectification significantly reduces the transport cost by aligning the learned trajectories directly along geodesics on the statistical manifold, allowing the model to map pure noise to target discrete data in a single step. Through extensive experiments on diverse real-world generative tasks, ranging from image and text to biological domains, we demonstrate ReSFlow's superior one-step generation quality, which truly embodies geodesically optimal and rapid categorical generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaohuanjia/ReSFlow.
papers.summary: Flow-based generative models for discrete data learn continuous vector fields on statistical manifolds, but because the learned flows are not constrained to follow geodesics they need many numerical integration steps at inference. Rectified Statistical Flow (`ReSFlow`) adapts the straight-and-fast idea of `Rectified Flow` from Euclidean space to the statistical manifold, explicitly learning trajectories that respect its Riemannian geometry, with a theoretical guarantee that rectified paths between prior and target approximate geodesics and thereby reduce transport cost. The authors claim **one-step generation from pure noise to discrete data with superior quality** across image, text, and biological tasks, and release code.

papers.title: Learning Schwarzschild Geodesic Motion with Lagrangian Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn dynamics from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving accelerations through the Euler--Lagrange equation, providing a variational inductive bias that improves physical consistency over purely data-driven models. LNNs have recently been extended to general relativistic settings, leaving Schwarzschild geodesics as an open challenge. Training on complex relativistic systems is hindered by the diversity of the dynamics, as well as numerical instabilities and the difficulty of adequately sampling physically relevant, diverse orbital regimes. We introduce two coordinated improvements: a decoupled position--velocity normalization scheme that independently rescales each coordinate and its time derivatives, reweighting acceleration targets to balance contributions across all channels; and an energy-constrained log-uniformly sampled dataset generation strategy informed by the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) structure. With these improvements, our model accurately reproduces perihelion precession and relativistic time dilation, conserves energy and angular momentum to within a few percent even after completing multiple orbits around the central mass and predicts orbital trajectories across eight orbital scenarios in close, medium, and far-field regimes. These results establish that LNNs, augmented with physically motivated normalization and sampling, can reliably learn geodesic dynamics in curved spacetime. Our work also represents the first successful training of LNNs on Schwarzschild geodesics and offers a promising direction for data-driven modeling of complex relativistic systems.
papers.summary: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn dynamics by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving accelerations through the Euler-Lagrange equation, but training them on relativistic systems has been hampered by diverse dynamics, numerical instability, and the difficulty of sampling physically relevant orbits. The authors add a decoupled position-velocity normalization scheme that rescales each coordinate and its time derivatives independently and reweights acceleration targets across channels, together with an energy-constrained, log-uniformly sampled dataset informed by the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO) structure. The resulting model reproduces perihelion precession and relativistic time dilation, **conserves energy and angular momentum to within a few percent over multiple orbits**, and predicts trajectories across eight orbital scenarios spanning close, medium, and far-field regimes, which the authors present as the first successful LNN training on Schwarzschild geodesics.

papers.title: How Reliable are AMR Parser Outputs? Uncertainty Estimation for AMR Parsing
papers.abstract: Recent advances have significantly improved the performance of Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers, yet determining when their outputs can be trusted remains largely unexplored. This work presents the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting using top-k beam-search candidates. Uncertainty is estimated from pairwise candidate similarities and evaluated using the Prediction Rejection Ratio. This work characterises the relationship between parsing performance and uncertainty, evaluates the reliability of beam candidate distributions, analyses the effect of evaluation metrics on uncertainty assessment, and identifies parsers that provide the strongest balance between performance and reliability. Experimental results show the value of uncertainty estimation as a complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers.
papers.summary: Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) parsers have improved substantially, but there has been no way to tell when a given parse can be trusted. The authors present the first study of uncertainty estimation for AMR parsers in a black-box setting, deriving uncertainty from pairwise similarities among top-k beam-search candidates and scoring it with the Prediction Rejection Ratio. The study characterizes how parsing performance relates to uncertainty, assesses the reliability of beam candidate distributions, examines how the choice of evaluation metric affects uncertainty assessment, and identifies the parsers with the best balance of accuracy and reliability, concluding that **uncertainty estimation is a useful complementary dimension for evaluating AMR parsers**.

papers.title: The Predictability Bias of Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning in Medical Imaging
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context. Point prediction summarizes the conditional target distribution and cannot reproduce variation that the context does not resolve. We call this constraint predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT), recurrent anatomy is predictable from context, whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not. We introduce TAP-JEPA, a ViT-B/3D trained on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with state-of-the-art encoders (COLIPRI, Merlin, VoxelFM) in scan-level classification. We then audit the learned predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used during training. Prediction lowers the mean Skill (prevalence-normalized average precision) from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology, but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy. Along the teacher direction, separating pathology from matched control regions in the same organ, prediction moves pathology 34.7% toward the controls and controls 13.6% toward pathology, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Replacing visible matched-control representations increases surrounding-target prediction loss more than fully replacing pathology representations across four pathology categories. Downstream, removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes. Together, these results show that contextual predictability is not a sufficient proxy for clinical relevance in medical representation learning. Training objectives should therefore retain diagnostic features regardless of their predictability from surrounding anatomy.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting teacher representations of masked regions from visible context, but point prediction can only reproduce variation that the context resolves, a limitation the authors call predictability bias. In computed tomography (CT) recurring anatomy is predictable from context whereas the sporadic, localized pathology that determines clinical interpretation often is not, so the authors train `TAP-JEPA`, a ViT-B/3D on 113,611 CT volumes that is competitive with encoders such as `COLIPRI`, `Merlin`, and `VoxelFM` on scan-level classification, and then audit its predictive pathway by replaying the exact masking, teacher, and predictor computations used in training. **Prediction lowers mean Skill, a prevalence-normalized average precision, from 0.388 to 0.271 for pathology but only from 0.921 to 0.873 for anatomy**, and along the teacher direction it moves pathology representations 34.7% toward matched controls, with larger shifts farther from visible context. Removing all final-layer pathology tokens reduces the decision margin by at most 0.45% in four of seven scan-level probes, leading the authors to argue that training objectives should retain diagnostic features regardless of how predictable they are from surrounding anatomy.

papers.title: State-OPD: State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
papers.abstract: On-Policy Distillation (OPD) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for transferring reasoning capabilities from frontier models to smaller models, while extending its success to multi-turn agentic environments remains challenging. We study agentic OPD through interaction states, distinguishing the objective task and executed action-observation record from the internal semantic trajectory of student reasoning. Through this lens, we identify two roles of student reasoning in multi-turn OPD: prior reasoning distorts teacher supervision, while current reasoning shapes the action alternatives sampled at the same state. Specifically, at matched interaction states, removing prior student reasoning improves teacher continuation success and changes the teacher's token-level targets, with larger continuation gains at later turns. Meanwhile, resampling complete reasoning-action responses yields greater action diversity at the same state than resampling actions under a fixed reasoning trace. We introduce State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation, a framework that grounds teacher supervision in interaction states and reallocates the sampling budget to generate multiple complete reasoning-action responses at states with high response entropy, while retaining full-history student generation. Comprehensive evaluations across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and WebShop demonstrate that State-OPD achieves the highest macro-average success rate among the evaluated methods for both Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B students. Notably, for Qwen3-4B, State-OPD raises macro-average success from 26.07\% with the strongest baseline to 31.74\% and surpasses its Qwen3-32B teacher on ALFWorld Seen. Further analyses reveal that State-OPD achieves higher task success with fewer supervised turn responses and substantially reduces persistent failed-action repetition; qualitative traces illustrate decision revision based on interaction feedback.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers reasoning from frontier models to smaller ones, but extending it to multi-turn agentic environments is hard because the student's own reasoning both distorts teacher supervision and shapes which actions get sampled. Analyzing interaction states, which separate the objective task and action-observation record from the student's internal reasoning trace, the authors find that removing prior student reasoning improves the teacher's continuation success and changes its token-level targets, especially at later turns, and that resampling complete reasoning-action responses yields more action diversity than resampling actions under a fixed reasoning trace. State-Grounded On-Policy Distillation (`State-OPD`) grounds teacher supervision in interaction states and reallocates the sampling budget to generate multiple complete responses at high-entropy states while keeping full-history student generation. Across `ALFWorld`, `ScienceWorld`, and `WebShop` it achieves the highest macro-average success among evaluated methods for `Qwen3-1.7B` and `Qwen3-4B` students, and **for Qwen3-4B it lifts macro-average success from 26.07% with the strongest baseline to 31.74% and surpasses its Qwen3-32B teacher on ALFWorld Seen**, with fewer supervised turn responses and far less repetition of failed actions.

papers.title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
papers.abstract: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. The correlation does not show what the judge responds to: the music, the text prompt, or the way the question is asked. We propose four probes that test each of these, three of them read against a control computed from the human ratings: removing the audio, replacing the clip with another model's clip for the same prompt, swapping the order of two clips in pairwise judging, and rewording the instruction. We apply them to five open judges on all 2,748 clips of MusicEval, and the last two to the SongEval songs. Without audio, no judge exceeds what the prompt alone predicts from the human ratings, and for prompt alignment every judge falls below it. With audio, every judge follows the clip it hears when rating prompt alignment, two do when rating musical quality, and the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts' alignment rating more than their quality rating. The pairwise verdicts of the four smaller judges follow the position of a clip in the pair (its slot) rather than its quality on both rating sets. For musical quality, rewording the instruction moves the correlation of most judges as much as changing the judge. MusicEval's prompt assignment bounds any prompt-only judge at the model level. We recommend reporting the four probes with every music judge.
papers.summary: Open audio-language models are increasingly used to judge generated music, and are validated by correlating their ratings with expert ratings, yet correlation alone does not reveal whether a judge responds to the audio, the text prompt, or the phrasing of the question. The authors propose four probes, removing the audio, swapping in another model's clip for the same prompt, reversing the order of two clips in pairwise judging, and rewording the instruction, with three of them read against a control computed from the human ratings, and apply them to five open judges on all 2,748 clips of `MusicEval` plus the `SongEval` songs. **Without audio, no judge beats what the prompt alone predicts from the human ratings**, and with audio the strongest judge's quality score tracks the experts' prompt-alignment rating more than their quality rating. The four smaller judges' pairwise verdicts follow a clip's slot in the pair rather than its quality, and rewording the instruction shifts most judges' correlation about as much as switching judges, so the authors recommend reporting all four probes with any music judge.

papers.title: Vision Transformers Learn Word Meaning from Images Alone
papers.abstract: Can a vision model learn what words mean from pixels alone? We show that the two largest DINOv3 vision transformers organize words rendered in images by word meaning, despite being pretrained using self-supervision on images only, without paired captions, class labels, or other language supervision. We derive word representations from embedding differences between word images and matched controls, then test whether semantically related words are neighbors within each model's embedding space, while controlling for spelling similarity. We find that brand names in the same industry group together, as do nouns from the same semantic domain. Country-capital pairs exhibit consistent vector offsets, similarly to word embeddings trained on text. These word representations also align with the representations of the visual object categories they name. DINOv3-H and DINOv3-7B are, to our knowledge, the first self-supervised vision models to show substantial semantic structure for rendered words. Comparisons with text and speech encoders reveal shared structure among representations of the same words. Contrastive alignment with either encoder further strengthened DINOv3-H's word-level semantic structure, while leaving the other finetuned vision models largely unchanged. Image-only training can therefore teach vision models not just what words look like, but also how their meanings relate.
papers.summary: The two largest `DINOv3` vision transformers, `DINOv3-H` and `DINOv3-7B`, turn out to organize words rendered as images by their meaning, despite being pretrained with self-supervision on images only and no captions, class labels, or other language supervision. The authors derive word representations from embedding differences between word images and matched controls and test whether semantically related words are neighbors while controlling for spelling similarity. **Brand names cluster by industry, nouns cluster by semantic domain, and country-capital pairs show consistent vector offsets like those in text word embeddings**, and these word representations also align with the representations of the visual object categories they name. Comparisons with text and speech encoders reveal shared structure among representations of the same words, and contrastive alignment with either encoder further strengthens DINOv3-H's word-level semantic structure while leaving the other fine-tuned vision models largely unchanged.

papers.title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow
papers.abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. Meanwhile, traditional alternatives like Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs) remain highly competitive and run efficiently on CPUs, suggesting that tabular tasks may not inherently require deep architectures. This contrast raises a fundamental question: can TFMs be simplified by removing architectural redundancies without sacrificing performance? To answer this, we introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of the blocks, leaving the rest unchanged. Evaluating eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets, we reveal that tabular transformers are vastly overparameterized: replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most $0.002$ median AUROC across all architectures, with the half-depth TabFM still outperforming every other full-depth TFMs and tuned GBDTs. Furthermore, different model families are overparameterized in different ways: TabPFN-3 relies on its encoders, maintaining performance regardless of which single block is retained. Other single-axis models spread computation thinly, needing only their first block, while dual-axis models concentrate it in one critical block. Ultimately, removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters, speeds up GPU inference by up to $6\times$ at a median cost of $0.03$ AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries $2.4\times$ faster using $6\times$ less memory at negligible cost.
papers.summary: In-context-learning tabular foundation models (TFMs) solve new tasks without training but stack many transformer blocks, while gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) stay competitive on CPUs, raising the question of whether tabular tasks need such depth at all. The authors introduce a closed-form, label-free affine translator that replaces a contiguous window of up to 96% of a model's blocks while leaving the rest untouched, and evaluate eight frontier TFMs on 171 classification datasets. **Replacing half of a model's blocks costs at most 0.002 median AUROC across all architectures**, and one half-depth model still outperforms every other full-depth TFM and tuned GBDTs. Families are overparameterized in different ways, with `TabPFN-3` relying on its encoders and keeping its performance whichever single block is retained, other single-axis models needing only their first block, and dual-axis models concentrating computation in one critical block, and removing depth saves up to 1.5B parameters and speeds GPU inference by up to 6 times at a median cost of 0.03 AUROC, while a single-block TabPFN-3 serves cached queries 2.4 times faster with 6 times less memory at negligible cost.

papers.title: CAST: Credit Alignment for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) requires aligning teacher and student sequences before their scores can be compared. Decoded-text alignment provides such correspondence at the chunk level, but leaves a distinct problem unresolved: credit alignment. A chunk-level signal specifies how much a span should change, but not how that signal should be distributed across student tokens, while tokens without teacher correspondence remain unconstrained. We propose CAST (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring), a shift-or-stay framework that addresses both issues. For aligned chunks, CAST redistributes each chunk's advantage across student tokens using predictive uncertainty and local teacher-signal smoothness, emphasizing learning opportunities supported by locally consistent teacher feedback while preserving the chunk's total advantage. The resulting weights exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem. For unaligned positions, CAST selectively anchors the student to its initial policy through a KL penalty, limiting drift where teacher supervision is unavailable. Because credit assignment is separated from chunk construction, CAST also applies to punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under shared tokenization. Across six mathematics, science, and code benchmarks, CAST improves the average over the strongest evaluated baseline by $2.45$ and $1.32$ points for cross-tokenizer transfer from Qwen3-8B to Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively, and by $2.10$ points for shared-tokenizer transfer to Qwen3-1.7B.
papers.summary: Cross-tokenizer on-policy distillation (OPD) must align teacher and student sequences before comparing scores, and decoded-text alignment gives chunk-level correspondence but leaves open how a chunk's signal should be spread across student tokens, while tokens with no teacher counterpart are left unconstrained. `CAST` (Chunk-aware credit Assignment with Selective Token Anchoring) redistributes each aligned chunk's advantage across its student tokens according to predictive uncertainty and local smoothness of the teacher signal, preserving the chunk total through weights that exactly solve a KL-regularized credit-allocation problem, and anchors unaligned positions to the student's initial policy with a KL penalty. Because credit assignment is decoupled from chunk construction, the method also works with punctuation-defined or fixed-length chunks under a shared tokenizer, and across six math, science, and code benchmarks **it beats the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.45 and 1.32 average points** when distilling `Qwen3-8B` into `Mistral-7B` and `Llama-3.1-8B`, and by 2.10 points for shared-tokenizer transfer to `Qwen3-1.7B`.

papers.title: Neural Surrogate Modeling of Ultrasonic Wave Propagation in Heterogeneous Media
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates provide computationally efficient auto-regressive modeling of wave propagation, enabling e.g. fast inverse solutions. Despite recent progress, the current surrogates are not yet sufficient for the needs of ultrasonic sensing, characterized by high frequency and heterogeneous propagation media. We show how methods building on Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) fail to capture essential signal features, such as reflections, whereas U-Net -based methods learn the wave fields well but lack the ability to transfer information across different spatial scales. We then propose a new surrogate that captures the best of the two worlds, by integrating FNOs and local-integral resampling into a U-Net architecture. We show it can be trained on limited data, and that the predictions are robust to input noise and work across spatial scales.
papers.summary: Neural surrogates can replace expensive autoregressive simulation of wave propagation, enabling fast inverse solutions, but existing ones fall short for ultrasonic sensing, which involves high frequencies and heterogeneous media. The authors show that methods built on Fourier Neural Operators (`FNO`) miss essential features such as reflections, while `U-Net` based models learn the wave fields well but cannot transfer information across spatial scales, and they propose a hybrid that integrates FNOs and local-integral resampling into a U-Net architecture. They report that **the hybrid surrogate trains on limited data, stays robust to input noise, and works across spatial scales**.

papers.title: Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Metric Learning for Cross-Head Attention in Transformers
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Cross-Head Attention (DAMCHA), a simple and effective attention mechanism that generalizes Multi-Head Attention (MHA) through the lens of metric learning. Standard MHA implicitly learns a static, head-wise Euclidean similarity corresponding to the diagonal blocks of a unified cross-head metric matrix, discarding all off-diagonal interactions across heads. DAMCHA addresses this limitation via two key innovations. First, it learns the full cross-head metric matrix, inducing a Mahalanobis-like similarity that explicitly captures inter-head interactions beyond the restricted block-diagonal structure of MHA. Second, it parameterizes the metric matrix as an input-dependent function, enabling the attention geometry to dynamically adapt to the intrinsic manifold structure of the data rather than remaining fixed after training. We further introduce principled regularization strategies, most notably stack-wise parameter sharing, to ensure computational efficiency and stable optimization. DAMCHA serves as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants in various Transformer architectures, delivering superior expressive power and learning performance with comparable or reduced computational overhead. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DAMCHA-based Transformers consistently outperform competing baselines across a range of benchmark tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/erwinmsmith/DAMCHA.
papers.summary: Standard multi-head attention (MHA) implicitly uses a static, per-head Euclidean similarity, which corresponds to the diagonal blocks of a unified cross-head metric matrix and discards all off-diagonal interactions between heads. Data-Adaptive Mahalanobis Cross-Head Attention (`DAMCHA`) learns the full cross-head metric, inducing a Mahalanobis-like similarity that captures inter-head interactions, and parameterizes that metric as an input-dependent function so the attention geometry adapts to the data manifold, with regularization strategies such as stack-wise parameter sharing to keep optimization stable and overhead low. The authors present it as a drop-in replacement for MHA and its variants and claim **consistent gains over competing baselines across a range of benchmark tasks with comparable or reduced computational overhead**, with code released.

papers.title: CV-OPD: Contrastive Vision On-policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) reveals versatility and convenience during VLM post-training, providing dense supervision for student from teacher. However, we observed an anomaly that the distilled VLM could still answer the questions accurately even when the related visual regions were masked or replaced with noise. Building on this observation, our quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that OPD, which uses the answer as a hint, has failed to teach students to genuinely seek out and rely on visual evidence. Our theoretical analysis suggests that this failure arises from a shortcut enabled by the lack of visual constraints during distillation. To address the issue, we introduce Contrastive Vision On-policy Distillation (CV-OPD), which compares teacher distributions induced by positive and negative crops while conditioning on the same student prefix and augments optimization with a margin-based contrastive constraint, which is modulated with discrepancy gating across token and sample level. Specifically, CV-OPD first introduces a negative teacher unrelated to the answer and designs a Contrastive Divergence Loss (CDL) that constrains the feature distribution of student by contrasting the positive and negative teachers, correcting how the student exploits visual regions. The CV-OPD introduces a Discrepancy Aware Gate (DAG) that uses token-level and sample-level discrepancies to select visually relevant tokens for optimization, directing the student's attention toward visual content. Extensive experiments across a broad range of fine-grained visual benchmarks demonstrate that CV-OPD substantially alleviates shortcut and consistently improves the visual reasoning capabilities of existing VLMs.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) gives vision-language models (VLMs) dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but the authors find that distilled students often answer correctly even when the relevant image regions are masked or replaced with noise, and they argue theoretically that answer-conditioned distillation opens a shortcut because nothing constrains the student to use visual evidence. Their fix, `CV-OPD`, pairs the usual positive teacher with a negative teacher that sees an answer-irrelevant crop, applies a Contrastive Divergence Loss that pushes the student's distribution toward the positive teacher and away from the negative one, and uses a Discrepancy Aware Gate to restrict optimization to tokens where the two teachers disagree at the token and sample level. **Across a range of fine-grained visual benchmarks, the method substantially reduces the masking shortcut while consistently improving visual reasoning** over standard distillation.

papers.title: Forgetting is Not Always Bad: A Neuro-Inspired Memory Repair Mechanism for Poisoned LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are highly vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks. Existing defenses primarily rely on external modules for either static memory isolation or continuous online auditing, resulting in low memory efficiency and high computational overhead. To address these limitations, inspired by neuroscientific mechanisms that weak reactivation can destabilize memories and induce decay in the absence of reinforcement, we propose an agent-intrinsic training-free memory repair framework, DREAM (Dynamic Reactivation for Engram Attenuation in Memory), that enables selective functional forgetting of poisoned memories. Specifically, DREAM implements a three-stage pipeline: perturbation-induced implicit reactivation to reveal the structural fragility of malicious memories, adaptive anomaly diagnosis based on multi-dimensional activation patterns to detect topological anomalies, and a dynamic memory repair module that selectively suppresses harmful memories while reinforcing benign ones. Extensive experiments across diverse attackers and real-world tasks demonstrate that DREAM reduces attack success rates by over 95\% against backdoor poisoning while preserving strong benign utility. DREAM also achieves competitive robustness against injection attacks. In terms of runtime and token consumption, DREAM achieves up to a 2.13$\times$ speedup and a 37.7\% reduction in token consumption compared with A-MemGuard. Furthermore, DREAM also achieves a task success rate of 92.96\% on poisoned multi-agent systems.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents with persistent memory are vulnerable to poisoning, and current defenses rely on external isolation or continuous auditing modules that cost memory and compute. `DREAM` (Dynamic Reactivation for Engram Attenuation in Memory) is a training-free, agent-intrinsic repair pipeline inspired by the neuroscience finding that weak reactivation without reinforcement destabilizes memories: it perturbs stored memories to expose structural fragility, diagnoses anomalies from multi-dimensional activation patterns, and then selectively suppresses the flagged entries while reinforcing benign ones. **Against backdoor poisoning it cuts attack success rates by over 95%** while preserving benign utility, remains competitive against injection attacks, runs up to 2.13 times faster with 37.7% fewer tokens than `A-MemGuard`, and reaches a 92.96% task success rate on poisoned multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis
papers.abstract: API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code, existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event - overlooking the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and market-driven evolution of these artifacts. To address this issue, we present Agent4Spec, an autonomous multi-agent framework featuring two distinct pipelines: (1) a validation pipeline that detects and self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and (2) a market analysis pipeline that conducts competitive research, identifies functional gaps against industry leaders, and automatically generates missing API-spec functionalities. We evaluate Agent4Spec on two curated datasets of API specifications spanning both general-purpose and industrial scenarios. Among 9 SOTA LLMs, the top-performer achieves 100% syntax error detection rates and over 95% implementation success for proposed corrections, while securing over 50% adoption rates for suggested endpoint improvements, representing a practical tool for API development.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can draft OpenAPI specifications from source code, but existing work treats generation as a one-off step and ignores ongoing validation, maintenance, and evolution against competing products. `Agent4Spec` is a multi-agent framework with two pipelines: one detects and self-corrects OpenAPI syntax errors, and the other performs competitive research against industry leaders, identifies functional gaps, and generates the missing endpoint specifications. Evaluated on two curated datasets covering general-purpose and industrial APIs with nine state-of-the-art LLMs, **the best-performing model detected 100% of syntax errors and implemented over 95% of proposed corrections successfully**, and more than half of its suggested endpoint additions were adopted.

papers.title: CopRoute: Dependence-Aware Conformal Routing for Language Models
papers.abstract: Set-based language model routing aims to increase the coverage of the event where at least one model answers a query correctly while controlling the number of inference calls made. Existing risk-controlled routing policies bound the all-miss risk (the probability that every model in the selected set fails) by calibrating a single conformal threshold and applying it to a nested family of model sets. Because each model is scored in isolation, these policies ignore the dependence structure of model failures. Models that share training data or architecture tend to fail on the same queries, so two individually strong models can be jointly redundant while a weaker but complementary model covers the queries that the others miss. To account for this dependence, which existing risk-controlled policies ignore, we propose CopRoute, which orders models by how many new queries each one answers correctly beyond those already selected, decides per query how far down that order to go, and then picks the smallest cutoff that still meets the target risk. We show that CopRoute's ordering attains, on the design data, the best guarantee any efficient fixed-ordering algorithm can give for the average number of calls to the first correct model, and that a separate calibration step certifies the all-miss risk of the deployed sets. On RouterBench and RouterEval, CopRoute attains the fewest certified calls on nine of ten datasets at a target risk of 0.05 and on eight of ten at 0.10, making up to 79 percent fewer calls (median 24 percent) than the state-of-the-art risk-controlled policy at the same certified all-miss risk.
papers.summary: Set-based routing calls several language models per query and tries to ensure at least one answers correctly while limiting inference calls, but existing risk-controlled policies score models independently and so ignore that models sharing data or architecture tend to fail on the same queries. `CopRoute` orders models greedily by how many additional queries each one covers beyond those already selected, decides per query how deep to go in that order, and calibrates a conformal cutoff that certifies the all-miss risk of the deployed sets. The authors show the ordering achieves the best guarantee available to any efficient fixed-ordering method for expected calls to the first correct model, and on `RouterBench` and `RouterEval` it attains the fewest certified calls on nine of ten datasets at a 0.05 target risk, **making up to 79% fewer calls (median 24%) than the state-of-the-art risk-controlled policy** at the same certified risk.

papers.title: Beyond the Final Embedding: Retrieving Memories from Token-Level Evidence
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve evidence from stored conversations and documents to answer queries. Most embedding-based retrievers compare single-vector representations of queries and memories, even when relevance depends on a small part of the content. Such local evidence can be matched to queries using the contextual token representations already computed by the same embedding models. Our method uses sparse token matching to improve retrieval without additional training. Each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories. The matching scores are aggregated for each memory and combined with whole-memory similarity to rank memories. An optional low-rank query adapter can be trained with supervision while keeping the encoder and stored memory representations fixed. Our method improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families without additional training. Query adaptation further increases the gains to 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on Qwen3-Embedding-4B. These retrieval gains translate into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.
papers.summary: Memory-augmented assistants retrieve past conversations and documents with single-vector embeddings, even though relevance often hinges on a small passage inside a long memory. The proposed method reuses the contextual token representations that the embedding model already computes: each query token retrieves a small set of matching tokens across candidate memories, the match scores are aggregated per memory, and the result is combined with whole-memory similarity for ranking, with no extra training required; an optional low-rank query adapter can be trained while the encoder and stored memory vectors stay frozen. The training-free variant improves retrieval across eight benchmarks and multiple model families, **and with query adaptation the gains reach 13.3 and 14.3 percentage points in average Recall@10 and NDCG@10 on `Qwen3-Embedding-4B`**, translating into higher question-answering accuracy on long-term memory benchmarks.

papers.title: MHR-Router: Multimodal Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing for VLM Inference
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit complementary capabilities, yet selecting the most suitable expert for a given image-question query remains challenging due to heterogeneous multimodal inputs and varying expert strengths. Existing routing approaches rely on text-based cues or static model profiles, failing to capture fine-grained visual evidence and expert-specific failure patterns. To address this, we propose MHR-Router, a multimodal heterogeneous retrieval-enhanced adaptive routing framework for VLM inference. It accurately dispatches each multimodal query to the most suitable VLM expert via local retrieval evidence. MHR-Router consists of two stages: (1) Multimodal Routing Representation, which fuses frozen multimodal features into a comprehensive query representation; and (2) Heterogeneous Retrieval-Enhanced Adaptive Routing, which retrieves expert-specific success and failure memories as local evidence and employs a shared scorer to adaptively select the optimal expert. Experiments show that MHR-Router effectively achieves heterogeneous modality routing and consistently improves accuracy over traditional baselines.
papers.summary: Different vision-language models (VLMs) excel at different image-question queries, but existing routers rely on text-only cues or static model profiles and miss fine-grained visual evidence and expert-specific failure modes. `MHR-Router` first fuses frozen multimodal features into a joint query representation, then retrieves each candidate expert's past successes and failures on similar queries as local evidence and feeds them to a shared scorer that picks the expert to dispatch to. **The retrieval-enhanced router consistently improves accuracy over traditional routing baselines** on heterogeneous multimodal queries.

papers.title: BoundaryEvo: Data-Model Co-Evolution at the Capability Boundary for Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Distilling long-chain reasoning trajectories from large teacher models provides an effective way to improve the reasoning ability of small language models. However, existing methods typically select a fixed training set before distillation, overlooking that the usefulness of a reasoning example changes as the student evolves. This mismatch becomes especially costly when only a small number of teacher trajectories can be used for training. Besides, examples already mastered provide little new supervision, while examples far beyond the capability of student may be difficult to learn from. Training data should therefore adapt as model capability evolves, yet reliable data selection is difficult when the student is initially weak. To address these challenges, our key idea is to first establish the basic reasoning capability and then adapt the training data to the evolving capability boundary of the student. We propose BoundaryEvo, a two-stage data--model co-evolution framework. In Capability Priming, we directly distill a small set of teacher-generated long reasoning trajectories without using a separate model to judge and filter them, allowing the student to acquire an initial reasoning capability before capability-aware data selection. In Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution, we repeatedly select questions that the current student has not mastered but the expert can reliably solve, and update the training data as the student evolves. With only 1,000 training examples, BoundaryEvo consistently outperforms static and dynamic data selection baselines across 11 reasoning benchmarks, raising the original Qwen3.5-4B accuracy from 62.9 to 75.3 on IMO-AnswerBench and from 26.8 to 46.0 on AMO-Bench. The code and data will be made publicly available.
papers.summary: Distilling long reasoning traces from a large teacher into a small student usually uses a fixed training set, even though an example's usefulness changes as the student improves and only a small number of teacher trajectories may be affordable. `BoundaryEvo` runs in two stages: Capability Priming distills a small unfiltered set of teacher traces to establish basic reasoning ability, and Capability-Boundary Co-Evolution then repeatedly selects questions the current student fails but the teacher reliably solves, refreshing the training data as the student evolves. **Using only 1,000 training examples, the method beats static and dynamic data selection baselines on 11 reasoning benchmarks**, lifting `Qwen3.5-4B` from 62.9 to 75.3 on `IMO-AnswerBench` and from 26.8 to 46.0 on `AMO-Bench`.

papers.title: Do Prompt Optimizers Break Requirements They Are Not Scored On? A Preregistered Study
papers.abstract: Prompt optimizers rewrite a prompt to raise one target metric, but prompts also state requirements the metric does not score, such as an output format, citations, or abstention. In a preregistered study, we run GEPA, MIPROv2, and TextGrad on HotpotQA, SQuAD 2.0, and IFEval and count per-item violations of unscored requirements with deterministic checks. By the preregistered criterion, all three optimizers produce regressions, substantially on HotpotQA, where net regression in citation validity reaches 10.7 to 41.6 points while exact match rises by 21 to 34 points. A post-hoc decomposition changes this reading. The optimized prompts elicit reasoning before the required JSON object, and under the 200-token output cap used throughout, 13.9% to 47.0% of responses end before any answer appears. Among parseable outputs, net regression is within 3 points of zero. With a 1,024-token cap, extraction failures disappear, content regression stays below 1 point, and exact match rises further. Two simple gates fail the preregistered criterion. The side effect is narrower than hypothesized: optimized prompts are more accurate and break an explicit output contract, and a lenient target metric does not show the cost.
papers.summary: Prompt optimizers maximize one scored metric, but prompts usually also carry unscored requirements such as output format, citations, or abstention, and this preregistered study asks whether optimization silently violates them. The authors run `GEPA`, `MIPROv2`, and `TextGrad` on `HotpotQA`, `SQuAD 2.0`, and `IFEval` and count per-item violations with deterministic checks; by the preregistered criterion all three optimizers regress, most sharply on `HotpotQA`, where citation validity drops 10.7 to 41.6 points while exact match rises 21 to 34 points. **A post-hoc decomposition attributes most of the damage to truncation: optimized prompts elicit reasoning before the required JSON object, so under the 200-token cap 13.9% to 47.0% of responses end before any answer appears, while among parseable outputs net regression is within 3 points of zero** and a 1,024-token cap eliminates the extraction failures. The side effect is narrower than hypothesized: optimized prompts are more accurate but break an explicit output contract that a lenient target metric fails to expose.

papers.title: Recovering Irreducible Three-Body Interactions with Lagrangian Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving the dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, biasing the model toward motion that respects the variational structure of mechanics. The interactions studied so far have been pairwise-additive, leaving open whether LNNs can recover an irreducible many-body interaction from motion alone.
