We address this using the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, the leading three-body dispersion term, whose dependence on the collective geometry of three particles cannot be represented by any sum of pairwise terms. We prescribe the kinetic energy exactly and learn only the potential, as a function of interparticle distances and angles. Combined with a signal-aware sampling strategy that concentrates training data where the three-body signal is strongest while preserving broad coverage of configuration space, this recovers the interaction from accelerations alone. The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and characteristic sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller interaction, and generates stable trajectories. Embedding it within a pairwise Lennard-Jones potential lets us examine its observability: the three-body term is recovered once its dynamical signature exceeds the residual modeling error, which it does cleanly at amplified coupling but not at the coupling of a real noble gas, bracketing the transition between the two. Finally, symbolic regression on the trained potential, with no assumed functional form, returns the Axilrod-Teller expression with angular numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact. An LNN with domain-specific structure can thus recover an irreducible three-body interaction from trajectories as a closed-form law, pointing toward learning interaction laws whose structure is not known a priori.
papers.summary: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, but prior work has only recovered pairwise-additive interactions. The authors test whether an LNN can recover the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, an irreducible three-body dispersion term that no sum of pairwise terms can represent, by fixing the kinetic energy exactly, learning only the potential as a function of interparticle distances and angles, and sampling training data where the three-body signal is strongest. **The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller term, and symbolic regression on it returns the closed-form expression with numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact**, though when embedded in a Lennard-Jones potential the term is only recoverable once its dynamical signature exceeds residual modeling error, which holds at amplified coupling but not at realistic noble-gas strength.

papers.title: PRIME: Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling Enhancement for Structured Document Retrieval-Real
papers.abstract: High-precision retrieval over external knowledge bases is essential for LLM agents to operate effectively. However, existing Information Retrieval (IR) research primarily optimizes query-side retrievers (e.g., ColBERT, BGE) and generators (e.g., Self-RAG, GraphRAG), while reducing corpus-side representation to chunking. This leaves index-side quality an underexplored lever. We propose Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling & Enhancement (PRIME), an index-side optimization framework built on two complementary tracks: an LLM-driven Semantic Restructuring (SR) track that transforms long documents into structured, information-dense sections, and a deterministic Metadata Synthesis (MS) and Hierarchical Retrieval (HR) track that extracts semantic anchors and heading structure for coarse-to-fine section retrieval. Our evaluations show that deterministic metadata matches structure-aware chunking's retrieval quality while cutting embedding computation by 45.8 $\times$ and index vector count by 22.4 $\times$. On top of these gains, Semantic Restructuring (SR) further improves Answer-F1 by 13.7% in full deployment, with characterized quality-fidelity-cost trade-offs. Across QASPER, BRIGHT, and NFCorpus, we further characterize three qualitative regimes that determine whether index-side optimization helps or degrades retrieval, while showing that these index-side effects are neutralized under a strong reranker.
papers.summary: Retrieval research for LLM agents has concentrated on query-side retrievers and generators while reducing the corpus side to chunking, leaving index quality largely unexplored. `PRIME` (Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling and Enhancement) optimizes the index with two tracks: an LLM-driven Semantic Restructuring track that rewrites long documents into structured, information-dense sections, and a deterministic Metadata Synthesis plus Hierarchical Retrieval track that extracts semantic anchors and heading structure for coarse-to-fine section retrieval. **Deterministic metadata matches structure-aware chunking's retrieval quality while cutting embedding computation 45.8 times and index vector count 22.4 times**, Semantic Restructuring adds a further 13.7% Answer-F1 in full deployment, and across `QASPER`, `BRIGHT`, and `NFCorpus` the authors identify three regimes governing whether index-side work helps or hurts, noting that the effects vanish under a strong reranker.

papers.title: Decoding Register Tokens Preserves Global Scene Details
papers.abstract: Pretrained vision transformers learn structured image representations spanning spatial patch tokens and non-spatial tokens. Recent analyses suggest that non-spatial register tokens encode global scene properties such as illumination, blur, and style. Yet patch-based image decoders discard these outputs, leaving the decoder to recover image appearance from patches alone. We investigate whether retaining register features improves decoding when the complete spatial patch representation is already available. We study this question using representation autoencoders (RAEs) with frozen register-equipped encoders. Our decoder processes four register tokens together with all patch tokens through joint self-attention. Appearance probes, paired reconstruction-error analysis, and fixed-decoder register substitutions examine which global image properties are accessible from registers and how their values affect reconstructed pixels. For generation, we train a multi-head attention pooling (MHAP) predictor to recover register features from sampled patches, keeping the pretrained diffusion model and its samples unchanged. On ImageNet-1K, our ViT-B decoders achieve mean reconstruction FIDs of 0.472 with DINOv2 and 0.442 with DINOv3, reductions of 9.5% and 5.2% relative to their respective patch-only baselines. The corresponding PSNRs are 19.73 and 20.54 dB. For generation, our DINOv2 models achieve a mean FID of 1.641, 9.8% below the patch-only baseline on identical sampled patches.
papers.summary: Pretrained vision transformers emit both spatial patch tokens and non-spatial register tokens, and recent analyses suggest the registers encode global properties such as illumination, blur, and style, yet patch-based image decoders discard them. Using representation autoencoders (RAEs) with frozen `DINOv2` and `DINOv3` encoders, the authors build a decoder that attends jointly over four register tokens and all patch tokens, then use appearance probes, paired reconstruction-error analysis, and register substitution to show which global properties the registers carry and how they shape reconstructed pixels; for generation, a multi-head attention pooling predictor recovers register features from sampled patches without changing the diffusion model. **On ImageNet-1K, ViT-B decoders reach reconstruction FIDs of 0.472 with `DINOv2` and 0.442 with `DINOv3`, 9.5% and 5.2% below patch-only baselines**, and generation FID with `DINOv2` falls 9.8% to 1.641 on identical sampled patches.

papers.title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
papers.abstract: Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from. Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences. Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next. We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio. The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens. Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments. Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training-inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts. To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference. On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision. It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations. Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.
papers.summary: Generating human motion in response to spatial audio requires modeling both what is heard and where it comes from, and prior methods work offline with the full audio sequence even though real listeners react without knowing what comes next. `Sonic-AMG` encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens and feeds them to a causal transformer with a flow head that produces continuous motion latents, decoded causally into motion segments; because teacher forcing derives motion history and source locations from ground truth while streaming inference must use generated motion, the authors add rehearsal training with short autoregressive self-rollouts and spatial feedback that recomputes source locations from generated root poses. **On the `SAM` benchmark it achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision** while supporting real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source positions.

papers.title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans
papers.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly deployed as panels, and disagreement among panel members is often read as a symptom of an unclear rubric. We test a label-free procedure that turns this disagreement into rubric repairs. The procedure decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested ones. An additional stage that moves text-checkable sub-criteria to deterministic checkers transferred none in our evaluation. Human labels are never used to select or edit clauses; they are used only to evaluate the outcome. We pre-specified four hypotheses in a version-controlled protocol and evaluated six rubric conditions with a panel of five judges from three providers on SummEval, the HealthBench meta-evaluation, and USR Topical-Chat, for a total of 129,770 judge requests, excluding retries. On SummEval, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's $\alpha$ by 0.069 (95% CI 0.046 to 0.092) over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that applied the same edits to an equal number of randomly chosen clauses that were not selected. Agreement with expert ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall $\tau$ difference -0.007, 95% CI -0.037 to 0.021). On HealthBench and USR, neither inter-judge agreement nor human agreement met the preregistered effect criteria. In a preregistered secondary comparison, human agreement after editing the contested clauses was lower than after editing the control clauses on all three datasets in point estimate, although no interval excluded zero. Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators. We will release code, frozen rubrics, item identifiers, and judge scores.
papers.summary: When panels of LLM judges disagree, the rubric is often blamed, so the authors test a label-free procedure that decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested clauses, with human labels used solely for evaluation. In a preregistered protocol with five judges from three providers on `SummEval`, the `HealthBench` meta-evaluation, and `USR Topical-Chat`, totaling 129,770 judge requests, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's alpha on `SummEval` by 0.069 over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that edited an equal number of random clauses. **Agreement with expert human ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall tau difference of -0.007), and on the other two datasets neither consensus nor human agreement met the preregistered criteria**, so disagreement-targeted edits make judges agree with each other more without bringing them closer to human annotators.

papers.title: DAG Structure Learning with Node-Varying Heavy-Tailed Disturbances
papers.abstract: DAG structures can be learned from observations by incorporating acyclicity via smooth constraints, such as DAGMA's log-determinant function. Typically, observations and the underlying DAG are related through linear structural equation models, with Gaussianity assumption on the disturbances at each node. Extending DAG learning methods that account for scale and tail behavior of disturbances that vary across nodes remains a challenge. We propose a node-varying Student-$t$ DAGMA that jointly estimates the graph structure, node-specific disturbance scales, and the degrees-of-freedom parameter. A Gaussian scale-mixture representation yields an iteratively reweighted formulation that down-weights large standardized residuals. Building on existing results, we also establish identifiability of the graph and disturbance parameters. Synthetic experiments demonstrate improved structural recovery under heterogeneous heavy-tailed disturbances, and experiments on real finance data show that the proposed method yields lower test negative log-likelihood than the evaluated baselines.
papers.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure learning methods such as `DAGMA` enforce acyclicity through smooth constraints but typically assume linear structural equations with Gaussian disturbances of equal scale, which breaks down when noise scale and tail heaviness vary across nodes. The authors propose a node-varying Student-t extension of `DAGMA` that jointly estimates the graph, per-node disturbance scales, and the degrees-of-freedom parameter, using a Gaussian scale-mixture representation to obtain an iteratively reweighted formulation that down-weights large standardized residuals, and they establish identifiability of both the graph and disturbance parameters. **Synthetic experiments show improved structural recovery under heterogeneous heavy-tailed noise**, and on real finance data the method achieves lower test negative log-likelihood than the evaluated baselines.

papers.title: MORAD: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Objective Rewards for RNA Inverse Design
papers.abstract: We introduce MORAD, an online reinforcement learning framework for backbone-conditioned RNA diffusion models that trains a single shared policy across diverse target backbones. Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences compatible with a target three-dimensional backbone, yet existing reinforcement learning approaches either optimize a separate policy for each target backbone or rely on offline preference optimization, leaving online post-training of a reusable backbone-conditioned model largely unexplored. MORAD combines backbone-conditioned group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective. Beyond existing RL rewards that primarily target tertiary structural quality, MORAD jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition. To aggregate these heterogeneous objectives despite differences in scale and optimization direction, MORAD maps each measurement to a bounded desirability score and combines them with a weighted geometric mean. Compared with a tertiary-structure-only reward, this multi-objective formulation improves 10 of the 11 evaluation metrics that have a preferred direction. Applied to pretrained RIDE, MORAD improves GDT-TS by 16.0% (from 0.3300 to 0.3827) and pairing MCC by 19.4% (from 0.6110 to 0.7295), while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5% (from 0.3906 to 0.2830). On the test set, MORAD outperforms RiboDiffusion, gRNAde, and RDesign across tertiary structural accuracy, secondary-structure pairing, and thermodynamic quality, establishing a new state of the art in structure-conditioned RNA inverse design.
papers.summary: Structure-conditioned RNA inverse design seeks nucleotide sequences that fold into a target 3D backbone, but existing reinforcement learning approaches either train a separate policy per backbone or rely on offline preference optimization. `MORAD` trains a single backbone-conditioned diffusion policy online using group sampling, group-relative reward normalization, and a forward-process diffusion objective, and it jointly optimizes six measurements spanning tertiary geometry, base pairing, ensemble behavior, and sequence composition by mapping each to a bounded desirability score and combining them with a weighted geometric mean. Applied to the pretrained `RIDE` model, **it raises GDT-TS by 16.0% and pairing MCC by 19.4% while reducing normalized ensemble defect by 27.5%**, improves 10 of 11 directional metrics over a tertiary-only reward, and outperforms `RiboDiffusion`, `gRNAde`, and `RDesign` on the test set.

papers.title: Structure-Aware Numerical Stabilization for Half-Precision Proximal Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Local online training on resource-constrained platforms requires low computational and training-state overhead. We study the numerical stability and computational efficiency of half-precision proximal policy optimization (PPO) on commodity GPUs. Directly converting PPO training to FP16 is unreliable because numerical errors feed back through policy updates and subsequent data collection, while PPO repeatedly compares a current policy with a fixed behavior policy. We propose PPO-FP16 with three structure-aware modules. Global scalar protection stabilizes statistics shared across a minibatch or parameter update. Policy-change residual protection extracts and preserves small differences between the current and behavior policies. Efficient persistent-update protection stabilizes optimizer state and parameter writeback while reducing state storage. These changes preserve the PPO objective, hyperparameters, and training budget. Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 achieves the lowest mean return-AUC rank (1.90) among the four methods and ranks first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons. Eight of nine performance configurations yield PPO update speedups ranging from 1.16 to 2.03 times. Relative to Full FP32 Adam, optimizer-state memory is reduced by 71.7 to 74.9 percent, and peak allocated GPU memory is reduced by up to 44.5 percent. The results show that protecting a small set of structurally important quantities can deliver stable, efficient FP16 PPO without retuning.
papers.summary: Online reinforcement learning on resource-constrained hardware needs low compute and training-state overhead, but naively running proximal policy optimization (PPO) in FP16 is unreliable because numerical errors feed back through policy updates and data collection, and PPO repeatedly compares a current policy against a fixed behavior policy. `PPO-FP16` adds three structure-aware protections: global scalar protection for statistics shared across a minibatch or update, policy-change residual protection that extracts and preserves the small differences between current and behavior policies, and persistent-update protection for optimizer state and parameter writeback, all without altering the PPO objective, hyperparameters, or training budget. Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds it achieves the best mean return-AUC rank among four methods and ranks first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons, **with PPO update speedups of 1.16 to 2.03 times, optimizer-state memory reduced 71.7 to 74.9%, and peak GPU memory reduced up to 44.5%** relative to full FP32 Adam.

papers.title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
papers.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
papers.summary: Data center energy use and the need for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings motivate pushing learning to the edge, treating the building itself as the data center. The authors validate resilient data acquisition chains on affordable Arduino hardware (Uno R4 WiFi with BME280 sensors) with Node-RED/MySQL archiving and rsync/SSH transfer, propose a lightweight orchestration framework called `KOptim` that is interoperable with the FIWARE standard for managing service level agreements, and adapt the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for principal component analysis on low-power microcontrollers using a buffered iterative scheme that sorts and preserves extreme samples to maintain diversity. **On the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data, the buffered GHA converges to results visually equivalent to full-memory processing** and reliably identifies two distinct operational states, at an O(W log W) sorting cost per buffer.

papers.title: JEPA-kMMVAE: CSI Prediction for Time-Varying Wireless Channels
papers.abstract: This paper considers channel state information (CSI) prediction using neural networks for time-varying multi-antenna channels from noisy historical observations. The main challenge is to exploit temporal correlation while distinguishing channel evolution from observation noise. We propose JEPA-kMMVAE, which combines a joint-embedding predictive architecture with a k-memory Markov variational autoencoder to predict future CSI through temporally structured latent representations. The framework supports direct prediction and residual corrections relative to the latest latent state and noisy CSI observation. Simulation results show that the residual configuration outperforms the evaluated baselines at moderate and high input CSI signal-to-noise ratios, while sequence baselines remain more accurate under stronger noise.
papers.summary: Predicting channel state information (CSI) for time-varying multi-antenna wireless channels from noisy historical observations requires exploiting temporal correlation while separating true channel evolution from observation noise. `JEPA-kMMVAE` combines a joint-embedding predictive architecture with a k-memory Markov variational autoencoder to forecast future CSI through temporally structured latent representations, supporting both direct prediction and residual corrections relative to the latest latent state and noisy observation. **In simulation, the residual configuration outperforms the evaluated baselines at moderate and high input signal-to-noise ratios**, while conventional sequence baselines remain more accurate under heavy noise.

papers.title: SBNO : Schr\"odinger Bridge Neural Operator for the Forward and Inverse Problems under Missing Information
papers.abstract: Partial differential equation (PDE) surrogate modeling often relies on either dense observations or access to governing equations/physics constraints. In practice, observations can be sparse and partial, and the underlying physics may be partially specified or unavailable. We introduce SBNO, an equation-free paired-data diffusion bridge matching framework that learns conditional operators for both forward and inverse PDE problems under partial observations. SBNO uses diffusion Schr\"odinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware endpoint coupling that preserves empirical input-solution pairing during training and supports both PDE-task directions within a single framework. At inference time, SBNO produces a deterministic point reconstruction by integrating the probability-flow ODE constructed from the learned drift pair, without inference-time observation or PDE guidance-weight tuning. On five PDE benchmarks with 5% observations, SBNO achieves superior or comparable accuracy to baselines while demonstrating lower test-instance error dispersion. Furthermore, SBNO is at least $9.7 \times$ faster and reduces GPU memory by at least $4.3 \times$ compared to guided-diffusion baselines.
papers.summary: Surrogate models for partial differential equations (PDEs) usually need dense observations or explicit physics constraints, but in practice measurements are sparse and the governing equations may be partially specified or unknown. `SBNO` is an equation-free framework that uses diffusion Schrödinger bridge matching to learn a pair of time-dependent drifts from a mask-aware coupling of paired inputs and solutions, handling both forward and inverse PDE problems in one model and producing deterministic reconstructions at inference by integrating the probability-flow ODE without observation guidance or guidance-weight tuning. **On five PDE benchmarks with only 5% of the field observed, it matches or exceeds baseline accuracy with lower error dispersion while running at least 9.7 times faster and using at least 4.3 times less GPU memory than guided-diffusion baselines.**

papers.title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Web crawling is a major source of large language model (LLM) pretraining data, yet data-selection pipelines discard a large share of crawled pages. We investigate how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts to collect more high-quality pretraining data. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host crawl coverage, we find that roughly half of the variation in classifier scores occurs between hosts. In the crawls we analyze, a few pages from a host also provide a useful estimate of the quality of its remaining pages. Common Crawl uses harmonic centrality, a graph centrality metric, to guide its crawl allocation. In our simulations, using centrality to choose which hosts to crawl yields limited gains over random ordering and performs worse for some classifiers. For deciding how deeply to crawl each host, sampling a few pages and then fetching more from hosts with higher-scoring samples collects several times more high-quality pages per fetch than uniform depth or centrality-based allocation. Finally, Common Crawl's observed per-host coverage has little correlation with the evaluated quality signals. We estimate that tens of millions of high-quality pages remain among known but uncrawled URLs in each crawl examined, with most concentrated on a small share of hosts.
papers.summary: Web crawls supply much of the pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet quality filters discard a large share of what is fetched, raising the question of how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host coverage, the authors find that about half of the variation in quality scores lies between hosts, that a few sampled pages predict a host's remaining quality well, and that the harmonic centrality Common Crawl uses to guide allocation offers limited gains over random host ordering and sometimes does worse. **Sampling a few pages per host and then crawling deeper into hosts whose samples score highly collects several times more high-quality pages per fetch than uniform depth or centrality-based allocation**, and the authors estimate that tens of millions of high-quality pages remain uncrawled in each crawl examined, concentrated on a small share of hosts.

papers.title: Taking Tokenization off the Host for Agentic LLM Serving
papers.abstract: Agentic workloads resend long contexts that barely change between calls. Prefix caching now skips most of their prefill, yet every request must still be tokenized in full before the cache can even be consulted. Tokenization, a CPU stage long treated as negligible, becomes the largest part of time-to-first-token (TTFT), and a frontend that tokenizes for a whole GPU fleet limits how many GPUs it can feed. We present GraphTok, a GPU tokenizer that runs the entire encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, as one replayable CUDA graph. GraphTok reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit on GPT-2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, DeepSeek-V3, and Gemma 3, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified vLLM and NVIDIA Dynamo. GraphTok encodes one million GPT-2 tokens in 1.7-3.2 ms including data transfers, and on Llama 3 it is 4.7-6.0x faster than gigatoken, the strongest CPU tokenizer. On TokTier's own single-request benchmark, it is 2.6-3.9x faster than gigatoken and up to 18.1x faster than TokTier. In vLLM with a cached prefix, it lowers mean TTFT by 2.1-2.4x. The largest gain is capacity. Within a 2 s P99 target, one Dynamo frontend with GraphTok sustains 518 requests/s of 121k-token traffic, the busiest-hour load of 56 GPUs, against 296 with gigatoken and 18.5 with the default tokenizer. Across 121k to one million tokens, this is 1.75-2.5x the load gigatoken sustains, with a P99 up to 64x lower where gigatoken's tail breaks.
papers.summary: In agentic serving, prefix caching skips most of the prefill, but every request still has to be tokenized in full on the CPU before the cache can be consulted, so tokenization becomes the dominant share of time-to-first-token (TTFT) and a single frontend can only feed a limited number of GPUs. `GraphTok` moves the whole encoding pipeline, from pre-tokenization through byte-pair encoding (BPE) merging to token-ID assembly, onto the GPU as one replayable CUDA graph, hands short inputs to a CPU engine where the GPU cannot win, and plugs into unmodified `vLLM` and `NVIDIA Dynamo`. It reproduces the reference token IDs bit-for-bit for `GPT-2`, `Llama 3`, `Qwen 2.5`, `DeepSeek-V3`, and `Gemma 3`, runs 4.7-6.0x faster than the `gigatoken` CPU tokenizer on Llama 3, and lowers mean TTFT by 2.1-2.4x in vLLM with a cached prefix. **Within a 2 s P99 target, one Dynamo frontend sustains 518 requests/s of 121k-token traffic, against 296 with gigatoken and 18.5 with the default tokenizer.**

papers.title: DuoRate: Two-Rate Per-Expert Precision Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Serving
papers.abstract: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store-read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. Online, it profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate-distortion allocation under the decode functional; routing frequency provably cancels from every per-expert decision, and the solve costs one dot product per expert and a bisection. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, DuoRate reading 2.3 bpw exceeds every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4-1.6 bpw more. The advantage is largest under long decoding: on GSM8K, DuoRate at 2.9 bpw matches or exceeds every 4-bit format and trails BF16 by only 0.25 points, and at 2.6 bpw it still matches or exceeds the 4.5-bit NF4 and FP4. Against controls in its own format, the allocation alone is worth 0.07-0.11 bpw of read rate. Code will be released upon publication.
papers.summary: Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint counts every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step reads only the experts it selects, and published per-expert quantization allocators constrain only the former. The authors call this the store-read gap and note that the released `BitsMoE` checkpoint stores 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) yet reads 7.50 bpw during decode. `DuoRate` stores a single uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream plus a precomputed distortion tensor, then at deployment profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate-distortion allocation under the decode cost, which needs one dot product per expert and a bisection and from which routing frequency provably cancels. **On `Qwen3-30B-A3B`, reading 2.3 bpw beats every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy**, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4-1.6 bpw more, trailing BF16 by only 0.25 points on `GSM8K`.

papers.title: Masked Diffusion Language Agents for Tool-Integrated Chemical Reasoning
papers.abstract: Designing tool-integrated reasoning agent systems for complex chemical tasks remains a fundamental challenge. Although recent chemical agents have demonstrated promising performance through the integration of external tools, they are still built on the autoregressive paradigm, which is inherently constrained by causal attention and left-to-right generation. As a result, they often struggle with bidirectional molecular understanding, global coordinated tool planning and multi-source evidence integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ChemDiffAgent, the first masked diffusion language agent for tool-integrated chemical reasoning. It reformulates chemical reasoning as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-use trajectories, enabling tool-use decisions to be jointly determined under full-trajectory context and thereby better aligning the agent's decision boundary with its knowledge boundary. We further analyze how this paradigm benefits agentic reasoning through harder infilling subproblems during training and flexible arbitrary-order decoding during inference. Then we develop a two-stage post-training framework, comprising agentic supervised fine-tuning and variance-reduced preference optimization, to enhance tool-use and reasoning capabilities. We also construct a comprehensive benchmark covering six chemistry tasks across both single-turn and multi-turn tool-use scenarios. Under matched budgets and evaluation, ChemDiffAgent consistently outperforms autoregressive agents, achieving an overall improvement of approximately 20%. Notably, our 8B model achieves performance comparable to, in some cases surpassing, significantly larger frontier models, such as GPT 5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7. Code is available at https://github.com/bilemond/ChemDiffAgent.
papers.summary: Chemical reasoning agents that call external tools have so far been autoregressive, and the authors argue that left-to-right generation with causal attention hampers bidirectional molecular understanding, globally coordinated tool planning, and integration of evidence from multiple sources. `ChemDiffAgent` instead casts the task as iterative denoising over interleaved reasoning and tool-call trajectories with a masked diffusion language model, so tool-use decisions are made jointly under full-trajectory context, and it is post-trained in two stages: agentic supervised fine-tuning followed by variance-reduced preference optimization. On a new benchmark spanning six chemistry tasks in single-turn and multi-turn tool-use settings, **it outperforms autoregressive agents by roughly 20% overall under matched budgets**, and the 8B model is reported to match or in some cases exceed much larger frontier models such as `GPT 5.5` and `Claude Opus 4.7`. Code is released.

papers.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
papers.abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.
papers.summary: Drawing on the robustness of large language models (LLMs) to noisy pre-training data and on the in-context learning mechanism of prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), the authors study in-context prediction of partial differential equation (PDE) solution fields from only approximate training data. `PDE-PFN` is a Transformer with self- and cross-attention that approximates the posterior predictive mean of a PDE solution given a context set, and it is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions produced by physics-informed neural networks rather than exact solvers. Across a range of two-dimensional PDEs, **the model generalizes across heterogeneous equations and remains robust under noisy priors while inferring with zero gradient updates**, and its predictive accuracy is competitive with or better than the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.

papers.title: AgentTune: A Unified Training Lifecycle for Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source-available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool-using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two-tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing. Building on this substrate, the library provides a shared agent runtime, tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a designed path toward self-healing agents. These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source-available library at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AgentTune
papers.summary: Building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining tool-using agents is typically handled by separate tools for each stage, each with its own trajectory format. `AgentTune` is a source-available Python library built around a two-tier `EventLog` representation that preserves raw agent trajectories while projecting them consistently for training, evaluation, and auditing. On that substrate it layers a shared agent runtime, tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a planned path toward self-healing agents, all exposed through composable interfaces so strategies, training methods, and recovery mechanisms can be mixed without separate pipelines. **The framework is demonstrated on agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications**, illustrating trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development.

papers.title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models
papers.abstract: Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest. Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored. To fill this gap and better understand how text-to-image Transformers allocate and route attention, we explore this phenomenon of text-to-image transformers across bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive models. Specifically, we explore whether attention sinks exist, where they emerge, and how they functionally influence generation. Through systematic attention analysis and targeted interventions, we identify that attention sinks emerge in both bidirectional diffusion and autoregressive models but exhibit distinct patterns. The autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, whereas the bidirectional models develop sinks near modality boundaries, within text regions, and at spatial corners. Moreover, these patterns vary across generation stages and are localized to a sparse subset of layers and heads. To assess their functional relevance, we perturb sink-related heads and token positions. It turns out that perturbing sink-ranked heads produces larger average changes than non-sink comparisons, while some sink-position perturbations have limited effects on bidirectional model scores. We further introduce register tokens to redistribute attention sinks and find that several configurations preserve or modestly improve generation performance. Overall, attention sinks are architecture-, inference-stage-, and component-dependent phenomena, providing a basis for mechanistic analysis and principled attention design in text-to-image transformers.
papers.summary: Attention sinks, positions that absorb disproportionate attention mass regardless of their semantic content, are well studied in large language models but largely unexamined in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers. The authors analyze attention maps and run targeted interventions on both bidirectional diffusion models and causal autoregressive image generators to ask whether sinks exist, where they form, and what they do. **Sinks appear in both model families but with distinct patterns: the autoregressive model concentrates attention on the first and global-scale tokens, while bidirectional models form sinks near modality boundaries, inside text regions, and at spatial corners**, with the patterns shifting across generation stages and confined to a sparse subset of layers and heads. Perturbing sink-ranked heads changes outputs more than perturbing non-sink heads, though some sink-position perturbations barely move bidirectional model scores, and adding register tokens to redistribute sinks preserves or modestly improves generation in several configurations.

papers.title: Understanding Mamba-3 Through Oscillatory Dynamics
papers.abstract: Mamba-3 introduces input-dependent rotations into recurrent state updates, but their contribution beyond state retention remains unclear. We interpret these ro- tations as underdamped second-order dynamics, providing a framework for in- vestigating the role of oscillation in sequence modeling. Controlled comparisons show that underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping regimes on state-tracking tasks, while language-model pretraining demonstrates benefits for long-context prediction and length generalization. Interventions in pretrained models further establish the importance of learned phase, and state analysis sug- gests that rotation regulates how retained information combines with incoming up- dates. Taken together, these findings identify underdamped dynamics as a useful mechanism for recurrent computation and suggest that oscillation supports long- context processing by regulating how information accumulates.
papers.summary: `Mamba-3` adds input-dependent rotations to its recurrent state updates, but what those rotations contribute beyond retaining state has been unclear. The authors interpret the rotations as underdamped second-order dynamics, giving a framework for studying the role of oscillation in sequence modeling. **In controlled comparisons, underdamped dynamics outperform non-oscillatory damping regimes on state-tracking tasks**, and language-model pretraining shows gains in long-context prediction and length generalization. Interventions on pretrained models establish that the learned phase matters, and state analysis suggests the rotation regulates how retained information is combined with incoming updates.

papers.title: Test-Time Memory Construction
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that defers memory construction to inference and progressively builds memory along the reasoning process. Specifically, T$^2$Mem extracts lightweight episode-level metadata offline to capture key events and temporal associations as retrieval cues, while retaining links to the original interactions to facilitate the reconstruction of dependencies across episodes. At test time, the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw interactions, progressively constructing query-specific memory as reasoning unfolds. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval show the effectiveness of T$^2$Mem by consistently outperforming strong baselines across different backbone LLMs while substantially reducing the overhead of memory construction. Further analysis demonstrates that deferring memory construction to inference enables the memory construction process to dynamically adapt to the information needs of individual queries. All code is available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/T2Mem.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories when the relevant evidence is scattered across distant sessions, and existing memory systems build elaborate memory representations offline before any query arrives, which is costly and cannot adapt to what a specific question needs. `T²Mem` defers memory construction to inference: offline it extracts only lightweight episode-level metadata capturing key events and temporal links as retrieval cues, keeping pointers back to the raw interactions, and at test time the LLM adaptively retrieves and organizes metadata and raw turns, building query-specific memory as its reasoning unfolds. **On `LoCoMo` and `LongMemEval` it consistently outperforms strong baselines across several backbone LLMs while substantially reducing memory-construction overhead**, and further analysis shows the constructed memory adapts to the information needs of individual queries. Code is released.

papers.title: Hidden Data Challenges in Clinical Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Widely reused preprocessing pipelines for electronic health records can encode assumptions about when information became available, what clinical episode a label represents, and what missingness means. These assumptions are rarely audited systematically and may propagate across subsequent studies when preprocessing pipelines are reused or adapted. Using MIMIC-IV as a case study, we identify and quantify violations of three complementary forms of preprocessing alignment, i.e., temporal, semantic, and population alignment, which manifest as temporal leakage, feature-task misalignment, and biased imputation. We show how ambiguities in timestamp semantics, episode definitions, endpoint construction, modality selection, and missingness handling can alter the information available to a model and affect the interpretation of its predictions. Through analyses of MIMIC-IV data and empirical case studies, we demonstrate that such choices may remain largely invisible in aggregate predictive performance while changing the signals on which models rely. We derive practical recommendations for temporally valid, clinically aligned, and reproducible preprocessing of MIMIC-IV and related electronic health record datasets. The code for our experiments, including our proposed preprocessing, is available at: https://github.com/m2l-lab/mimic-iv-preprocess.
papers.summary: Widely reused preprocessing pipelines for electronic health records encode assumptions about when information became available, which clinical episode a label refers to, and what missing values mean, and these assumptions are rarely audited yet propagate as pipelines are copied across studies. Using `MIMIC-IV` as a case study, the authors identify and quantify violations of three forms of alignment, temporal, semantic, and population, which surface as temporal leakage, feature-task misalignment, and biased imputation. **Choices about timestamp semantics, episode definitions, endpoint construction, modality selection, and missingness handling can remain invisible in aggregate predictive performance while changing the signals a model actually relies on.** The work closes with practical recommendations for temporally valid, clinically aligned, and reproducible preprocessing of MIMIC-IV and similar datasets, with code and a proposed preprocessing pipeline released.

papers.title: EmoGavel: Grounding-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Multimodal Emotion Preference Learning
papers.abstract: Multimodal emotion preference learning uses pairwise comparisons to identify which open-ended emotion descriptions align more closely with human judgments. However, existing methods primarily focus on the final preference decision and provide little explicit supervision for localizing and correcting erroneous content. To address this limitation, we propose EmoGavel, a Grounding-Aware reinforcement learning framework with Verifiable rewards for multimodal Emotion preference Learning. We first introduce grounded supervised fine-tuning (Grounded SFT), which exploits controlled-error construction information to jointly learn preference prediction, error localization, repair, and missing-evidence recovery. We then optimize these verifiable outcomes with grounding-aware group relative policy optimization (GA-GRPO), combining preference-gated grounding rewards with dynamic zero-variance rescue to prioritize preference correctness and recover learning signals from all-wrong groups. Experiments on EmoPrefer and controlled-error evaluation sets show that EmoGavel improves both natural preference prediction and controlled-error discrimination while maintaining strong error-grounding performance. Our code and model checkpoints will be released once the paper is accepted.
papers.summary: Multimodal emotion preference learning asks a model to judge, from pairwise comparisons, which of two open-ended emotion descriptions better matches human judgment, but existing methods supervise only the final preference and give no explicit signal for locating and fixing wrong content. `EmoGavel` first applies grounded supervised fine-tuning (`Grounded SFT`), which uses controlled-error construction information to jointly learn preference prediction, error localization, repair, and recovery of missing evidence, then optimizes these verifiable outcomes with grounding-aware group relative policy optimization (`GA-GRPO`), combining preference-gated grounding rewards with a dynamic zero-variance rescue that recovers learning signal from groups where every sample is wrong. **On `EmoPrefer` and controlled-error evaluation sets, it improves both natural preference prediction and controlled-error discrimination** while keeping strong error-grounding performance.

papers.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
papers.abstract: The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation. Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts. Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences. Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble. But how much of the strategy must be specified? The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win. AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble. In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning. The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete. The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner. For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
papers.summary: The `NIST Assembly Task Board #1` demands precise contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts over short horizons and recovery and coordination over long ones, and prior learning-based methods have leaned on demonstrations, task decomposition, or dense progress rewards to specify how to assemble. Drawing an analogy to the move from `AlphaGo` to `AlphaGo Zero`, the authors ask whether a sparse binary task reward, plus the task diversity such a task-agnostic reward permits, is enough for reinforcement learning to discover assembly strategies on its own. **In simulation, a single policy trained from scratch across all 20 board tasks reaches 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning**, and the same framework trains policies that complete ten assembly pairs in one episode in any order, rewarded only when all ten are simultaneously done. The learned policies show planning-like behavior such as choosing grasps with later assembly in mind, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and setting one part aside to assemble another before returning to finish it, with no explicit planner.

papers.title: SWE-Critix: Post-Training Generalist Verifiers for Assessing Coding-Agent Trajectories
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly deployed for end-to-end software engineering tasks, where a readily available oracle evaluator that defines the success criteria is often absent. This motivates verifications for coding agents that can reliably judge and explain their behavior. However, verification is non-trivial as coding agents are increasingly capable of solving long-horizon software engineering tasks. Their execution trajectories can be extremely long, containing hundreds of iterative interactions with code repositories and external tools. Existing verifiers either rely on general-purpose LLMs without specialized training or train dedicated critics that predominantly focus on producing scalar rewards, highlighting the relatively limited exploration of training-based generalist verification. We introduce SWE-Critix, a post-training pipeline for training generalist verifiers of coding-agent trajectories. Given a task and its execution trajectory, the learned verifier predicts the completion label and generates a natural-language analysis that explains its judgment. Our pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) and trains a series of 30B models on trajectories from CodeForge-Preview. On a held-out test set, SWE-Critix improves classification accuracy from 57% for the base Qwen3-30B-A3B reasoning model to 66% after SFT and 78% after RL. We release our models, datasets, and training code to facilitate further research.
papers.summary: Coding agents increasingly tackle end-to-end software engineering tasks with no oracle evaluator defining success, so a verifier that can judge and explain an agent's behavior is needed, yet trajectories can run to hundreds of tool and repository interactions, and existing verifiers either use untrained general-purpose LLMs or train critics that emit only scalar rewards. `SWE-Critix` is a post-training pipeline that teaches a model to read a task and its execution trajectory, predict whether the task was completed, and write a natural-language analysis justifying the verdict, combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL) on trajectories from `CodeForge-Preview`. **On a held-out test set, classification accuracy rises from 57% for the base `Qwen3-30B-A3B` reasoning model to 66% after SFT and 78% after RL.** Models, datasets, and training code are released.

papers.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?
papers.abstract: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.
papers.summary: As coding agents are commissioned to build other agents tailored to a user's workflow, there is an unstated assumption that the delivered agent faithfully serves its requirement rather than merely appearing to, and no benchmark had tested it. `AgentSWE` spans three stages of the agent development lifecycle, creating a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, editing production agent codebases, and optimizing toward a measurable target, across 25 tasks framed as commissions: the builder iterates against a few illustrative cases while acceptance runs the frozen submission on held-out cases graded by requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates, or against the source benchmark's own objective for optimization. **Across a range of coding agents, models, and harnesses, none comes close to delivering what the requirement asks for, and the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm rather than the corner case.** Analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring modes including overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck
papers.abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a standard technique for improving conditional generation in diffusion models, yet its activation schedule is usually selected heuristically. In practice, most existing CFG-based methods rely on a pre-defined activation policy throughout inference, while recent dynamic variants often depend on hand-designed schedules without a principled theoretical explanation of when conditional information is most useful. In order to understand how the informational relevance between conditioning inputs and the score function evolves over the course of generation, we explore when guidance should be activated from an information-theoretic perspective. In this work, we formulate the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the effectiveness of conditional information is not uniform throughout sampling, but becomes significantly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition. Motivated by this insight, we propose a training-free dynamic CFG strategy for inference. Rather than prescribing a fixed schedule in advance, our method constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and activates guidance when the estimated guidance gain crosses a prescribed threshold. This yields an adaptive activation rule that aligns condition injection with the underlying generation dynamics, while also recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Extensive experiments across diverse architectures and tasks, demonstrate that our method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable. Beyond empirical improvements, our framework provides an interpretation of dynamic guidance methods and a principled foundation for inference-time control in conditional diffusion models.
papers.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is standard for conditional diffusion sampling, but when to activate it is usually chosen heuristically, with fixed schedules or hand-designed dynamic variants that lack a principled account of when conditioning information is most useful. The authors model the diffusion trajectory as a time-dependent information bottleneck and show that the usefulness of conditional information is not uniform across sampling but **becomes markedly stronger after a critical stage characterized by a Fisher-information balance condition**. Building on this, they propose a training-free dynamic CFG rule that constructs a stochastic process from conditional and unconditional score statistics and switches guidance on when the estimated guidance gain crosses a threshold, recovering interval-based guidance as a limiting special case. Experiments across diverse architectures and tasks are reported to show the method is effective, robust, and broadly applicable, and the framework also offers an interpretation of existing dynamic guidance methods.

papers.title: Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become the standard architecture for frontier LLMs. The multiple parallel experts in each transformer block theoretically enable expert specialization according to categories such as domains, languages, or modalities during pretraining. However, when data is imbalanced across categories, minority categories can become concentrated in a small fraction of the expert pool or spread inefficiently across them, effectively limiting their available capacity. In this work, we demonstrate that category-conditioned expert-selection biases can preferentially route tokens from different categories toward specialized expert pools. By applying biases based on input category, we provide a simple way to induce soft category-aligned specialization. This intervention encourages categories toward distinct expert subsets while retaining cross-category sharing when useful. More importantly, it enables the over-allocation of expert capacity to categories that would otherwise be disadvantaged by data scarcity. We observe performance improvements across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters. At our smallest and largest model scales, these gains are equivalent to allocating 18.5% and 2.7% additional baseline training tokens, respectively. Overall, our results show that expert biases can serve as a lightweight control for category-level expert allocation, making room for low-resource categories while retaining standard MoE inference.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can in principle let experts specialize by domain, language, or modality during pretraining, but when training data is imbalanced across such categories, minority categories end up squeezed into a small slice of the expert pool or spread thinly across it, limiting their effective capacity. The authors add category-conditioned expert-selection biases that steer tokens from each category toward designated expert subsets, inducing soft category-aligned specialization while still allowing cross-category sharing, and in particular letting them over-allocate expert capacity to data-scarce categories. **Gains appear across modalities, low-resource languages, and code in models up to 10.6B parameters, equivalent to 18.5% more baseline training tokens at the smallest scale and 2.7% at the largest.** Because the intervention only changes routing biases, inference proceeds as in a standard MoE.

papers.title: From Structure to Validity: Mechanism-Guided Generation and Refinement of LLM Rubrics
papers.abstract: Rubrics have been widely used to evaluate and optimize language models on open-ended tasks. However, existing work primarily focuses on generating better rubrics, with limited understanding of what makes rubric design effective. In this work, we conduct a systematic mechanistic analysis of rubric design across criterion organization, criterion operationalization, and score aggregation. Our analysis shows that structural organization enables more comprehensive criterion construction, semantic specification alone does not ensure effective criterion-level judgments, and sophisticated score aggregation provides limited additional gains. Guided by these findings, we introduce Adaptive Rubric Tree Search with Hybrid refinement (ARTS-Hybrid), which combines adaptive tree construction with semantic-first, response-calibrated refinement. Experiments across benchmarks show that ARTS-Hybrid improves both end-to-end evaluation performance and intrinsic rubric quality. Further experiments suggest that, beyond evaluation, rubrics generated by ARTS-Hybrid provide effective signals for model optimization.
papers.summary: Rubrics are widely used to evaluate and optimize language models on open-ended tasks, but most work focuses on generating better rubrics without understanding what makes a rubric design effective. The authors run a systematic mechanistic analysis across criterion organization, criterion operationalization, and score aggregation, finding that **structured organization yields more comprehensive criteria, semantic specification alone does not guarantee sound criterion-level judgments, and sophisticated score aggregation adds little**. Guided by this, they introduce Adaptive Rubric Tree Search with Hybrid refinement (`ARTS-Hybrid`), which pairs adaptive tree construction with semantic-first, response-calibrated refinement. Across benchmarks it improves both end-to-end evaluation performance and intrinsic rubric quality, and the rubrics it generates also serve as effective signals for model optimization.

papers.title: BLOKS: Scaling Kernel Solvers with Sketched Block Preconditioning
papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically sound algorithm for nonparametric learning, which is also often used to investigate properties of deep learning. However, the exact KRR formulation incurs time and memory costs preventing applicability to large datasets, motivating the development of approximate solvers. These algorithms rely on (i) iterative methods, to avoid the computational burden of direct solutions; (ii) sketching or batching, to reduce the problem size; and (iii) preconditioning, to accelerate convergence. While crucial for fast convergence, preconditioning incurs memory costs that can be managed by lowering the number of free parameters of the model, potentially at the expense of expressivity and hence accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose BLOKS, a Conjugate Gradient-based solver for Nystr\"om-sketched KRR built around a novel preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching. The BLOKS preconditioner has memory cost independent of both the dataset size and the number of parameters, allowing scaling to large models. We provide a memory-efficient, GPU-accelerated implementation and show that BLOKS achieves excellent accuracy while retaining favorable time/memory complexity. Indeed, on standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers, BLOKS achieves comparable or better performances than state-of-the-art methods.
papers.summary: Kernel Ridge Regression (KRR) is a theoretically grounded nonparametric learner, often used to probe properties of deep learning, but its exact form has time and memory costs that rule out large datasets, so approximate solvers combine iterative methods, sketching or batching, and preconditioning, where the preconditioner's memory cost is usually tamed by reducing the model's number of free parameters at a possible cost in accuracy. `BLOKS` is a Conjugate Gradient solver for Nyström-sketched KRR built around a preconditioner that combines a block Jacobi approximation with sketching, **giving a preconditioner whose memory cost is independent of both dataset size and parameter count**. With a memory-efficient GPU implementation, it reaches accuracy comparable to or better than state-of-the-art methods on the standard large-scale datasets used to benchmark kernel solvers while keeping favorable time and memory complexity.

papers.title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection
papers.abstract: Stance detection remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to implicit opinions, sarcasm, and context-dependent expressions of stance. Although automatic prompt optimization offers an alternative to fine-tuning without updating model parameters, existing structured approaches are not specifically designed around stance-label semantics and class-specific ambiguities. We introduce MoPrO-SD, a stance-specific prompt optimization framework that decomposes prompts into functional semantic modules and refines them sequentially using LLM-based feedback. We study three refinement strategies: instruction-only optimization (I), instruction with reasoning (I+R), and instruction with per-example reasoning (I+R+E), using class-conditioned errors for stance-label refinement. We also introduce VaccineStance, a new human-annotated benchmark for vaccine stance detection. Experiments across four datasets and five open-weight LLMs show that MoPrO-SD improves upon the human-written Base prompt in many settings. On SemEval-2016, class-conditioned feedback achieves higher mean Macro-F1 than pooled feedback for four of five backbones. Both reasoning-based strategies, I+R and I+R+E, achieve strong performance, with their relative effectiveness varying across models and datasets, while remaining competitive with recent prompt optimization methods. The MoPrO-SD code and VaccineStance dataset are available on GitHub.
papers.summary: Stance detection is hard for large language models (LLMs) because opinions are often implicit, sarcastic, or context-dependent, and existing automatic prompt optimization methods are not designed around stance-label semantics or class-specific ambiguities. `MoPrO-SD` decomposes a prompt into functional semantic modules and refines them sequentially with LLM feedback, comparing three strategies, instruction-only, instruction with reasoning, and instruction with per-example reasoning, and using class-conditioned errors to refine stance-label definitions; the authors also release `VaccineStance`, a human-annotated benchmark for vaccine stance. Across four datasets and five open-weight LLMs the method improves on the human-written base prompt in many settings, and **on `SemEval-2016` class-conditioned feedback beats pooled feedback in mean Macro-F1 for four of five backbones**, with the two reasoning-based strategies both strong but trading places depending on model and dataset.

papers.title: PlacePulse: Learning Transferable Place Representations from Structural Geographic Data
papers.abstract: Geospatial machine learning often depends on task-specific feature engineering over large collections of sociodemographic, business, and environmental variables. Geospatial foundation models offer reusable representations of place, but leading approaches typically encode dynamic signals, such as mobility and search activity, or visual signals from satellite imagery. Few models represent the static structural composition of places (who lives and works there, which businesses operate there, and which risks they face) as transferable embeddings at fine spatial resolution. We introduce PlacePulse, a structural geospatial foundation model that compresses 572 attributes, expanded to 2,288 inputs through H3 neighborhood aggregates, into 256-dimensional unit-norm embeddings for 1,055,537 H3 resolution-7 cells in the United States. We also introduce a reusable two-axis benchmark that separates intrinsic representation quality from downstream predictive utility across multiple targets and spatial supports. Intrinsically, the embeddings reconstruct standardized inputs with mean $R^2 = 0.853$, use 251 of 256 approximately decorrelated dimensions, and show strong spatial organization, with Moran's $I = 0.93$ on the leading principal component and autocorrelation persisting beyond the input radius. Extrinsically, across 74 held-out targets from 12 external sources and four spatial supports, PlacePulse outperforms a dimensionality-matched feature-selection baseline on targets unrelated to the training inputs and is competitive with Google's Population Dynamics Foundation Model, leading on health, economic, election, economic-mobility and social-vulnerability outcomes, with relative strengths that vary by domain. These findings position structural composition as a distinct and complementary modality for geospatial foundation models, not simply a fallback where behavioral or imagery data are unavailable.
papers.summary: Geospatial machine learning usually relies on task-specific feature engineering over large collections of sociodemographic, business, and environmental variables, and existing geospatial foundation models mostly encode dynamic signals like mobility and search activity or satellite imagery rather than the static structural makeup of a place. `PlacePulse` compresses 572 attributes, expanded to 2,288 inputs through H3 neighborhood aggregates, into 256-dimensional unit-norm embeddings for 1,055,537 H3 resolution-7 cells covering the United States, and the authors add a two-axis benchmark that separates intrinsic representation quality from downstream predictive utility. The embeddings reconstruct standardized inputs with mean R² of 0.853, use 251 of 256 roughly decorrelated dimensions, and show strong spatial organization, with Moran's I of 0.93 on the leading principal component. **Across 74 held-out targets from 12 external sources and four spatial supports, PlacePulse beats a dimensionality-matched feature-selection baseline on targets unrelated to its training inputs and is competitive with Google's `Population Dynamics Foundation Model`, leading on health, economic, election, economic-mobility, and social-vulnerability outcomes.**

papers.title: ProgramGym: Scaling Training Environments for Long-Horizon Program Reproduction Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to build programs from scratch as software engineers do rather than to resolve issues within a repository or to generate a repository from a given requirements document. However, scalable verifiable training environments that force agents to discover what is required and to decide how the system should be designed remain scarce. Moreover, existing agent workflows also cannot sustain long-horizon development in which the agent explores the reference program before implementation.
