To address these challenges, we introduce ProgramGym, a framework consisting of Program-Env and Program-Agent for scalable training environments of long-horizon program reproduction agents. Specifically, Program-Env constructs verifiable training environments from repositories through a feedback-driven loop that repairs runtime sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests. Using this novel pipeline, we obtain 1,648 training environments spanning C, C++, Go, and Rust. Program-Agent combines a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review with revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. Experiments on ProgramBench show that both Program-Env and Program-Agent improve performance on program reproduction. Fine-tuning on trajectories with these constructed environments raises the performance of Qwen3.8-27B from 34.87% to 42.84%. Program-Agent further raises the base and SFT models to 55.71% and 56.25%, both exceeding some flagship models. We will release the ProgramGym to support further research on coding agents that build programs from scratch.
papers.summary: Coding agents are increasingly asked to build programs from scratch rather than fix issues in an existing repository, but verifiable training environments that force an agent to discover requirements and make design decisions are scarce, and current workflows cannot sustain the long-horizon loop of exploring a reference program before implementing it. `ProgramGym` pairs `Program-Env`, which turns repositories into verifiable environments through a feedback-driven loop that repairs sandbox builds and the quality of black-box tests and yields 1,648 environments across C, C++, Go, and Rust, with `Program-Agent`, a role-isolated workflow of analysis, implementation, and review plus revision management for compilation checks and failure recovery. **On `ProgramBench`, fine-tuning `Qwen3.8-27B` on trajectories from these environments lifts its score from 34.87% to 42.84%, and running the base and fine-tuned models inside Program-Agent raises them to 55.71% and 56.25%**, exceeding some flagship models.
papers.highlight_summary:
`ProgramBench`-style program reproduction asks an agent to rebuild a program's observable behavior from its documentation and a reference executable, with no source or network, but almost no verifiable training environments exist and single-session harnesses forget early exploration evidence over long horizons. `ProgramGym` addresses both halves with `Program-Env`, an automated pipeline that turns GitHub repositories into sandboxed environments with a reference binary and validated black-box tests, and `Program-Agent`, a role-isolated analyst/implementer workflow with compile-gated revisions.

- `Program-Env` wraps a `Claude Code` harness in feedback loops that split online dependency fetching from offline compilation, generate tests per functional module in parallel, and discard tests that fail on the reference, flake across runs, accept a dummy implementation, or carry weak assertions, yielding **1,648** environments in C, C++, Go, and Rust from 30,459 candidate repositories with **665,512** validated tests and mean coverage of **72.99%**.
- `Program-Agent` runs one Analysis session that records behavioral evidence from the reference program, then alternates Implement and Review sessions that pass only markdown handoff artifacts, with the Implement stage never seeing the reference, each round compiled from a clean snapshot, and failures rolled back to the last validated revision.
- Fine-tuning on `Program-Env` trajectories raises `Qwen3.8-27B` from **34.87%** to **42.84%** Tests Passed under `Claude Code`, and `Program-Agent` with K=5 rounds lifts the base and SFT models to **55.71%** and **56.25%**, above `Claude Opus 4.7` at 50.90% under `mini-SWE-agent`, with most of the iteration gain already present at K=3 (54.13%).
- The scaffold does nearly all the work, since SFT adds only +0.54 on top of `Program-Agent` and `Program-Agent` adds just +1.29 for the stronger `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731`, and the flagship comparison is cross-scaffold rather than apples to apples.
- Whole-program reproduction remains unsolved, with Resolved at most **0.50%** and Almost Resolved at most 5.5% in every configuration, SFT actually dropping Almost Resolved under `Claude Code` from 3.50% to 1.50%, an environment set skewed to 1,492 easy versus 5 hard tasks, and construction costing roughly 83M tokens per environment.

papers.title: Model-free Bayesian Clustering and Multimodal Posterior Summarisation
papers.abstract: We develop a model-free, noise-aware Bayesian clustering framework that constructs a martingale posterior over clusterings from a predictive Bayesian perspective. This avoids explicit likelihood-prior model specification, expensive MCMC sampling, and mode-seeking variational approximations, while accommodating irregular cluster shapes and enabling parallel generation of posterior draws. To interpret the posterior over high-dimensional, noise-aware clusterings, we introduce a Wasserstein-type summarization method. Using a novel noise-aware loss, this approach compresses the large collection of posterior draws into a small set of weighted representatives, capturing distinct cluster structures and noise assignments. Further, we marginalise the uncertainty in the density level, avoiding reliance on a specific choice. We establish theoretical properties of the proposed loss and guarantees for the level-marginal posterior approximation. Results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in capturing clustering and noise uncertainty.
papers.summary: Bayesian clustering usually requires specifying a likelihood and prior, running Markov chain Monte Carlo, or using mode-seeking variational approximations, and the resulting posterior over clusterings is hard to interpret. The authors build a model-free, noise-aware framework that constructs a martingale posterior over clusterings from a predictive Bayesian viewpoint, which handles irregular cluster shapes and lets posterior draws be generated in parallel. To make the high-dimensional posterior readable, they introduce a Wasserstein-type summarisation with a noise-aware loss that **compresses many posterior draws into a small set of weighted representative clusterings**, and they marginalise over the density level rather than fixing it. Theoretical properties of the loss and guarantees for the level-marginal approximation are established, with experiments showing the method captures both clustering and noise-assignment uncertainty.

papers.title: Towards the Roof of the World: NLP Progress in Tibetan Languages
papers.abstract: Tibetan, spoken by some seven million people on and around the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, remains underrepresented in natural language processing (NLP). We present, to our knowledge, the first peer-reviewed systematic bibliometric survey of Tibetan NLP: 140 publications from 2004 to 2026 in the ACL Anthology and DBLP, annotated for venue type, research area, first-affiliation country, and resource release. Output has grown rapidly, with 84% of the publications appearing since 2018, and has expanded bottom-up along the NLP pipeline, from corpora and word segmentation through script, speech, and applications to large language models (LLMs). Researchers based in China first-authored 87% of the publications, which span all 25 represented research areas, whereas work from other countries concentrates on Classical Tibetan. We argue that this full-pipeline paradigm, realized under the compounded constraints of a complex script, dialectal diversity, and geographic remoteness, offers a reference model for other low-resource languages of the Global South. We also identify gaps in dialect coverage, responsible NLP, native and comparable evaluation, cross-community visibility, and resource release (only 29% of the publications release data, code, or models), and recommend open science, shared standards, and community participation for the LLM era.
papers.summary: Tibetan is spoken by roughly seven million people yet remains underrepresented in natural language processing (NLP). A bibliometric survey of 140 publications from 2004 to 2026 in the ACL Anthology and DBLP, annotated by venue, research area, first-affiliation country, and resource release, traces how the field grew bottom-up along the pipeline from corpora and word segmentation to script, speech, applications, and large language models (LLMs). **84% of the publications appeared since 2018**, and researchers based in China first-authored 87% of them, while work from other countries concentrates on Classical Tibetan. The survey argues this full-pipeline paradigm, achieved despite a complex script, dialectal diversity, and geographic remoteness, can serve as a reference for other low-resource languages, and it flags gaps in dialect coverage, responsible NLP, native evaluation, and resource release, since only 29% of publications release data, code, or models.

papers.title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
papers.abstract: Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) tutoring systems personalise responses using memory and retrieval, but the pedagogical reasoning that links a learner's history to a teaching strategy is often left implicit. `RegulaTutor` is a tutoring harness grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) research that operationalises a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework to derive evidence-backed learner interpretations and teaching policies, which keep links to their supporting evidence and update as new observations arrive. A companion offline procedure, `PairRoute`, uses intermediate execution records to separate harness failures from model failures and mixed failures, proposes and tests targeted harness revisions, and builds reviewed stage-level supervision for the model failures that remain. Across the evaluated model configurations, **`RegulaTutor` improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average**, and `PairRoute` yields an endpoint gain in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory.

papers.title: Why Linear Models Can Still Work in a Complex and Changing World
papers.abstract: Linear models can predict well in complex domains even when underlying mechanisms are nonlinear. We argue that this can occur because the complexity of the world exceeds the complexity that can be learned reliably from finite, partially observed data. Flexible models can exploit curvature, thresholds, and interactions that fit one hospital, period, population, policy setting, or measurement process but fail elsewhere. When this instability lies mainly in the nonlinear component, omitting it can give linear models lower prediction error in a new environment. We connect this claim to work on simple linear rules, bias and variance, regularization, best linear prediction, measurement error, distribution shift, invariance, Rashomon sets, and underspecification. Proposition 1 gives a simple squared-error case in which a nonlinear rule learned in the training environment raises target error because it transfers too weakly; finite-sample estimation error can strengthen this result. Partial observation alone is not enough: the link between observed variables and unobserved factors must vary across environments. Stable nonlinear structure favors flexible models, and linear models remain vulnerable to linear spurious relationships. Model complexity should therefore be chosen by cross-environment stability as well as training-data accuracy.
papers.summary: Linear models often predict well in domains whose underlying mechanisms are plainly nonlinear, and the authors argue this happens because the world's complexity exceeds what can be learned reliably from finite, partially observed data. Flexible models can latch onto curvature, thresholds, and interactions that hold in one hospital, period, population, or measurement process but fail elsewhere, so when that instability sits mainly in the nonlinear component, dropping it lowers prediction error in a new environment. A squared-error proposition formalises the case where a nonlinear rule learned in training raises target-environment error because it transfers too weakly, and the argument is tied to prior work on bias and variance, regularisation, measurement error, distribution shift, invariance, Rashomon sets, and underspecification. The conclusion is that **model complexity should be chosen by cross-environment stability as well as training accuracy**, since partial observation alone is not enough, stable nonlinear structure still favours flexible models, and linear models remain exposed to linear spurious relationships.

papers.title: Desertification Forecasting in Semi-Arid Regions: Using Deep Learning to Probe the Observability Limits of Land Degradation Dynamics
papers.abstract: Forecasting desertification has received far less attention than mapping it. We use a convolutional LSTM (ConvLSTM) trained on ten annual Earth Observation (EO) variables (2000-2023) over the semi-arid state of Cear\'a, Brazil, on a 256x206 grid at roughly 2.2 km resolution, to measure how much of the year-to-year evolution of a MapBiomas-derived degradation index (IDV) can be predicted from satellite data. The network predicts a bounded change on top of the last observed state, is trained in two stages (single-step, then recursive rollout) and is evaluated on a contiguous spatial and temporal holdout. State-wide mean IDV rose from 0.238 to 0.350 between 2000 and 2023, about 0.005 per year, but cell-level change is dominated by year-to-year jumps, and a gradient-boosting model given all channels explains only 4.7% of its variance. Against this ceiling, the ConvLSTM lowers RMSE relative to persistence by 1.6% one year ahead and 4.4% four years ahead in a held-out southern band (p < 0.001), beats persistence with a constant drift and reproduces 53-69% of the regional drift. Drift-aware baselines only help from the third year onward, by up to 4.4% in RMSE at six years. An earlier formulation that redrew the whole field each year predicted changes unrelated to the observed ones (correlation -0.06) and produced a spurious decline when run recursively. Channel knockouts suggest that elevation and EVI degrade the forecast, while slope and aspect have no measurable effect. Monte Carlo dropout and stochastic scenario maps convey the uncertainty that the expected-value forecast hides. Under climatological forcing, mean IDV rises from 0.350 in 2023 to 0.370 in 2030. EO-based desertification forecasting is therefore reliable for the regional trend, not for individual cells.
papers.summary: Desertification has been mapped far more often than it has been forecast. A convolutional long short-term memory network (`ConvLSTM`) trained on ten annual Earth Observation (EO) variables from 2000 to 2023 over the semi-arid state of Ceará, Brazil, predicts bounded year-to-year changes in a `MapBiomas`-derived degradation index (IDV) on a grid of roughly 2.2 km cells, using single-step then recursive training and a contiguous spatial and temporal holdout. Cell-level change is dominated by year-to-year jumps of which a gradient-boosting model with all channels explains only 4.7% of the variance, and against that ceiling the `ConvLSTM` cuts root mean squared error relative to persistence by 1.6% one year ahead and 4.4% four years ahead while reproducing 53-69% of the regional drift. Channel knockouts suggest elevation and the enhanced vegetation index (EVI) hurt the forecast, Monte Carlo dropout exposes uncertainty hidden by the mean forecast, and the authors conclude that **satellite-based desertification forecasting is reliable for the regional trend but not for individual cells**.

papers.title: Accelerating Linear Bandits with Persistent Candidate Sets
papers.abstract: Exhaustive optimistic scoring can make action selection costly in linear bandits with a large fixed set of $K$ actions, requiring $\mathcal{O}(K)$ score evaluations per round. We introduce Persistent Candidate LinUCB (\textsc{PC-LinUCB}), which maintains $k$ active actions and samples $q$ challengers uniformly from the remaining $K-k$ actions at each round. By scoring only these $k+q$ candidates, \textsc{PC-LinUCB} reduces the number of score evaluations per round to $\mathcal{O}(k+q)$. We establish problem-independent and problem-dependent high-probability regret bounds consisting of a standard linear-bandit learning term and an additive discovery cost of order $\mathcal{O}\left((K-k)\log(K-k)/q\right)$ at fixed confidence. Notably, this additional cost does not grow with the horizon. For fixed gaps and sufficiently long horizons, we establish an $\Omega\left((K-k)/q\right)$ regret lower bound under uniform challenger sampling, showing that partial candidate access itself imposes an unavoidable regret cost. Experiments show that \textsc{PC-LinUCB} substantially accelerates LinUCB while maintaining comparable regret, and that the persistent candidate mechanism can extend beyond LinUCB.
papers.summary: In linear bandits with a large fixed set of K actions, optimistic scoring of every action costs O(K) evaluations per round. `PC-LinUCB` (Persistent Candidate LinUCB) keeps k active actions and samples q challengers uniformly from the rest each round, scoring only those k+q candidates. High-probability regret bounds, both problem-independent and problem-dependent, consist of the usual `LinUCB` learning term plus an additive discovery cost of order **O((K-k) log(K-k)/q) that does not grow with the horizon**, and an Ω((K-k)/q) lower bound under uniform challenger sampling shows that partial candidate access carries an unavoidable regret price. Experiments show the method substantially speeds up `LinUCB` at comparable regret, and the persistent-candidate mechanism extends to other algorithms.

papers.title: In-Context Learning for System Identification: Probabilistic Formulation, Long-Sequence Handling, and Benchmark Validation
papers.abstract: Traditional system identification typically involves two steps: initially, training data is processed to estimate a model of the system of interest; then, the model is used to predict outputs for new input queries. In contrast, recent in-context learning approaches learn a meta model that maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in a zero-shot fashion, bypassing explicit model estimation. This approach leverages a meta model trained offline, on large sets of synthetically generated data, to emulate the behavior of a system identification algorithm. In this work, we advance this meta-learning framework for system identification in three directions. First, we develop a unified probabilistic meta-identification architecture that combines a Transformer-based encoder-decoder with tailored mechanisms for handling long training sequences, enabling calibrated predictions over long horizons. Second, we show how a pre-trained meta model can act as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator for classical system identification, providing task-specific data that regularize parametric models when real data are scarce. Third, we systematically evaluate the framework on standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and on a challenging out-of-distribution scenario, demonstrating competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art methods and strong generalization, including cases where input-only adaptation is sufficient to handle significant distribution shifts.
papers.summary: Classical system identification first fits a model to training data and then uses it to predict outputs for new inputs, whereas in-context approaches train a meta model offline on large synthetic datasets so it maps directly from training data and query inputs to outputs in zero-shot fashion. The authors extend this meta-learning framework with a probabilistic Transformer encoder-decoder architecture that includes mechanisms for long training sequences, giving calibrated predictions over long horizons. They also show that a pre-trained meta model can serve as an uncertainty-aware synthetic data generator, supplying task-specific data that regularises parametric models when real measurements are scarce. On standard nonlinear system identification benchmarks and an out-of-distribution scenario, the framework reaches **accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art methods** and generalises well, including cases where adapting on inputs alone handles substantial distribution shifts.

papers.title: Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents. Nevertheless, as users expect agents to complete long-horizon, end-to-end tasks, they increasingly need to conduct broad information gathering, perform browser actions, and revisit acquired evidence within a single trajectory. Yet our preliminary analyses reveal that existing access models struggle to meet these demands. They primarily support either information gathering or browser interaction, while combining their capabilities can involve substantial costs or performance trade-offs. To this end, we present Web\$hell, an interface that unifies web access under a single access model. Using a common schema defined by WebContract, WebCompiler compiles live webpages into addressable information and action objects. These objects are maintained in WebCache and handled through a shared set of operations, providing agents with consistent, operable, and persistent web access. Through extensive experiments across web search, web navigation, and deep research benchmarks, we show that Web\$hell achieves strong task performance at lower cost. Our results further indicate the importance of interface design for effective web access, with Web\$hell opening new possibilities for more capable and efficient LLM agents on the web.
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly need to gather information broadly, perform browser actions, and revisit evidence within one long-horizon task, but existing access models, whether search-augmented, browser-based, or filesystem-based, mostly support either information gathering or browser interaction, and combining them brings cost or performance trade-offs. `Web$hell` unifies web access under a single model: using a common schema defined by `WebContract`, a `WebCompiler` turns live webpages into addressable information and action objects, which are kept in a `WebCache` and manipulated through one shared set of operations so access is consistent, operable, and persistent. Across web search, web navigation, and deep research benchmarks, **the unified interface achieves strong task performance at lower cost** than existing access models, and the results point to interface design as a lever for more capable web agents.

papers.title: One Thing Leads to Another: The Essentials of Time Series Causal Discovery
papers.abstract: Time series causal discovery --- the process of detecting causation between time series --- has its roots in signal processing research from over a half century ago. It has since received active and widespread interest, evolving into different forms across domains such as statistics, dynamical systems and machine learning. Entering this fragmented and constantly evolving research landscape can be daunting. This tutorial provides a unified overview of time series causal discovery across research communities. We introduce the key principles invoked by modern discovery methods, and we discuss their limitations and assumptions. We also discuss how discovery methods are evaluated, benchmarked and fine-tuned. We further discuss how causal discovery for time series is becoming crucial for downstream tasks in agriculture and Earth science, in healthcare, and in artificial intelligence systems. We believe that this tutorial will serve as a valuable resource in navigating the deluge of recent causality research, as well as an invitation to signal processing audiences to contribute to causal problems. To further help readers, we host a companion repository to link to useful code packages and resources at https://github.com/CHAI-UK/Awesome-Time-Series-Causal-Discovery.
papers.summary: Time series causal discovery, the detection of causal relations between time series, grew out of signal processing research half a century ago and has since fragmented across statistics, dynamical systems, and machine learning. The tutorial provides **a unified overview across those communities**, introducing the key principles behind modern discovery methods together with their assumptions and limitations, and explaining how such methods are evaluated, benchmarked, and tuned. It also surveys why causal discovery for time series is becoming central to downstream work in agriculture and Earth science, healthcare, and artificial intelligence systems, and it is pitched partly as an invitation to signal processing researchers to take up causal problems. A companion repository collects code packages and related resources.

papers.title: Does Financial Speech Need Continual Learning Regularization? A Study of EWC and mini-KFAC on Earnings Call ASR
papers.abstract: Earnings call transcription presents a realistic continual learning scenario where Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) systems are updated with new recordings but risk catastrophic forgetting of previously learned financial speech patterns. Adapting Whisper-small from a general-domain speech corpus to the Earnings22 benchmark reveals the opposite: all evaluated methods exhibit improvement on held-out financial speech from the same domain during adaptation rather than forgetting. This task complementarity makes regularization counterproductive. Nevertheless, when regularization is warranted, a layer-wise mini-Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (mini-KFAC) approximation seems to achieve lower word error rates (WERs) and more stable optimization than standard diagonal Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). The results suggest that task complementarity should be assessed before applying continual learning constraints, and prefer mini-KFAC EWC over diagonal EWC when needed.
papers.summary: Earnings call transcription looks like a natural continual learning setting: an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system is updated with new recordings and risks catastrophically forgetting earlier financial speech patterns. Adapting `Whisper-small` from a general-domain corpus to the `Earnings22` benchmark shows the opposite, since **every evaluated method improves rather than forgets on held-out financial speech during adaptation**, so the tasks are complementary and regularisation becomes counterproductive. When regularisation is nonetheless warranted, a layer-wise mini-Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (mini-KFAC) approximation appears to give lower word error rates (WERs) and more stable optimisation than standard diagonal Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). The recommendation is to check task complementarity before imposing continual learning constraints, and to prefer mini-KFAC over diagonal EWC when a constraint is needed.

papers.title: CNN-Transformer with Sigmoid Label for High-Resolution Sub-Degree DOA Estimation
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the grid quantization error of deep-learning (DL)-based direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation. Classification- based DOA methods discretize the continuous angular space into a grid, so that with a peak-based read-out, the accuracy and resolution are limited by the grid step and by the width of the label peak. To address this issue, we propose a sigmoid label that encodes the sources' DOAs as the sum of angle-shifted monotonic sigmoid functions. Differentiating the output of a CNN-Transformer network trained with the sigmoid label produces sharp spectral peaks at the source DOAs. Combined with a moderately refined grid step of 0.25 degrees, the CNN-Transformer with the proposed sigmoid label attains sub-degree accuracy and a 1-degree resolution, breaking the limit of the grid quantization error. Under the unified CNN-Transformer backbone, we compare the proposed Sigmoid label with the Gaussian label, the 0-1 hard label, and the binary cross-entropy (BCE) baseline. Numerical results demonstrate that the Sigmoid label attains the highest accuracy and superior resolution compared to other labels.
papers.summary: Deep-learning (DL) direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimators that treat the problem as classification discretise the angular space into a grid, so a peak-based read-out is limited by both the grid step and the width of the label peak. The proposed sigmoid label instead encodes source directions as a sum of angle-shifted monotonic sigmoid functions, so differentiating the output of a `CNN-Transformer` trained on it produces sharp spectral peaks at the source angles. With a moderately refined 0.25-degree grid, **the sigmoid label reaches sub-degree accuracy and 1-degree resolution**, breaking the grid quantization limit. Under the same `CNN-Transformer` backbone it outperforms Gaussian, 0-1 hard, and binary cross-entropy (BCE) labels in both accuracy and resolution.

papers.title: PPG-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for PPG Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is increasingly recorded by wearable and clinical devices at enormous scale, and a growing number of PPG foundation models (FMs) have been developed to compute reusable representations for various downstream tasks. These models are difficult to compare: different evaluations use different datasets, task definitions, preprocessing, downstream heads, hyperparameter tuning, and baselines. We present PPG-Bench, a unifying open-source benchmark evaluating five public PPG FMs across nine open-access datasets and 26 tasks spanning cardiovascular state estimation, activity, sleep, screening, and identification. We evaluate models under four downstream regimes of increasing adaptability (linear probing, random forests, frozen MLP probes, and end-to-end finetuning), with model-specific hyperparameter optimization and subject-disjoint cross-validation. We also evaluate against three controls: random/constant baseline, a deterministic pulse-rate-variability (PRV) feature set, and a generic time-series FM (MOMENT). Across all 68 task-regime combinations, 35.3% show no meaningful FM advantage over the random/constant baseline, and in 83.8% no PPG-specific FM outperforms both PRV and MOMENT. We also find that added downstream head capacity generally improves performance, but can cause significant degradation if the model is performing at chance/constant level. Current PPG FMs therefore cannot yet claim to provide generalised and transferrable representations of PPG signals, and future evaluation in this field should include checks against simple, non-learned controls. Code for the benchmark and instructions to evaluate more models can be found here - https://github.com/mannas-ai/ppg-bench.
papers.summary: Photoplethysmography (PPG) foundation models (FMs) are hard to compare because published evaluations differ in datasets, task definitions, preprocessing, downstream heads, tuning, and baselines. `PPG-Bench` evaluates five public PPG FMs on nine open-access datasets and 26 tasks covering cardiovascular state estimation, activity, sleep, screening, and identification, under four downstream regimes from linear probing to end-to-end finetuning, with per-model hyperparameter optimisation and subject-disjoint cross-validation, and against three controls: a random/constant baseline, a deterministic pulse-rate-variability (PRV) feature set, and the generic time-series FM `MOMENT`. Across the 68 task-regime combinations, 35.3% show no meaningful advantage over the random/constant baseline, and **in 83.8% no PPG-specific FM beats both the PRV features and `MOMENT`**. Extra downstream head capacity generally helps but can sharply degrade models already at chance level, leading the authors to conclude that current PPG FMs cannot yet claim generalised, transferable representations and that future evaluations should include simple non-learned controls.

papers.title: Local Diagnostics of Learned Event Representations for Anomaly Detection at the HL-LHC
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection, the identification of collision events that deviate from Standard Model expectations, is one of the most promising model-agnostic strategies for new-physics searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Searching for rare events in learned low-dimensional representations removes the need to commit to hand-crafted observables a priori, but sacrifices the immediate physical interpretation those observables provide. For anomaly detection to enter a discovery pipeline, flagged events must therefore be diagnosed locally, both to distinguish potential new physics from mismodeling or detector effects and to identify observables for targeted follow-up searches. We evaluate supervised and self-supervised neural embedding strategies on COLLIDE-2V, a 750-million-event dataset simulated under realistic High-Luminosity LHC conditions, using the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained in the learned latent space as the anomaly score. Across the configurations and benchmark signals considered, supervised objectives, which exploit simulation process labels during training, generally outperform their self-supervised counterparts and, in their best configurations, improve on an autoencoder trained directly on kinematic features, raising the signal efficiency at 10% background acceptance on all held-out processes. We further introduce a local diagnostic pipeline that fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to the SM latent space, profiles each component through high-level observables without process labels, localizes the flagged events, and ranks observables by their local discriminating power. The ranking recovers the defining kinematics of the held-out processes, while correlating the anomaly score with the same observables quantifies how closely the score tracks them, revealing cases where the most discriminating observable is not the one the score follows most closely.
papers.summary: Anomaly detection at the Large Hadron Collider searches learned low-dimensional representations for collision events that deviate from Standard Model (SM) expectations, but this gives up the physical interpretability of hand-crafted observables, which a discovery pipeline needs in order to tell new physics from mismodelling and to choose observables for follow-up searches. The authors compare supervised and self-supervised embedding strategies on `COLLIDE-2V`, a 750-million-event simulation under realistic High-Luminosity LHC conditions, scoring anomalies by the reconstruction error of an autoencoder trained in the learned latent space. **Supervised objectives that use simulation process labels generally outperform self-supervised ones** and, in their best configurations, raise signal efficiency at 10% background acceptance on all held-out processes compared with an autoencoder on raw kinematic features. A local diagnostic pipeline fits a Gaussian Mixture Model to the SM latent space, profiles each component with high-level observables, localises flagged events, and ranks observables by local discriminating power, recovering the defining kinematics of held-out processes while revealing cases where the score does not track the most discriminating observable.

papers.title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. We introduce Rollout-Time Intervention (RTI), a technique designed to elicit successful trajectories beyond the policy's intrinsic exploration capacity. RTI operates by leveraging reward-side evidence (i.e., evaluation rubrics) during rollout to convert erroneous trajectories into successful ones, providing effective learning signals for tasks that the policy rarely solves on its own. Although intervention trajectories are inherently off-policy, we find that they can effectively guide policy optimization when trajectories with excessive distributional shifts are filtered out. Extensive experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that RTI consistently outperforms RL baselines, enabling the post-trained policy to approach the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs and, more importantly, transcend its original capability boundary. The code is available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents hits an on-policy bottleneck: when tasks lie beyond the model's current capability, successful trajectories become so sparse that training often collapses. Rollout-Time Intervention (`RTI`) uses reward-side evidence such as evaluation rubrics during rollout to convert failing trajectories into successful ones, supplying learning signal for tasks the policy rarely solves alone. Although these intervened trajectories are off-policy, they guide policy optimisation effectively once trajectories with excessive distributional shift are filtered out. Across five benchmarks `RTI` consistently beats RL baselines, and **the post-trained policy approaches the performance of substantially stronger contemporary LLMs** while moving past its original capability boundary.

papers.title: Collective Autonomous Vehicle Routing Needs Social Awareness for Coexistence with Human Drivers
papers.abstract:
Collective Autonomous Vehicle (AV) route choices in real-world traffic networks can create externalities for Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), as routes that benefit AVs may increase travel times for other road users. To address this, we introduce a social component, the marginal cost, to the selfish travel time AV reward. Marginal cost captures an AV's impact on other road users by comparing their travel times with those in a counterfactual simulation in which the AV is removed.
  We study AV route choice in mixed-autonomy traffic settings using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where AVs learn routing policies through repeated interactions with the traffic environment. Experiments on the real-world networks of Ingolstadt and Provins show that incorporating marginal cost into the AV reward not only limits the increase in HDV travel times and shortens AV travel times relative to selfish AV routing, but also improves overall system performance. In Ingolstadt, selfish routing of 40\% AVs increases the travel times of other vehicles by 1.7\%, and this drops to 1.1\% when the social reward is included. Interestingly, not only does overall system performance improve, but the AVs are also better off when acting socially.This effect is consistent across tested cities, penetration rates, and replications, yet when the weight of the social component in the reward increases, the system fails to reach the desired performance.
  For a more scalable approach to social AV routing in mixed-autonomy traffic, we compute the marginal cost only for the AVs whose route choices most affect the traffic system. This reduces the number of counterfactual simulations and achieves similar performance at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that AV routing should go beyond selfish rewards and, for the benefit of all traffic participants, include a social component in its objective.
papers.summary: When autonomous vehicles (AVs) choose routes selfishly in mixed traffic, they can lengthen travel times for human-driven vehicles (HDVs). The authors add a marginal-cost term to the AV reward that measures each AV's effect on other road users by comparing their travel times against a counterfactual simulation with that AV removed, and they train routing policies with multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) on real networks of Ingolstadt and Provins. **Social routing limits the HDV slowdown, shortens AV travel times, and improves overall system performance compared with selfish routing**, with the travel-time increase for other vehicles in Ingolstadt at 40% AV penetration falling from 1.7% to 1.1%, although weighting the social term too heavily makes the system miss its target. Computing marginal cost only for the AVs whose choices most affect the network cuts the number of counterfactual simulations while reaching similar performance.

papers.title: Revisiting Accent Classification with DistilHuBERT: Speaker-Disjoint Evaluation and Cross-Corpus Generalization
papers.abstract: Recent accent classification systems can achieve high accuracy in standard in-corpus evaluations. However, when speakers overlap between the training and test sets, such results may overestimate model robustness compared with real-world deployment scenarios. This study revisits the robustness of DistilHuBERT-based accent classification by using L2-ARCTIC and multiple external English accent datasets. The comparison covers file-level and speaker-disjoint splits, along with balanced external-data training and teacher-student pseudo-labeling. The large performance gap between in-corpus and external evaluations suggests that file-level evaluation substantially overestimates performance, while speaker-disjoint evaluation can provide a more realistic estimate of the generalization to unseen speakers. In this study, models trained on external data alone do not reliably generalize to L2-ARCTIC. Among the tested configurations, balanced external-data training offers the most promising supervised setting. The pseudo-labeling experiments further indicate that confidence-based filtering alone is insufficient under domain mismatch. Overall, this study suggests that robust accent classification evaluation should simultaneously include speaker-disjoint evaluation and cross-corpus testing.
papers.summary: Accent classifiers report high in-corpus accuracy, but when speakers overlap between training and test sets those numbers can overstate robustness relative to deployment. Using `DistilHuBERT` with `L2-ARCTIC` and several external English accent datasets, the study compares file-level and speaker-disjoint splits alongside balanced external-data training and teacher-student pseudo-labelling. **File-level evaluation substantially overestimates performance**, speaker-disjoint evaluation gives a more realistic estimate of generalisation to unseen speakers, and models trained only on external data do not reliably transfer to `L2-ARCTIC`. Balanced external-data training is the most promising supervised setting, confidence-based filtering alone proves insufficient for pseudo-labelling under domain mismatch, and the authors recommend evaluations that combine speaker-disjoint splits with cross-corpus testing.

papers.title: Learning by Compression: Risk Estimates Attain the Law-of-Large-Numbers Rate
papers.abstract: Compression schemes provide a general framework for deriving data-dependent risk bounds for learning algorithms. For learning rules based on preferent compression, existing results upper-bound the risk in terms of a sample-dependent complexity $\boldsymbol{k}$, defined as the cardinality of the compression augmented by the training examples on which the reconstructed hypothesis is inappropriate. These results, however, yield a margin of order $O(\sqrt{\ln N/N})$ above $\boldsymbol{k}/N$. In this paper, we establish that the logarithmic factor is not intrinsic. We prove that, for every fixed confidence level $1-\delta$, the risk is bounded with probability at least $1-\delta$ by $$ \frac{\boldsymbol{k}}{N} + O\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right), $$ uniformly over all possible values of $\boldsymbol{k}$. Thus, risk estimates for learning algorithms based on preferent compression attain the same law-of-large-numbers rate as the empirical estimate of the probability of a fixed event. We also show that the leading term $\boldsymbol{k}/N$ is necessary and investigate its relation to the empirical risk. In particular, we identify regimes in which the empirical risk retains the $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ convergence rate, as well as regimes in which it converges more slowly or ceases to be consistent, while the complexity-based estimator preserves the $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ rate.
papers.summary: Compression schemes yield data-dependent risk bounds for learning algorithms, and for rules based on preferent compression existing bounds express risk through a sample-dependent complexity k, the size of the compression set plus the training examples on which the reconstructed hypothesis is inappropriate, with a slack of order sqrt(ln N / N) above k/N. The authors show the logarithmic factor is not intrinsic: for any fixed confidence level, **the risk is bounded by k/N + O(1/sqrt(N)) uniformly over all values of k**, matching the law-of-large-numbers rate of estimating the probability of a fixed event. They also prove the leading k/N term is necessary and study its relation to empirical risk, identifying regimes where empirical risk keeps the O(1/sqrt(N)) rate and others where it converges more slowly or stops being consistent while the complexity-based estimator keeps the fast rate.

papers.title: O\'ido: Open-Vocabulary Speech Recognition on a $5 Microcontroller without a Neural Accelerator
papers.abstract: Speech recognition on low-cost microcontrollers is, in practice, limited to keyword spotting or a fixed list of commands. We present O\'ido, an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English speech recognition entirely on an ESP32-S3 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX7, 512 KB of SRAM, 8 MB of PSRAM, 16 MB of flash, no neural accelerator). O\'ido executes a 13M-parameter Conformer-CTC model with int8 weights, per-frame dynamic int8 activations and int8 attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule designed around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other the on-device arithmetic reaches 3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER), within 0.12 points of full precision, and 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model; a transducer head gives 2.99%/6.67% and an int4 variant fits in 8.3 MB. This is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer on the same chip, and fewer than Whisper tiny.en and Moonshine tiny in full precision on a laptop, including in real noise and reverberation. Measured on a physical board, the firmware runs at 1.97x the duration of the audio on one core, with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator: accurate, but not yet real time (a 4 s command is transcribed about 8.7 s after it ends). The two-core schedule gives wrong results on silicon and is disabled. A streaming variant shows partial text while the speaker talks and delivers the final text 4.1-11.1 s after clips of 3.6-10.6 s (7.2-22.4 s in utterance mode) at 4.86%/11.03% WER; a Spanish model makes 34-60% fewer errors than multilingual Whisper tiny. Code and models are released.
papers.summary: Speech recognition on cheap microcontrollers has in practice meant keyword spotting or a fixed command list. `Oído` is an inference engine that runs open-vocabulary English recognition on an `ESP32-S3` (dual-core 240 MHz, 512 KB SRAM, 8 MB PSRAM, no neural accelerator) by executing a 13M-parameter `Conformer-CTC` model with int8 weights, activations, and attention on the chip's SIMD instructions, with a schedule built around flash and PSRAM bandwidth. On `LibriSpeech` test-clean and test-other it reaches **3.70%/8.23% word error rate (WER) on device, within 0.12 points of full precision**, improving to 3.33%/7.15% with an on-chip 1.3M-parameter language model and 2.99%/6.67% with a transducer head, which is 2.3-2.8x fewer errors than the vendor's recognizer and fewer than `Whisper tiny.en` and `Moonshine tiny` at full precision on a laptop. On a physical board the firmware takes 1.97 times the audio duration on one core with transcripts identical to an instruction-exact emulator, so it is accurate but not yet real time, a streaming variant shows partial text while the user speaks, a Spanish model cuts errors 34-60% versus multilingual `Whisper tiny`, and code and models are released.

papers.title: Agentic Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) already shape decisions through writing and question answering, and the book asks what changes when they can act in the world directly and interact with one another. Agentic LLMs combine language models with the ability to take actions, and the text covers **how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact with each other, and what this means for users**. It is a book-length treatment rather than a single experimental result.

papers.title: Towards Enriching Design-Time Models with Evidence from Simulation and Operational Activities
papers.abstract: Cyber-Physical Systems are developed through multiple model based activities, comprising several stages of development. As the development progresses through simulation, experimentation, and operation, observations of system execution may reveal missing, uncertain, or invalid design knowledge. The path from execution results to persistent design-time enrichment, however, is often implicit. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing an evidence driven workflow for systematically transferring knowledge produced during simulation and operation back into design-time models. We demonstrate the workflow using an Influence Model, a design-time artefact used to represent how design artefacts and environmental factors jointly affect system response properties, using a sign-following robot use case. We show how simulation evidence can enrich Influence Models by supporting participant pruning decisions, interaction characterisation, influence-function abstraction, and validity-scope information. The application demonstrates the feasibility of the workflow for simulation-based evidence and its potential benefits to improve design-time reasoning and feedback in subsequent development iterations.
papers.summary: Cyber-physical systems are developed through many model-based activities, and as development moves through simulation, experimentation, and operation, observed executions can expose missing, uncertain, or invalid design knowledge that rarely flows back into design-time models. The authors propose an evidence-driven workflow for systematically transferring knowledge gained during simulation and operation into those models. They demonstrate it on an Influence Model, a design-time artefact capturing how design artefacts and environmental factors jointly affect system response properties, using a sign-following robot, and show how simulation evidence supports **participant pruning, interaction characterisation, influence-function abstraction, and validity-scope information**. The case study shows feasibility for simulation-based evidence and suggests benefits for design-time reasoning in later iterations.

papers.title: SqueezeBench: Saturation-Resilient Evaluation of Mathematical Capability
papers.abstract: AI systems are making rapid progress in mathematics, but this progress is hard to measure. Benchmarks of solved problems saturate, and in benchmarks of open problems each problem can be resolved for the first time only once. We present SqueezeBench, a benchmark that is resilient to saturation: a success raises the bar instead of removing the problem. Each problem fixes an integer function $f(n)$ whose values are known only for small $n$, and the benchmark keeps a lower and an upper record on it. A record is a computable Lean function with a machine-checked proof that it bounds $f$. A submission proposes a new function and proves that it bounds $f$, that it is no worse than the current record at any $n$, and that it is strictly better at some $n$. Once accepted, it becomes the record that the next submission has to beat. The system thus chooses the bound as well as its proof, and it may improve the record at a single $n$ or its growth rate. At every $n$, the gap between the two records shows how far the certified bounds are from determining $f(n)$. Every proof is checked by two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics. The checks also reject a function that computes $f$ by exhaustive search at small $n$, and a maintainer only reads the submitter's report and looks for such a search at larger $n$. We release ten problems from extremal combinatorics with twenty proved initial records and the admission tools. As a baseline, agents based on a frontier language model, with at most one hour per record, had 82 submissions accepted and improved every record, without going beyond the published literature. Agents based on two newer models then started from these records, had 60 more submissions accepted and improved 19 of the 20 records again. For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound.
papers.summary: Benchmarks of solved math problems saturate, while open problems can be resolved for the first time only once, which makes progress in machine mathematics hard to measure. `SqueezeBench` instead poses ten extremal-combinatorics problems, each defined by an integer function whose values are known only for small inputs, and maintains lower and upper records on that function as computable Lean functions with machine-checked proofs; a submission is accepted only if two independent Lean kernels verify that it bounds the function, is no worse than the current record everywhere, and is strictly better somewhere, so each success raises the bar instead of retiring the problem. Agents built on a frontier language model, given at most one hour per record, had **82 submissions accepted and improved every one of the twenty initial records**, and agents on two newer models then improved 19 of the 20 again, though for eight of the ten problems at least one record still trails the best published asymptotic bound.

papers.title: When MLLMs miss what humans read: diagnosing and learning to read squint text
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure (text a human recovers by squinting) and report that no text is present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench, comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl, a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. Frozen-weight analysis shows that hidden text leaves a coarse signal while glyph identity is weakly represented; identity becomes substantially more accessible when the correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as a major bottleneck. Suppressing high-frequency content also improves reading at a fixed visual-token budget, while visual token count may also contribute. These findings motivate Squint OPSD: a frozen teacher receives a downscaled view and the ground-truth transcription as privileged context, and its token-level distributions supervise a student along on-policy trajectories. At inference, the student reads the original image alone. Squint OPSD reaches 88.61 ANLS on SquintBench, versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone, 24.44 for the best general-purpose model on the original view, and 68.60 at best for an off-the-shelf model under a downscaled view. These results substantially narrow the gap between available visual evidence and its generated read-out without auxiliary views at inference.
papers.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure, the kind a human recovers by squinting, and instead report that no text is present, a failure the authors traced through a production content-moderation pipeline. They release `SquintBench`, 1076 production-derived moderation images, and `SquintCtrl`, a controlled synthetic suite for diagnosing the mechanism; frozen-weight analysis shows the hidden text leaves a coarse signal but glyph identity is weakly represented and becomes far more accessible once the correct spatial regions are supplied, implicating spatial selection as the main bottleneck. The proposed `Squint OPSD` distills on-policy from a frozen teacher that sees a downscaled view plus the ground-truth transcription, while the student reads only the original image at inference, reaching **88.61 average normalized Levenshtein similarity (ANLS) on `SquintBench` versus 26.50 for the unadapted backbone** and 68.60 for the best off-the-shelf model given a downscaled view.

papers.title: A Better Metric Will Not Save You: What You Compare Beats How You Compare It
papers.abstract: Representational similarity measures (RSA, CKA, Procrustes) are chosen for the transformations they treat as irrelevant, and all of them take the set of conditions as given. That set is fixed by two decisions, which inputs are admitted and how they are grouped, both taken before the matrix a measure operates on exists: no invariance property reaches them. We measure what they are worth where the arrangement the conditions ought to have is known independently of the systems compared, the acoustic organisation of vowels, across fifteen languages and twenty-seven representations. Changing which categories are compared, at a fixed number of them, moves the gap between two representations by more than twice the effect being measured, while changing how many moves it not at all. In this setting rankings of models are identified under these choices, and rankings across languages are not.
papers.summary: Representational similarity measures such as representational similarity analysis (RSA), centered kernel alignment (CKA), and Procrustes distance differ in which transformations they ignore, but all of them take the set of compared conditions as given, a set fixed by two upstream choices: which inputs are admitted and how they are grouped. The authors test how much those choices matter in a setting where the correct arrangement of conditions is known independently of the systems compared, the acoustic organization of vowels, across fifteen languages and twenty-seven representations. **Changing which vowel categories are compared, at a fixed number of categories, shifts the gap between two representations by more than twice the effect being measured**, while changing how many categories are compared shifts it not at all; rankings of models survive these choices, but rankings across languages do not.

papers.title: Harmonic analysis and circuit approximation of Sobolev functions on quantum input spaces
papers.abstract: We derive approximation rates for Sobolev functions defined on the complex unit sphere and complex projective space, representing quantum states, and on the special and projective unitary groups, representing quantum unitary operations. By using harmonic analysis on compact groups and compact homogeneous spaces, we characterize the corresponding Peter--Weyl decompositions and Sobolev spaces via irreducible representations and the Laplace--Beltrami operator. Combining spectral truncation with finite-depth quantum-circuit approximation, invoking the Solovay--Kitaev theorem, we establish quantitative rates that separate the spectral truncation error from the circuit approximation error.
papers.summary: Approximating smooth functions whose inputs are quantum states or quantum operations requires relating function regularity to the geometry of those input spaces. The authors derive approximation rates for Sobolev functions on the complex unit sphere and complex projective space, which represent quantum states, and on the special and projective unitary groups, which represent quantum unitaries, using harmonic analysis on compact groups and homogeneous spaces to characterize the Peter-Weyl decompositions and Sobolev spaces through irreducible representations and the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Combining spectral truncation with finite-depth quantum-circuit approximation via the Solovay-Kitaev theorem, they obtain **quantitative rates that separate the spectral truncation error from the circuit approximation error**.

papers.title: A Local Agentic AI Framework to Generate Edge Case Scenarios for Safety Assurance
papers.abstract: Generating edge case scenarios is crucial for training, testing and safety assuring autonomous systems. This identifies hazardous failures to increase system reliability and robustness, ensures the system can still function safely on the boundaries of its operational design domain and learns the expected system behaviour for these edge cases. The rapid advancement in the generation and analysis capabilities of language models (LMs) has expanded their applicability and recent work has investigated LM scenario generation. However, many recent approaches rely on human-in-the-loop or rule-based strategies. This restricts the LM's ability to generate diverse and edge case scenarios; the long tail of the distribution. Our work uses local LMs in a laptop-based agentic AI framework for adaptive scenario generation. This is cheap, fully-controlled, ensures data privacy and security. It uses think, act, observe, update, and continue loops with lightweight JSON encoding to generate scenarios. We use the system requirements, system description and environment description as knowledge bases in contextual prompts for an LM to ensure scenario realism. A second, independent LM critiques each scenario using domain specific criteria so it can be refined. The refined scenarios are run in simulation and evaluation metrics collected. These metric scores are analysed and similar scenarios are created for edge cases (exploitation) or novel scenarios are generated to explore the scenario space. Post-hoc clustering using metric scores and thematic-type analysis of the rich-text scenario descriptions produced by the LM pinpoints functional gaps and their triggering conditions. This creates traceable evidence for the safety assurance case. Our work highlights the potential of a flexible and adaptive local agentic AI framework for automating edge case generation and producing traceable safety assurance evidence.
papers.summary: Generating edge-case scenarios is essential for testing and safety-assuring autonomous systems, but many recent language-model-based approaches rely on human-in-the-loop or rule-based strategies that limit how far into the long tail of scenarios they reach. The proposed framework runs entirely on local language models on a laptop, using think, act, observe, update, and continue loops with lightweight JSON encoding: one model generates scenarios grounded in the system requirements, system description, and environment description, a second independent model critiques each scenario against domain-specific criteria, and the refined scenarios run in simulation to collect metric scores that steer the next round either toward similar edge cases (exploitation) or toward novel regions of the scenario space (exploration). Post-hoc clustering on the metric scores plus thematic analysis of the generated scenario descriptions pinpoints functional gaps and their triggering conditions, **producing traceable safety-assurance evidence without cloud models, data leaving the machine, or hand-written rules**.

papers.title: A Scalable Learned Iterative Solver for Nonlinear MPC via Temporal Decomposition
papers.abstract: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) can be applied to large nonlinear systems with complex objectives while enforcing constraints, but the cost of solving the underlying optimization problems limits real-time application for systems with fast dynamics or many states. Neural networks can reduce this online cost by approximating the control law, but may violate constraints and typically require many precomputed optimizer solutions for training. The learning-based iterative solver for constrained optimization (LISCO) instead learns to predict primal-dual steps toward satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions through self-supervised training without precomputed solutions, but its dense, monolithic architecture grows with the prediction horizon. We remove this horizon dependence by exploiting the temporal structure of the problem in the solver architecture, which makes the network size independent of the horizon while leaving the training loss and the solver iteration unchanged. A closed-loop resampling strategy further aligns the training distribution with closed-loop operation at no additional sampling cost. On an economic NMPC benchmark of a CSTR cascade, the proposed solver scales to larger problems than monolithic LISCO and achieves median speedups of up to a factor of four over IPOPT. In closed loop, it achieves comparable control performance to IPOPT with no observed constraint violations.
papers.summary: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) handles large constrained nonlinear systems, but solving its optimization problems online is too slow for fast dynamics or many states, and neural approximations of the control law can violate constraints and need many precomputed optimizer solutions to train. The learning-based iterative solver for constrained optimization (`LISCO`) avoids precomputed solutions by learning primal-dual steps toward the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, but its dense monolithic network grows with the prediction horizon; this work exploits the problem's temporal structure so the network size becomes horizon-independent while the training loss and solver iteration stay unchanged, and adds closed-loop resampling that aligns the training distribution with closed-loop operation at no extra sampling cost. On an economic NMPC benchmark of a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) cascade, the solver scales to larger problems than monolithic `LISCO`, **reaches median speedups of up to four times over `IPOPT`**, and matches `IPOPT`'s closed-loop control performance with no observed constraint violations.

papers.title: Branching On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides teacher supervision on student-generated trajectories, but a single trajectory realizes only one continuation at each decision, limiting supervision coverage under a finite sampling budget. We propose BranchOPD (Branching On-Policy Distillation), which selects informative decision points using student uncertainty and teacher-student disagreement, resamples student-policy continuations from shared prefixes, and applies token-level teacher supervision to both main trajectories and branches. BranchOPD operates at token-level decisions in mathematics and within-turn decisions in agent tasks. Shared-prefix reuse reduces student-generated token costs by approximately 19% on ALFWorld and 31% on WebShop relative to seven independent trajectories. We also introduce protocol-boundary repair (PBR), which uses targeted supervision under protocol constraints to mitigate repetition and wasted generation. BranchOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD and Multi-Rollout OPD (n=7) across all evaluated benchmarks, with gains over Vanilla OPD of 18.55 percentage points in mean mathematics accuracy over 16 sampled answers (avg@16) and 13.8 points in mean ALFWorld ID/OOD success. Mechanistic analyses and selection ablations show that branching at uncertain decisions expands subsequent behavior coverage and outperforms random selection and turn-initial branching.
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) supervises a student on its own generated trajectories, but each trajectory realizes only one continuation at every decision point, so a finite sampling budget covers few alternatives. Branching On-Policy Distillation (`BranchOPD`) selects informative decision points using student uncertainty and teacher-student disagreement, resamples student continuations from shared prefixes, and applies token-level teacher supervision to both main trajectories and branches, operating at token-level decisions in mathematics and within-turn decisions in agent tasks; a protocol-boundary repair (PBR) component adds targeted supervision under protocol constraints to curb repetition and wasted generation. Shared-prefix reuse cuts student-generated token costs by about 19% on `ALFWorld` and 31% on `WebShop` relative to seven independent trajectories, and `BranchOPD` beats both vanilla OPD and seven-rollout multi-rollout OPD on every benchmark, with **gains over vanilla OPD of 18.55 points in mean mathematics accuracy over 16 sampled answers and 13.8 points in `ALFWorld` in- and out-of-distribution success**; ablations show branching at uncertain decisions expands subsequent behavior coverage and outperforms random or turn-initial branching.

papers.title: Proactive Agentic Orchestration
papers.abstract: Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub-agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. To address these limitations, we introduce POrchestra, an on-the-fly proactive agentic orchestration framework. It allows sub-agents to proactively communicate with the orchestrator at any logical point to request harness adjustments while maintaining continuity of local execution. This mechanism not only enables sub-agents to adapt seamlessly to dynamic environments but also naturally inspires On-Policy Orchestration Distillation (OPOD) based on hindsight feedback. OPOD attributes sub-agents' proactive revision requests back to preceding orchestration decisions to derive targeted improvement signals, and leverages these signals as process supervision alongside the final reward to optimize the orchestration policy. We evaluate POrchestra on three long-horizon agent benchmarks spanning deep research, dynamic digital assistance, and software engineering. POrchestra improves task success by an average of 9.1% relative to the strongest baseline; combined with OPOD, it improves small-orchestrator success by an average of 10.0% relative to existing training baselines. POrchestra also achieves a more favorable cost-performance trade-off. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/XueyangFeng/POrchestra.
papers.summary: Agentic orchestration extends the execution horizon of large language model agents by delegating tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, but current methods fix each sub-agent's goals and harness at creation time and learn the orchestration policy only from sparse, delayed feedback. `POrchestra` lets sub-agents proactively message the orchestrator at any logical point to request harness adjustments while continuing their local execution, and those revision requests drive On-Policy Orchestration Distillation (`OPOD`), which attributes each request back to the preceding orchestration decision to produce targeted process supervision alongside the final reward. Across three long-horizon benchmarks spanning deep research, dynamic digital assistance, and software engineering, **`POrchestra` raises task success by an average of 9.1% over the strongest baseline**, `OPOD` lifts small-orchestrator success by an average of 10.0% over existing training baselines, and the system reaches a more favorable cost-performance trade-off; the code is public.

papers.title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
papers.abstract: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. These findings suggest that their benefits may not persist across versions, which motivates a workflow-level approach in which agents build on one another's work across sessions. We model these alternating agent sessions as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP) and establish sufficient conditions for alternation to exceed single-agent reference limits, derive an explicit experiment-budget bound, and characterize when session caps preserve this advantage. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Humanize MLE Agents (HMA), which alternates two agents on a shared workspace, limits each session to at most k experiments and resets the context between sessions, without additional task-specific harness or prior knowledge supplements. Across 75 Kaggle tasks in MLE-bench, HMA reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, exceeding the strongest open-source baseline by 8.0 points with a quarter of its time budget. Moreover, among six configurations spanning five heterogeneous agent pairs, HMA improves any-medal rate over the constituent baselines by 6.4 points on average, demonstrating cross-pair generality. A supplementary case on kernel optimization reaches 878 cycles, within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader, demonstrating applicability beyond MLE.
papers.summary: Long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) agents usually rely on custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience, but the authors find that reasoning intensity and progress both decay as a single session lengthens (long-horizon deceleration) and that the benefit of custom harnesses vanishes as the underlying model improves (harness staleness). They model alternating agent sessions on a shared workspace as a context-reset semi-Markov decision process (CR-SMDP), derive sufficient conditions and an experiment-budget bound under which alternation beats a single agent, and instantiate this as Humanize MLE Agents (`HMA`), which alternates two agents with at most k experiments per session and a context reset between sessions, with no task-specific harness or extra prior knowledge. On 75 Kaggle tasks in `MLE-bench`, **`HMA` reaches a state-of-the-art any-medal rate of 78.2%, 8.0 points above the strongest open-source baseline with a quarter of its time budget**, improves over its constituent agents by 6.4 points on average across five heterogeneous agent pairs, and a kernel-optimization case lands within 1.6% of the community leaderboard leader.

papers.title: Beyond Temporal Proximity: Explanatory World Models for Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Generative Recommenders increasingly use Reinforcement Learning (RL) to optimize outcomes that may appear hundreds or thousands of interactions after a decision. Standard RL propagates reward according to temporal proximity rather than explicit relevance, attenuating the signal assigned to distant but important actions and creating a source of sample inefficiency. We introduce Explanatory World Models (EWM), an attribution framework that uses explanations to identify the earlier events that plausibly contributed to a realized outcome. We instantiate EWM with a frontier language model and use its explanations as learning signals using a conservative hierarchical operator that recursively redistributes reward while preserving the undiscounted episode return. To investigate what constitutes a useful explanation, we operationalize three complementary variants inspired by Halpern's actual causation, Lombrozo's explanatory simplicity, and Deutsch's hard-to-vary explanations. We evaluate EWM on two controlled long-horizon RL benchmarks, a public sequential-recommendation benchmark, and an industry-scale generative recommender. On Crafter and WordCraft, EWM substantially outperforms PPO and LaRe, with its largest gains when rewards are most delayed. On KuaiRand, EWM outperforms SFT and LaRe offline and A2C online. Finally, in an offline evaluation of an industry generative recommender, EWM considerably improves Recall and increases behavioral proxies.
