papers.abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on AMLworld's smallest test splits is costly because each of over a million targets requires a separate graph prompt. Sampling reduces this cost, but small balanced subsets change unweighted precision and F1. We introduce AMLworld-Compact, an evaluation set that retains every illicit test transaction and samples benign transactions from supervised-score strata. Its HT-Coreset protocol reduces evaluation targets by 271x and 611x on HI-Small and LI-Small. Horvitz-Thompson weights give unbiased full-test confusion-count estimates for fixed predictions; recall is exact, while precision and F1 are ratio estimates. In a held-out study using Graph Feature Preprocessor (GFP) features, one boosted-tree family defines strata for evaluating the other over 500 draws per configuration. At the released sizes, F1 RMSE is 0.00-2.58 percentage points versus 4.44-7.41 for uniform sampling with HT weights; conservative intervals remain broad. Under the evaluated graph prompts, seven open-weight LLMs have weighted precision near the predict-all-illicit baseline. In an outcome-stratified audit of 1,000 HI-Small few-shot outputs from one run per model, lexical checks pass for 84.5% of correct and 56.2% of incorrect binary verdicts, so these markers do not establish correctness. We release the evaluation sets, construction code, and audit tools at https://huggingface.co/datasets/typhoon-ai/AMLworldCompactEval and https://github.com/nat-nischw/AMLworld-Compact.
papers.summary: Evaluating LLMs on the `AMLworld` anti-money-laundering test splits is expensive because each of over a million target transactions needs its own graph prompt, and naive balanced subsampling distorts unweighted precision and F1. `AMLworld-Compact` keeps every illicit test transaction and samples benign ones from strata defined by supervised model scores, using Horvitz-Thompson weights to produce unbiased estimates of full-test confusion counts; recall is exact while precision and F1 are ratio estimates. The `HT-Coreset` protocol **reduces evaluation targets by 271x and 611x on HI-Small and LI-Small**, with F1 root-mean-square error of 0.00-2.58 percentage points versus 4.44-7.41 for uniform sampling. Under the evaluated graph prompts, seven open-weight LLMs show weighted precision near the predict-all-illicit baseline, and an audit finds that lexical reasoning markers pass for 56.2% of incorrect verdicts, so they do not establish correctness.

papers.title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
papers.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies emit sparse action targets that reach the robot controller with irregular delay, so even a sensible predicted action can turn into abrupt motion near people, and existing remedies are hard to compare because they are tested on different streams, delays, and metrics. `JitterVLA` replays identical command and arrival traces through alternative controllers so the controller's contribution to motion quality can be isolated, and is applied to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, 838 episodes from three open VLA pipelines, and a physical `UR3` arm. Interpolation **cut modeled p99 jerk by 83% on human motion with 200 ms delay** at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, replicated on 598 new episodes, while jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at larger tracking cost. Entropy-based gating helped in one pipeline but not another, and on the real arm interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% across six exploratory pairs.

papers.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
papers.abstract: Attention Residuals (AttnRes) enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth, which can be viewed as single-stream softmax attention along the depth axis. Inspired by the success of multi-head attention along the sequence axis, we introduce Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of AttnRes that generalizes this mechanism to multi-head depth attention, yielding substantial performance gains with minimal additional overhead. MSAR draws stream diversity from sequence context through multi-scale causal convolutions, allowing different heads to retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views while preserving the integrity of the hidden representation. The retrieved streams are combined through lightweight adaptive mixing to generate the single-stream layer input. By retaining single-stream sources and expanding them on demand, MSAR supports multi-stream computation without requiring persistent multi-stream storage or communication. Across all 12 downstream benchmarks at the 18B and 28B MoE scales, MSAR consistently outperforms prior residual variants, including standard residual connections, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), and AttnRes. Scaling-law experiments yield an iso-loss compute speedup of $1.58\times$ over the standard residual baseline, compared with $1.35\times$ for AttnRes and $1.30\times$ for mHC. These results make MSAR a promising residual architecture for large-scale pre-training.
papers.summary: Attention Residuals (`AttnRes`) let a layer retrieve from earlier layers through content-dependent softmax attention along the depth axis, but only as a single stream. `MSAR` generalizes this to multi-head depth attention, deriving stream diversity from multi-scale causal convolutions over the sequence so that different heads retrieve historical representations through distinct contextual views, then recombining them with lightweight adaptive mixing; because single-stream sources are expanded on demand, no persistent multi-stream storage or communication is needed. At 18B and 28B mixture-of-experts scales it outperforms standard residuals, manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (`mHC`), and `AttnRes` on all 12 downstream benchmarks, and scaling-law experiments show **an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58x over the standard residual baseline**, versus 1.35x for `AttnRes` and 1.30x for `mHC`.

papers.title: Private and Distributionally Robust Federated Multiclass Classification
papers.abstract: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries requires multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data collected across geographically distributed client sites. Federated learning enables collaborative training without centralizing data, but most approaches do not provide formal privacy guarantees for individual records stored at client sites and can degrade under label noise. To address these limitations, we develop a differentially private, distributionally robust framework for federated multiclass classification that provides sample-level privacy for records stored at each client. We build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved using an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm. To protect the released client updates, our method injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local distributionally robust variable before aggregation at the central server, and we quantify the cumulative privacy loss using the moments accountant. We provide per-round sample-level $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy guarantees and an overall composed privacy guarantee across all training rounds, together with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. Experiments on simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmark datasets show that our method outperforms differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent baselines in most tested settings, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.
papers.summary: Fault diagnosis in asset-intensive industries needs multiclass models trained on noisy, sensitive data spread across distributed client sites, yet most federated learning methods offer no formal privacy guarantee for individual records and degrade under label noise. The authors build on a federated Wasserstein distributionally robust multiclass objective with the Crammer-Singer loss, solved via an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm, and inject calibrated Gaussian noise into the proximal linearized client updates of both the local model and the local robustness variable, tracking cumulative privacy loss with the moments accountant. They provide per-round and composed sample-level epsilon-delta differential privacy guarantees along with convergence results and an explicit privacy-utility tradeoff. On simulated industrial fault data and UCI benchmarks, **the method beats differentially private federated empirical risk minimization and SGD baselines in most settings**, with the largest gains under strong privacy-induced noise.

papers.title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erd\H{o}s Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. More broadly, a single agent session remains brittle on difficult problems: early errors can propagate, missing domain knowledge can stall progress, and apparent success can mask a misinterpretation or weakening of the original task. We introduce HOA (Humanize Olympiads Agent), an open, flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three complementary feedback channels. First, an independent reviewer evaluates each candidate and provides actionable feedback. Second, a structured wiki supplies task-specific knowledge that may be missing or unreliable in model pretraining. Third, a verifier checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With GPT-5.6 Sol, HOA achieves perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on the IChO 2026 problem set, and solves all 672 problems (100%) on PutnamBench. On the Lean-Eval leaderboard, HOA ranks first, solving 251 of 304 problems (82.6%). We further evaluate HOA with open models. Using Kimi-K3, HOA achieves full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI, and a gold-level score of 97.1% on the IChO. These results closely match the closed-source GPT-5.6 Sol + /Goal baseline on the IMO and IPhO, while exceeding it on the IChO and IOI, demonstrating that systematic feedback can help bridge substantial differences in base-model capability.
papers.summary: Single agent sessions remain brittle on hard olympiad-level problems: early errors propagate, missing domain knowledge stalls progress, and apparent success can hide a misread or weakened task. `HOA` is an open flow-level framework that coordinates multiple agent sessions through three feedback channels: an independent reviewer that critiques each candidate, a structured wiki that supplies task-specific knowledge the base model may lack, and a verifier that checks generated Lean proofs against trusted challenge statements. With `GPT-5.6 Sol`, it reports perfect scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI 2026, near-full marks on IChO 2026, **solves all 672 problems on `PutnamBench`**, and ranks first on `Lean-Eval` with 251 of 304 problems. With the open model `Kimi-K3` it also reaches full scores on the IMO, IPhO, and IOI and 97.1% on IChO, suggesting systematic feedback can bridge large gaps in base-model capability.

papers.title: PANDA: Prior-guided Attentional Dual-path Architecture
papers.abstract: Hypergraph Neural Networks (HNNs), designed to model higher-order relations beyond pairwise interactions, typically rely either on fixed structural weights or on normalised attention. Fixed weights can propagate misleading information in heterophilic settings, while normalisation makes attention coefficients competitive, in the sense that, in a message-passing framework, increasing the weight of one sender must reduce the weight of others in the same aggregation set. Our main contribution is the introduction of PANDA (Prior-guided AttentioNal Dual-path Architecture), a plug-in for two-stage message passing HNNs applicable to both undirected and directed settings. The main path interpolates between learned receiver-normalised attention and structural incidence priors, while a non-competitive (not normalised) auxiliary path lets each sender contribute its own transformed information. We also show that, with fixed structural coefficients, PANDA recovers a certain complex-valued convolution operator adopted in previous works. Across four HNNs spanning spatial and spectral methods in both directed and undirected settings, plugging PANDA in yields an average improvement of 5.18 percentage points across eight real-world benchmark datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/jainris/panda.
papers.summary: Hypergraph Neural Networks (HNNs) typically aggregate messages with either fixed structural weights, which can propagate misleading information in heterophilic settings, or normalized attention, which forces senders in the same aggregation set to compete for weight. `PANDA` is a plug-in for two-stage message-passing HNNs in both undirected and directed settings: its main path interpolates between learned receiver-normalized attention and structural incidence priors, while a non-normalized auxiliary path lets each sender contribute its own transformed information without competition. With fixed structural coefficients, the design recovers a complex-valued convolution operator used in prior work. Plugged into four spatial and spectral HNNs, it **improves accuracy by an average of 5.18 percentage points across eight real-world benchmark datasets**.

papers.title: Model-agnostic Knowledge Augmented Machine Learning for Weakly Annotated Bioimaging Data
papers.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used for automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data, such as microscopy and cytomorphology images. Due to the sole dependency of automated feature extraction, existing methods yield inconsistent classification performance across weakly annotated datasets. Here, we propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that enables ML models to exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction can capture. The proposed approach improves classification performance across seven ML architectures. When integrated with masked autoencoder-based self-supervised learning, our method achieves the strongest overall performance, improving precision by 2.9% over the next-best method on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks. We perform nucleus-level classification based on mislocalization of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, a phenotype linked to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), using three independent microscopy datasets of motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells. Accurate quantification of this phenotype at scale remains challenging and may contribute to inconsistencies across studies. Application of the best-performing model to these microscopy datasets reveals biological interpretations related to ALS, including dose-dependent effects of the proteasomal stressor, MG132, and the oxidative stressor, sodium arsenite (SA), on TDP-43 mislocalization, variable pathology in motor neurons from sporadic and familial ALS donors, and a lack of protection of the pharmacological compounds, edaravone and niclosamide, against SA-induced TDP-43 mislocalization. Together, our pipeline enables in-vitro cellular image analysis to advance understanding of ALS-associated pathology and potential treatments.
papers.summary: Automated feature extraction from weakly annotated bioimaging data such as microscopy and cytomorphology images gives inconsistent classification results across datasets. The authors propose a model-agnostic knowledge augmentation method that lets machine learning models exploit domain knowledge beyond what automated feature extraction captures, improving classification across seven architectures. Combined with masked autoencoder self-supervised learning, it **improves precision by 2.9% on three in-house microscopy datasets and by an average of 6.8% across three public cytomorphology benchmarks** over the next-best method. Applied to nucleus-level classification of TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) mislocalization in motor neurons derived from human induced pluripotent stem cells, the pipeline recovers Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS)-relevant findings, including dose-dependent effects of the stressors `MG132` and sodium arsenite and a lack of protection from edaravone and niclosamide.

papers.title: Learning Size Independent Constraint Models from Input Data and Positive and Negative Example Solutions
papers.abstract: In this paper we describe a Constraint Acquisition Tool that generates size independent constraint programs from input data and positive and negative example solutions of multiple problem instances. The system finds size specific models based on typical constraint patterns over global and binary constraints, then generalizes the models to a size independent model that can be run on unseen input data. The system produces MiniZinc code as well as a textual description of the model. We evaluate the tool on the example problems of the PTHG21 Challenge and show the feasibility of the approach.
papers.summary: Writing a constraint program by hand requires expertise, and models learned from examples are usually tied to a single instance size. The described Constraint Acquisition Tool takes input data plus positive and negative example solutions from multiple problem instances, finds size-specific models based on typical patterns over global and binary constraints, and then generalizes them into a size-independent model that runs on unseen input data. It emits `MiniZinc` code together with a textual description of the model, and **the approach is shown to be feasible on the example problems of the `PTHG21 Challenge`**.

papers.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.
papers.summary: Practitioners choosing a feature selection method face benchmarks built on outdated models, ad hoc protocols, or synthetic data that does not reflect real problems. `SelectArena` compares 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets spanning classification and regression, with standardized protocols and state-of-the-art tabular foundation models as downstream learners, measuring predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. **Tree-based `CART` and `RFImportance` together with `F-Test` are Pareto-optimal on performance versus runtime**, with `F-Test` also leading on stability and validity and emerging as the most balanced choice. Search-based methods are slow, unstable, and low-performing, and the benchmark is released as an extensible platform.

papers.title: Electron-Density-Informed Molecular Property Prediction Using Surrogate Functionals
papers.abstract: Machine learning methods are increasingly used to predict chemical properties directly from the molecular structure to bypass the often prohibitive cost of quantum mechanical calculations. Recent work has shown that including the ground-state electron density as input to the machine learning model can improve accuracy in this setting. This work employs the recent surrogate functional framework originally developed for orbital-free density functional theory and extends it to predicting molecular properties. We show that passing the ground-state density as input to the model, while simultaneously enforcing it to be the minimum of the surrogate functional, surpasses state-of-the-art performance for six out of seven extensive properties of the QM9 dataset. Additionally, the approach shows improved generalization to larger molecules taken from the QM40 dataset. On all extensive properties of both datasets, our approach outperforms models that are informed by the ground-state density but do not enforce the surrogate functional constraints.
papers.summary: Machine learning models that predict chemical properties from molecular structure can gain accuracy by also taking the ground-state electron density as input. The authors adapt the surrogate functional framework, originally developed for orbital-free density functional theory, to property prediction by feeding the model the ground-state density while simultaneously enforcing that density to be the minimum of the surrogate functional. The constrained approach **surpasses state-of-the-art performance on six of seven extensive properties of the `QM9` dataset** and generalizes better to the larger molecules of `QM40`, and on all extensive properties of both datasets it beats density-informed models that do not enforce the surrogate functional constraints.

papers.title: A Critical Look at Power Sampling when Test Time Sharpening LLMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved LLM reasoning, yet growing evidence suggests it mainly performs distribution sharpening: concentrating probability mass on reasoning paths the base model already produces. Recent work therefore seeks RLVR's gains without needing reward signals, by sampling from the power distribution $\pi_\alpha \propto \pi_{\text{base}}^\alpha$ via Markov chain Monte Carlo or sequential Monte Carlo. We show that these samplers fail to converge to $\pi_\alpha$ under realistic compute budgets, and that their gains are largely recreated via simple Best-of-$N$ with appropriate grading . This suggests they succeed by selecting high-probability sequences, not by approximating $\pi_\alpha$, raising a natural question: is the power distribution itself a worthwhile target? We test this hypothesis directly by fine-tuning the base model to match $\pi_\alpha$, sidestepping sampler convergence issues entirely. Despite approximating the target far more faithfully than existing samplers, this strategy yields gains that are noisy and specific to certain models and sampling tasks. Together, our results suggest that the value of power sampling lies not in faithfully targeting $\pi_\alpha$, but in the simpler goal of extracting sequences the base model already deems likely.
papers.summary: Evidence suggests reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) mainly sharpens the base model's distribution onto reasoning paths it already produces, prompting reward-free methods that sample from the power distribution proportional to the base policy raised to alpha via Markov chain Monte Carlo or sequential Monte Carlo. The authors show these samplers do not converge to the power distribution under realistic compute budgets and that **their gains are largely recreated by simple Best-of-N with appropriate grading**, implying they work by selecting high-probability sequences rather than approximating the target. To test whether the power distribution is itself worth targeting, they fine-tune the base model to match it directly, sidestepping sampler convergence; despite a far more faithful approximation, the gains are noisy and specific to certain models and tasks. The conclusion is that power sampling's value lies in extracting sequences the base model already deems likely, not in faithfully targeting the power distribution.

papers.title: TabReliBench: Evaluating Tabular Foundation Models Beyond Predictive Accuracy
papers.abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are increasingly popular for their strong predictive performance. Many also provide posterior predictive distributions (PPDs), whose reliability remains less studied. We assess reliability through point prediction, distributional quality, marginal and subgroup calibration, and interval efficiency. We then introduce TabReliBench, a large classification and regression benchmark for these comparisons and dataset-level analyses. We find that TFMs' rankings change between TabArena and our benchmark and across reliability metrics. Regression TFMs usually achieve near-nominal marginal coverage and retain narrow intervals, but this favorable marginal behavior does not imply valid conditional coverage. Dataset-level analyses show that classification difficulty often accompanies poor calibration, whereas regression predictive performance is not a reliable indicator of calibration. Ensembling improves predictive performance but does not consistently improve calibration of PPDs; TFMs also benefit little from conformal post-processing, which does not reliably resolve subgroup gaps. Reliable TFM selection therefore requires multidimensional evaluation beyond aggregate rankings. Code is available at https://github.com/Tianqi-Zhao/TabReliBench.
papers.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) are prized for predictive accuracy, but the reliability of the posterior predictive distributions (PPDs) many of them provide is understudied. `TabReliBench` is a large classification and regression benchmark that assesses point prediction, distributional quality, marginal and subgroup calibration, and interval efficiency, with dataset-level analyses. **TFM rankings shift between `TabArena` and this benchmark and across reliability metrics**; regression TFMs usually reach near-nominal marginal coverage with narrow intervals, but this does not imply valid conditional coverage, and classification difficulty tends to accompany poor calibration while regression accuracy does not predict calibration. Ensembling improves predictive performance without consistently improving PPD calibration, and conformal post-processing helps little and does not reliably close subgroup gaps, so selecting a TFM requires multidimensional evaluation.

papers.title: Scalable Sparse Autoregressive Variational Inference for Non-Gaussian Spatial Fields
papers.abstract: Latent field models are essential for spatial statistics, but the posterior distribution of the latent field, even with a Gaussian process (GP) prior, is analytically intractable whenever the likelihood is non-Gaussian. Existing approximations are either too slow or too restrictive for large non-Gaussian datasets. We present a scalable variational inference framework that mirrors the sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure of the prior in the variational family, uses normalizing-flow conditionals for expressiveness, and amortizes all variational parameters via a single shared neural conditioner. Doubly stochastic optimization with reduced ancestor sets achieves polylogarithmic complexity per iteration.
papers.summary: In spatial statistics, the posterior over a latent field with a Gaussian process (GP) prior becomes analytically intractable once the likelihood is non-Gaussian, and existing approximations are either too slow or too restrictive for large datasets. The proposed variational inference framework mirrors the prior's sparse nearest-neighbor autoregressive structure in the variational family, uses normalizing-flow conditionals for expressiveness, and amortizes all variational parameters through a single shared neural conditioner. Doubly stochastic optimization with reduced ancestor sets **achieves polylogarithmic complexity per iteration**.

papers.title: Pretraining and Test-Time Training Budgets Matter for ARC: A Controlled Study of VARC and TRM
papers.abstract: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) is increasingly used to evaluate whether neural networks can infer task-specific transformations from few demonstrations. Recent ARC models differ in architecture, but also in broader training and evaluation protocols, including pretraining data, data augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, making conclusions about architecture benefits debatable. In this work, we study how the performance of the vision-inspired VARC and recursion-based TRM models is affected by pretraining and test-time training (TTT) budgets under a common inductive protocol on ARC-AGI-1. We cross five pretraining budgets with four TTT budgets for each test task. Each budget specifies a task-variant count and total sample presentations, defining the controlled training budgets. We observe that increasing TTT sample presentations improves the standard ARC pass@2 metric in all settings for both models. Increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only TRM, whereas VARC often performs better with fewer variants. VARC also remains competitive without pretraining, while TRM benefits much more from it. These results show that pretraining and TTT budgets affect ARC evaluation and motivate reporting at comparable budgets.
papers.summary: Recent models for the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) differ not only in architecture but also in pretraining data, augmentation, test-time setup, and optimization budgets, which muddies conclusions about which architectural choices actually help. The authors place the vision-inspired `VARC` and recursion-based `TRM` under a common inductive protocol on `ARC-AGI-1`, crossing five pretraining budgets with four test-time training (TTT) budgets, each defined by a task-variant count and total sample presentations. **Increasing TTT sample presentations improves pass@2 in every setting for both models**, but increasing the TTT task-variant count consistently helps only `TRM`, while `VARC` often does better with fewer variants. `VARC` also stays competitive without pretraining whereas `TRM` depends on it much more, motivating reporting of ARC results at comparable budgets.

papers.title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
papers.abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.
papers.summary: Many machine learning methods are two-level: an expert picks a class of models, and then the choice of key components within that class is critical and usually manual. The proposed multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework uses three roles, analyst, coder, and recorder, with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment, and generates code only for specified components while leaving the overall network structure unchanged, rather than rewriting whole scripts or searching a discrete architecture space. It is validated on tuning a spiking neural network with correlation learning and on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) for high-order differential equations across five tasks. The agent beats baselines throughout, with **classification accuracy 13 points higher on `MNIST` and 6 points higher on `Digits`**, a roughly 2491-fold reduction in error against the analytical single-soliton solution of the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE), and a 14-fold drop in mass drift on the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) problem.

papers.title: A Step Harder, Not a Step Too Far: The Benefits and Limits of Curriculum Difficulty Progression in GRPO
papers.abstract: Curriculum learning typically organizes training samples from easy to hard. In GRPO, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are more likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, and prioritizing them can improve training efficiency. However, it remains unclear whether persistently selecting such samples also leads to the strongest final model performance, or whether training can benefit from progressing toward harder samples. Meanwhile, sample difficulty changes as the policy evolves, so fixed difficulty estimates can become misaligned with the current policy. We therefore re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and, inspired by the easy-to-hard principle of curriculum learning, design and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. Experiments on GSM8K show that persistent medium-difficulty selection does not achieve the strongest observed performance. Across three random seeds, progressing to a moderately harder difficulty band improves test accuracy to $0.6591 \pm 0.0077$, compared with $0.6449 \pm 0.0024$ for the fixed-medium curriculum. However, further progression to a harder difficulty band reduces accuracy to $0.6405 \pm 0.0053$. These results show that staged difficulty progression can outperform persistent medium-difficulty selection, but its benefit is non-monotonic. Effective GRPO curricula can therefore benefit from progressing beyond medium difficulty, while avoiding excessive progression toward overly difficult samples.}
papers.summary: In `GRPO`, medium-difficulty samples are attractive for online selection because they are most likely to yield informative group-relative learning signals, but it is unclear whether always selecting them produces the best final model or whether training should progress toward harder samples as the policy improves. The authors re-estimate sample difficulty under the current policy and evaluate a staged curriculum that progressively shifts the active difficulty band toward harder samples. On `GSM8K` across three seeds, **progressing to a moderately harder band improves test accuracy to 0.6591 versus 0.6449 for the fixed-medium curriculum**, but pushing further to a harder band drops accuracy to 0.6405. The benefit of difficulty progression is therefore non-monotonic: effective curricula should move beyond medium difficulty without advancing to overly difficult samples.

papers.title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
papers.abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. For redirection, we find that under a fixed generation budget, the tested inline injections fail to reliably redirect reasoning, whereas presenting the same instruction in a new user turn changes the model's course. The resulting correction framework, UPTURN (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), requires no LLM fine-tuning: it retains a selected prefix, injects an instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the suffix. Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks, UPTURN improves average accuracy in every setting over a 32-rollout baseline. It outperforms self-correction and reflection-token injection baselines under matched correction budgets, transfers across reasoners and to GPQA-Diamond without retraining, and complements GRPO and self-correction methods.
papers.summary: Large language models rarely manage to spot and fix errors in their own reasoning, and most fixes require fine-tuning the model to produce revisions or feedback. The authors instead train a small 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder, supervised only by final-answer correctness, to decide where in a failed rollout to intervene, and find that presenting the redirect instruction as a fresh user turn changes the model's course where inline token injection does not. The resulting method, `UPTURN` (User-Prompt TURN injection at a learned position), keeps a chosen prefix, inserts the instruction as a new user turn, and regenerates the rest without touching model weights. **Across four reasoners and six math benchmarks it improves average accuracy over a 32-rollout baseline in every setting**, beats self-correction and reflection-token baselines at matched budgets, transfers to `GPQA-Diamond` without retraining, and stacks with GRPO and self-correction methods.

papers.title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels
papers.abstract: Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query-key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. Motivated by this heterogeneity, we propose Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization (OAL), a dimension-aware method for constructing quadratic attention approximations. Starting from a second-order Taylor approximation, we introduce a Hadamard-product formulation that makes individual query-key contributions explicit. This formulation relaxes globally shared coefficients to support dimension-specific linear terms and cross-dimensional quadratic interactions while preserving separable evaluation. To retain this flexibility with fewer parameters, OAL groups dimensions with similar contribution scales to share coefficients, while allowing distinct treatment of the few outliers. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and admits linear-time evaluation with respect to sequence length for fixed head dimensions. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, OAL reduces frozen-attention output relative MSE by approximately 8.9% compared with DiJiang. Replacing middle-layer attention modules and jointly fine-tuning the kernel coefficients with LoRA further lowers WikiText-103 perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50 compared with a learned global quadratic, while improving accuracy on PIQA, HellaSwag, and ARC-E. These results demonstrate the value of outlier-aware dimension grouping for both attention approximation and pretrained-model conversion. The code is available at https://github.com/wuqianyue09/OAL
papers.summary: Replacing softmax attention with a linear-time kernel can speed up Transformer inference, but keeping the behaviour of pretrained attention is hard. The authors show that a handful of outlier dimensions dominate query-key dot products and account for much of the approximation error, and propose Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization (`OAL`), which starts from a second-order Taylor expansion, rewrites it with Hadamard products so each dimension's contribution is explicit, and groups dimensions by contribution scale so the few outliers get their own coefficients while the rest share parameters. The resulting positive quadratic kernel is calibrated against pretrained attention outputs and evaluates in linear time in sequence length. On `Qwen2.5-0.5B` it cuts frozen-attention relative MSE by about 8.9% versus `DiJiang`, and **swapping middle-layer attention and fine-tuning kernel coefficients with LoRA lowers `WikiText-103` perplexity from 31.71 to 27.50** relative to a learned global quadratic, with gains on `PIQA`, `HellaSwag`, and `ARC-E`.

papers.title: On the Encoding of Calendar Features in Covariate-Informed Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) increasingly offer covariate support, with calendar information being the most common type of categorical covariate in practice, as it is available for every point in time. However, how these features are encoded is largely treated as an implementation detail rather than as an object of study, despite encoding being one of the few design choices left for pretrained models at inference time. With the present study, we demonstrate that the way information is propagated into the model substantially affects forecast accuracy of TSFMs. Therefore, we systematically compare seven calendar encodings, including three conventional target-agnostic representations (ordinal, one-hot, and cyclic) and four target encodings, across four state-of-the-art TSFMs on nine datasets from multiple domains in a zero-shot rolling evaluation. The nine datasets are influenced by social activities, such as weekends and holidays, making calendar information particularly relevant for forecasting. We find that encoding choice affects forecast accuracy across all models, with MASE differences of up to 9.9 % on non-holidays and 83 % on holidays within a single model. Effectiveness and utilization vary substantially across models. Improvements are concentrated around holidays, where calendar information provides signals unavailable from target history, while some model encoding combinations also improve non-holiday forecasts. A SHAP-based attribution analysis locates the contribution of the covariates relative to the autoregressive component and explains why some model-encoding combinations degrade performance. Our findings suggest that current benchmarks for covariate-informed TSFMs can distort model comparisons by imposing fixed encoding strategies.
papers.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) increasingly accept covariates, and calendar features are the most common categorical covariate since they exist for every timestamp, yet how they are encoded is usually treated as an implementation detail. The authors systematically compare seven calendar encodings, three target-agnostic ones (ordinal, one-hot, cyclic) and four target encodings, across four state-of-the-art TSFMs on nine datasets shaped by weekends and holidays, in a zero-shot rolling evaluation. Encoding choice affects accuracy for every model, with **MASE differences of up to 9.9% on non-holidays and 83% on holidays within a single model**, and the gains cluster around holidays where the target history carries no signal. A SHAP-based attribution analysis explains why some model-encoding pairs degrade performance, and the authors argue that benchmarks that impose a fixed encoding can distort comparisons between covariate-informed TSFMs.

papers.title: Retractions Revisited: A Replication, Extension, and Mechanistic Evaluation of Linguistic Obfuscation Effects in Fraudulent Science
papers.abstract: Prior work suggests fraudulent scientists write their articles with higher rates of linguistic obfuscation than genuine scientists, with a possible mechanism suggesting obfuscation makes research more costly for a reader to analyze. This result has not undergone additional empirical scrutiny in the open science era, nor have other psychological mechanisms been evaluated. The current replication and extension addressed this opportunity by comparing 800 fraudulent and 800 genuine control papers (2013-2025). The results supported the linguistic obfuscation hypothesis, suggesting fraudulent papers were more obfuscated than genuine ones. A parallel mediation model evaluated three competing mechanisms, finding that reality monitoring, as measured through decreased rates of adjectives, best explained the link between fraudulent science and linguistic obfuscation. Cross-validated detection accuracy using obfuscation features (60.7%) and an elastic net of over 100 language dimensions (71.6%) were significantly greater than chance. Implications for scientific fraud and psychology of language research are discussed.
papers.summary: Earlier work found that fraudulent scientists write with more linguistic obfuscation than genuine ones, possibly to make their papers costlier to scrutinize, but that result had not been retested in the open science era or compared against other psychological mechanisms. This replication and extension compares 800 fraudulent papers with 800 genuine controls from 2013 to 2025 and confirms that fraudulent papers are more obfuscated. A parallel mediation model tests three competing mechanisms and finds that reality monitoring, measured through lower adjective rates, best explains the link. Cross-validated detection reached 60.7% accuracy with obfuscation features alone and **71.6% with an elastic net over more than 100 language dimensions**, both significantly above chance.

papers.title: X-AVDD: Cross-Attentive Audio-Visual Dataset Distillation
papers.abstract: Audio-visual dataset distillation aims to synthesize a small dataset from a large paired audio-visual dataset, while nearly preserving the training utility for neural networks. Existing approaches such as DM and AVDD face two critical limitations: 1) they are memory-intensive, making them difficult to scale to complex architectures and higher samples-per-class (SPC) settings, and 2) they often fail to preserve strong cross-modal semantic correspondence. To tackle these issues, we propose X-AVDD, a cross-attention-based distillation method that explicitly captures inter-modal relationships during synthesis. By decoupling cross-modal alignment from joint optimization, X-AVDD is substantially more memory-efficient, reducing end-to-end synthesis cost by $\sim 8\times$ GPU-hours, while producing highly aligned synthetic data. Empirically, X-AVDD significantly outperforms other audio-visual distillation methods. On VGGSound, an audio-visual dataset of short YouTube clips, X-AVDD improves top-1 test accuracy from $8.2\%\rightarrow24.0\%$ at SPC=$10$ and $9.8\%\rightarrow26.5\%$ at SPC=$20$. Furthermore, X-AVDD improves cross-architecture generalization (e.g., $25.5\%\rightarrow35.3\%$ for a ViT target on AVE dataset at SPC $=50$) and successfully scales to complex architectures such as AudioCLIP, achieving $62.3\%$ accuracy using only $5.65\%$ of the full dataset, against the full dataset accuracy of $72.4\%$ while completing in $9\times$ lower training time compared to the full dataset.
papers.summary: Audio-visual dataset distillation compresses a large paired audio-visual dataset into a small synthetic one that trains networks nearly as well, but existing methods such as `DM` and `AVDD` are memory-hungry and often lose cross-modal semantic correspondence. `X-AVDD` uses cross-attention to capture inter-modal relationships explicitly during synthesis and decouples cross-modal alignment from the joint optimization, cutting end-to-end synthesis cost by roughly 8x in GPU-hours. **On `VGGSound` it raises top-1 accuracy from 8.2% to 24.0% at 10 samples per class and from 9.8% to 26.5% at 20**, improves cross-architecture transfer (25.5% to 35.3% for a ViT target on `AVE` at 50 samples per class), and scales to `AudioCLIP`, reaching 62.3% accuracy with 5.65% of the data versus 72.4% for the full dataset at 9x lower training time.

papers.title: VQIL: Visible Quantum Interference Learning for Perturbation Response Ranking on Graphs
papers.abstract: Learning how local perturbations affect a network is important for identifying which components drive or absorb a system's response. We formulate this as seed-conditioned response ranking: given a perturbation at one seed node, ranking all other nodes by response strength. This is challenging when the model is given only the interaction topology, while the mechanism governing how perturbations propagate must be learned from data. We present VQIL (Visible Quantum Interference Learning), a trainable Szegedy quantum walk for seed-conditioned ranking. Edge weights, link phases, and per-node phase rotations are optimized end-to-end by backpropagation while the walk operator remains unitary throughout training. Node scores are obtained from a geometrically discounted coherent sum of quantum-walk amplitudes, enabling quantum interference before the final squared-norm readout. Because each learned parameter is attached to a named edge or node, the trained model provides directly inspectable hypotheses about the roles of individual graph components in the propagation mechanism. On AC power-flow perturbations over six transmission grids, with electrical parameters withheld from the model, VQIL improves Spearman rank correlation from 0.147 for the untrained walk to 0.831 and outperforms an identically trained random-walk model. On gene perturbation over five protein-protein interaction networks with Perturb-seq supervision, VQIL improves rank correlation from 0.171 to 0.620, outperforming the strongest learned classical and neural baselines. These results show that trainable quantum-walk interference provides a scalable and interpretable inductive bias for learning seed-conditioned response rankings on graphs.
papers.summary: Predicting how a perturbation at one node of a network spreads to the others matters for finding which components drive or absorb a system's response, and it is hard when only the topology is known and the propagation mechanism must be learned from data. Visible Quantum Interference Learning (`VQIL`) is a trainable Szegedy quantum walk whose edge weights, link phases, and per-node phase rotations are optimized by backpropagation while the walk operator stays unitary, with node scores read out from a geometrically discounted coherent sum of amplitudes so that interference happens before the squared-norm readout. Because each parameter belongs to a named edge or node, the trained model yields inspectable hypotheses about component roles. On AC power-flow perturbations across six transmission grids with electrical parameters withheld, **Spearman rank correlation rises from 0.147 for the untrained walk to 0.831**, and on gene perturbation over five protein-protein interaction networks with Perturb-seq supervision it rises from 0.171 to 0.620, beating the strongest classical and neural baselines.

papers.title: Transformer-based In-Context Score Operator Learning for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion models typically learn the generative dynamics of a single target distribution or a family of distributions indexed by conditioning variables fixed during training. This limits their ability to adapt to a previously unseen distribution from only a small set of examples. We introduce an in-context solution operator learning framework for diffusion models, in which each target distribution is treated as a task drawn from a meta-distribution and is specified at inference time by an empirical context set. Our method learns an in-context score operator that maps the context samples, a noisy query point, and the diffusion time to the task-dependent score, enabling reverse-diffusion sampling on unseen tasks without retraining or parameter updates. A key observation is that the task-dependent score admits a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean representation. Its empirical Nadaraya--Watson approximation can be represented exactly by a model in our constructed transformer class, providing a principled foundation for the proposed query-dependent attention architecture. The operator is trained through amortized denoising score matching across task distributions. We establish generalization-error bounds that quantify the effects of the context size, the numbers of training tasks and within-task samples, model complexity, and intrinsic and ambient dimensions. Numerically, we evaluate the method on a range of scientific and visual datasets, including Navier-Stokes, ERA5 climate data, QuickDraw sketches, and Food-101. The results show that the proposed method performs well on relatively simple task families, while its performance degrades as task complexity increases, thereby illustrating both the promise and the limitations of in-context learning for diffusion models.
papers.summary: Diffusion models usually learn one target distribution, or a family indexed by conditioning variables fixed at training time, so they cannot adapt to a new distribution from a few examples. The authors treat each target distribution as a task drawn from a meta-distribution, specified at inference by an empirical context set, and learn an in-context score operator that maps context samples, a noisy query, and the diffusion time to the task-dependent score, enabling reverse-diffusion sampling on unseen tasks without parameter updates. The design rests on the observation that the task-dependent score has a Gaussian-kernel conditional-mean form whose Nadaraya-Watson estimate is exactly representable by their transformer class, and the paper provides generalization bounds in terms of context size, number of tasks, samples per task, model complexity, and intrinsic and ambient dimension. On `Navier-Stokes`, `ERA5`, `QuickDraw`, and `Food-101`, **the method does well on simpler task families but degrades as task complexity grows**.

papers.title: Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient is Nearly Minimax-Optimal
papers.abstract: Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.
papers.summary: Policy gradient methods suffer from high variance in their Monte Carlo updates, and existing variance-reduced variants only reach optimal sample complexity under restrictive assumptions such as uniformly bounded importance weights or with impractical second-order operations. The authors introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced Policy Gradient (`LVR-PG`), a framework covering first-order estimators that combine recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including `PAGE-PG` and `STORM-PG`. **They prove last-iterate global convergence with sample complexity of order epsilon to the minus two, up to logarithmic factors, under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies**, using only first-order updates and no gradient preconditioners. Extending existing lower bounds to continuous parametric policies gives a matching lower bound of the same order, so the framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic and horizon terms.

papers.title: Calibration in One Go: Jointly Learning Accurate and Calibrated Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Neural networks (NNs), while highly flexible and versatile, are often poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration methods adjust the outputs of an already trained model using a separate calibration dataset and additional calibration parameters. This process adds overhead that requires separate optimization of the calibrator and subsequent model selection. In this paper, we show that standard (post-hoc) calibrators can be trained end-to-end with the backbone via a bilevel Stackelberg formulation. This formulation eliminates the need for a separate calibration set or a dedicated calibration loss by jointly optimizing accuracy and calibration using cross-entropy, introducing only one additional hyperparameter: the calibrator learning rate. Although our framework supports calibrators ranging from temperature and matrix scaling to NN layers, our results show that using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no additional parameters. Our approach outperforms SOTA calibrators with minimal added complexity, while also avoiding the multiplicative overhead of separate calibration components in settings such as multi-task learning.
papers.summary: Neural networks are often poorly calibrated, and post-hoc calibrators fix this with a separate calibration set, extra parameters, and a second optimization and model-selection pass. The authors show that standard post-hoc calibrators can instead be trained end-to-end with the backbone through a bilevel Stackelberg formulation that optimizes accuracy and calibration jointly with cross-entropy alone, adding only one hyperparameter, the calibrator learning rate, and needing no separate calibration set or loss. The framework supports temperature scaling, matrix scaling, and neural calibrators, but **using the final classification layer itself as the calibrator yields accurate, well-calibrated models with no extra parameters**. The approach outperforms state-of-the-art calibrators with little added complexity and avoids the multiplicative cost of separate calibration components in settings like multi-task learning.

papers.title: Verifiable Retrieval for Legal Reasoning through Structure-driven Knowledge Graph
papers.abstract: Any automation within reliability-critical contexts such as medicine or law has to be transparent and verifiable. Despite their advantages, current LLM-based systems do not meet these requirements due to their inherent black-box nature. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) attempts to ground the generative process in the relevant interpretable documents, thereby reducing the risk of AI 'hallucinations' and potentially enabling verification of the initial generation context. However, as the number and size of potential sources increases, naive retrieval approaches tend to perform worse, ignoring critical context elements. In this paper we aim to tackle this problem in the context of German Legal Code. Using structure-driven parsing to create a Knowledge Graph (KG) for the source document navigation and retrieval, we compare several KG-informed chunking and retrieval strategies and evaluate their effect on the accuracy of retrieved citations.
papers.summary: Automation in reliability-critical domains like law must be transparent and verifiable, which black-box LLM systems do not deliver on their own. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds generation in interpretable source documents, but naive retrieval degrades as the number and size of sources grows and misses critical context. Working on German legal code, the authors use structure-driven parsing to build a Knowledge Graph (KG) for navigating and retrieving from the source documents, then compare several KG-informed chunking and retrieval strategies. **The evaluation measures how each strategy affects the accuracy of the retrieved citations**, with the aim of making the generation context verifiable.

papers.title: A Baseline Assessment for the Agentic Web Technology Stack
papers.abstract: The fast pace in which protocols, frameworks, and technologies are being proposed for LLM-based agents results in a complex scenario for anyone aiming to create state-of-the-art AI solutions. Without an assessment on how different protocols, frameworks, and libraries work together to compose an Agentic Web solution, developers and organizations face different challenges (e.g., skilling, governance, infrastructure) even before becoming part of the Agentic Web ecosystem. In this context, we propose a system for performing Agentic Web evaluations called MASTIF (Multi-Agent System TestIng Framework) and present a baseline assessment of Agentic Web technologies, including 3 LLMs, 3 protocols, and 4 agent implementation frameworks, against 300 Mind2Web benchmark tasks. Results suggest that selecting a task-specific technology stack may result in gains of task completion rate, efficiency score, and social value stability scores; and reductions in verbosity and time to complete tasks. With the presented results, we expect to present a baseline in terms of metrics and results for this complex and fast evolving scenario for those aiming at designing, assessing, and developing multi-agent systems.
papers.summary: The rapid churn of protocols, frameworks, and libraries for LLM-based agents makes it hard for developers to know which combinations work together to build an Agentic Web solution, creating skilling, governance, and infrastructure hurdles before a team even gets started. The authors present `MASTIF` (Multi-Agent System TestIng Framework), a system for running Agentic Web evaluations, and use it for a baseline assessment of 3 LLMs, 3 protocols, and 4 agent implementation frameworks on 300 tasks from the `Mind2Web` benchmark. **Choosing a task-specific technology stack can raise task completion rate, efficiency score, and social value stability** while reducing verbosity and time to completion. The results are offered as baseline metrics for anyone designing, assessing, or building multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Adaptive DHiSparse: Speculative Decoding over a Load-Adaptive KV Hierarchy
papers.abstract: Long-context serving runs out of KV memory before the hardware reaches its useful throughput. HiSparse stores history in host memory and fetches only the selected entries, but it uses one cache budget at every load and does not handle draft-model speculative decoding such as DSpark and DFlash2. We present Adaptive DHiSparse, which supports speculative decoding over hierarchical sparse KV and adapts residency to load. It protects the required working set, retains additional history while GPU memory is spare, and recovers the rest through exact fused retrieval. DSpark and DFlash2 keep their proposal and acceptance rules: queries share missing-row retrieval, draft KV uses a window-bounded ring, and verification staging is reused across layer groups. At 100K context and concurrency 128, GLM-5.3 with DFlash2 delivers 793 output tokens/s per decode GPU, 1.45$\times$ HiSparse and 1.27$\times$ non-speculative adaptive serving. Held to the same latency bounds as HiSparse, it sustains up to 4$\times$ the concurrency and 2.3 to 3.7$\times$ the output, depending on the per-token bound. On DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 500K context and concurrency 512, Adaptive DHiSparse with DSpark delivers 1.85$\times$ the output of resident serving with DSpark. In a load step, optional residency reduces host fetches from 14.2% to 1.4% of selected rows at low load and releases memory under pressure.
papers.summary: Long-context LLM serving exhausts KV cache memory well before the GPU reaches its useful throughput. `HiSparse` already keeps history in host memory and fetches only selected entries, but it uses a single cache budget regardless of load and does not support draft-model speculative decoding such as `DSpark` and `DFlash2`. Adaptive `DHiSparse` runs speculative decoding over a hierarchical sparse KV cache and adapts residency to load, protecting the required working set, keeping extra history while GPU memory is spare, and recovering the rest through exact fused retrieval, with the drafters' proposal and acceptance rules left untouched. **At 100K context and concurrency 128, `GLM-5.3` with `DFlash2` reaches 793 output tokens per second per decode GPU, 1.45x `HiSparse`**, sustains up to 4x the concurrency under the same latency bounds, and on `DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash` at 500K context and concurrency 512 delivers 1.85x the output of resident serving with `DSpark`.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Training of GFlowNets: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn policies that sample discrete objects in proportion to a positive reward. They are trained by minimizing balance objectives, whose exact satisfaction guarantees correct sampling. However, a comprehensive theory linking nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially under evolving sampling distributions and backward policies, is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we develop a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. We first bound terminal symmetric KL by the square root of the expected balance loss. Then, we show that approximate stationarity controls this distribution error up to a tangent-space residual measuring parameterization incompleteness. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling and fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions, with fixed or controlled sampling and a fixed or balance-trained backward policy, the expected loss is $O(\bar\epsilon^2+T^{-1})$ and expected terminal symmetric KL is $O(\bar\epsilon+T^{-1/2})$ under uniform coverage. For a separately updated backward policy, we characterize the sufficient update decay to approach the residual neighborhood and preserve these rates. These results connect balance objectives to sampling accuracy and clarify how parameterization, coverage, and moving components govern GFlowNet training.
papers.summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) learn to sample discrete objects in proportion to a reward by minimizing balance objectives, but there has been no comprehensive theory tying a nonzero balance loss and approximate stationarity to sampling accuracy, especially when the sampling distribution and backward policy evolve during training. The authors build a unified theory for Flow Matching, Detailed Balance, and Trajectory Balance in this regime. **They bound the terminal symmetric KL divergence by the square root of the expected balance loss**, show that approximate stationarity controls distribution error up to a tangent-space residual reflecting parameterization incompleteness, and prove finite-time convergence under fixed or controlled sampling with fixed, balance-trained, or separately updated backward policies. Under standard smoothness assumptions and uniform coverage, the expected loss and terminal symmetric KL decay at rates set by the stationarity tolerance and the number of iterations, and the paper characterizes how fast a separately updated backward policy's steps must shrink to preserve those rates.

papers.title: Machine Unlearning for Federated Socially Fair k-Means Clustering
papers.abstract: Federated clustering can support applications such as patient stratification across hospitals and customer segmentation across distributed financial datasets. Responsible AI calls for fair representation of demographic groups and support for data deletion, motivated in part by rights such as the GDPR's right to erasure. These goals interact: deleting records can change the balance between groups and alter the clustering of the remaining population. We study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair $k$-means, whose objective is to minimize the largest group-average squared distance to the nearest center. Our approach keeps separate local summaries for each group, so summaries at unaffected institutions remain valid as global fairness weights change. For two groups, we prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling, and we show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. Reuse pays off most when a whole client withdraws: across three datasets, replay is $35.8\times$ faster than retraining for the initialization-only model and remains $2.4\times$ and $1.7\times$ faster with one and two fair-refinement rounds, which improve worst-group cost. For individual record deletions, gains are modest (about $1.06\times$), and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves. These results map where exact unlearning can profitably reuse computation. Code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/arareddy/mufsc.
papers.summary: Federated clustering across hospitals or banks must represent demographic groups fairly and honor deletion requests such as the GDPR right to erasure, and the two goals interact because deleting records shifts the balance between groups and changes the clustering of what remains. The authors study exact machine unlearning for federated socially fair k-means, which minimizes the worst group-average squared distance to the nearest center, by keeping separate local summaries per group so that summaries at unaffected institutions stay valid when global fairness weights change. For two groups they prove an initialization approximation guarantee independent of client group proportions under ideal sampling and show that same-seed replay reproduces retraining exactly. **Replay is 35.8x faster than retraining when a whole client withdraws for the initialization-only model**, dropping to 2.4x and 1.7x with one and two fair-refinement rounds, while individual record deletions gain only about 1.06x and certifying cached assignments can cost more than it saves.

papers.title: Enhancing Legal Reasoning in Pre-trained Language Models via Knowledge Graph-Guided Multi-Task Pre-training
papers.abstract: Legal language understanding requires reasoning over semi-structured regulatory documents, yet standard pre-training objectives do not explicitly target this structural capability. Because current legal language models rely solely on masked language modeling, they treat statutory text as flat token sequences and ignore the underlying hierarchical constraints. To bridge this gap, we present a multi-task pre-training approach for German traffic law (StVO). Our approach combines three complementary objectives: Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), Knowledge Graph (KG) Guided Clustering (CLU), and Knowledge Graph (KG) Aware Paragraph Classification (CLS). This approach explicitly encodes structured legal knowledge directly into the model weights. This encoding enables zero-shot legal reasoning at inference time and removes the need for discrete graph traversal. We evaluate our approach across nine Transformer-based encoders and 324 experimental runs. On synthetic StVO question answering, our models demonstrate consistent relative improvements between 10.3% and 155.0% over baselines. Furthermore, relative to the established LexGLUE baselines (Chalkidis et al., 2022), our models improve over prior results on four of seven legal benchmarks. It also achieves consistent zero-shot transfer gains between 3.4% and 15.8% on Austrian driving regulations. These experimental results indicate that our training approach generalizes successfully beyond the initial training legal domain.
papers.summary: Legal language understanding requires reasoning over semi-structured regulatory text, but legal language models trained only with masked language modeling treat statutes as flat token sequences and ignore their hierarchy. The authors propose a multi-task pre-training approach for German traffic law (`StVO`) that combines Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), Knowledge Graph (KG) Guided Clustering (CLU), and KG Aware Paragraph Classification (CLS) so that structured legal knowledge is encoded directly into model weights, enabling zero-shot legal reasoning without discrete graph traversal. Across nine Transformer encoders and 324 runs, **models show relative improvements of 10.3% to 155.0% over baselines on synthetic StVO question answering**, beat established `LexGLUE` baselines on four of seven benchmarks, and gain 3.4% to 15.8% in zero-shot transfer to Austrian driving regulations.

papers.title: Amortized Counterfactual Prediction with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Counterfactual inference asks how an observed outcome might have differed under different circumstances, such as whether a patient would have recovered had they received a different treatment. Such questions arise whenever decisions depend on the outcomes of alternatives that were not observed. Answering counterfactual queries generally requires knowledge of the underlying causal structure, which is often unavailable in practice. A common approach is therefore to first estimate the causal graph from observational data and then perform counterfactual inference. However, errors in the estimated causal graph can propagate to downstream counterfactual predictions. To address this challenge, we introduce the Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (CFGNP), an end-to-end approach that answers counterfactual queries directly from observational data without first estimating a causal graph. CFGNP uses Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to exploit the dual-graph structure by restricting cross-world message passing to corresponding factual--counterfactual variables. Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks, CFGNP achieves stronger predictive performance than existing approaches, including on the German Loan benchmark, where it reduces MSE from $4.51 \times 10^{-2}$ to $0.19 \times 10^{-2}$. Furthermore, on synthetic causal graphs, a model trained only on 10-node graphs maintains strong predictive performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes, without retraining.
papers.summary: Counterfactual questions, such as whether a patient would have recovered under a different treatment, usually require knowing the causal structure, and the common workaround of first estimating a causal graph from observational data lets graph errors propagate into the counterfactual predictions. The Counterfactual Graph Neural Process (`CFGNP`) answers counterfactual queries end-to-end from observational data without estimating a causal graph, using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) over a dual-graph structure in which cross-world message passing is restricted to corresponding factual and counterfactual variables. Across synthetic and image-based benchmarks it outperforms existing approaches, and **on the `German Loan` benchmark it reduces MSE from 0.0451 to 0.0019**. A model trained only on 10-node synthetic graphs keeps strong performance on graphs with up to 30 nodes without retraining.

papers.title: SeoulMMOD: A Large-Scale Multimodal Origin-Destination Flow Benchmark
papers.abstract: Origin-destination (OD) flow forecasting supports urban mobility decisions by predicting the volume and patterns of human movement across a city. Most existing public OD benchmarks provide only a partial view of citywide mobility, covering a single transport service or at most two modes. With partial mode coverage, observed demand changes are difficult to separate into shifts across transport modes and changes in total travel. We introduce SeoulMMOD, a large-scale public benchmark for citywide multimodal mobility in Seoul. SeoulMMOD provides three years of hourly OD flows estimating total mobility for 6 urban travel modes across 25 districts and 426 sub-districts, together with travel-time, travel-distance, calendar, rainfall, and point-of-interest (POI) signals. Using SeoulMMOD, we benchmark 14 forecasting baselines under a common protocol and analyse the effects of spatial scaling, joint versus mode-separate training, and cross-year generalization. Results show that several spatio-temporal models that work at district level do not scale to sub-district OD forecasting, and that naive joint multi-mode training does not consistently improve accuracy. Together, the dataset and benchmark establish a reproducible testbed for multi-mode, multi-year OD forecasting at the city scale.
