papers.summary: Origin-destination (OD) flow forecasting predicts how people move across a city, but public OD benchmarks typically cover one transport service or at most two modes, so shifts between modes cannot be separated from changes in total travel. `SeoulMMOD` is a large-scale public benchmark providing **three years of hourly OD flows for 6 urban travel modes across 25 districts and 426 sub-districts of Seoul**, alongside travel-time, travel-distance, calendar, rainfall, and point-of-interest signals. The authors benchmark 14 forecasting baselines under a common protocol and study spatial scaling, joint versus mode-separate training, and cross-year generalization. Several spatio-temporal models that work at district level fail to scale to sub-district forecasting, and naive joint multi-mode training does not consistently help.

papers.title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies are bottlenecked by the cost of collecting embodied interaction data, and egocentric human videos, while plentiful, carry no robot action labels and are hard to annotate reliably under real-world visual complexity. `LAPT-Scale` pairs a latent action model, `LAPT-Scale-LAM`, that learns continuous latent actions explaining frame-to-frame transitions in human video, with `LAPT-Scale-Policy`, a VLA policy trained through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized latent action models, the continuous latent space preserves fine-grained motion, and perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals supplement pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, the approach yields consistent scaling gains, **raising real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video grows from 1K to 5K hours**, and the policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

papers.title: Orthros: Phase-Aware Heterogeneous Attention for Efficient Transformers
papers.abstract: Efficient attention mechanisms, such as linear and sliding window attention, aim to reduce the computational complexity of Transformers from quadratic to linear. However, their degraded in-context recall often necessitates interleaving full attention layers, leaving the quadratic bottleneck unresolved in long-context processing. To address this, we introduce Orthros attention, which shifts the efficiency paradigm from structural allocation to phase-aware decoupling. As a unified module, it dynamically switches its computation pattern across different phases of sequence processing, enabling linear complexity prefilling and full attention decoding. Our design grants Orthros attention a lower asymptotic complexity compared to vanilla Transformers in prevalent long-context scenarios characterized by heavy prefilling and light decoding. Beyond theoretical formulation and complexity analysis, extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate Orthros's superiority across multiple dimensions. First, we validate its fundamental language modeling capabilities, demonstrating scalability across varying model sizes and strong competitiveness in comprehensive architectural comparisons. Second, Orthros exhibits exceptional conversion feasibility via a data-efficient Transformer-to-Orthros conversion, yielding performance that even surpasses the original Transformer. Finally, Orthros achieves a $21.9\times$ prefilling speedup over Transformers with end-to-end inference gains, while preserving long-context capabilities, as demonstrated by near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results and Transformer-level performance on real-world in-context recall tasks. Overall, these advantages in high performance, flexibility, and efficiency position Orthros as a promising candidate to succeed the Transformer in industrial applications.
papers.summary: Linear and sliding-window attention reduce Transformer cost from quadratic to linear but weaken in-context recall, so practical models interleave full attention layers and the quadratic bottleneck persists for long contexts. `Orthros` attention instead decouples by phase: a single module switches its computation pattern between linear-complexity prefilling and full-attention decoding, which gives lower asymptotic cost than a vanilla Transformer in the common regime of heavy prefill and light decode. Experiments show competitive language modeling across model sizes and architectural comparisons, plus a data-efficient Transformer-to-Orthros conversion that even surpasses the original Transformer. **It achieves a 21.9x prefilling speedup over Transformers** with end-to-end inference gains, near-perfect 128K needle-in-a-haystack results, and Transformer-level performance on real-world in-context recall tasks.

papers.title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.
papers.summary: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often carry constraints on a shared objective or collective safety, and a team-level violation cost cannot say which agents' actions drove the violation. `SafeDiSTL` is a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that assigns credit from joint constraint measurements by using Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation as running-maximum cost increments, then using smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics to compute action sensitivities that split each increment across agents at the same decision time while accounting for delayed effects. On cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control, **it reaches 1.6 to 5.1x the safe-success rate of constrained baselines in transport**, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50 to 68% more traffic throughput, while keeping the performance of unconstrained policies.

papers.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
papers.summary: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce, but the strongest versions rely on video diffusion transformers too expensive for edge devices. `SmolWAM` is derived from the 2B-parameter `Cosmos Policy` by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding the inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of the original 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in a single rectified-flow step. After only 3.6 GPU-hours of training, the model **succeeds in 95.5% of 400 `LIBERO` episodes at 57 ms per 16-action chunk**, running 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory while its world head still forecasts scene motion.

papers.title: A Privileged Teacher That Only Scores Cannot Search: Critique-Conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation promises to replace the sparse outcome signal of verifiable-reward RL with dense token-level credit: a teacher conditioned on the reference solution scores the student's own rollout, and the resulting distributional shift is distilled back into the policy. We investigate whether this scoring signal actually contains corrective credit. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, we test the two signals consumed by self-distillation objectives, the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio, for two properties: whether they localize errors and whether they push probability away from erroneous student tokens. They exhibit neither of these properties nor can they reliably distinguish correct from incorrect rollouts within the same problem. We argue that this failure is structural: locating an error in a reasoning trace is itself a search problem, while a scoring teacher is never explicitly asked to perform that search. The same model, with the same privileged information, localizes errors substantially better when allowed to generate a critique. This forms the motivation for \emph{critique-conditioned self-distillation}: first generate a critique of the current rollout, then condition the scoring teacher on that critique. The resulting signal localizes errors, is corrective within error spans, and shifts probability toward tokens that initiate backtracking such as ``Wait'', ``But'', and ``Actually''. We further show that the critique is useful both at test time, where resuming a wrong rollout with the critique in context converts math problems the model cannot solve by sampling, and in cold-start GRPO, where it provides an advantage signal on prompts for which verifiable rewards alone provide none.
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation promises dense token-level credit for reasoning by having a teacher conditioned on the reference solution score the student's own rollout, and the authors ask whether that scoring signal actually carries corrective information. Using gold error spans in student rollouts, they test the full-distribution KL and the token log-ratio and find that **neither signal localizes errors, pushes probability away from erroneous tokens, or reliably separates correct from incorrect rollouts** on the same problem. They argue this is structural, since locating an error is itself a search problem that a scoring teacher is never asked to perform, and show that the same model with the same privileged information localizes errors far better when allowed to write a critique. Conditioning the scoring teacher on a generated critique yields a signal that is corrective within error spans and favors backtracking tokens like 'Wait' and 'Actually', and the critique also helps at test time and provides an advantage signal in cold-start `GRPO` on prompts where verifiable rewards alone give none.

papers.title: Studying the Effects of Task Diversity Using Small Mathematical Worlds
papers.abstract: Basic mathematical tasks like modular addition have been a valuable tool for illuminating aspects of neural network behavior that are challenging to see in noisy, unverifiable, large-scale, real-world settings. These studies have typically focused on a single task. However, modern language models are exposed to a vast number of tasks despite being trained with a next-token prediction objective. In this work, we introduce two mathematical task ecosystems, IntWorld and PermWorld, built from distinct but related tasks on integers and permutations. Both are designed to simulate task diversity within a cohesive mathematical 'world' where tasks are distinct but related. Because the datasets are procedurally generated, we can precisely vary the number of tasks, allowing us to begin to disentangle the role of task variety from other factors in training. After describing the datasets, we provide some initial results obtained from these datasets which support the idea that increasing task diversity increases the richness of a model's internal representations.
papers.summary: Small algorithmic tasks such as modular addition have illuminated neural network behavior, but those studies almost always train on a single task, while real language models see an enormous variety of tasks under one next-token objective. The authors introduce `IntWorld` and `PermWorld`, two procedurally generated ecosystems of distinct but related tasks on integers and permutations, designed so the number of tasks can be varied precisely while holding other factors fixed. Initial experiments on these datasets **support the idea that increasing task diversity enriches a model's internal representations**, offering a controlled testbed for disentangling task variety from scale and data volume.

papers.title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
papers.abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. MCGPO defines comparison contexts with pre-action state summaries and observed rubric progress, annotated by task rules. Two-action support selects among ordered exact and coarse matching rules. Fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient their preferences, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside shared GraphGPO task learning. MCGPO reuses rollout data and each response's original history, preserving critic-free training. Across six environment-backbone settings with three training seeds each, MCGPO improves mean success over matched GraphGPO: by 0.47-1.46 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B, and by 3.96 and 5.16 points on WebShop with Qwen3-4B and 8B. The ALFWorld gains build on baseline success above 92%, where remaining headroom is limited. Integrated success improves in three of four Qwen2.5 settings. Three-seed factorial controls support opposite-fold evidence and evidence weighting; joint state-rubric matching achieves the highest mean in all four representation-control settings.
papers.summary: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback, and comparisons between sibling rollouts are only useful when they share a comparable context. Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (`MCGPO`) builds weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories: comparison contexts are defined by pre-action state summaries and rubric progress, ordered exact and coarse matching rules select pairs, fixed folds separate candidate decisions from the terminal outcomes used to orient them, and support-dependent evidence weights scale an auxiliary pairwise objective alongside the shared `GraphGPO` task loss, all without a critic. Across six environment-backbone settings with three seeds each, `MCGPO` improves mean success over matched `GraphGPO` by 0.47 to 1.46 points on `ALFWorld` and `WebShop` with `Qwen2.5` 1.5B and 7B models, and by **3.96 and 5.16 points on `WebShop` with `Qwen3-4B` and `Qwen3-8B`**, with factorial controls supporting the opposite-fold evidence and weighting design.

papers.title: How Well Do Prior-Data Fitted Networks Amortize Bayesian Inference?
papers.abstract: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution (PPD) of a synthetic prior, yet results about the approximation quality are surprisingly thin. Taking an empirical risk minimization perspective, we decompose the deployment error of PFNs into prior, context, and amortization error, and measure the latter against a reference PPD under a realistic prior. Results show that PFNs generally recover the targeted PPD very well. Nevertheless, we find that parts of the residual amortization error persist, especially in \textit{rare} settings under the prior pretraining distribution, even when scaling the model size, which manifests in disagreement between independently pretrained PFNs and leaves uncertainty about the predictor at inference time. As a remedy, we study multiple types of Bayesian model averages and find that these can consistently reduce this uncertainty and improve predictions up to full-size TabICLv2 models.
papers.summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) are trained to approximate the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution (PPD) of a synthetic prior, yet little is known about how well they actually do so. Taking an empirical risk minimization view, the authors decompose a PFN's deployment error into prior, context, and amortization components and measure the amortization error against a reference PPD under a realistic prior. PFNs recover the target PPD well overall, but **residual amortization error persists in settings that are rare under the pretraining prior even as model size scales**, showing up as disagreement between independently pretrained PFNs. Bayesian model averaging over multiple PFNs consistently reduces this uncertainty and improves predictions up to full-size `TabICLv2` models.

papers.title: When Edge Independence Fails: Joint Graph Diffusion with Latent Sociability Priors
papers.abstract: Discrete graph diffusion models corrupt graph structure through independent edge updates with a Markovian noise model. Combined with the exchangeability requirement on the output distribution, the terminal prior is necessarily an Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi (E-R) random graph. This has a fundamental consequence for unconditional graph generation without node features: in the large graph limit, any GNN denoiser applied to an E-R graph approximately outputs an E-R graph, making effective denoising difficult. In practice, generated graphs fail to recover meaningful node heterogeneity and higher-order structure. Previous models introduced specialized node features to compensate, framing this as an expressivity problem, while the role of the prior remained unexamined. We instead address the root cause by introducing the Latent Sociability Prior (LSP) and a join} diffusion process that co-evolves latent node sociability variables and graph structure, removing edge independence while preserving exchangeability. Unlike existing latent graph diffusion methods, the sociability mechanism requires no complex encoder: its sole role is to guide edge updates and preserve node heterogeneity throughout the trajectory. We validate our approach on multiple graph generation datasets and show that the proposed framework more accurately captures graph distributions than baseline methods without node features.
papers.summary: Discrete graph diffusion models corrupt structure through independent, Markovian edge updates, and combined with the exchangeability requirement this forces the terminal prior to be an Erdős-Rényi (E-R) random graph, so in the large-graph limit a graph neural network denoiser applied to an E-R graph approximately outputs another E-R graph. The authors argue that the resulting failure to recover node heterogeneity and higher-order structure is a problem of the prior rather than of denoiser expressivity, which prior work addressed with specialized node features. They introduce the Latent Sociability Prior (LSP) and a joint diffusion process that co-evolves latent per-node sociability variables with the graph structure, removing edge independence while preserving exchangeability and requiring no encoder. On multiple graph generation datasets the framework **captures graph distributions more accurately than baselines that use no node features**.

papers.title: Shortcut Learning in Geospatial Foundation Model Embeddings for Cross-Disaster Damage Assessment
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models can support disaster damage assessment, but high accuracy on familiar disasters may hide shortcut learning: prediction from event or scene characteristics rather than evidence that transfers to a new disaster. We study embeddings from TerraMind, Prithvi-EO-2.0, DOFA, and DINOv3 on the multi-disaster datasets xView2 and BRIGHT. Holding out an entire disaster, instead of randomly splitting image tiles, reduces mean balanced accuracy from 0.807 to 0.638 on xView2 and from 0.818 to 0.568 on BRIGHT. Four sets of tests examine what information supports prediction: event and acquisition context, before/after image inputs, building count, and correct image pairing. Pre-event images remain predictive, and a classifier given only the annotated number of buildings reaches balanced accuracy of 0.629 and 0.653. Combining before/after features performs best on average on xView2, but does not improve over pre-only features on BRIGHT. Shuffling image pairs within the same disaster and damage class causes modest losses. Motivated by these findings, we test whether feature transformations learned only from training disasters improve generalization to unseen disasters. These transformations improve performance, with supervised contrastive learning performing best on xView2 and PCA on BRIGHT. Our results highlight the importance of evaluation on unseen domains for assessing model robustness and show that simple feature-level transformations can improve generalization. Code and experiments can be found at https://github.com/alishibli97/gfm-shortcut-learning.
papers.summary: Geospatial foundation models can support disaster damage assessment, but high accuracy on familiar disasters may reflect shortcut learning from event or scene characteristics rather than transferable damage evidence. The authors evaluate embeddings from `TerraMind`, `Prithvi-EO-2.0`, `DOFA`, and `DINOv3` on the multi-disaster datasets `xView2` and `BRIGHT`, and find that **holding out an entire disaster instead of randomly splitting tiles drops mean balanced accuracy from 0.807 to 0.638 on `xView2` and from 0.818 to 0.568 on `BRIGHT`**. Further tests show pre-event images alone remain predictive, a classifier given only the annotated building count reaches balanced accuracy above 0.62, and shuffling image pairs within a disaster causes only modest losses. Feature transformations learned solely from training disasters, supervised contrastive learning on `xView2` and PCA on `BRIGHT`, improve generalization to unseen disasters.

papers.title: DualQuant: Dual-scale Calibration-free Weight-and-Activation Quantization for LLMs
papers.abstract: Low-bit inference on accelerators with native 4-bit support requires quantizing both weights and activations to realize the full throughput gains these formats provide. While post-training weight quantization has been extensively studied, activation quantization remains considerably more challenging and typically requires calibration data. In this work, we introduce DUALQUANT, a dual-scale, calibration-free post-training quantization framework that directly minimizes the weight-reconstruction Mean Squared Error (MSE) and, as an immediate by-product, yields per-channel activation rescalings prior to activation quantization. Our key observation is that the scaling factors obtained by minimizing weight-reconstruction error provide effective activation rescalings, enabling competitive activation quantization without calibration data. We formulate DUALQUANT as a non-differentiable weight-reconstruction problem and develop an efficient solver based on variable splitting and block coordinate descent, where each subproblem admits a closed-form update. DUALQUANT provides a unified algorithm supporting a wide range of formats, including the full MX family and NVFP4. To our knowledge, DUALQUANT is the first dual-scaling method to formally support MX and NV block formats. Across Llama and Qwen models evaluated on WikiText-2, C4, and zero-shot downstream tasks, DUALQUANT matches or exceeds the accuracy of calibration-based SmoothQuant across most models and formats, and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, with large gains for MX and NV block formats. We validate these gains with a real packed W4A4 inference path for Llama-3.1-8B on an RTX 4090. The resulting implementation closely matches the accuracy of fake quantization while delivering up to 2.61x memory reduction and up to 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16.
papers.summary: The (epsilon, delta) guarantee of DP-SGD does not directly say what an adversary can reconstruct from a trained model. The authors derive a distortion bound, computable before training, that holds even against an adversary who observes the full parameter trajectory, knows every other training record, and knows the population distribution. The framework separates the information revealed by training, measured through conditional mutual information and depending only on sampling rates and noise multipliers, from the uncertainty already in the data, measured through source entropy, and combines them via rate-distortion theory into a lower bound on the expected error of any reconstruction attack in an analyst-chosen representation. Instantiated in pixel space and in `LPIPS` feature space, it gives **the first lower bound on reconstruction distortion measured directly by `LPIPS`**, and on several image datasets establishes non-trivial unavoidable error within recommended privacy budgets, with comparisons to strong attacks identifying the main sources of remaining slack.

papers.title: From Pixels to Privacy-Sensitive Features: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Reconstruction Bounds
papers.abstract: What can an adversary recover from a model trained with DP-SGD? Its $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ guarantee does not answer this question directly. We derive a distortion bound that can be computed before training and applies even to an adversary who observes the parameter trajectory during training, knows every other training record and the population distribution from which the training records are drawn. The analyst may choose the representation in which error is measured, allowing the bound to target the aspects of reconstruction that are privacy-sensitive in a given application. Our information-theoretic framework separates two contributions: the information about a record revealed by training, measured through conditional mutual information, and the uncertainty already present in the data distribution, measured through source entropy. Rate-distortion theory combines them into a lower bound on the expected error of every reconstruction attack. For DP-SGD, the leakage bound depends only on the sampling rates and noise multipliers, while the source entropy is lower-bounded from a sample with finite-sample confidence. An orthogonal block construction keeps the resulting bound informative for high-dimensional images. We instantiate the framework in pixel space and in LPIPS feature space, obtaining, to our knowledge, the first lower bound on reconstruction distortion measured directly by LPIPS. On a range of image datasets the bounds establish non-trivial unavoidable expected reconstruction error within heuristically recommended privacy-budget ranges and beyond. Experiments compare the bounds with strong reconstruction attacks and identify the principal sources of the remaining slack.
papers.summary: Accelerators with native 4-bit support only deliver their full throughput when both weights and activations are quantized, but activation quantization is harder than weight quantization and typically requires calibration data. `DualQuant` is a calibration-free post-training method that directly minimizes weight-reconstruction mean squared error (MSE) and obtains per-channel activation rescalings as a by-product, based on the observation that scaling factors from weight reconstruction also work well for activations. The non-differentiable problem is solved by variable splitting and block coordinate descent with closed-form updates, and the method supports the full MX family and NVFP4 formats. Across `Llama` and `Qwen` models on `WikiText-2`, `C4`, and zero-shot tasks it matches or beats calibration-based `SmoothQuant` and substantially outperforms calibration-free baselines, and a real packed W4A4 path for `Llama-3.1-8B` on an RTX 4090 delivers **up to 2.61x memory reduction and 2.46x throughput speedup over BF16**.

papers.title: Geometry-Aware Multi-Objective Optimization: Norm-Constrained Oracles with Entropic Weight Updates
papers.abstract: Multiple-gradient descent is typically formulated in Euclidean geometry, whereas matrix-aware optimizers use directions induced by other norms. We analyze a single-loop multi-objective method combining a norm-constrained linear minimization oracle with entropic updates of task weights. For any finite-dimensional norm pair, we establish an $O(T^{-1/2})$ ergodic stationarity rate in the deterministic setting, deriving the required trajectory gradient bound from smoothness and lower-boundedness in the unregularized case. With stochastic gradients and a bounded-gradient assumption, one persistent blended-gradient momentum buffer yields an $O(T^{-1/4})$ rate whose leading term has no explicit dependence on the number of tasks. We also establish static regret for the inner weighting objective on arbitrary bounded gradient sequences and, with entropy regularization and a weight floor, iteration-wise inner-gap control after burn-in while retaining ergodic stationarity, conditional on a trajectory gradient bound. The optimal blended gradient can be nonunique in spectral and sign geometries, motivating a selection-independent inner gap. Our analysis extends the spectral construction studied by concurrent MOON to general norms. Experiments compare the method with existing multi-task optimizers and examine its oracle, weighting, and momentum choices.
papers.summary: Multiple-gradient descent for multi-objective optimization is usually formulated in Euclidean geometry, whereas matrix-aware optimizers follow directions induced by other norms. The authors analyze a single-loop method that pairs a norm-constrained linear minimization oracle with entropic updates of task weights, extending the spectral construction of the concurrent `MOON` method to arbitrary finite-dimensional norms. They prove an **O(T^-1/2) ergodic stationarity rate in the deterministic setting and an O(T^-1/4) rate with stochastic gradients** using a single blended-gradient momentum buffer whose leading term has no explicit dependence on the number of tasks, plus static regret and iteration-wise inner-gap control under entropy regularization. Experiments compare the method with existing multi-task optimizers and examine its oracle, weighting, and momentum choices.

papers.title: ReplaySSM: Cache SSM Inputs, Not State
papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) maintain a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it at every decoding step can bottleneck hybrid models. This eager state management causes large state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding no cheap rollback, and feeds state quantization error into subsequent recurrent updates. We introduce ReplaySSM, which unrolls the recurrence to represent the state as a checkpoint and a buffer of recent SSM inputs. This separates output computation from checkpoint updates. By updating the checkpoint periodically, ReplaySSM avoids state writes on most steps and roughly halves the dominant state memory traffic. Keeping recent inputs also makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation and enables output-only verification without materializing intermediate states. The same separation allows a low-precision checkpoint to serve output computation on most steps while a higher-precision checkpoint serves recurrent updates, so rounding error in the low-precision copy never enters later updates. We implement ReplaySSM in vLLM for Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet. At serving batch size 256, it accelerates standard decoding by $1.20$--$1.47\times$ over a tuned vLLM baseline across four hybrid models, and delivers about $1.8\times$ the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on the two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and downstream accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.
papers.summary: State-space models (SSMs) keep a fixed-size recurrent state, but reading and writing it on every decoding step creates heavy state I/O with low arithmetic intensity, leaves speculative decoding without a cheap rollback, and feeds quantization error back into later updates. `ReplaySSM` unrolls the recurrence so the state is represented as a periodic checkpoint plus a buffer of recent SSM inputs, which avoids state writes on most steps, makes speculative rollback a buffer-pointer operation, and lets a low-precision checkpoint serve output computation while a higher-precision one serves recurrent updates. Implemented in `vLLM` for `Mamba-2` and `Gated DeltaNet`, it **speeds up standard decoding by 1.20x to 1.47x over a tuned `vLLM` baseline at batch size 256** across four hybrid models and gives about 1.8x the throughput of vLLM's speculative decoding on two 120B-class models. Separate state precisions also reduce output KL divergence and accuracy losses compared with a shared low-precision checkpoint.

papers.title: UkrMeme: Multimodal Explainable Persuasion Detection in Ukrainian Memes
papers.abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). We introduce UkrMeme, a dataset of 200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques, and PTM-UA, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the Propaganda 950 benchmark that preserves original visual content while translating meme text. We evaluate VLMs in a zero-shot prompting setup across image, text, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1 metrics. Finally, we compare Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) and model-generated token attributions and analyze the semantic categories of evidence emphasized by each explanation method.
papers.summary: Wartime memes combine visual and textual cues to persuade, and detecting the techniques they use is understudied outside English. The authors release `UkrMeme`, a dataset of **200 organically produced Ukrainian wartime memes annotated for persuasion techniques**, and `PTM-UA`, a Ukrainian translation of a subset of the `Propaganda 950` benchmark that keeps the original visuals while translating meme text. Vision-language models (VLMs) are evaluated zero-shot across image-only, text-only, and multimodal inputs using hierarchical F1. The study also compares Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) with model-generated token attributions and analyzes which semantic categories of evidence each explanation method emphasizes.

papers.title: Your Discrete Graph Diffusion Model is Secretly Memorizing
papers.abstract: Discrete graph diffusion models (GDMs) corrupt the graph structure by adding noise independently to nodes and edges under a Markovian noise model. In the unconditional setting without node features, an equivariant denoiser trained on a single graph is able to generate novel graphs and sample-level metrics such as edge overlap and WL kernel similarity find no evidence of memorization. In this work, we challenge this view and show for the first time that graph diffusion models indeed exhibit memorization. Analyzing the reverse diffusion trajectories of GDMs trained on two-block stochastic block models (SBMs), we find a strong train-data bias: the model recovers a corrupted training graph almost perfectly compared to a held-out test graph. We term this conditional memorization, as it surfaces only when the reverse trajectory is conditioned on a corrupted training graph and is not apparent during inference. It coincides with a growing generalization gap, where the training loss improves as the loss on held-out graphs degrades, and it cannot be mitigated by early stopping. The onset of memorization always precedes the emergence of community structure in the generated graphs, thus every checkpoint earlier produces structureless graphs. This behavior holds across all node sizes we test.
papers.summary: Discrete graph diffusion models (GDMs) trained on a single graph can generate novel graphs, and sample-level metrics such as edge overlap and Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel similarity show no sign of memorization. Analyzing reverse diffusion trajectories of GDMs trained on two-block stochastic block models (SBMs), the authors find a strong train-data bias: **the model recovers a corrupted training graph almost perfectly while failing to recover a corrupted held-out graph**. They call this conditional memorization because it only surfaces when the reverse trajectory is conditioned on a corrupted training graph and is invisible at ordinary inference time. It coincides with a growing generalization gap that early stopping cannot fix, and its onset always precedes the emergence of community structure in generated graphs, so every earlier checkpoint produces structureless outputs across all tested graph sizes.

papers.title: Optimal Algorithms for Nonsmooth Nonconvex Stochastic Optimization with Constraints
papers.abstract: We present new algorithms for stochastic optimization problems in which the objective is neither smooth nor convex, subject to a convex constraint set. Our algorithms return a $(\delta,\varepsilon)$-Goldstein stationary point, as recently defined for constrained problems by Liu et al. (2024), with improved complexities, and are the first to achieve optimal convergence rates for this task in several settings. In particular, we design projection-based and projection-free algorithms that achieve a $\widetilde O(\delta^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate using stochastic gradients, which we show to be optimal, and a $\widetilde O(d\delta^{-1}\varepsilon^{-3})$ rate using zeroth-order queries, which is also optimal in its dependence on the dimension $d$ and improves over prior work. Notably, our lower bound is given in terms of the Frank-Wolfe gap and holds even for smooth problems, which is of independent interest. These results show that in nonconvex stochastic optimization, the convergence rate is degraded neither by the presence of constraints nor by nonsmoothness. Our analysis is based on a reduction to online linear optimization, extending a related technique from unconstrained optimization.
papers.summary: The work targets stochastic optimization where the objective is neither smooth nor convex and the variable is restricted to a convex constraint set, using the (delta, epsilon)-Goldstein stationarity notion recently defined for constrained problems. The authors design projection-based and projection-free algorithms via a reduction to online linear optimization, extending a technique from the unconstrained case. They achieve **an optimal O(delta^-1 epsilon^-3) rate with stochastic gradients** and an O(d delta^-1 epsilon^-3) rate with zeroth-order queries that is optimal in dimension and improves on prior work, with a matching lower bound stated in terms of the Frank-Wolfe gap that holds even for smooth problems. The results show that neither constraints nor nonsmoothness degrade the convergence rate in nonconvex stochastic optimization.

papers.title: Randomized Momentum Transport with Cheap Predictors
papers.abstract: Momentum methods such as STORM and second-order momentum track the gradient by adding a transport correction to momentum, at the cost of an extra oracle call per iteration. We introduce randomized momentum transport, which evaluates the correction with probability $q$ and otherwise uses a cheap prediction, with importance weighting that preserves the conditional mean and adds $(q^{-1}-1)$ times the prediction loss to the variance. Under transport-bias, second-moment, and residual-control assumptions, linear minimization oracle (LMO) updates, including normalized, sign, and exact spectral (Muon) directions, retain an $O(T^{-1/3})$ stationarity bound for each fixed $q>0$ with a single-gradient initialization. For unnormalized STORM, some $q<1$ lowers the leading coefficient of our sufficient gradient budget if and only if the gradient-difference noise modulus exceeds the smoothness constant, by at most about $10\%$. An online diagonal predictor admits a regret-to-convergence guarantee. At approximately equal oracle cost, querying a quarter of the corrections lowers the final training loss by $18$ to $43\%$ on MNIST1D and raises the test accuracy of Hessian-vector transport on CIFAR-10 by $1.5$ points.
papers.summary: Momentum methods such as `STORM` and second-order momentum track the gradient by adding a transport correction, which costs an extra oracle call every iteration. Randomized momentum transport evaluates the correction only with probability q and otherwise substitutes a cheap prediction, with importance weighting that keeps the conditional mean and adds (1/q - 1) times the prediction loss to the variance. Under transport-bias, second-moment, and residual-control assumptions, linear minimization oracle (LMO) updates including normalized, sign, and spectral `Muon` directions keep an O(T^-1/3) stationarity bound for any fixed q, and for unnormalized `STORM` some q below 1 lowers the leading gradient-budget coefficient by at most about 10% exactly when gradient-difference noise exceeds the smoothness constant. At roughly equal oracle cost, **querying a quarter of the corrections lowers final training loss by 18 to 43% on `MNIST1D`** and raises test accuracy of Hessian-vector transport on `CIFAR-10` by 1.5 points.

papers.title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
papers.abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential cases, exhibiting a 20.0-point gap. Humans attain higher accuracies of 63.4% versus 68.5% for direct and inferential images, respectively, with no significant gap. To locate this failure, we introduce OccludeTrace, a four-stage diagnostic that isolates where the visual reasoning process breaks down. The bottleneck emerges when models must recover the relevant object from the projection within the full image: they succeed on only 50% of failed examples, compared with 91% of examples they answer correctly. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting yield inconsistent improvements and do not reliably eliminate the gap. In contrast, an inpaint-then-confront intervention, which prompts models to first generate a candidate hidden object and then evaluate that hypothesis against the visible physical cue, reduces the gap to a statistically non-significant difference for both models with image-generation capabilities. Together, our results establish a tractable, controlled diagnostic for isolating how VLMs reason about visual content that is missing from an image.
papers.summary: `OccludeBench` is a manually curated benchmark testing whether vision-language models (VLMs) can identify fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains, separating direct cases that depend on a specific physical cue like a shadow or reflection from inferential cases solvable from broader scene context. Across five VLMs, **accuracy averages 42.7% on direct cases versus 62.7% on inferential ones, a 20-point gap** that humans do not show, scoring 63.4% and 68.5% respectively. A four-stage diagnostic called `OccludeTrace` locates the bottleneck at recovering the relevant object from its projection within the full image, where models succeed on only half of failed examples versus 91% of correct ones. Extended reasoning, tool use, and few-shot prompting help inconsistently, but an inpaint-then-confront intervention, in which the model generates a candidate hidden object and then checks it against the visible cue, shrinks the gap to statistical insignificance for both models with image-generation capabilities.

papers.title: Not Just an Evaluation: A Case Study of Discourse Particle Sensitivity in Language Models
papers.abstract: Discourse particles subtly shape the flow of discourse by reflecting conversational context and interlocutor attitudes, often leaving the truth-conditional meaning untouched. They are also often polyfunctional, with distinct senses which partially overlap with other particles; for example, the exclusive use of English "just" and "only" ("John only/just drinks water"). Despite the frequency of these words in natural language, they have gone largely unstudied due to the subtle nature of their effects. We investigate LLM sensitivity to "just" and "only" in natural conversations using behavioral and mechanistic analyses. First, we find that LLMs and humans similarly prefer the presence of these particles in context, and both are more sensitive to "just" compared to "only". Second, when sampling from LLMs with and without these particles, we find LLMs consistently rate generations as more likely, given their source context, demonstrating their particle sensitivity. In both experiments, instruction tuning increases sensitivity. Finally, we localize particle-sensitive units within LLMs and find the overlap between "just" and "only" is asymmetric: "only" units transfer selectively to exclusive "just", while all "just" units transfer to "only" equally well regardless of sense, suggesting LLM lexical-level particle representations are partially organized by sense. We release our code, sense-labeled dialogue stimuli, and human preference annotations at https://github.com/JiahuiKChen/Not_Just_an_Evaluation.
papers.summary: Discourse particles such as English 'just' and 'only' shape conversational flow and attitude without changing truth-conditional meaning, are polyfunctional, and have gone largely unstudied in language models because their effects are subtle. Using behavioral and mechanistic analyses on natural conversations, the authors find that large language models and humans similarly prefer the presence of these particles in context and are both more sensitive to 'just' than 'only', that models rate their own generations as more likely given the source context when the particle is present, and that instruction tuning increases sensitivity in both experiments. Localizing particle-sensitive units reveals an **asymmetric overlap in which 'only' units transfer selectively to exclusive 'just' while all 'just' units transfer equally well to 'only' regardless of sense**, suggesting lexical-level particle representations are partly organized by sense. Code, sense-labeled dialogue stimuli, and human preference annotations are released.

papers.title: REFLECT: Role-Aware Detection of Sentiment, Emotion, Politeness, and Formality
papers.abstract: Detecting communicative meaning in dialogue requires modeling not only lexical content but also the participant-role structures through which sentiment, emotion, politeness, and formality (SEPF) are expressed. Existing approaches rely on contextual language representations while leaving semantic roles implicit. We introduce a role-aware transformer architecture that maps the four SEPF dimensions to theory-grounded Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) configurations, incorporating these configurations directly into the transformer's self-attention mechanism. Role-aware attention models non-directional internal states (sentiment and emotion), while directional role-aware attention captures initiator-to-recipient relations for external cues (politeness and formality). The resulting role-aware representations are fused with contextual embeddings through a learned gate that adaptively weights how much role information each input contributes, rather than appending semantic roles as an auxiliary feature vector. Across four benchmark datasets, the framework yields statistically reliable gains over strong BERT-based baselines for emotion, politeness, and formality, with gains concentrated in theoretically predicted cases such as low-frequency, complex emotions and highly polite expressions; sentiment improvements are marginal and non-significant, suggesting that sentiment is conveyed more through lexical choice than participant-role structure. Additional evaluation on real-world data demonstrates that the framework improves both predictive performance and model traceability. These results demonstrate that linguistically grounded modifications to transformer self-attention improve the detection of communicative meaning, generalize beyond benchmark datasets to real-world mental-health data, and yield traceable, role-grounded explanations that extend beyond predictive performance to interpretability.
papers.summary: Detecting sentiment, emotion, politeness, and formality (SEPF) in dialogue depends on participant-role structure, which existing contextual representations leave implicit. The proposed role-aware transformer maps each SEPF dimension to theory-grounded Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) configurations and injects them into self-attention, using non-directional role-aware attention for internal states like sentiment and emotion and directional attention for initiator-to-recipient cues like politeness and formality, then fuses the role-aware representations with contextual embeddings through a learned gate. Across four benchmark datasets the approach **yields statistically reliable gains over strong `BERT`-based baselines for emotion, politeness, and formality**, concentrated in low-frequency complex emotions and highly polite expressions, while sentiment gains are marginal, suggesting sentiment is carried more by lexical choice than by role structure. Evaluation on real-world mental-health data shows improved prediction along with traceable, role-grounded explanations.

papers.title: Adaptive Variance Reduction without Knowing Oracle Smoothness
papers.abstract: Variance reduction improves the convergence rate of stochastic non-convex optimization under the average smoothness condition. Existing adaptive variance reduction methods are especially designed for average smoothness and do not adapt to standard smoothness. In this paper, we study how one algorithm can adapt to these two settings and the noiseless setting without knowing the smoothness constants or the variance bound. Given the gradient budget $T$, we develop a two-phase method. The first phase compares two independent gradients and switches to normalized momentum when their difference exceeds a threshold. This phase provides both a candidate with standard smooth and noiseless guarantees and also ensures a bounded expected function gap for the second variance reduction phase. The resulting rates are $O(T^{-1/3})$ under average smoothness, $O(T^{-1/4})$ under standard smoothness, and $O(T^{-1/2})$ without noise. When $T$ is unknown, we propose a method with two paths that attain the corresponding rates with logarithmic factors in the stochastic settings. Here, we use a variance reduction path to deal with average smoothness and employ the AdaGrad-Norm for standard smoothness and noiseless setting. Neither method restarts from the initial point or requires a growing number of oracle calls in each round.
papers.summary: Variance reduction speeds up stochastic non-convex optimization under average smoothness, but existing adaptive variants are built for that condition alone and do not adapt to standard smoothness or the noiseless case. The authors develop a two-phase method for a known gradient budget T: the first phase compares two independent gradients and switches to normalized momentum when their difference exceeds a threshold, supplying a candidate with standard-smooth and noiseless guarantees and a bounded expected function gap for the second, variance-reduction phase. Without knowing smoothness constants or the variance bound, the method attains **O(T^-1/3) under average smoothness, O(T^-1/4) under standard smoothness, and O(T^-1/2) without noise**. When T is unknown, a two-path variant combining a variance reduction path with `AdaGrad-Norm` achieves the same rates up to logarithmic factors, and neither method restarts from the initial point or needs a growing number of oracle calls per round.

papers.title: Constrained Probabilistic Numerics: Gaussian Process Solvers for Linear PDEs under Linear Inequality Constraints
papers.abstract: Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors rather than point estimates, but they condition only on equality information: the PDE residual, boundary data, and measurements. Many solutions of interest also obey inequality constraints, including nonnegativity, monotonicity, and absence of arbitrage, which equality conditioning cannot enforce. We prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite-dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially in terms of Borel measures on the solution space. The physics-informed posterior is therefore a valid prior for the inequality update at virtual points. The combined law is non-Gaussian yet computable through truncated-Gaussian moments, and neither the PDE conditioning nor the inequality update requires modification. We evaluated the construction on a Poisson benchmark, option-price surfaces, and air-quality fields. Under incomplete boundary data, a monotonicity constraint lowered the error of a two-dimensional Poisson reconstruction by $63\%$. On a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to $20$ retained quotes, no-arbitrage constraints reduced held-out extrapolation error by $22\%$ and cut the calendar-arbitrage rate from $10\%$ to $1\%$. On four real air-quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a Gaussian moment-based sub-zero-tail proxy by $74\%$ at the sparsest monitor count. Changes in mean accuracy and constraint diagnostics differed across data regimes. The probability of the noisy virtual constraint event under the equality posterior measures agreement with the specified bounds before the update. The construction turns admissibility from a post-processing step into conditioning information for probabilistic PDE solvers.
papers.summary: Gaussian process solvers for linear partial differential equations (PDEs) return posteriors, but they condition only on equality information such as PDE residuals, boundary data, and measurements, and cannot enforce inequality constraints like nonnegativity, monotonicity, or absence of arbitrage. The authors prove that conditioning a Gaussian process prior jointly on linear equality observations and a finite-dimensional inequality event is equivalent to conditioning sequentially, so the physics-informed posterior serves as a valid prior for an inequality update at virtual points, with the resulting non-Gaussian law computable via truncated-Gaussian moments and no change to either step. On a Poisson benchmark with incomplete boundary data a monotonicity constraint cut reconstruction error by 63%, and on a real S&P 500 option chain thinned to 20 quotes, **no-arbitrage constraints reduced held-out extrapolation error by 22% and cut the calendar-arbitrage rate from 10% to 1%**. On four real air-quality snapshots, nonnegativity reduced a sub-zero-tail proxy by 74% at the sparsest monitor count, turning admissibility from post-processing into conditioning information.

papers.title: FORTE: A Production Framework for Feature Evaluation and Deprecation in Industrial Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Production recommender systems have feature-lifecycle asymmetry: adding new features must produce gains on some metric, while feature removal must not regress any metric. In practice, feature deprecation is hard to prioritize as a feature can fail to be removed if it interacts with other features, its importance changes daily, it cannot be evaluated before production models change or data drift occurs, it is in contention for A/B test space with other launches, it causes regressions in an online A/B test, or it is consumed by multiple models that need to coordinate its deprecation. We present FORTE, a model-agnostic production framework for discovering, validating, and removing features. Its efficient perturbation implementation allows daily feature evaluation. To account for interactions, it evaluates candidate feature sets constructed from all the low-rank features through grouped ablation and its offline results are sufficiently predictive of online A/B tests to allow deprecations to proceed to online testing with confidence. Lineage tracing identifies all downstream consumer models to realize the full savings of removing a feature from the training set. We validate FORTE over 2 large-scale recommender systems and find that it identifies deprecable feature sets which do not cause online regressions, while the impact on efficiency depends on model characteristics. On a search-relevance model, FORTE resulted in 3 nested candidate sets of 32, 48, and 59 features. Online guardrails rejected the largest treatment. The 48-feature set was selected for deprecation, removing 43.3% of the model's features. On a large ranking model, FORTE identified 8 candidates for removal. Retraining and A/B testing confirmed no regression. Its launch reduced the trainable parameters by 29.9%, improved serving throughput by 19.8-25.5%, and reduced annual training costs by hundreds of thousands of dollars.
papers.summary: Production recommender systems can add features freely but struggle to retire them, since a removal must regress no metric while features interact, drift in importance daily, and are shared across models. `FORTE` is a model-agnostic framework that scores features daily with an efficient perturbation implementation, groups low-importance features into candidate sets evaluated by grouped ablation, and traces lineage to find every downstream consumer model. Across two large-scale systems its offline results predicted online A/B outcomes well enough to ship deprecations: a search-relevance model had 43.3% of its features removed, and a large ranking model shed **29.9% of its trainable parameters** with serving throughput up 19.8% to 25.5% and no regression.

papers.title: Error Rate is Not Enough: Costs of Augmentation in Low-Resource ASR
papers.abstract: Data augmentation is standard practice for low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR), but its benefits are almost always reported as aggregate error rates, leaving open why and when a method helps. On four low-resource languages and English at five data sizes, we cross two augmentations that modify existing audio (speed perturbation and SpecAugment) with two that modify text transcriptions and synthesize audio from it. We analyze errors at the phoneme level and find that they help for complementary reasons. SpecAugment has the most reliable aggregate improvements, but increases tone and palatalization errors, whereas text-based methods introduce consonant insertions; in combination, each reduces the errors the other introduces. This complementarity is predictable. Tone and palatalization are each signaled by a single acoustic property and occur least frequently in training (lowest training exposure), and text-based methods that flatten word frequency raise their frequency by 37--38%, reversing those errors while further improving aggregate error. The improvement from combining the methods exceeds the sum of their individual improvements; the superadditivity vanishes by 100 hours, limiting the complementarity to the low-resource regime. Where specific error types matter, we recommend selecting augmentation by training exposure and acoustic properties, both measurable before any training.
papers.summary: Augmentation for low-resource automatic speech recognition (ASR) is almost always judged by aggregate error rates, which hides when and why a method helps. Four low-resource languages plus English at five data sizes were used to cross two audio-modifying augmentations, speed perturbation and `SpecAugment`, with two that rewrite transcriptions and synthesize audio from them, and the errors were then analyzed at the phoneme level. `SpecAugment` gives the most reliable aggregate gains but adds tone and palatalization errors, while text-based methods add consonant insertions, and each repairs what the other breaks; **the combined improvement exceeds the sum of the individual ones**, a superadditivity that vanishes by 100 hours of data. The authors argue the right augmentation can be picked in advance from training exposure and the acoustic properties of the contrasts at stake.

papers.title: Diversity-Aware Ensemble of Quantum-Classical Models via Combinatorial Fusion
papers.abstract: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are highly sensitive to circuit architecture, yet most quantum machine learning pipelines select a single best design and discard the remaining candidates. This paper addresses whether the structural diversity across quantum circuit search spaces can be used to produce stronger predictions through model fusion. We apply Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (CFA), a model fusion framework that selects and combines multiple scoring systems using rank-score function (RSF) and cognitive diversity (CD), to a pool of 29 architecturally diverse classical models and quantum circuits. Using a diversity-aware model selection method, we identify subsets of maximally diverse models and combine them with both score and rank combination. Experiments on four binary classification benchmarks covering different domains demonstrate that CFA-based hybrid classical-quantum fusion consistently outperform the best individual model on every dataset considered with improvements up to 6.03% in accuracy. When comparing with relevant literatures, the CFA framework further achieves superior performance across all four datasets.
papers.summary: Variational quantum circuits are highly sensitive to architecture, yet typical quantum machine learning pipelines keep only the single best design and discard the rest. Combinatorial Fusion Analysis (`CFA`), which selects and merges scoring systems using rank-score functions and a cognitive diversity measure, is applied to a pool of 29 architecturally diverse classical models and quantum circuits, picking maximally diverse subsets and combining them by both score and rank. On four binary classification benchmarks from different domains, the fused hybrid ensembles beat the best individual model on every dataset, with **accuracy improvements of up to 6.03%**.

papers.title: Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard source of query expansion terms but they hallucinate. They inject non existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise and can hurt strong retrievers. Existing remedies such as corpus grounding, mutual verification and preference alignment treat hallucinated terms as an undifferentiated nuisance to be filtered by agreement heuristics, without a mechanistic account of why a given term appears or a principled criterion for how many terms to keep. We propose Subsequence-Association Filtered, breadth-aware query expansion (SAFE-QE), a training-free, retriever agnostic method that draws on the subsequence-association account of hallucination. We score each candidate expansion term by its corpus conditioned cross-context reproducibility, terms that reappear under randomised query contexts yet lack support in the pseudo-relevant set are flagged as products of dominant hallucinatory associations and down-weighted. Drawing on the characterisation of language generation as a trade-off between consistency (no hallucination) and breadth (coverage), we cast term selection as constrained coverage maximisation over the pseudo-relevant set, keeping a set that is approximately broad but consistent and stable across resampling. We also introduce the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate, a query side faithfulness metric that counts injected expansion terms no relevant document supports. We evaluate our approach on benchmarked TREC and BEIR collections. Our SAFE-QE is statistically indistinguishable from generative and corpus-steered expansion on nDCG@10 while injecting fewer unsupported terms 4.3 per query against 27.8 for Query2doc and 57.5 for HyDE and on a strong learned sparse retriever, where every expansion method regresses. Faithfulness is therefore available at no measurable cost in ranking quality.
papers.summary: Large language models are now a standard source of query expansion terms, but they inject non-existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise, and existing remedies filter them with agreement heuristics rather than any account of why a term appeared. `SAFE-QE` is training-free and retriever-agnostic: it scores each candidate term by corpus-conditioned cross-context reproducibility, down-weighting terms that recur under randomized query contexts yet lack support in the pseudo-relevant set, then casts final selection as constrained coverage maximization to keep a set that is broad but consistent under resampling. A companion metric, the Hallucinated Expansion Term Rate, counts injected terms no relevant document supports, and on `TREC` and `BEIR` collections the method matches generative and corpus-steered expansion on nDCG@10 while injecting **4.3 unsupported terms per query against 27.8 for `Query2doc` and 57.5 for `HyDE`**.

papers.title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. Existing quantum benchmarks measure whether a model produces a correct solution, but not whether its tests can distinguish correct implementations from faulty ones. We introduce QTestBench, a framework that evaluates LLM-generated quantum test suites against independent benchmark checkers, never treating the tests themselves as ground truth. For each task, QTestBench prompts models to produce syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test verdict with the checker's label under three validation cohorts, each answering a distinct diagnostic question. We benchmark five LLMs on eight PennyLane QHack challenges and ten Qiskit HumanEval tasks. Generated suites almost always execute, but discrimination lags behind: the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval, so executability alone overstates test quality. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates when natural faulty solutions are scarce, as on three of ten Qiskit tasks that yield none. QTestBench offers a reproducible, cross-framework benchmark for the trustworthiness of LLM-generated quantum tests.
papers.summary: Whether language models can write trustworthy unit tests for quantum software is unclear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. `QTestBench` prompts models for syntactic, semantic, and behavioral tests, injects candidate solutions at runtime, and compares each test's verdict against an independent benchmark checker under three validation cohorts, never treating the tests as ground truth. Across five models on eight `PennyLane` QHack challenges and ten `Qiskit HumanEval` tasks, generated suites almost always execute but discriminate poorly: **the best generator reaches a test quality of 0.71 on QHack and only 0.34 on Qiskit HumanEval**. Oracle-verified synthetic mutants stabilize bug-detection estimates on the tasks where no naturally faulty solutions exist.

papers.title: Spanning Diffusion and Flow-based Posterior Sampling via Exact Gaussian Conditioning
papers.abstract: Flow-matching and diffusion models are increasingly used as priors for linear inverse problems, however, most methods are bespoke to one class of trajectory prior. Plug-and-play methods have been proposed, however these implicitly decorrelate the guided trajectory, resulting in broad priors that can struggle when data is sparse. This work proposes $\beta$-Flow: a general plug-and-play method indexed by a correlation parameter $\beta$ that generalises over flow, diffusion, and decorrelated priors, and a confidence parameter $\kappa$ that controls how strongly the path distribution is enforced. Each step requires only one forward evaluation of a denoising network, followed by a Gaussian conditioning step. This step is an exact Kalman update that is not dependent on network gradients. We show that many existing guided samplers can be interpreted as instances or approximations of our method, each implicitly using a different trajectory prior and operator in place of the Kalman gain. From this viewpoint, we provide a qualitative comparison of methods in terms of their implicit biases and assumptions. We demonstrate consistently state-of-the-art level performance across 7 inverse problems over 4 datasets in terms of PSNR and SSIM. Moreover, we demonstrate the utility of this prior control, by showing that confident high correlations (strict priors) work best when observations are less informative, while low correlation is preferred when observations are more informative, reflecting the complementary roles of the prior and likelihood in Bayesian inference.
papers.summary: Flow-matching and diffusion priors for linear inverse problems are usually built for one trajectory type, and plug-and-play variants implicitly decorrelate the guided trajectory, producing broad priors that struggle when measurements are sparse. `beta-Flow` introduces a correlation parameter that interpolates across flow, diffusion, and decorrelated priors plus a confidence parameter setting how strictly the path distribution is enforced, with each step needing one denoiser evaluation followed by an exact Kalman update that uses no network gradients. Many existing guided samplers can be read as instances or approximations of this scheme, each silently assuming a different trajectory prior and a different stand-in for the Kalman gain. Performance is **at state-of-the-art level on seven inverse problems across four datasets** by PSNR and SSIM, and strict high-correlation priors help most when observations are uninformative while low correlation wins when they are informative.

papers.title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.
papers.summary: Generalist robot policies learned by imitation are capped by their demonstrations, and reinforcement learning can extend them either by fine-tuning weights or by training a small module that steers a frozen generative policy's input noise, but sequential tasks make both forget earlier skills. `Dream to Remember` keeps the generalist frozen and trains the steering module on each new task while a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, needing no replay buffer and no new data. On `CALVIN` it improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, **lifting average success from 63.7% to 74.8% where LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence collapses to 11.7%**. With off-the-shelf `pi-0` and `A2World` it learns unseen `LIBERO-90` tasks in the environment while preserving prior LIBERO performance even though the world model is too inaccurate for policy optimization, and three tasks on a real Franka arm improve in sequence.

papers.title: TabMF: Learning Dataset Representations with Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Representations of supervised datasets support higher-level machine-learning tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring. However, existing approaches typically rely either on hand-crafted meta-features or on dataset encoders trained specifically for representation learning. We introduce TabMF, a framework that repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models (TFMs) as encoders of supervised datasets. TabMF equips a predictive TFM with an architecture-aware dataset-level readout and adapts the model end-to-end using contrastive post-training on stochastic views of synthetic supervised datasets. We instantiate TabMF on TabICLv2 and TabPFN-2.5 and evaluate the resulting representations across six tasks on unseen real datasets. Simple frozen TFM readouts yield competitive representations, indicating that predictive pretraining already induces substantial dataset-level structure. The two TabMF encoders obtain the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated learned and classical dataset representations, with particularly strong results in dataset retrieval, compact benchmark construction, and distribution-shift severity assessment.
papers.summary: Representations of entire supervised datasets support higher-level tasks such as dataset retrieval and distribution-shift monitoring, but are normally built from hand-crafted meta-features or encoders trained only for that purpose. `TabMF` instead repurposes pretrained tabular foundation models as dataset encoders, adding an architecture-aware dataset-level readout and adapting the model end to end with contrastive post-training on stochastic views of synthetic supervised datasets. Instantiated on `TabICLv2` and `TabPFN-2.5` and tested on six tasks over unseen real datasets, **the two encoders achieve the strongest aggregate performance among the learned and classical representations compared**, and even frozen readouts are competitive, suggesting predictive pretraining already induces dataset-level structure.

papers.title: Shared Canonical Component Removal Beyond Expert Views
papers.abstract:
In clinical practice, experts often begin by converting raw inputs into a set of expert features before making a decision. While black-box models trained on raw input can outperform models trained on expert views, it remains unclear what predictive signal the raw model exploits beyond what the expert view captures. We introduce an audit framework to quantify this gap using Shared Canonical Component Removal (SCCR). Unlike standard residualization or concept erasure, SCCR selectively removes only those directions strongly shared between learned raw and expert embeddings.
