  Evaluations on synthetic data, coronary artery disease (CAD) detection, antidepressant treatment dropout prediction, and skin lesion classification using SkinCon annotations show that SCCR identifies the ways in which expert views are insufficient and recovers residual predictive signal while minimizing redundancy with the expert view.
papers.summary: Clinicians usually compress raw inputs into a set of expert features before deciding, and black-box models trained on the raw signal often do better without revealing what extra information they use. Shared Canonical Component Removal (`SCCR`) audits that gap by stripping out only the directions strongly shared between learned raw-input and expert-view embeddings, rather than residualizing or erasing concepts wholesale. Tested on synthetic data plus coronary artery disease detection, antidepressant treatment dropout prediction, and skin lesion classification with `SkinCon` annotations, **it recovers residual predictive signal while keeping redundancy with the expert view minimal**, making concrete where the expert representation falls short.

papers.title: Can Language Models Learn When to Abstain? Policy Learning and Calibrated Answer Selection
papers.abstract: A useful language model should know when to answer and when to say "I don't know." Can we improve that decision by training the model itself or by training a separate component to check its answers? We study both approaches on Qwen3-14B for factual questions, using a score that rewards correct answers, penalizes mistakes, and allows abstention. Across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds, a learned answer selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the original model's calibrated confidence filter. On TriviaQA, mean coverage increases from 20.2% to 30.9%, while the pooled error rate among scored answers decreases from 23.0% to 14.5% under exact-match grading. The tested reinforcement-learning changes do not establish consistent gains. On NQ-Open, the selector improves threshold-averaged utility over the filter but still performs worse than always abstaining. A partial human-reviewed audit preserves the TriviaQA finding. Our results support learning to select answers in this setting while showing that reliable abstention across datasets remains unresolved.
papers.summary: A model that answers only when it should can be built by training the model itself or by training a separate component to vet its answers, and both routes are compared on `Qwen3-14B` for factual questions under a score that rewards correct answers, penalizes mistakes, and allows abstention. Across three training seeds and two held-out confidence thresholds, a learned answer selector beats the model's own calibrated confidence filter on threshold-averaged utility, and on `TriviaQA` **coverage rises from 20.2% to 30.9% while the pooled error rate among scored answers falls from 23.0% to 14.5%** under exact-match grading, a result that survives a partial human-reviewed audit. The reinforcement-learning variants tested show no consistent gains, and on `NQ-Open` the selector beats the filter yet still scores worse than always abstaining, so dependable abstention across datasets stays unresolved.

papers.title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
papers.abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. At temperature 0, between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows change their operator output over five executions, depending on the model, and up to 24.0% on one task. Plans amplify these changes exponentially in the number of rows an answer exposes, as a possible-worlds model predicts: on UDA-Bench, a few percent of extracted values change, but about two thirds of the answers do. In SemBench's published results, 21% of text results change quality between executions, including on engines whose plans are deterministic. Several per-query system comparisons, and 16 of 28 tests of LRO-Bench's implementation recommendations, are not settled by the executions the benchmarks run. Changing rows are rows on which models disagree with each other; identical requests within one execution disagree as often as across executions; and one execution's decision margin or reasoning length predicts which rows change. Voting reduces the variance but does not remove it, and a calibrated cascade keeps its guarantee while the rows it returns change. We derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.
papers.summary: Semantic query engines ask a language model to judge individual rows, and benchmarks rank those engines from a handful of executions at temperature 0. Re-running the text and tabular workloads of `SemBench`, `LRO-Bench`, and `UDA-Bench` through their own harnesses while logging all 1.2 million model calls shows that at temperature 0 between 0.07% and 10.2% of rows flip their operator output across five executions, and up to 24.0% on one task. Query plans amplify this exponentially in how many rows an answer exposes: on `UDA-Bench` a few percent of extracted values change but **roughly two thirds of the answers change**, and 21% of `SemBench`'s published text results shift in quality between runs, including for engines whose plans are deterministic. Sixteen of 28 tests of `LRO-Bench`'s implementation recommendations are not settled by the executions the benchmark runs, voting damps the variance without eliminating it, and the authors derive reporting rules for benchmarks and design rules for engines.

papers.title: OpenPA: Forced-alignment-free Multi-granular Pronunciation Assessment with Mixed-transcript Adaptation
papers.abstract: Recent advances in automatic pronunciation assessment (APA) have driven a shift from scripted to free-form assessment. However, existing methods often rely on multi-stage pipelines with forced alignment and separate feature extractors, limiting their practicality across response settings. In light of this, we propose OpenPA, a novel APA framework that leverages Whisper's cross-attention mechanism to jointly predict word- and utterance-level pronunciation scores without forced alignment. Through mixed-transcript adaptation and adaptive substitution weighting, OpenPA accommodates heterogeneous transcripts across closed- and open-response settings within a single model. Trained solely on speechocean762, OpenPA achieves the strongest overall performance among evaluated systems under in-domain closed and simulated open-response conditions, while maintaining its performance zero-shot on MultiPA. An additional cross-task evaluation on oral-cancer speech suggests its potential applicability beyond non-native speech.
papers.summary: Automatic pronunciation assessment is shifting from scripted prompts to free-form speech, but current systems chain forced alignment with separate feature extractors, which limits their practicality across response formats. `OpenPA` reads `Whisper`'s cross-attention to predict word-level and utterance-level pronunciation scores without forced alignment, and handles both closed- and open-response transcripts in a single model via mixed-transcript adaptation and adaptive substitution weighting. Trained only on `speechocean762`, it **records the strongest overall performance among the systems evaluated under in-domain closed and simulated open-response conditions** while holding its accuracy zero-shot on `MultiPA`, and a cross-task test on oral-cancer speech suggests use beyond non-native speakers.

papers.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
papers.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source-target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source
papers.summary: Claims that an embodied agent improves itself from experience are hard to verify, because a saved memory or a successful final action can reflect carried-over resources, unequal exposure to the source task, or early execution failures rather than a durable new skill. `MC-EvoBench` is a controlled Minecraft benchmark with 19 registered evolution chains, representing each task as a task-state graph with stage-level environment verifiers, assigning matched source and target roles, resetting the target world, and letting only one declared agent artifact cross the boundary, measured under no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions at matched step budgets over five seeds. Planner-backed agents consistently outperform controller-only variants on direct capability, but **related experience produces no stable transfer, with every reported interval including zero**. Stage audits also show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks frequently leave later capabilities unobserved.

papers.title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
papers.abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? We term this ability Active Spatial Mentalization (ASM), an intrinsic component of visual intelligence that remains substantially underdeveloped in current LVLMs. To bridge this gap, we introduce SpatialASM, a scalable framework to internalize ASM into LVLMs through training-time spatial simulation. SpatialASM employs an allocentric novel-view generator to ground hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence and produces two complementary forms of supervision: i) explicit ASM trajectories that teach LVLMs when and how to adaptively invoke view planning and imagination during spatial reasoning, and ii) automatically-constructed perspective-taking tasks that further strengthens viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. On seven benchmarks spanning relatively perception-oriented spatial understanding to more challenging tasks requiring multi-image, cross-view and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, SpatialASM yields performance gain on LVLMs of four LVLM backbones in spatial reasoning while retaining their original general vision capabilities. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves average accuracy across the seven spatial benchmarks. And the synthesis of ASM trajectories provides a scalable pathway to alleviate the scarcity of spatial Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision for eliciting active viewpoint exploration and mental scene simulation.
papers.summary: People solve hard spatial problems by mentally moving to a task-relevant viewpoint and reconstructing the layout from there, an ability the authors call active spatial mentalization and find largely absent in large vision-language models (LVLMs). `SpatialASM` instills it at training time using an allocentric novel-view generator that grounds hypothetical viewpoints in visual evidence, yielding both explicit trajectories that teach when and how to invoke view planning and imagination, and automatically constructed perspective-taking tasks that strengthen viewpoint-conditioned scene imagination. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial perception through multi-image, cross-view, and viewpoint-transformation reasoning, **all four LVLM backbones gain average spatial accuracy while retaining their general vision capabilities**, offering a scalable substitute for scarce spatial chain-of-thought supervision.

papers.title: On the Design Space of Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) promise to bring the benefits of continuous flow modelling to language, including accelerated sampling and controllable generation. The field has grown rapidly, and the capabilities of CDLMs have begun to rival those of discrete diffusion. Yet, unlike for continuous modalities such as images or videos, our grasp of the levers that matter when training CDLMs remains limited. In this work, we focus on two of these levers, namely self-conditioning and embedding geometry, and shed light on some of the mechanisms behind them, which in turn suggest cheaper and more effective designs. We begin by showing that self-conditioning corrects a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that are otherwise rare during training. These gains can be recovered without an extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant, coined $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, which improves TinyGSM accuracy more than threefold. Self-conditioning also aids in recognising tokens dominated by large-norm Gaussians$\unicode{x2013}$an issue known as token identifiability. To address it directly, we introduce discrete reveals to $\mathrm{DoubleCat}$, yielding $\mathrm{SemiCat}$, which achieves discrete diffusion-level performance on TinyGSM, reaching $49.94\%$ with standard training hyperparameters and a tuned sampler. At the $1.7$B scale, $\mathrm{SemiCat}$ outperforms discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations, and surpasses one-hot flows on unconditional generation. On embedded spaces, we find that cross-entropy drives embeddings towards a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot one. We briefly explore a range of further options, such as hybrid corruption processes and noise schedules, including asynchronous ones. We believe this exploration can help the community better understand and advance the design space of CDLMs.
papers.summary: Continuous diffusion language models now rival discrete diffusion, yet which training choices actually matter remains poorly mapped compared with images or video. Two levers are dissected: self-conditioning turns out to fix a train/inference mismatch by exposing the model to inference-like states that training rarely visits, and the same benefit is recovered without the extra forward pass by a two-level interpolant called `DoubleCat`, which **more than triples `TinyGSM` accuracy**. Adding discrete reveals gives `SemiCat`, which hits 49.94% on `TinyGSM` with standard hyperparameters and a tuned sampler, matching discrete diffusion, and at 1.7B parameters beats discrete diffusion on four of six likelihood-based evaluations and one-hot flows on unconditional generation. Cross-entropy training is also shown to push embeddings toward a geometry whose decoding error rate closely matches the one-hot case.

papers.title: Specialists Learn Faster: Knowledge Organization in Pre-training Shapes Knowledge Update Efficiency
papers.abstract: An ideal (language) model must continually update its knowledge. Existing work largely focuses on making these updates efficient after training. We investigate how the organization of time-varying knowledge during pre-training shapes the efficiency of subsequent updates. Models trained on chronologically ordered knowledge specialize in the most recently encountered knowledge; we call them specialists. In contrast, models trained on the same knowledge in randomly shuffled order perform well across all represented time periods; we call them generalists. Surprisingly, specialists require far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge. To explain this advantage, we derive a law from first principles that relates update cost to the model's optimization dynamics and that closely predicts empirical results. Guided by these findings, we design a strategy for organizing pre-training data that preserves stable historical knowledge while enabling efficient updates to current knowledge. We also show that the benefits of temporal knowledge organization extend to real-world pre-trained models and existing knowledge update tools, and generalize to other knowledge orderings. Project page: https://horizon-lab.org/specialist/
papers.summary: Work on keeping a language model's knowledge current mostly optimizes the update procedure; the question here is how knowledge organization during pre-training affects later update cost. Training on chronologically ordered facts yields specialists that excel on the most recently seen period, while the same data shuffled yields generalists that perform evenly across periods, and **specialists need far fewer update steps than generalists to acquire new knowledge**. A law derived from first principles relates update cost to optimization dynamics and closely predicts the measured results, motivating a data-ordering strategy that preserves stable historical knowledge while keeping current knowledge cheap to refresh, with the effect also appearing in real pre-trained models, existing knowledge-update tools, and other orderings.

papers.title: Studying Comics at Scale with Artificial Intelligence: The PAGE Framework and Three Studies of American Comics and Japanese Manga
papers.abstract: Comics are one of the great visual records of the twentieth century: hundreds of thousands of pages in which a mass readership saw its leaders, its wars and its heroes. Most of this record has never been studied as a whole; comics scholarship proceeds one book at a time. We argue that artificial intelligence, including generative models, can change this to the benefit of the medium itself. We propose PAGE, a framework that makes artificial intelligence an instrument for comics research. It parses every scan into panels, text and a bibliographic record; annotates each page with a vision-language model that follows a written codebook, as a human coder would; grounds samples of these readings in human annotation; and explains change across an archive, with estimates controlled for publisher and genre. We demonstrate the framework on 3,929 American comic books (1938--1956) and 87 volumes of Japanese manga, in three studies, each resting on a different capability. The first pairs text search with visual reading to recover how a mass medium portrayed political power. The second measures the page's visual form across an industry and recovers the hand of individual artists. The third follows who speaks across two comics traditions, checked against human annotation. Beyond research, the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn, open comics to blind and low-vision readers, and help preserve fragile collections and credit uncredited artists. We outline a research agenda in which artificial intelligence strengthens the study, preservation and reach of the medium.
papers.summary: Comics are a vast twentieth-century visual record that scholarship has largely examined one book at a time. `PAGE` is a framework for studying them at archive scale: it parses each scan into panels, text, and a bibliographic record, annotates every page with a vision-language model following a written codebook as a human coder would, grounds samples of those readings in human annotation, and estimates change across the archive with controls for publisher and genre. Demonstrated on **3,929 American comic books from 1938 to 1956 plus 87 volumes of Japanese manga**, three studies recover how a mass medium portrayed political power, measure page form well enough to identify individual artists' hands, and track who speaks across the two traditions. The authors also argue the same instruments can make archives searchable by what is drawn and open them to blind and low-vision readers.

papers.title: Returning to Development States: When Full Sandbox Snapshots Help Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents often make useful progress before they fail, but retry-from-scratch discards the machine state created along the way. This makes failure recovery an interesting search problem: if intermediate environment states preserve meaningful progress, restoring and branching from them could outperform repeatedly restarting from the initial state. We implement Go-Explore-style search over full Daytona snapshots and find that higher and more efficient solve rates depend mainly on progress that sits outside the repository, such as databases, services, and other runtime state. Our results suggest that full-snapshot search is most effective when long-horizon coding work spans multiple services whose state cannot be reconstructed from a single diff.
papers.summary: Coding agents often make real progress before failing, and retrying from scratch throws away the machine state that progress created, which turns failure recovery into a search problem over intermediate environment states. The authors implement Go-Explore-style search over full `Daytona` sandbox snapshots so an agent can restore and branch from promising earlier states instead of restarting from the initial one. **Higher and more efficient solve rates depend mainly on progress that lives outside the repository**, such as databases, running services, and other runtime state, indicating that full-snapshot search pays off for long-horizon work spanning several services whose state cannot be rebuilt from a single diff.

papers.title: Inference-Time Steering Across Scaffolds and Epitopes for Sample-Efficient De Novo Nanobody Design
papers.abstract: Generative molecular design typically relies on over-generation and post-hoc filtering. Inference-time steering methods like Feynman-Kac (FK) steering improve efficiency by biasing trajectories toward high-reward candidates, yet they optimize within a single fixed configuration. In de novo nanobody design, upfront commitment to conditioning choices like scaffold identity or target epitope creates a bottleneck. Since yield varies across these conditions, steering unpromising setups wastes compute. We recast generative condition selection as an inference-time resource-allocation problem. We propose two dynamic budget allocators: a joint Global Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations concurrently, and a decoupled approach adapting Batched Successive Elimination (BaSE). Empirically, these dynamic allocators increase the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly 5$\times$ without sacrificing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.
papers.summary: Generative molecular design usually over-generates and filters afterwards, and inference-time steering such as Feynman-Kac steering is more efficient but optimizes inside one fixed configuration, so committing up front to a nanobody scaffold or target epitope spends compute on setups that will not pay off. Generative condition selection is recast as an inference-time resource-allocation problem with two dynamic budget allocators: a joint global sequential Monte Carlo formulation that steers and allocates compute across configurations at once, and a decoupled adaptation of batched successive elimination. Both **raise the yield of designable candidates per GPU-hour nearly fivefold** without reducing diversity across distinct therapeutic targets and generative configurations.

papers.title: Finite-Sample Guarantees for Fully Discrete Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: We establish finite-sample guarantees for conditional diffusion models learned from data and implemented with finitely many denoising steps. Our approach aligns the score-training objective with the sampling grid, allowing statistical estimation and numerical discretization errors to be analyzed together. Under a smooth conditional density model, we derive high-probability bounds on the generated distribution's error and quantify the required number of score evaluations. For every smoothness index $\beta>0$, a suitable grid yields averaged conditional Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence $\widetilde O_p(n^{-2\beta/(d_x+d_y+2\beta)})$ relative to the original target with or without early stopping. Both the full and early-stopped samplers attain average target total-variation (TV) error $\widetilde O_p(n^{-\beta/(d_x+d_y+2\beta)})$. Here $n$ is the sample size, $d_x,d_y$ are the data and conditioning dimensions, and errors are averaged over the conditioning variable. The total-variation bound matches the rate established in existing conditional distribution-estimation theory, up to logarithmic factors.
papers.summary: Guarantees for conditional diffusion models typically assume exact scores or continuous-time sampling, leaving the practical case of a learned score run for finitely many denoising steps unanalyzed. Aligning the score-training objective with the sampling grid lets statistical estimation error and numerical discretization error be bounded jointly, giving high-probability bounds on the generated distribution under a smooth conditional density model along with the number of score evaluations required. For every smoothness index a suitable grid attains averaged conditional Kullback-Leibler divergence of order `n^(-2b/(dx+dy+2b))` with or without early stopping, and **both the full and early-stopped samplers reach average total-variation error of order `n^(-b/(dx+dy+2b))`, matching known conditional distribution-estimation rates up to logarithmic factors**.

papers.title: Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization via Zeroth-Order Residual Tracking
papers.abstract: Many optimization problems provide direct access to only part of the gradient, while the remaining component must be inferred from function evaluations. This structure arises in performative prediction, performative reinforcement learning, and bilevel optimization with a black-box lower level. We introduce Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization (PISO), which combines the available gradient component with a running estimate of the residual. By centring each zeroth-order observation on this estimate, PISO makes the variance due to random probing depend on the tracking error rather than the residual's magnitude. This yields a randomized sketch iteration with an explicit contraction mechanism and a principled interpretation of momentum. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence guarantees that depend on the residual's variation and initial magnitude, without requiring a uniform bound on the unavailable gradient component. With independently sampled function evaluations and Gaussian or spherical probes, PISO attains leading function-evaluation complexities of \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-6})\) under Lipschitz gradients and \(O(d^{2}\varepsilon^{-5})\) under an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption. These rates require only one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-component sample per update. The analysis also quantifies how batching trades observations for fewer deployments. Across five settings, PISO variants improve on the tested baselines with comparable oracle access in three, reach a comparable solution faster in bilevel routing, and perform best among methods without response-model derivatives in performative reinforcement learning.
papers.summary: Many optimization problems expose only part of the gradient directly, with the remainder observable only through function evaluations, as in performative prediction, performative reinforcement learning, and bilevel optimization with a black-box lower level. `PISO` (Partially Informed Stochastic Optimization) combines the known gradient component with a running estimate of the unknown residual, centring each zeroth-order probe on that estimate so the probing variance scales with the tracking error rather than the residual's magnitude. For smooth nonconvex objectives the method converges without any uniform bound on the hidden component, and with one probe direction, two function samples, and one known-component sample per step it reaches **function-evaluation complexities of O(d² ε⁻⁶) under Lipschitz gradients and O(d² ε⁻⁵) with an additional Lipschitz-Hessian assumption**. Across five test settings, `PISO` variants beat baselines with comparable oracle access in three, reach a comparable solution faster in bilevel routing, and perform best among methods without response-model derivatives in performative reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Prediction Is Not a Sufficient Memory State
papers.abstract: A memory that reproduces every current prediction may still have forgotten how to learn from the next observation. We characterize this distinction for exact cumulative learning and attention. For smooth convex residual losses with unrestricted real features and labels, a continuous recurrent state of fixed dimension exists exactly when the loss is polynomial. With ordinary, unweighted observations, degree $D$ requires precisely $r=\binom{d+D}{D}-1$ coordinates; even among histories with one fixed current predictor, exactly $r-d$ coordinates can remain necessary for continuation. Nonpolynomial losses have unbounded requirements on such equal-prediction histories. Bounded scalar logistic examples retain this obstruction after fixing any finite derivative jet. For ridge regression, the hidden evidence is the design matrix: the exact state costs $dp+d(d+1)/2$, versus $dp$ for the predictor. On a well-conditioned zero-prediction family, optimal $B$-bit compression has average one-update error of order $d^{-1}2^{-2B/s_d}$, $s_d=d(d+1)/2$, even with arbitrary randomized codes. Kernel attention gives a second exact closure classification. The results identify what future updates reveal, rather than proposing a new regression algorithm or asserting trained-model gains.
papers.summary: A learner's state can reproduce every current prediction yet lack the information needed to update correctly on the next observation, raising the question of how much extra state exact cumulative learning really requires. For smooth convex residual losses with unrestricted real features and labels, a continuous recurrent state of fixed dimension exists exactly when the loss is polynomial, a degree-D loss needs precisely C(d+D, D) − 1 coordinates, and nonpolynomial losses such as bounded scalar logistic examples have unbounded requirements even after fixing any finite derivative jet. For ridge regression the hidden evidence is the design matrix, so **the exact state costs dp + d(d+1)/2 numbers versus dp for the predictor alone**, and any B-bit compression of that state incurs one-update error of order d⁻¹ 2^(−2B/s_d) with s_d = d(d+1)/2 even with arbitrary randomized codes. A parallel exact-closure classification is given for kernel attention, and the results are framed as characterizing what future updates reveal rather than as a new regression algorithm.

papers.title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross-service paths. Existing red-teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions or decompose harmful objectives specified by humans or LLMs into seemingly benign action combinations. However, generation is biased toward patterns learned during training, potentially favoring familiar tool combinations and leaving novel cross-service interactions underexplored. To address this, we propose X-AgentRed, a self-evolving red-teaming framework that discovers harmful tool call paths through a graph of tool dependencies and expands and refines them using execution feedback. By analyzing each tool's effects, potential harms, and preconditions for execution, the red-teaming agent constructs a directed graph that captures how one tool's effects can satisfy another's execution preconditions. Recipes sampled from this graph are instantiated as realistic scenarios in which agents can produce harmful outcomes. Execution feedback enables self-improvement by diversifying paths that produce harm through tool substitution and refining preconditions at blocked steps in unsuccessful paths to enable further execution. Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves $1.77\times$ the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding $2.99\times$ the tool coverage on average.
papers.summary: Personal agents that call tools across many web services can cause harm while fulfilling benign requests, because the effects of actions accumulate and interact across services, and existing red-teaming approaches that prompt large language models to propose harmful paths tend to favor familiar tool combinations. `X-AgentRed` is a self-evolving red-teaming framework in which an attacker agent analyzes each tool's effects, potential harms, and execution preconditions, builds a directed dependency graph capturing how one tool's effects satisfy another's preconditions, and samples recipes from that graph to instantiate realistic harmful scenarios. Execution feedback then drives self-improvement by substituting tools to diversify harmful paths and refining preconditions at blocked steps of failed paths. Across four frontier agentic models, it finds **1.77 times the harmful path rate of `STAC`** and covers 2.99 times as many tools on average.

papers.title: RATED: Reliability-Aware AI Agent Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics
papers.abstract: As AI agents increasingly rely on external tools, accurate retrieval is essential for reliable behavior. Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution. To address this gap, we propose RATED (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics), a retrieval framework that combines robust semantic matching with dynamic reliability adaptation. RATED employs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching, and a lightweight contextual bandit module that re-ranks candidates based on real-time execution feedback. This design enables rapid adaptation to runtime tool failures without expensive model retraining. We introduce EcoAgent, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that RATED achieves a 52.2% relative MRR improvement over the ToolLLM API retriever on real-world queries, and reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Elliotes/EcoAgent.
papers.summary: Tool retrieval for agents usually optimizes semantic relevance alone and ignores whether a tool will actually be available at execution time. `RATED` (Reliability-Aware Tool Retrieval via Execution Dynamics) pairs a frozen dual-encoder with contrastive fine-tuning for semantic matching with a lightweight contextual bandit that re-ranks candidates from real-time execution feedback, so runtime failures are absorbed without retraining the model. The authors also release `EcoAgent`, a benchmark of 5,172 real-world tools and over 210,000 query-tool pairs for offline retrieval and dynamic reliability evaluation. `RATED` improves mean reciprocal rank by 52.2% relative to the `ToolLLM` API retriever on real-world queries and, under outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, **cuts the fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9%** while adding under 1 ms of latency over encode-only inference.

papers.title: Task Context Shapes Component Roles in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. Here, we compare fixed model components across tasks using identical graph facts, statements specifying which directed connections are present. We measure how interventions affect attention heads and the activation state in later layers (influence), as well as the answer (importance). Task changes redistribute the influence in five open-weight models spanning four families and 1.5-14 billion parameters. In Gemma-2-9B and Qwen3-14B, an activation edit changes an early internal activation vector and switches which fact the model reads while the written instruction stays fixed. The same heads then respond to different graph facts and influence later components differently. For each prompt, we construct two linear response maps, one before the edit and one after it. Each map predicts a later head's response from a measured change in an earlier head. For a separate factual intervention, the map for the corresponding condition reduces mean squared prediction error by 53.6% in Gemma and 5.0% in Qwen compared with the average of the two maps. These findings show that task context changes both which graph facts the shared components respond to and how their outputs affect later computation. A network account may help explain how models use shared parameters to perform different computations. Measurements of task-dependent influence could also guide interventions intended to alter one behavior while preserving others.
papers.summary: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but knowing which heads are shared does not explain what they do differently in each task. Drawing on the idea of task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, the authors compare fixed components across tasks that use identical graph facts, measuring how interventions affect attention heads and later-layer activations (influence) as well as the final answer (importance), across five open-weight models from four families spanning 1.5 to 14 billion parameters. Changing the task redistributes influence, and in `Gemma-2-9B` and `Qwen3-14B` an activation edit to an early layer switches which fact the model reads while the written instruction stays fixed, after which the same heads respond to different facts and affect later components differently. Per-prompt linear response maps fitted before and after the edit predict a later head's response from an earlier head's change, and for a separate factual intervention the matching map **reduces mean squared prediction error by 53.6% in Gemma** and 5.0% in Qwen compared with averaging the two maps.

papers.title: Structural Automata for Neural Semantic Parsing
papers.abstract: Neural semantic parsers generate meaning representations token by token, yet well-formedness depends on references, scope, and graph relations that unfold during generation. Constrained decoding prevents locally invalid tokens but does not guarantee that a valid prefix can be completed within a fixed output-length limit. We investigate structural automata at three stages of DRS parsing (decoding, post hoc processing, and training) and additionally evaluate decoding on AMR. For decoding, we introduce accepting-path decoding (APD), which maintains a verified completion within the remaining length limit and follows the model's preferred token whenever that token can also be completed. APD guarantees an accepted output without retracting tokens. Under tight length limits, it improves Smatch++ over local masking by 5.1 and 2.4 points on DRS and by 6.4 and 3.2 points on AMR, comparable to rollback under the same limit, which retracts tokens. For post hoc processing, invalid outputs concentrate on the same inputs: eight unconstrained samples yield no valid output for 10.2% of inputs with limited training data, compared with 0.4% with full data, where filtering comes within 0.2 Smatch++ points of APD. For training, penalizing automaton-rejected tokens improves development Smatch++ by 3.6-11.0 points after 10% of training, but this advantage diminishes as cross-entropy alone reduces the probability assigned to rejected tokens from 14% to below 2% within the first sixth of training with limited data.
papers.summary: Neural semantic parsers emit meaning representations token by token, but well-formedness depends on references, scope, and graph relations, and standard constrained decoding blocks locally invalid tokens without guaranteeing that a valid prefix can be completed within a fixed output length. The authors study structural automata at the decoding, post hoc processing, and training stages of Discourse Representation Structure (`DRS`) parsing and also evaluate decoding on Abstract Meaning Representation (`AMR`). Their accepting-path decoding (`APD`) keeps a verified completion within the remaining length budget and follows the model's preferred token whenever that token is still completable, which guarantees an accepted output without retracting tokens; under tight length limits it **improves `Smatch++` over local masking by 5.1 and 2.4 points on `DRS` and 6.4 and 3.2 points on `AMR`**, comparable to rollback decoding that does retract tokens. Invalid outputs concentrate on the same inputs, so sampling eight candidates and filtering fails on 10.2% of inputs with limited training data but only 0.4% with full data, and penalizing automaton-rejected tokens during training helps early (3.6 to 11.0 points after 10% of training) but the advantage fades as cross-entropy alone drives rejected-token probability from 14% to below 2%.

papers.title: Hitting-Time Bounds for Asynchronous Q-Learning
papers.abstract: We study the last iterate of standard asynchronous Q-learning from a single trajectory of a finite Markov decision process. The trajectory follows a fixed behavior policy whose state--action chain is irreducible and may be periodic. For discount factor $\gamma$, write $H=(1-\gamma)^{-1}$, and let $\mu_{\min}$ be the minimum stationary state--action probability and $\mathfrak h_\star$ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse state--action chain. We prove that zero-initialized Q-learning with a constant step size achieves sup-norm error at most $\varepsilon$ with high probability using $\widetilde{O}(H^4/(\mu_{\min}\varepsilon^2)+\mathfrak h_\star)$ transitions, for $0<\varepsilon\le1$. The statistical term retains the quartic effective-horizon dependence of standard Q-learning, while initialization cost is additive in $\mathfrak h_\star$. For aperiodic behavior chains, a comparison with mixing time yields a transient term $\widetilde{O}(t_{\mathrm{mix}}/\mu_{\min})$. An empirical state--action count rule selects a constant step size for a subsequent training run and attains the same rate without prior knowledge of model parameters, target accuracy, or confidence level. The output is the last training iterate, with both stages included in the sample count. The proof uses two deterministic Bellman envelopes to separate statistical error from fixed-policy initialization error and adapts reverse-time hitting-cost compensation from TD learning to state--action propagation. An exploration lower bound holds for arbitrary predictable step sizes. Together with the existing statistical lower bound and its extension to pilot-selected constant steps, it yields matching mean-square rates up to logarithmic factors on the stated large-sample parameter classes.
papers.summary: The analysis concerns the last iterate of standard asynchronous Q-learning run on a single trajectory from a finite Markov decision process under a fixed behavior policy whose state-action chain is irreducible but possibly periodic. With H the effective horizon 1/(1−γ), μ_min the minimum stationary state-action probability, and h⋆ the largest expected hitting time of the reverse state-action chain, zero-initialized Q-learning with a constant step size reaches sup-norm error ε with high probability using **Õ(H⁴/(μ_min ε²) + h⋆) transitions**, so the initialization cost enters additively rather than multiplying the statistical term, and for aperiodic chains a mixing-time comparison gives a transient term of Õ(t_mix/μ_min). A step size chosen from empirical state-action counts in a pilot run attains the same rate without knowing model parameters, target accuracy, or confidence level, with both stages counted toward the sample total. The proof separates statistical from initialization error via two deterministic Bellman envelopes, and an exploration lower bound for arbitrary predictable step sizes, combined with existing statistical lower bounds, yields matching mean-square rates up to logarithmic factors.

papers.title: Revisiting Tabular Deep Regression: Objectives and the Limits of Global Early Stopping
papers.abstract: While deep learning models for tabular data have recently received significant research attention, the choice of objective functions for regression tasks remains an understudied degree of freedom. Several lines of research offer alternatives to the standard Mean Squared Error (MSE), but differences in datasets, backbones, and evaluation protocols make their practical benefits difficult to compare. In this work, we address this gap by performing a systematic re-evaluation of regression objectives across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and multiple neural backbones. Our comparison reveals that many proposed objectives provide limited or inconsistent gains over a properly tuned MSE baseline, while quantile loss yields consistent aggregate improvements over MSE across the tested backbones. We then identify a limitation that remains even with this strong objective: regions with different levels of target noise can reach their best predictive performance at different training epochs. Consequently, a single global early-stopping checkpoint can impose a compromise between uncertainty regions, even when the objective can represent heteroskedastic target distributions. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce a heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss that uses input-dependent label smoothing as a potential remedy and improves over quantile loss on several backbones. Overall, our results provide a modern empirical picture of regression objectives for tabular deep learning and highlight how differences in optimal stopping times across uncertainty regions can limit the effectiveness of global early stopping. The code is available at https://github.com/yandex-research/tabular-regression.
papers.summary: The choice of loss function for deep tabular regression is rarely studied systematically, and proposed alternatives to Mean Squared Error (MSE) are hard to compare because they were evaluated on different datasets, backbones, and protocols. A re-evaluation across a broad collection of established tabular datasets and several neural backbones finds that most proposed objectives give limited or inconsistent gains over a well-tuned `MSE` baseline, while **quantile loss delivers consistent aggregate improvements over `MSE` across the tested backbones**. The authors then show that regions of the input space with different target-noise levels reach their best performance at different epochs, so a single global early-stopping checkpoint forces a compromise even when the objective can model heteroskedastic targets. A heteroskedasticity-aware extension of quantile loss using input-dependent label smoothing partially remedies this and improves on plain quantile loss on several backbones.

papers.title: When VLMs Destroy What They Know: Spatial Representations Fall Below Lexical Priors
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly analyze and reason about images, yet it remains unclear whether their internal representations faithfully encode the structured relations required for such reasoning. We introduce EICS (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for testing whether representations consistently encode concepts under controlled one-concept interventions, and CASP-VL (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of causally controlled spatial perturbations derived from Visual Genome scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, we find that spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information, even when the same models score well above chance on compositional benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost when the sentence is aggregated into a global representation, whether through the (EOS) token or by mean pooling. These findings reveal a systematic failure invisible to output-based evaluation: VLMs do not preserve, in the representation used downstream, relational information that is present in their own input.
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score well on compositional reasoning benchmarks, but it is unclear whether their internal representations actually encode the structured spatial relations such reasoning needs. The authors introduce `EICS` (Evaluation-Invariant Concept Stability), a metric for whether representations encode a concept consistently under controlled single-concept interventions, and `CASP-VL` (Causally controlled Spatial Perturbations for Vision-Language models), a benchmark of spatial perturbations derived from `Visual Genome` scene graphs. Across multiple VLM architectures, **spatial relations are represented substantially less faithfully than lexical information**, even in models well above chance on compositional benchmarks. The relation is identifiable at the predicate's own tokens but is lost once the sentence is aggregated into a global representation through the end-of-sequence token or mean pooling, a failure invisible to output-based evaluation.

papers.title: RSI-Anything: Unlocking Recursive Self-Improvement with World Models
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) aims to transform interaction experience into persistent improvements, yet external feedback is costly and world-model predictions may become unreliable as policies evolve. We introduce RSI-Anything, a domain-general framework built on JEPA-Anything that uses predictive world models to guide action and learning-data selection. Observed feedback drives policy or workflow improvement and conditional world-model adaptation, while component and compatibility checks govern the retention of updated policy-model pairs. Across diverse computational and scientific domains, RSI-Anything demonstrates substantial gains. In code repair, with the coder fixed, success increases from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% through predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation, at comparable test usage. Graphical user interface (GUI) evaluations showed higher task completion, while average actions decrease by 39.4%. Across five successive policy versions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01%. In reaction optimization, RSI-Anything achieves 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization under the same 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application further connects workflow evolution and predictive modeling with therapeutic hypothesis generation. These results demonstrate how predictive world models and retained system updates enable recursive improvement across diverse environments.
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to turn interaction experience into lasting gains, but external feedback is expensive and a world model's predictions can drift out of date as the policy changes. `RSI-Anything`, built on `JEPA-Anything`, uses predictive world models to select both actions and training data, lets observed feedback drive policy or workflow updates and conditional world-model adaptation, and gates retention of each updated policy-model pair behind component and compatibility checks. In code repair with a fixed coder, **success rises from 26.3% with a static verifier to 29.2% with predictive selection and 31.2% after world-model adaptation** at comparable test usage; graphical user interface (GUI) tasks show higher completion with 39.4% fewer actions, laboratory-planning scores more than double from 21.80% to 46.01% over five policy versions, and reaction optimization reaches 96.15% mean best observed yield versus 82.16% for Bayesian optimization on a 40-experiment budget. An end-to-end immune-science application links workflow evolution and predictive modeling to therapeutic hypothesis generation.
papers.highlight_summary:
Recursive self-improvement needs external feedback that is costly to collect, and the world models that could stand in for it become unreliable as the policy they predict for changes. `RSI-Anything` builds on `JEPA-Anything` predictive world models to decide which candidate actions receive real feedback, then retains an updated policy and world-model pair only when it passes both component-level and compatibility checks.

- Each round the world model ranks candidates and only the executed one yields a paired prediction and observation, which drives policy or workflow revision while the predictor adapts only when a reliability check flags it unreliable with sufficient data and budget, and a final pair check decides which policy and model versions carry into the next round.
- In code repair with `ReasonFlux-Coder-7B` held fixed on 200 `CodeContests` tasks across three seeds, hidden-test success rose from **26.3%** with a static verifier to **29.2%** with fixed world-model selection and **31.2%** after world-model adaptation, at roughly 3.7 online test calls per task throughout, though the first step's 95% interval of +0.17 to +5.50 points barely clears zero.
- Five successive retained versions of a 4B policy on `LabHorizon` F200 Level-2 climbed from **21.80% to 46.01%**, edging the Actor–Simulator–Selector reference at 45.32%, and in a flow Suzuki–Miyaura screen the mean best yield reached **96.15% versus 82.16%** for Bayesian optimization at a matched 40-experiment budget.
- On `MiniWoB++` click-checkboxes success went from **51% to 99%** with **39.4%** fewer actions per episode and repeated clicks dropping from 237 to 0, but a World-based control reached 98% on the same task, so the GUI headline is barely distinguishable from the control.
- No single experiment runs the full loop, since code repair fixes the coder and lab planning only tracks policy versions, so sustained joint policy and world-model improvement remains unproven, lab scores measure protocol similarity rather than physical execution, and the immune-science therapeutic hypothesis has not been tested experimentally.

papers.title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
papers.abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14\% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57\% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent $K_{\mathrm{D}}$ of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.
papers.summary: De novo protein design models usually need a dedicated input representation for each property they condition on, which limits the design objectives they can support. `Prompteina` is an all-atom structure generation model conditioned on free-form natural language, trained on `Prompteina-Data`, a paired corpus of 1.8 million structures and over 50 million captions describing global and residue-level structural and functional properties, by adapting the pretrained `Proteina-Complexa` model through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their descriptions. It outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties, leads on at least 13 of 20 binder-design targets with 14% higher interface confidence than the strongest baseline, and gains 57% more from iterative in silico feedback than the next-best method on the hardest targets. In wet-lab validation against `GM2A`, a target with no previously reported de novo binders, **nine binders were identified, the strongest with an apparent dissociation constant of 107 nM**.

papers.title: DyssomniaNN: Multi-Scale Spiking Neural Modeling of Human Sleep Disorders and Perceived Restedness
papers.abstract: Clinical sleep medicine repeatedly documents profound divergences between objective sleep duration and subjective daytime impairment, notably exemplified by sleep state misperception in paradoxical insomnia and boundary instability in narcolepsy type 1. Here, we present DyssomniaNN: a multi-scale biophysical computational framework coupling Borb\'ely's two-process regulation of sleep homeostasis and circadian drive with Saper's hypothalamic reciprocal flip-flop circuit and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network. We formalize five clinical cohorts across an identical 72-hour photoperiod: healthy control, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (delayed-phase), chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1. The synthetic local field potential converges closely with empirical human electroencephalography spectra from the PhysioNet Sleep-EDF database across all canonical frequency bands (spectral mean absolute error of 0.33--0.35). Furthermore, we introduce the Well-Rested Index to quantify restorative efficacy. Simulations reveal that sleep duration fails to predict restorative recovery: paradoxical insomnia achieves normal total sleep time (21.15 h) yet yields low restoration (37.6%) from unsuppressed cortical beta-band intrusion, whereas hypocretin deficiency in narcolepsy produces severe nocturnal fragmentation (781 min of wake after sleep onset) and 35 sleep-onset rapid eye movement periods. DyssomniaNN provides an in silico platform for mechanistic sleep research and virtual neuropharmacology.
papers.summary: Clinical sleep medicine documents large gaps between objectively measured sleep and subjective daytime impairment, as in the sleep state misperception of paradoxical insomnia and the unstable sleep-wake boundaries of narcolepsy type 1. `DyssomniaNN` is a multi-scale biophysical model coupling Borbély's two-process model of homeostatic and circadian drive, Saper's hypothalamic flip-flop switch, and a recurrent corticothalamic leaky integrate-and-fire spiking network, simulated for five cohorts (healthy, delayed-phase circadian disorder, chronic insomnia, paradoxical insomnia, and narcolepsy type 1) over an identical 72-hour photoperiod. The synthetic local field potential matches human electroencephalography spectra from the `PhysioNet Sleep-EDF` database across canonical frequency bands with a spectral mean absolute error of 0.33 to 0.35. A proposed Well-Rested Index shows that **sleep duration does not predict restoration**: simulated paradoxical insomnia reaches a normal total sleep time of 21.15 hours yet only 37.6% restoration because of unsuppressed beta-band intrusion, while simulated hypocretin deficiency yields 781 minutes of wake after sleep onset and 35 sleep-onset REM periods.

papers.title: Goal-Oriented Bundle Management and Flow Control for Deep-Space Communications via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Deep-space communications operate under intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and relay storage constraints. In such networks, the Bundle Protocol enables store-carry-forward communication, requiring relay nodes to manage limited storage and scarce contact opportunities. Relay-side scheduling and dropping decisions are inherently goal-oriented: transmission resources should be allocated to bundles most valuable to downstream mission objectives. Conventional schedulers, such as FIFO, do not explicitly optimize task utility and may provide unfair service across heterogeneous planetary sources. This paper presents a closed-loop modeling and learning framework for relay-side bundle and flow management in a contact-driven deep-space network, where lunar and Martian updates are forwarded through a shared-buffer relay to Earth. We quantify destination-side information freshness using excess age $\Delta_i^e(t)=[\Delta_i(t)-d_i(t)]^+$, where $\Delta_i(t)$ denotes the Age of Information of source $i$ and $d_i(t)$ is a source-dependent delay baseline. Based on this metric, we define a goal-oriented loss that supports source-dependent nonlinear penalties, allowing prioritization according to mission relevance. We formulate relay control as a constrained semi-Markov decision process (CSMDP) and solve it using masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can complete within the remaining contact window. DTNSim simulations indicate improved age-based utility and inter-flow fairness compared with baseline schedulers. The proposed framework jointly optimizes relay-side bundle scheduling, dropping, and flow control under contact-driven dynamics with explicit fairness considerations across heterogeneous sources.
papers.summary: Deep-space networks suffer intermittent connectivity, long propagation delays, and limited relay storage, so relays running the Bundle Protocol's store-carry-forward scheme must decide which bundles to forward or drop, and conventional schedulers such as FIFO ignore downstream mission value and can serve heterogeneous planetary sources unfairly. The authors model a shared-buffer relay forwarding lunar and Martian updates to Earth, measure destination-side freshness with an excess-age metric that subtracts a source-dependent delay baseline from the Age of Information, and define a goal-oriented loss with source-specific nonlinear penalties to encode mission relevance. Relay control is cast as a constrained semi-Markov decision process and solved with masked Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (`PPO`), where feasibility-aware action masking restricts transmissions to bundles that can finish within the current contact window. In `DTNSim` simulations the learned policy **improves age-based utility and inter-flow fairness over baseline schedulers** while jointly handling scheduling, dropping, and flow control.

papers.title: KL Before and After Mixing: A Round-Complexity Separation in Parallel Sampling
papers.abstract: A parallel sampler can choose at random which coordinates to generate together. For a target $p$ and the output law $q_U$ of a schedule $U$ drawn afresh for each output, we compare the schedule-averaged divergence $\mathbb{E}_U D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_U)$ with the output-law divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\mathbb{E}_U q_U)$, in nats. Rounds commit independent draws from exact conditional marginals frozen at the round's start, each output's schedule is drawn before sampling from a finite mixture of schedules, and every scheduled round is charged. For the uniform distribution on binary strings of even length $n$ with $n/2$ ones, the least expected number of rounds at a fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ is $\Theta_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ under the first criterion but $(e^{-\varepsilon}+o(1))\log_2\ln n$ under the second, and the double-logarithmic order is attainable with the same round count on every run. For this target, a count-state recursion gives the exact least output divergence at every round cap over all causal randomized policies. The separation extends to weighted fixed-count targets with bounded weight ratios and quota fractions bounded away from zero and one, without permutation symmetry, and to the full-support Beta$(1,1)$--Bernoulli target, where the sharp expected cost under the output-law criterion is $(e^{-\varepsilon}/2+o(1))\log_2\log_2n$, attained with rare $n$-round runs. Prior work implies the order of the schedule-averaged cost on the balanced target and its $O_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ upper bounds on both extensions.
papers.summary: A parallel sampler that randomly chooses which coordinates to generate together can be judged either by the schedule-averaged divergence E_U KL(p‖q_U) or by the divergence of the mixed output law KL(p‖E_U q_U), and the two criteria turn out to demand very different numbers of rounds. For the uniform distribution over even-length binary strings with exactly n/2 ones, the least expected number of rounds at a fixed tolerance ε is **Θ((log n)²) under the schedule-averaged criterion but only (e^(−ε)+o(1)) log₂ ln n under the output-law criterion**, with the double-logarithmic count attainable with the same round count on every run. A count-state recursion gives the exact minimal output divergence at every round cap over all causal randomized policies for this target. The separation extends to weighted fixed-count targets with bounded weight ratios and quota fractions bounded away from zero and one, without permutation symmetry, and to the full-support Beta(1,1)-Bernoulli target, where the sharp expected cost is (e^(−ε)/2+o(1)) log₂ log₂ n, attained with rare n-round runs.

papers.title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
papers.abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task - a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.
papers.summary: Capability evaluations assume that a model's hidden dangerous capabilities can be elicited before deployment, and the authors show this assumption fails adversarially by embedding encrypted neural networks inside a host model's weights that are decrypted and executed only when a secret trigger appears. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits are **provably hard to elicit or interpret under cryptographic assumptions even with full access to model weights**, extending earlier work from hiding fixed strings to hiding arbitrary computations. Proof-of-concept constructions implemented in PyTorch resist fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training on a small chemical reaction prediction task used as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. The models are released to support work on defenses, and the results mark a limit of elicitation-based capability audits.

papers.title: Constructive Bounds for the Topological Expressivity of Neural Networks
papers.abstract:
The expressivity of a neural network $\Phi$ describes the class of functions that a network can express. The term topological expressivity refers to a family of measures particularly suited to understand binary classification and is often formulated in terms of the Betti numbers of a decision boundary $\beta (\Phi^{-1}(0))$. Despite its popularity, this measure is not as useful for regression and other problems that do not involve a decision boundary. Instead, we propose to study topological expressivity in terms of the Betti numbers of the output of a neural network $\beta(\Phi(X))$. We formally prove that a ReLU network with architecture $(d,\sum\limits_{k=1}^{d
  } \beta_k(3k+2),\sum\limits_{k=1}^{d}\beta_k(k+1))$ can express spaces homotopy equivalent to wedge sums of spheres with arbitrary Betti numbers. This gives upper bounds for any arbitrary connected ($\beta_0=1$) sequence of Betti numbers, but by constructing spaces homotopy equivalent to products of $N$ spheres of dimension $d_1,...,d_N$ we achieve much better bounds $(\sum\limits_{n=1} d_n, 3\sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + 2N, \sum\limits_{n=1}\limits^N d_n + N) $ for Betti numbers given by $\prod_n (1+x^{d_n})$. Finally we conjecture a much stronger tight bound which gives the architectural bound $(d,d+1,d+1)$ for a space homeomorphic to the sphere.
papers.summary: Topological expressivity of neural networks is usually measured through the Betti numbers of a decision boundary, which says little about regression and other tasks without one, so the authors instead study the Betti numbers of a network's output set Φ(X). They prove that a ReLU network with architecture (d, Σ_k β_k(3k+2), Σ_k β_k(k+1)) can express spaces homotopy equivalent to wedge sums of spheres with any prescribed Betti numbers, giving upper bounds for any connected Betti sequence. By constructing spaces homotopy equivalent to products of N spheres of dimensions d_1 through d_N they obtain **much tighter bounds of (Σ d_n, 3Σ d_n + 2N, Σ d_n + N) for Betti numbers given by Π_n(1+x^{d_n})**. They conjecture a stronger tight bound implying that a (d, d+1, d+1) architecture suffices for a space homeomorphic to the sphere.

papers.title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models
papers.abstract: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. We propose Hide and Seek (HnS), a new method for concept-level attribution that does not require access to model weights or labeled concept datasets. HnS can interpret a wide range of vision models. Given a concept and image set, HnS retrieves concept-aligned images using a vision-language model, localizes the concept within each image, masks the localized region, and measures attribution from the change in the black-box model's output between the original and masked images. This enables faithful attribution by directly measuring the model's behavior and supporting local attributions. We validated HnS on CelebA and COCO-Stuff. Compared to existing methods, HnS showed better agreement with ground-truth attributions. We demonstrated the applicability of HnS on diverse tasks, including image captioning and satellite image segmentation, where no existing concept attribution method can be used. We provided our anonymous code in the supplementary material.
papers.summary: Concept-based attribution methods explain vision models through human-understandable concepts, but existing ones handle only classification and regression, need model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and mostly cannot give image-level attributions. Hide and Seek (`HnS`) needs neither weights nor concept labels: given a concept and an image set, it retrieves concept-aligned images with a vision-language model, localizes the concept in each image, masks that region, and measures attribution as the change in the black-box model's output between original and masked inputs, which directly probes model behavior and supports local attributions. On `CelebA` and `COCO-Stuff`, **`HnS` agrees with ground-truth attributions better than existing methods**, and it extends to image captioning and satellite image segmentation, where no prior concept attribution method applies.

papers.title: Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
papers.abstract: Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from document collections too large to index. This task is difficult when it requires specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, players must reach a target article using only article links. We compared sentence embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them. This allows the study of language models' navigation capabilities without relying on third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks. The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, languages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics, with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly used to retrieve information from document collections too large to index, which is hard when specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge is needed. The Wikipedia Game, in which a player must reach a target article by following only article links, serves as an analogous navigation task for comparing sentence embedding models and large language models across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-literature datasets, with very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and `OpenAlex` paper citations built so the study needs no third-party APIs. Against human and `TF-IDF` baselines, **no model significantly outperformed humans**, though the best models (`GPT-o3 mini`, `GPT-4o`, `QwQ:32B`, and `DeepSeek-R1:70B`) reached comparable success rates. Performance and model rankings varied across languages and topics, which matters for practitioners choosing among these techniques.
